1. Pre-commit to what kills H1. "All three tiers spike ~proportionally" kills a *tier-specific* pricing artifact, but doesn't necessarily kill a *global* pricing change (uniform price increase, billing-cycle shift, packaging change applied across tiers). Worth deciding now whether uniform = dead, or uniform = H1 reshaped into a sub-hypothesis you test separately.

The framing I'd push back on slightly is "the comforting explanations." Competitor-cycle in particular isn't just "Feb historically looks like this" — the comp answer only really kills *seasonal* (Feb being a heavy month). Denominator sanity check — three I'd actually run before saying h2 out loud:

  1. v1 cohort def (50–200 seats) applied literally to historical — confirm Feb 2021 and Feb 2022 are using the same seat-band as today, not a back-applied "mid-seg as understood back then." If mid-seg got defined retroactively, prior Feds could be running a different band.
  2. Cancel effective vs logged date — churn historically can be logged on cancel-effective (calendar month of last active day) vs cancel-logged (calendar month of the cancel event). Those shift which Feb a churn lands in by up to ~30 days, which on a small mid-seg base can swing the rate. Confirm Feb 2021/2022 used the same convention as Feb 2023.
  3. Exclusions — trial-to-paid conversions, paused accounts, downgrade-to-below-50-seat "soft churn." If any of those were handled differently historically (especially anything CS-touchy), the headline rate isn't comparable.

If all three hold, h2 publishes directionally per Owen's cadence — and the 1-pager should still split the kill: seasonality out (historical comp flat), competitor cycle partially out (no long-running cycle visible), but a Feb-specific competitor event is not addressed by the comp at all. The thing that would actually be an emergency is if, after the checks below, the direction is wrong (v3 > v2) or there's a real product-side signal hiding under the drift. So the right move is to run the checks, not to escalate.

Frame the explanation to Owen like this:
- Two different activation definitions, two different views. Dashboard defaulted to v3, notebook is still pinned to v2.
- v3 is the canonical/superseded read. v2 is legacy.
- Lower v3 number is structurally expected — v3 is a stricter gate.
- Late-May signups haven't hit day-14 under v3 yet, so even v3 is going to drift up as the window closes for the most recent cohort.

Then say you want to run a few parity checks before either of you forwards May numbers anywhere or relabels anything.

Checks before anyone edits labels or cites a May number:

Definition parity (are the views using what you think they're using?)
1. Confirm the dashboard query is bound to the v3 reference table, not just "labeled v3 in a comment somewhere."
2. Confirm the notebook query is bound to v2.
3. Confirm "first integration" resolves to the same event in both — specifically whether it's install vs. first successful sync. Drift here would be a real bug.
4. Confirm the 14-day clock starts on the same anchor (signup? first session? account create?) in both views.
5. Confirm what counts as an "in-product event" for v3 — any event, or a specific allowlist. If it's an allowlist, confirm it's been stable across May.

Cohort parity (are we slicing the same users?)
6. Same signup date window in both views. A trailing-14-from-today view compared against a calendar-May view will disagree for reasons that have nothing to do with activation.
7. Same segment filters. If the notebook is mid-segment only and the dashboard is everyone, that's a gap, not a definition story.
8. Same exclusion rules (test accounts, internal users, suspended, etc.).
9. Cohort completeness for v3: anyone who signed up after ~May 17–18 hasn't had a full 14-day window yet. v3 rate on a calendar-May slice will look artificially low and will tick up over the next ~2 weeks.

Math sanity (does the direction even make sense?)
10. v3 rate should be ≤ v2 rate. If v3 > v2, that's not a definitional artifact and you do have something to look at — most likely an event-mapping bug, a clock-anchor mismatch, or the notebook's denominator drifting.
11. Size the gap by computing the v2-only cohort (integrated + 2-logins but no in-product event in 14d). If that cohort is small and stable, you can describe the delta concretely. If it's large and weird (e.g., concentrated in a single week), that's worth a second look before forwarding anything.

Before forwarding or relabeling
12. Decide the canonical "May activation" number. It's v3, with v2 as the legacy comparison row, not the other way around.
13. If anyone needs a single number to share this week, cite v3 with the definition footnote AND the cohort-completeness caveat (latest cohort hasn't hit day-14). Don't publish a "final" May number until the window closes for the last signup.
14. Do not relabel the notebook to "v3" by editing the query in place. That's exactly what the versioned tables exist to prevent. If you want a v3 notebook, build it as a new artifact bound to the v3 table.
15. Don't change dashboard labels or "default view" until the parity checks above are clean. A label change in this state is what creates the next round of this same email.

**Addendum — Apr 17 cohort artifact (growth-side read, for the Apr reliability review)**

The Apr 17 second-post-ship cohort showed a +1.4 pt dip in mid-segment activation that, on inspection, was a measurement artifact rather than a conversion-logic regression. Root cause was a ~36-hour outage of the CS-team-owned auto-onboarding-nudge between Apr 15 and Apr 16: with the nudge down, a block of 50–75-seat accounts activated later than their expected window, shifting the activation event off its normal cadence and pulling the cohort cut onto a noisier part of the curve. During the same window the segment job also misclassified a chunk of 50–75-seat accounts as mid-tier while the onboarding send read stale membership from cache, so the cohort denominator was wrong before any retention math ran.

To be explicit on scope: `lifecycle_onboarding_trigger_v2` behaved as designed across this window. v2 fires off the activation event it observes; when activation is delayed upstream, v2 correctly fires later relative to signup but no longer aligns with the cohort cut, which is what produced the apparent dip. Read together with the contaminated segment denominator, this looked like a conversion problem in the activation-day cut on Apr 21 even though no activation logic changed. The framing we'd suggest for the reliability record is that two upstream systems — CS nudge availability and segment/membership freshness — were out of spec during Apr 15–16, and v2's observed behavior is fully accounted for by that.

Matrix (six rows × three buckets; each cell splits eligibility signal from product constraint)

Row 1 — First integration
- Green
    - Eligibility: standard integration path, no SSO/SCIM/custom-API ask at purchase.
    - Product constraint: in-product setup + activation event v3 carry it; existing instrumentation covers the funnel.
- Yellow
    - Eligibility: integration that has historically required human troubleshooting (legacy, regulated, edge connectors).
    - Product constraint: first failure → docs; second failure → human handoff. Do not auto-route to assisted onboarding.
- Red
    - Eligibility: SSO or SCIM required at purchase, custom API integration, regulated-data residency.
    - Product constraint: routes to mid-market assisted path. Refusal language: "this shape needs hands-on onboarding to land cleanly — we'd rather route you there than have you hit walls in self-serve."

Row 2 — Admin and permissions complexity
- Green
    - Eligibility: one clear admin owner, default RBAC.
    - Product constraint: admin_count telemetry exists; Day-10 invite touch fires only when admin_count > 1.
- Yellow
    - Eligibility: more than one active admin during setup, RBAC requests beyond default roles, ownership unclear but recoverable.
    - Product constraint: permissions check routed to docs then human if it persists; admin_count = 0 suppresses Day-10 touch.
- Red
    - Eligibility: SSO, granular/complex permissions, audit log requirement, no identifiable admin owner.
    - Product constraint: refused-list flag fires in-product and surfaces upgrade path; never blocks signup silently. Refusal language: "the admin model here is going to need a guided setup — let's get you on the right path before you start."

Row 3 — Import help
- Green
    - Eligibility: no import request at setup, or volume well below the support cap.
    - Product constraint: none; activation v3 starts clean.
- Yellow
    - Eligibility: small import volume, defined schema, customer willing to self-serve the mapping.
    - Product constraint: gated on import-volume threshold before setup starts; above cap routes to human handoff, below cap → docs.
- Red
    - Eligibility: large migration/import volume, competitive-takeover migration, schema mapping that requires human review.
    - Product constraint: refused in self-serve. Refusal language: "imports at this scope are where setup usually breaks — we'd rather hand you off to a migration specialist than risk a broken first week."

Row 4 — Billing exceptions
- Green
    - Eligibility: standard card billing, self-serve invoice under threshold.
    - Product constraint: billing automation covers it; no human load.
- Yellow
    - Eligibility: NET terms, custom invoice formatting, PO-required billing.
    - Product constraint: routing rule (not a refusal) — billing-ops human handoff above invoice threshold; standard self-serve below.
- Red
    - Eligibility: custom MSA, procurement-led purchase, legal redlines, custom contract terms.
    - Product constraint: refused in self-serve. Refusal language: "these terms need a real contract — let's route you to sales so the paperwork matches what you actually need."

Row 5 — Migration support
- Green
    - Eligibility: greenfield, no prior-tool data to bring in.
    - Product constraint: none; activation v3 starts clean.
- Yellow
    - Eligibility: small data migration importable via the standard import path.
    - Product constraint: same routing as Row 3 Yellow — do not duplicate the rule.
- Red
    - Eligibility: multi-day human migration, custom data transformation, parallel-run migration support.
    - Product constraint: refused in self-serve. Refusal language: "a migration at this scope is a project, not a setup — let's plan it together so nothing breaks on day one."

Row 6 — Support handoff risk
- Green

- Yellow
    - Eligibility: one failed integration, import at edge of cap, owner identified but inactive.

- Red

WORDING TRAPS TO AVOID

1.  "Under 50 is fine" / "under 50 is bad" — both overclaim. The cut tracks deployment shape × first-week integration, not seat count.

5.  "Permissions / import / billing / migration are gaps we close in Q3" — they're refusal risks for the first eligibility model, not product work. Eng can document future requirements; Q3 doesn't commit to fixing them.

6.  Collapsing the 50-75 band into "under 50" — erases the band separation that makes the cut readable. Keep the 50-75 on its own line, every time.

7.  Saying "Helio Start" in the same breath as revenue or Q3 numbers — keeps the working name from drifting into a public product name or a launch promise.

What the split supports

2. Lift is real in a slice, but the slice isn't an accident. Deep-integration × multi-admin accounts are the ones that were already on a path to expand — they're using the product. The prompt didn't create usage; it landed on accounts that had usage to monetize. That's a genuine signal about who to talk to, not about whether the prompt itself raises expansion across the segment.

3. Low-depth accounts being flat is informative on its own. The prompt isn't pulling expansion out of accounts that haven't earned it. Reading that as "the prompt doesn't work for shallow accounts" is correct, but the corollary is: shipping the prompt to all 75–200 won't move the segment average much, because the un-monetizable accounts are a large share of the population.

What it doesn't support

A within-cell causal claim. The 2x2 is an observational split, not a randomized one. Deep accounts were already there — they're correlated with high expansion propensity regardless of treatment. Owen's table tells you which slice the treated average is being lifted by; it doesn't tell you what would have happened to those same deep accounts under control. The standard error on the deep cell is almost certainly wide enough that the apparent lead could be half noise.

The trap Marcus is going to fall into

He's going to read the deep slice as "we found the audience, ship to them," and want to widen. The three things that will make that feel right to him and wrong to you:

- Selection looks like targeting. "Deep integ + multi-admin" sounds like a feature, not a confound. He's going to frame it as a clean segment we can route the nudge to.
- The sub-cell revenue is real dollars, just small. Even if the deep-slice lift is genuine at +$X/account, that cell is a minority of the population. Widening the flag to "deep slice only" won't move Q3 — it'll move a footnote. He'll commit to a number the segment can't deliver.
- A prompt that only works for users who were going to expand anyway is a routing decision dressed up as a growth experiment. If you widen on this, you're committing to a "right person, right time" product motion without having tested whether the prompt did anything or just coincided with the purchase intent. The next quarter you won't be able to tell those apart.

Helio Start — first-motion eligibility (refusal-rule copy, revised draft)

The Helio Start first self-serve motion is built for workspaces that can complete initial setup without hands-on help from our team. The signals below describe a workspace that would be better served by sales-assisted onboarding for its first motion, rather than the self-serve path. None of these are judgments about the customer — they describe conditions under which the self-serve setup itself would be likely to fail before the workspace reaches value.

Migration help in flight
The workspace is mid-migration from another tool (HubSpot, a custom CRM, a spreadsheet-based pipeline, etc.) and needs our team to assist with import, mapping, or data carry-over during setup. Routing this through self-serve would put the workspace into the first-motion flow before its data is settled — the failure mode the eligibility rule exists to prevent.

Agency-shared or multi-party admin permissions
The workspace will be administered by more than one party (an agency partner, a fractional admin, a contractor team, etc.) and the admin model is not yet defined inside a single owner. The first self-serve motion assumes one integration owner with enough permission context to make setup decisions; without that, the workspace will stall at the integration step before reaching activation.

Manual billing exception
The workspace needs a manual invoice, custom contract terms, or another billing arrangement the self-serve checkout does not support. The self-serve motion cannot honor the billing terms the workspace needs, so the account belongs on the sales-assisted path for its first motion.

Heavy support needs at setup
The workspace has indicated (in pre-sales conversation, support tickets, or onboarding notes) that it will need hands-on help from our team to complete setup, configure integrations, or troubleshoot early issues. Routing this through self-serve would mean the workspace hits the first wall alone — exactly the failure the eligibility rule is designed to prevent.

How refusal rules route
A workspace matching any of the above is not a Helio Start first-motion candidate and is not framed as one internally or externally. The handoff is to sales-assisted onboarding, where the workspace gets the hands-on setup it needs before it returns to a self-serve cadence. The refusal list is a protective filter for the customer's first motion, not a tier judgment — and "Helio Start" stays a working label, not a public plan name.

**Helio Start discovery candidate intake — backfill rule (for Owen)**

Scope: rows in the discovery candidates sheet. This intake is discovery input, not readiness evidence. The rule below decides what can be filled in from existing notes and how the source is named.

**1. What can be backfilled**

Backfill is allowed only from one of these named sources, with the source itself required in the cell or a sibling "source" column:
- AE notes (CRM, dated)
- Onboarding kickoff / onboarding notes (dated)
- A documented spot-check or reconciliation (date + reviewer)

Backfill is allowed for these fields when the source is explicit:
- deployment shape
- admin / permissions complexity
- support-handoff risk

Backfill is not allowed for these fields, regardless of source. Leave them unknown and route to a named owner:
- first-week first integration status — system-tracked only; an inferred value here is worse than blank
- import or migration help needed — too often ad-hoc; needs the person who fielded the request
- manual billing exceptions — sensitive; needs explicit owner sign-off, not inference

If a field isn't on the allowed list, do not fill it. Note the owner in open questions.

**2. How to label source and staleness**

Every backfilled value carries two labels:
- Source: `<type> | <date> | <reviewer>` — e.g., "AE note | 2023-04-22 | M. Park" or "onboarding kickoff | 2023-05-09 | unsigned"
- Staleness: notes older than 90 days at the time of entry are tagged "stale." Notes older than 180 days cannot be the sole source — they can mark a field as known, but the row stays "needs reconfirmation" until a current source lands.

Blank cells are not backfilled silence. If a source was checked and didn't say, the cell reads "unknown, checked <source> <date>." That's a different state from blank, and it matters — the 6/20 spot-check showed how much "checked but missing" can hide in plain columns.

(90/180-day thresholds are my defaults — flag if you want different numbers.)

**3. How to keep unknown rows out of beta-ready language**

- Sheet title stays "Helio Start discovery candidates." No rename. No "beta", "qualified", "eligible", or "ready" column or status anywhere on the sheet.
- A row exists as a discovery candidate if and only if account name + current seats are present. Everything else is required for the row to become usable downstream, not for it to exist.
- Any field reading "unknown" — or absent — blocks that field's downstream use. Specifically: a row with an unknown deployment shape, unknown support-handoff risk, or any field tagged stale cannot be described as a beta candidate in a note, a deck, or a Slack post.
- Unknowns are owned, not ignored. Each unknown on a row needs a named owner to become fillable. If you find an unknown on a row you're already touching, name the owner in the open-questions column the same day.

**Summary:** backfill is allowed only when the source is named and recent; everything else stays unknown with an owner; the sheet's language stays discovery-only; unknown rows are unusable, not just unfilled.

Here is a rewrite and a short note explaining why each phrase is wrong.

REWRITTEN BLURB

  Helio Start: a narrow, discovery-only controlled beta approved to begin in August, running through a non-public path. Participation is gated to discovery candidates meeting explicit eligibility criteria — complete profile fields, simple deployment, no manual billing or migration help, and clear admin ownership — and remains contingent on the eligibility, instrumentation, lifecycle, and support gates. Pricing-page exposure and paid acquisition remain blocked until taxonomy/entitlements and the lifecycle fork are live. Helio Start is a working name for the scenario; it is not a public product name and not a Q3 revenue commitment.

WHY EACH PHRASE IS WRONG

  `live this week`
    Reads as a public launch on a date. Helio Start is a gated beta — it can't be "live" until the four gate conditions clear, and even then only for the narrow eligible population. A week-anchored phrase makes it look like a release event and invites the org to treat it as one.

  `teams under 50 seats`
    Two problems stacked. First, it collapses the 50-75 band into "under 50" — the band has to stay separate in measurement so we don't lose visibility into how the boundary segment behaves. Second, it implies seat count is the qualifying dimension, when the actual eligibility is about deployment shape, profile completeness, and admin ownership. Framing it as a seat-tier plan makes it sound like a packaged product offer rather than a discovery instrument.

  `new self-serve plan from the pricing page`
    Pricing-page exposure is explicitly blocked until taxonomy and entitlements land. Writing it as if it's already on the pricing page either announces a motion that hasn't been approved, or signals to the org (and to readers downstream) that the pricing-page gate is open. Either way the phrasing does work the gate is supposed to prevent.

  `August pipeline`
    Pipeline framing turns the beta into a revenue wedge. The point of the controlled beta is to learn — eligibility fit, refusal patterns, support load, lifecycle behavior — not to feed a Q3 forecast. Once it shows up as "pipeline," exec and board conversations will treat it as a number rather than a learning, and any underperformance will get read as a miss against a commitment we never made.

PATTERN TO APPLY GOING FORWARD

  Lead with the beta framing (narrow, discovery-only, gated). Name the gate conditions explicitly. Name what remains blocked (pricing page, paid acquisition). Treat "Helio Start" as a working scenario label — never as a product name, never as a launch, never as a revenue line. If a sentence can't survive that filter, it doesn't go in the blurb.

WHAT TO AVOID (so it doesn't slip into the wrong read):
- Don't tie it to event taxonomy. The events are doing their job. Linking permissions questions to instrumentation invites a "fix the telemetry" reaction and relitigates the gate that's already closed.
- Don't let "events clean" carry over into "path clean." Events clean only means telemetry is healthy. It says nothing about whether the user got where they wanted to go.
- Don't soften it into "minor confusion." It happened repeatedly and it's the dominant permissions pattern — name it that way.
- Don't bury it in the activation numbers. Permissions tickets are a support-load signal; they belong next to support load, not inside activation.

A few facts first, so the frame is grounded:

  - One send, 0.42% unsub vs ~0.18% normal — roughly 2.3x baseline
  - Complaints low + "felt irrelevant" (not "angry" or "misleading") → relevance signal, not deliverability
  - Refreshed subject line + possible stale-trial leak → two plausible causes, not one
  - "Don't overreact" + "don't make her wait a week" → next send is the lever, not this one

Practical triage frame

Separate the two questions before doing anything. They have different evidence and different fixes.

  1. Segment risk (cheaper to test, easier to fix)
     - Pull the recipient list for this send
     - Cut: % of workspaces that are trial-only, no paid history, or no activity in last 60-90 days
     - If a meaningful slice is stale trial (rule of thumb: >10-15%), the spike is segment-driven. Subject line is not the story. Fix the exclusion for the next send, copy stays.
     - If the stale slice is small, segment is probably not it.

  2. Copy risk (judgment call, harder to test)
     - Only worth opening if the segment came back clean
     - Read subject + first 2 lines against a healthy retained account: "would they expect this and find it useful?"
     - Refreshed subject lines are a known cause of relevance-reaction unsubs when the body still talks to the prior expectation. That pattern fits here.

  3. Urgency calibration
     - One send at 2.3x baseline is signal, not alarm — don't pull copy based on n=1
     - The next send in the program is the real lever. If it's within 3-5 days, hold it. If it's a week+ out, you have time to check first.
     - Either way: decision within 1-2 days, not a week. Ines shouldn't be sitting on it.

  4. Action ladder (in order)
     - Today/tomorrow: Ines pulls recipient list, runs the stale-workspace cut
     - If slice is meaningful → fix exclusion, resume next send, leave subject alone
     - If slice is small → you and Ines read the send together, decide if subject walks back or holds
     - Either path: capture the learning in the segment rules so this doesn't re-happen at the next subject refresh

The discipline here: don't let the subject-line refresh become the scapegoat before checking whether stale trials were even in the audience. Segment hygiene is the cheaper hypothesis and the one with a clear yes/no answer.

The churn risk in Daniela's second sentence is that it routes the user to a person they may not be able to identify — every "who's my admin?" reply becomes another ticket. The fix is to swap "ask your admin to generate the key" for a self-check the user can do in-product, and to keep "reply with workspace URL" as the escape hatch rather than the default.

Refined beta-only UI hint (one line at the disabled control):

    API keys are admin-only. Check your role at Settings → Members —
    the workspace creator is the admin until they promote someone.

Refined CS macro (matches the UI hint):

    Your workspace role is viewer-level, so API keys are admin-only in
    this workspace. The two most common reasons this happens are
    (1) the workspace was created under a different email than the one
    you're logged in with, and (2) the original admin hasn't promoted
    you yet. Check Settings → Members to confirm your role — the
    workspace creator is the admin until they promote someone. Two paths
    forward: ask the workspace creator to promote you and retry, or
    reply with the workspace URL and we'll check who the current admin
    is.

What changed vs. Daniela's draft:

  - Dropped "ask your admin to generate the key" from the UI hint.
    That sentence assumed (a) the user knows who their admin is and
    (b) the admin will do it for them — both assumptions generate
    tickets.
  - Replaced it with a self-check: Settings → Members shows their
    role in-product, and the workspace-creator rule is a deterministic
    default everyone can verify without asking us.
  - CS macro mirrors the same two moves (role check + creator default)
    so the support reply and the in-product hint point at the same
    resolution path.
  - "Reply with workspace URL" stays as the escape hatch in the macro,
    but it's now the second path, not the first. Default expectation is
    self-resolution; escalation is for genuine edge cases.
  - Beta-only, no plan/upgrade language, no onboarding doc links,
    no apologies.

Why this holds the line on "no unclear admin ownership acceptable":
the creator rule means admin ownership is never actually unclear —
it's whoever created the workspace, full stop. The escape hatch
(reply with workspace URL) only fires when the user can't reconcile
that with what they see, which is a real edge case and not a
normalization of ambiguity.

Six questions for the Friday 1pm CT Growth Ops Analyst slot. Five minutes each in a 30-minute interview — if you want time for their questions at the end, you can drop Q4 or Q5; both are useful but Q6 is the highest-signal synthesis test.

1. Cohort instinct confirmation
"Walk me through how you decided to look at cohort mix before the subject line in the take-home. What was the trigger, and what would have made you skip that step?"
Listening for: whether they can articulate the diagnostic order or got lucky once.

2. Causal discipline
"On the six-point trial-completion bump — you wrote it up as causal. What would have to be true for that to actually be causal, and what's the earliest evidence you'd want before you said it that way in a stakeholder read?"
Listening for: holdout thinking, what would change their mind, or just squirming.

3. Audience quality before tactic
"Your first recommendation was more lifecycle email. If the audience file turned out to be six months stale, how would that change your ranking of next steps, and what checks would you run on the data before suggesting any send?"
Listening for: whether they revise the ranking or defend the original call.

4. SQL / data hygiene
"Your active-workspace filter ran before the workspace_role join. What could fall out of that, how would you know it happened, and how would you restructure the query?"
Listening for: row-drop risk, self-awareness vs. defensive.

5. Denominator and chart hygiene
"One chart, no stated denominator. If a VP reads it and walks away with the wrong number, where does the responsibility sit, and how would you redesign the chart to prevent it?"
Listening for: analyst owns the framing vs. "reader should have asked."

6. Synthesis under pressure
"Activation drops four points week-over-week in a single segment. You have 48 hours for a one-page read. What do you look at first, what do you explicitly NOT do in those 48 hours, and what's the earliest point at which you'd say 'I don't know yet'?"
Listening for: do they name the temptation (more email, more nudges) and refuse it; do they put a real "not yet" boundary on the read.

The shape across the six: Q1-Q2 test the analytical strengths and the calibration wobble you already saw; Q3 is the direct test for the lifecycle-email reflex; Q4-Q5 are the stakeholder-communication calibration checks; Q6 is end-to-end judgment under messy conditions, which is the actual job.

30-MIN PANEL — GROWTH OPS ANALYST
Fri Sep 15, 1:00pm Central

North star: does the candidate reach for diagnosis before reaching for a send/dashboard? Restraint is the test, not volume of ideas.

Prior read (from 9/9 take-home review): lean-yes pending stakeholder-comm calibration and causal-language guardrails. Panel should either confirm or break that — not reset it.

Time budget
  2 min  opener
  5 min  take-home walkthrough (the two concerns)
  8 min  live messy-data probe
  5 min  audience-quality drill
  5 min  rewrite their own summary
  5 min  situational + candidate questions

Opener (2 min)
  "We have steady mid-funnel diagnosis work. I'm testing whether this role stays useful between 'we noticed something' and 'we did something about it' — without defaulting to more sends or more dashboards."

1. Causal overreach (3 min)
  Q: "Take-home had a +6pt trial-completion bump tied to a subject line. Walk me through how you ruled out other changes that week."
  Good: lists confounders (other lifecycle moves, signup-mix shift, billing changes, seasonality), names a cut that would disambiguate.
  Bad: "the timing lined up."
  Listen for: do they retrofit one story, or generate hypotheses first?

2. Audience freshness (2 min)
  Q: "You recommended two more reminder emails. Before that — how do you check whether the audience is current admins vs. stale-role contacts? First thing you pull."
  Good: workspace_role + last-active, prior-email engagement split by role, suppression-list overlap, CS-handoff-recent cohort.
  Bad: just adds sends, or punts to "ask the data team."
  Listen for: who-is-in-the-bucket check before any more-volume recommendation.

3. Live messy probe (8 min)
  Setup: "Week of Aug 28. Retained-mid activation -4pt WoW. That week: Tuesday subject-line change, Friday price-page A/B end, CS-handoff rate 18%→31%, billing-side plan migration. What do you do first?"
  Good: lists candidates, ranks by plausibility + ease-of-cut, proposes ONE diagnostic before any change, holds off on growth-side sends.
  Bad: opens a new email test, picks the loudest change, or "I'd build a dashboard to track this weekly."
  Follow-up: "If the CS-handoff jump turns out to be the explanation — what's your move?"
  Good: routes to CS owner, doesn't touch the lifecycle program.
  Bad: sends a "sorry about the handoff" email or rewrites copy.
  Listen for: do they know when growth-side shouldn't move?

4. Audience-quality drill (5 min)
  Q: "Take-home summary said 'lifecycle email drove a retention lift.' Rewrite for an exec who's going to ask hard questions in the room. What changes?"
  Good: identifies the overclaim, softens to "associated with" or "consistent with," names what would strengthen the read, leaves the supported parts intact.
  Bad: gut-rewrites ("may have driven"), or doesn't see the issue.
  Listen for: epistemic calibration, not prose polish.

5. Rewrite their own summary (5 min)
  Show one paragraph from the take-home stakeholder summary. Ask: "Two sentences you'd cut or rewrite before this goes to Marcus or Daniela. Why those two."
  Good: targets confidence overclaims, names what the data actually supports, leaves the supported parts intact.
  Bad: edits for tone only; restructures without changing confidence levels.
  Listen for: do they edit for accuracy, or for prose?

6. Situational + candidate questions (5 min)
  Setup: "Day one. You inherit: declining week-2 retention in growth-tier, a stale activation-helped email flagged too CS-led for growth-tier, an onboarding-trigger flag at 0% rollout, and a recent copy-drift incident. 8 hours this week. Walk me through what you do AND what you don't."
  Good: triages, identifies dependencies, holds off on send-side changes pending diagnosis, names which item belongs to which owner.
  Bad: opens new sends, restructures dashboards, picks the loudest thing.
  Close: "A time you recommended NOT sending something because the data wasn't there."

SCORECARD (post-panel, /4 each)
  Causal reasoning     — hypotheses before recommendations?
  Audience discipline  — checks who's in the bucket before adding volume?
  Stakeholder comms    — calibrates language to data, not desired story?
  Restraint            — says don't / wait when that's right?
  Cross-functional     — routes findings to right owner instead of absorbing?

  Threshold for lean-yes: 12+/16, no 1 in causal or restraint.

Two things I'd want to change before merge. Both small. Both worth doing because entitlement naming is the line that's been drifting (the 7/19 spec says capture at workspace creation, update on support handoff + billing changes, NOT plan-name inference — that's the rule).

First, the framing is fair: admin proof is its own thing, and a read-only helper scoped to a reporting query is a different surface than production entitlement writes. I don't think this breaks anything that's live. But it creates a code path that future engineers will copy if we don't fence it off, and the field name is the part that does the damage.

1. The field name. Calling the derived value `entitlement_tier` is what worries me, not the helper. If someone later imports this from the beta reporting module into a place that touches production entitlement, the name tells them it's authoritative. Either rename to something that signals "reporting label, not entitlement truth" (e.g., `beta_legacy_plan_label`, `reporting_plan_segment`), or — preferred — drop the helper and write the legacy rows as proper backfill events with `entitlement_source=backfill_2023_07` so they show up in the same shape as everything else.

2. "Without requiring a separate entitlement event" — that phrase is the real issue. The 7/19 spec has a backfill mechanism specifically so we don't end up with two ways to populate entitlement fields. If legacy rows genuinely lack entitlement events, the fix is the one-shot backfill script, not a derived helper that reads plan_name at query time. Otherwise we end up with: production rows get `entitlement_source=workspace_created` / `support_handoff_created` / `manual_billing_exception_added`, and beta rows get "whatever plan_name starts with." Two source populations, same field name, different meanings.

If the scope really is "I need this for a beta reporting query tomorrow and don't want to run the backfill before then," I'd accept the helper with:
- rename the derived value to something that's NOT `entitlement_tier`
- the helper lives in the reporting module only, with no import path into entitlement code (a CI grep on `from reporting import` inside `entitlement/` is cheap)
- a TODO + ticket to replace it with the proper backfill before beta exits

Otherwise happy to merge once we run the backfill the spec already defines.

The burr-find + rinse was the right move. A few hours of residual licking tonight is normal — the pad was just irritated, and his first instinct is to clean it. Most burr-between-pad incidents clear up overnight once the debris is out. Here's a calm plan.

TONIGHT — one look, then leave it alone
  - In good light, check the pad where the burr was:
    - small red dent or tiny scrape = fine, expected
    - any remaining fragment you can see = try to lift gently with clean fingers; if it won't come free easily, stop and call tomorrow
    - a spot or two of blood = fine; steady ooze = not
  - Compare to the other front paw: same size, same color, no swelling. Slight pink where the burr was = expected. Hot, swollen, or visibly bigger = not.
  - Check the other pads and between toes on that paw — burrs travel in packs sometimes.
  - Watch his walk over the next hour or two: gradual return to even steps = good. Increasing limp = not.

TONIGHT — okay to just watch
  - Low-level licking, especially right before bed
  - Slight favoring for the first 30–60 min after the rinse (stings a bit)
  - Normal eating, drinking, settling, greeting you at the door
  - Wanting to be near you (a little uncomfortable — allowed)

TONIGHT — call urgent/ER vet if:
  - Paw swells rapidly or feels hot compared to the other
  - Bleeding you can't stop with a minute of gentle pressure
  - He refuses to bear any weight on the paw at all
  - He yelps when you touch near it, or suddenly much more withdrawn than usual
  - Pale gums, hard panting at rest, or anything that looks systemic (very unlikely from a burr, but the threshold)
  - You find something embedded that won't budge with gentle pressure — don't dig; they can numb and get it clean

TOMORROW MORNING — daylight recheck
  - Before breakfast, look again in daylight. Press gently along the pad and between toes — he should tolerate this. Pulling away hard or yelping = call the vet.
  - On the first walk: still favoring, or back to even? Even = done. Still favoring after a few minutes = call your regular vet for a same-day slot.
  - Occasional lick = fine. Persistent obsessive licking that doesn't taper by midday = vet call.

TOMORROW — routine vet call (not urgent)
  - Still licking the paw by midday
  - Any discharge, smell, or crusting between pads
  - Mild limp that doesn't fully resolve by the second walk
  - Redness that's spread or looks angrier than last night

PRACTICAL FOR TONIGHT
  - Skip a real walk — grass only if he needs a quick potty break, then back in. Fresh pad + pavement = sting.
  - Don't use hydrogen peroxide or Neosporin without a vet's nod; peroxide damages healing tissue, and he'll lick most ointments off. Plain dog paw balm or a thin smear of Vaseline is fine, or just leave it.
  - Don't preemptively cone him. If licking becomes nonstop and the paw can't air out, a soft inflatable collar or a loose sock taped above the wrist is the move — but try without first.
  - Water down, fan/AC if it's warm, low lights, let him decompress. Sam's slot stays protected; this is a Kibo evening, not a Helio one.

Light enough to borrow?
Light for Owen, Ines, you, Priya — four lines, fits on an index card, and the two safeguards from 10/6 are both visible (item 2 carries the effect size; item 4 carries the first-significance / stabilization-cohort split). Lightness holds inside that circle.
It stops being light the moment it travels to someone who hasn't sat in the operating-note cadence with Priya. "Hypothesis stack," "stabilization-cohort confirmation," and "decision boundary" are terms-of-art that compress a sentence each. A borrower who hasn't seen the shape before will fill them in with whatever sounds closest.

What would be confusing?
- "Hypothesis stack." Reads like a count (more than one hypothesis). The real meaning is layered — directional expectation + effect-size expectation + the alternative if neither holds. A borrower can write one bullet and call it done. The September CS readout had exactly this failure: shape present, effect-size layer dropped.
- "Effect size, not just direction." Accepts either expected or observed, but doesn't say *which* effect size when several honest ones exist. The onboarding-trigger rerun had two — +3.4 on the n=200 cut, +3.1 pooled on n=420. A borrower who picks the flattering slice is technically following the rule.
- "Decision boundary." Sounds statistical. The three options are listed, so the borrower picks a label. The checklist labels the state; it doesn't restrict the action. "First significance" is the easiest box to tick, and it's the one that licenses the most.
- "Stabilization-cohort confirmation." Assumes the borrower already has a stabilization cohort defined. If they don't, they'll reach for "first significance" because it sounds more advanced than "observation that should not ship yet." That's the September growth-team failure mode in compressed form.

Where would a lifecycle or analyst reader accidentally overclaim?
- Lifecycle reader (Ines's neighborhood): the temptation is to read "first significance" as a green light because copy is cheap to revert and feels low-stakes. Pattern — fill in effect size + first significance, treat the doc itself as the ship-decision, act on Monday. The September CS readout walked this path with the hypothesis-stack shape and the effect size missing; the shape was enough to authorize action.
- Analyst reader (Owen's neighborhood): the temptation is to upgrade "observation" to "stabilization-cohort confirmation" once the math looks clean, because the analyst trusts numbers more than process labels and the checklist is self-classifying. Pattern — write the effect size, decide the cohort is stable by assertion, skip the second reader. The September growth-team summary did the first half of this.

What's not on the four items but is load-bearing for either reader
- Who decides if it ships. The boundary is self-labeled; nothing forces a second pass.
- Sample composition. Item 3 names cohort and window but doesn't ask whether the cohort is the one the claim should generalize to — a single-channel slice can carry a real effect size and still not travel.
- Reversibility. Copy is cheap; pricing and entitlement are not. The checklist doesn't ask the borrower to weigh what "should not ship yet" actually costs.

Tightening that keeps it light
- A one-line example filled in for a known past case (the onboarding-trigger rerun is the obvious one) buys back the missing meaning without adding items. Lightness-by-illustration rather than lightness-by-omission.
- If you want to defuse the analyst overclaim specifically, rename "Decision boundary" to "Ship-status" or "Read-status." The statistical framing is what invites the upgrade-by-assertion move.
- If you want to keep the four items exactly as they are, then add the second-reader rule verbally when Owen or Ines borrow it — that's the part the checklist can't carry on its own.

v0.2 — borrowed-shape thinking aid (Q4, lighter)

For when you're reusing the investigation shape on a readout, experiment, or decision. Not a template to fill in — a way to slow down before you call it.

  1. What's the call?
     One line. What are you deciding, and who decides it?

  2. What do you believe, and how big does it need to be?
     Stack your hypotheses biggest-to-smallest. For each one, hold both:
       - the effect size you actually saw
       - the minimum effect that would change the call
     Keeping these together is what stops a "yes" from sneaking through on a
     number that doesn't matter.

  3. What are you measuring, on whom, over what window?
     Metric, cohort, window. Specific enough that someone else could rebuild it
     without asking you.

  4. What would make you wait instead of ship?
     Ask this before you look at the first significant number. Then name:
       - the trigger: the result that pulls you into the conversation
       - the wait-check: the thing you'd still want to see before you act
     Most borrowed-shape mistakes happen when the trigger gets treated as the answer.

When you're borrowing this shape:
  - Effect size and the "big enough to matter" threshold travel with the
    hypothesis — don't split them up.
  - The wait-check is set before the result, not justified after.
  - Q4 guidance for borrowing the shape. Not a process rollout, not a launch
    checklist.

Confirming your read and adding three points you didn't make that I think are worth pressing on:

1. Segmentation on job title from the signup form is the wrong axis. Job title is low-quality self-reported data (people default to "Founder" or skip it), and the trigger condition already gives you a behavioral split that matters more — invite state vs integration state are likely different failure modes with different remedies. Segmenting on the demographic and treating both blocked states with the same five-email cadence wastes sends and conflates two distinct problems. The first analytical move is to look at the conditional distribution: of users who hit day 5 with no teammates and no integration, what fraction are blocked on access/ownership vs blocked on technical setup vs just gone? Five emails should not be drafted before that distribution is on the page.

2. The metrics are vanity. Open rate and reply rate measure whether the email was interesting, not whether activation moved. The decision-relevant metrics for this trigger are activation rate (integration connected within the trial), time-to-activation, trial-to-paid conversion, and a downstream retention check at 30/60 days. "Open rate above 35%" is a threshold, not an effect — even if it's met, you haven't answered whether the sequence caused activation to lift or just made the email more clickable. Reply rate at 5% is especially weak as a primary metric because it conflates engaged-but-stuck users (the ones you want) with confused users reporting problems (the ones you don't).

3. The rollout decision is built wrong. "If those are met after two weeks, I would roll the sequence out to all starter trials" is a within-subjects step on the same population — anyone measured in the treatment becomes part of the rollout baseline, and the comparison group disappears. There is no holdout, no cohort boundary, no definition of a decision-relevant effect size, and no mention of what would make you *stop* the rollout. Even a minimal version — concurrent control = no sequence, treatment = sequence, decision threshold = "activation rate increases by X absolute points with at least Y days of data" — would be a real evaluation. As written, the "two weeks and ship" rule is arbitrary and would commit to a permanent lifecycle change on a 14-day read of two weak metrics.

One probe worth adding to your Friday list, distinct from the six already drafted:

  "You're proposing five emails before any diagnosis. Walk me through what you'd actually look at first about a day-5 starter trial user with no teammates and no integration — what data, in what order, before you draft a single email. And tell me explicitly what would make you send zero emails."

That tests diagnosis-before-prescription directly, and the "tell me when you'd send nothing" half forces them to defend restraint, which is the muscle the response shows they don't have.

Worth flagging as a pattern: this is the second candidate in a row whose first move on a lifecycle question is more email before audience/stage diagnosis. Candidates who skip that instruction are telling you what you need to know.

CLEANING THE TIN

Before you open it again to paint:
- Dry dust first. A clean soft brush (a makeup brush or a hake works) over the pans and into the lid corners. Get the loose grit off before any moisture touches anything.
- If a pan looks grimy, lay a barely-damp soft cloth on it for a few seconds, then lift. Don't rub.
- The metal case: dry microfiber. If you want, a cloth barely dampened with water, then immediately dried. Old tins hate standing moisture.
- The cracked mixing tray: don't try to fix it, don't glue it, don't tape it shut. While painting, lay a small piece of wax paper or a cut-up plastic baggie under it as a moisture shield so water doesn't seep through the crack onto the table.

What NOT to do:
- No running water over the pans. The pigment is bound with gum arabic; soaking dissolves the binder and pans pit or crumble. Sponge-bath only.
- No soap, no dish detergent, no vinegar, no rubbing alcohol — anything you'd reach for "to clean" will either leave residue or attack the binder.
- No scrubbing. No paper towel on the pan surface (lint + abrasion in one move).
- No heat — no hair dryer to "speed up drying." Warps the metal, can extend the tray crack.
- Don't pry the lid past its natural arc. Old hinges snap clean.

FIRST SWATCH ON A QUIET SUNDAY

Small setup:
- A scrap sheet or test page, taped down (tape before coffee — tradition).
- Two water cups: one for picking up pigment, one for rinsing.
- A soft round brush, size 6 or 8. Maybe a small flat for the washes.
- A scrap of paper towel.
- The wax-paper shield under the tray if you're going to mix on it.

Order of operations:
1. One drop of water per pan, one at a time. Wait. Don't flood the tin.
2. Pick up with a damp brush and lay each color in a small labeled square on the scrap.
3. Note which pans release fast and which fight you. The blue, per history, will probably want a longer sit — 20–30 seconds with the drop on the pan before you try to lift it. Don't try to bully it.
4. Then one tiny low-stakes study: a leaf, the shadow under a mug, the corner of a window. Not a "real" painting. You're just listening to what the tin still wants to do.
5. Close the tin between sessions. Brushes rest on the table, not back in the tin wet.

While painting, DON'T:
- Drip into the cracked tray.
- Press hard on the pans.
- Dig at a sad pan with the brush to "wake it up" — that's the surface coming off.

Here's a draft for Priya — a follow-up probe that uses a neutral SaaS scenario so the candidate is being judged on judgment, not on knowing Helio's vocabulary. Two pieces: the prompt itself, and a private scoring guide.

==============================================================
FOLLOW-UP EXERCISE — "The September onboarding nudge read"
==============================================================

Time box: 15 minutes. Hand the candidate the prompt on a single
page. Give them ~5 minutes to think and respond; probe from there.

THE PROMPT (read aloud or handed over)

  You're a growth analyst at a B2B SaaS company. A PM ran a one-week
  A/B test on a new onboarding nudge — a tooltip that points new
  users to a key setup step. Here is the read:

    - Variant: tooltip shown in the user's first session
    - Cohort: US SMB signups, week of Sept 11–17
    - Sample: 1,203 users exposed to the variant; 1,187 in holdout
    - Headline: "+18% relative lift in D7 activation, p < 0.05"
    - Absolute: ~+2.3 percentage points on a 13% baseline
    - No second-cohort replication yet
    - PM context: "Can we roll out next week? I want it in the
      October board update."

  The PM wants a recommendation by EOD. Walk through how you'd
  think about this before answering.

PROBES IF THE CANDIDATE DOESN'T SURFACE THEM NATURALLY

  - "What's the denominator here, and is it the right one?"
  - "Is +2.3pp on a 13% base the number that would change a
    decision? Is there a smaller or larger number that would?"
  - "What's the difference between this result being significant
    and being ready to ship?"
  - "What would you want to see in a second read before scaling?"

==============================================================
SCORING GUIDE (PRIVATE — DO NOT SHARE WITH CANDIDATE)
==============================================================

We are listening for four things. Each can show up strongly,
partially, or not at all.

  1. DENOMINATOR DISCIPLINE
     Strong: distinguishes exposed users from eligible population
     from all signups in the window. Asks whether the week has
     seasonal or signup-quality issues that narrow the cohort.
     Notices that n is comfortable for the headline but small
     enough that subgroup reads (plan tier, integration status)
     would be noisy.
     Partial: names the denominator but doesn't interrogate it
     (e.g., cites 1,203 without asking whether that's the right
     population to make a decision on).
     Missing: uses the headline number at face value.

  2. EFFECT SIZE JUDGMENT
     Strong: translates +18% relative into +2.3pp absolute and
     asks whether that's the decision-relevant effect. Separates
     the observed effect from the effect that would actually
     change the call (Owen's point — these aren't always the
     same number). Raises multiple-testing or pre-registration
     risk if relevant to the shape.
     Partial: translates to absolute but doesn't frame it as a
     decision question, or names decision-relevance without
     anchoring it to a number.
     Missing: treats the relative lift as the whole story, or
     can't articulate why observed ≠ decision-relevant.

  3. SHIP BOUNDARY (first significance vs stabilization)
     Strong: refuses to call "p < 0.05 on one cohort" a ship
     trigger. Names a concrete replication condition — a second
     cohort, a stabilization window, a pre-registered success
     criterion — before recommending scale.
     Partial: acknowledges the read isn't final but frames the
     wait as "we'll see" rather than a concrete gate.
     Missing: treats first significance as sufficient to ship,
     or recommends rollout/rejection without a wait-condition.

  4. RECOMMENDATION SHAPE
     Strong: held pending replication, narrow scope first (e.g.,
     one segment or one channel), with a concrete unblock date.
     Partial: held, but no scope discipline or no date.
     Missing: binary roll-out / don't-roll-out answer driven by
     the PM's deadline or the headline number.

TIERS

  Strong signal: 3 or 4 dimensions strong, none missing.
  Mixed signal:  1–2 dimensions strong, or one missing plus the
                 rest partial. Most candidates land here.
  Weak signal:   2+ dimensions missing, or any red flag below.

RED FLAGS (any one of these is a weak signal regardless of tier)

  - Confuses statistical significance with decision-relevance.
  - Recommends scaling based on a single cohort without naming a
    replication or stabilization condition.
  - Cannot articulate a wait-condition at all.
  - Treats the PM's deadline as the decision boundary.

==============================================================
NOTES FOR PRIYA
==============================================================

  This is a judgment probe, not a knowledge probe. There is no
  single correct answer; we want to know whether the candidate's
  default mode is to name the denominator, separate the effect
  from the decision, and hold the ship trigger until the read
  stabilizes — without being told to.

  If they only get the right answer after probing, that's still
  partial credit. The question is whether they would have gotten
  there on their own with five minutes and a clean page.

  The scenario deliberately lives in a neutral lane (onboarding
  tooltip on activation) so it doesn't tip into growth-stage
  sensitivities. If you want to swap it for something with a
  sharper lifecycle-email shape, fine — but the four listening
  dimensions stay the same.

A couple of choices worth flagging:
  - The "no second-cohort replication yet" line is doing real
    work. It's the cheapest way to make the ship-boundary question
    obvious without spelling it out. If a candidate misses it,
    that's the dimension they missed.
  - The PM's deadline is in the prompt on purpose. We're testing
    whether the candidate treats the deadline as the boundary or
    pushes back on it. Strong candidates reframe the question;
    weak ones absorb the urgency.

Want me to also draft a 2-minute back-pocket variant (one
paragraph, no probes) for if the panel is running long, or a
sharper lifecycle-email-shaped version if you'd rather test the
same dimensions closer to a sensitive lane?

**Scenario.** A lifecycle retention experiment has been running 14 days. The treatment arm reduced 30-day activation churn from 18.2% → 17.1% (Δ = -1.1pp, p = .04, n ≈ 12k treatment / 12k control). The experiment owner has asked you for a ship/no-ship recommendation by end of day.

Candidate evaluation prompt — Churn investigation readout shape

Context. You're handed a draft one-pager investigating a churn signal in a mid-segment cohort (the kind of write-up we cut from an investigation after the Feb–Apr '23 mid-segment churn retrospective). The draft may or may not be shippable. Your job is not to issue a ship/no-ship verdict. Your job is to read it the way a reviewer would, surface the gaps that would matter if this readout were the basis for a decision, and recommend specific edits.

Deliverable. A short written critique (roughly one page) with four sections, in this order:

1. Problem statement. Restate, in one sentence, what the readout claims to explain. Flag whether the framing is the real question or a more convenient one.

2. Hypothesis stack with effect size and denominator. List the explanations the readout considers, in order. For each: the observed effect size (with sign and magnitude, in the units the readout uses) and the decision-relevant effect size — i.e., the size that would actually change a decision, against whatever baseline or guardrail is in play. Write the denominator out explicitly: accounts, users, events, or MRR — which, and why this is the right one for the claim being made. If the readout only names a direction (e.g., "effect is positive"), flag it.

3. Metric, cohort, and window. Name the metric, the cohort definition, and the time window. State whether those cuts are the right ones for the question, or just the easy ones. If the cohort or window looks chosen to make the signal visible rather than to test it, say so.

4. Decision boundary. Where does this readout actually sit? Three options, and only three:
 - first significance — one window, one cohort, no replication;
 - stabilization-cohort confirmation — a second window or cohort consistent with the first;
 - observation that should not ship yet — interesting, not decision-grade.
Say which one, and what would have to be true for it to move up a level.

Before recommending any lifecycle or comms action (extra email, in-app nudge, CS outreach), answer two screening questions in writing:
 - Is the audience fresh enough that this is a setup problem and not a fatigue problem?
 - What setup blockers exist that would keep this cohort from converting even with another send?
If either answer is "unknown" or "no," the recommendation has to wait, regardless of the p-value.

Scoring rubric (for the candidate's evaluator, not for the candidate to see). Score on:
 - Reasoning rigor: does the critique name the assumptions and the cuts, or just the conclusion?
 - Denominator/effect-size discipline: does it write both observed and decision-relevant effect sizes out, and pick the right denominator?
 - Decision-boundary naming: does it place the readout in one of the three buckets and articulate the move-up condition?
 - Resistance to tactic-before-diagnosis: does it refuse to bless an extra send until the two screening questions are answered?
A candidate who produces a clean yes/no ship verdict on the draft without those four moves has failed the prompt, regardless of how confident the verdict sounds.

---

Why this prompt tests reasoning instead of baiting a yes/no.

A "should we ship this?" prompt invites the candidate to pattern-match on confidence and reach for the most plausible send. That's exactly the failure mode we've already seen twice in this cycle: the candidate reaches for an extra lifecycle email before checking audience freshness or setup blockers, and treats the first statistically significant window as a decision instead of a signal. A yes/no ship prompt also flatters the wrong skill — decisiveness under ambiguity looks like judgment only until you watch someone be decisive in the wrong direction.

The four-block structure forces the work the decision actually depends on. The hypothesis stack can't be skimmed if both the observed and the decision-relevant effect size have to be written down with a denominator attached. The decision-boundary block forces a choice among three named states instead of a vibes-based "looks promising." And the two screening questions before any comms recommendation are the cheap, decisive filter: they cost almost nothing to answer and they kill most premature sends on contact. A candidate who skips them — or answers them with "trust me, the audience is fine" — is telling you, in writing, that they will reach for a tactic before they diagnose the audience. That's the failure mode you're screening for, and a yes/no prompt can't see it.

The rubric is also doing real work. Scoring on reasoning rigor, denominator/effect-size discipline, boundary naming, and tactic-before-diagnosis resistance gives you four independent signals; a yes/no score collapses them into one. Two candidates can give the same verdict for opposite reasons, and only the four-block scoring tells them apart.

In short: the prompt is designed so that the only way to do well is to do the work a reviewer would do, and the only way to do badly is to do what we'd already seen the previous candidates do. A ship/no-ship prompt rewards the second behavior; this one penalizes it.

Safe order, least invasive → most. Stop and call maintenance at anything in the stop list below.

1. Hot water + dish soap, now. Squirt a generous amount of dish soap down the drain, then pour a full kettle of just-off-boil water in 2–3 slow pours with a minute between each. This often clears grease/soap film in the trap arm and is safe overnight.

2. Clean the P-trap (most likely real fix, since the plunge only helped a little). Bucket under the U, hand-loosen the two slip nuts, drop the trap out. Expect black gunk, sometimes a bottle cap or food scrap. While it's off, shine a flashlight into the stub-out in the wall — if you see standing water past the first couple of inches, the blockage is past the wall and you should stop and reassemble + call maintenance.

3. Reassemble with the same rubber washers (replace if squished/cracked). Hand-tight plus a quarter turn with channel locks. Run both basins hot for a minute and check the trap AND the cabinet floor for any drip before walking away. Even one drop = don't leave it for Mom's visit.

4. If the basin is still slow after a clean trap: the clog is in the wall lateral. That's maintenance, not a DIY job — stop.

Stop and call maintenance if:
- Slip nuts won't budge or the trap is corroded/cracked on removal
- You see standing water past the trap arm when you look in
- Any drip after reassembly, even small
- The dishwasher backs up or gurgles when you run the disposal
- Any sewer smell at any point (vent issue, not a clog)

Time-pressure note: if it's already late and you're tired post-cleanup, the cleanest move is to skip the left basin overnight, leave a short note ("left basin draining slow, not using it, calling maintenance in the morning"), and book the call first thing before Mom arrives. A slow drain won't cause damage overnight as long as you don't run that basin hard or put a lot down it. P-trap work is a 15-minute job when fresh, not a tired-after-cooking job.

Patch is reasonable here. A single pinhole from a known small shard, casing visually clean, and you have a patch kit on hand — that's exactly what patches are for, and you save the spare for a real commuter failure.

The August lesson still applies, though: the previous "failed patch" wasn't the patch — it was a rim tape split. So treat this patch as a *repair + diagnostic*: if it goes soft again, the next move is rim tape, not another patch. With that framing, here's the sequence.

DECISION: PATCH now, keep the spare tube in the bag.

INSPECTION CHECKLIST (do all of these before mounting the patched tube):

  1. Find and inspect the hole in the old tube *before* patching it. Inflate it just enough to find the leak, mark it, then fully deflate. Confirm it's a single pinhole and not a slit, rim-side wear mark, or two adjacent holes (multiple holes = rim tape or spoke issue, not patch territory).
  2. Run a fingertip *slowly around the entire inside of the tire casing*. The shard that punctured the tube is almost certainly still lodged in the tread or casing — find and remove it. A 2nd piece left in = guaranteed repeat flat on the new tube. This is the step most likely to save you.
  3. Inspect the outside of the tire at the puncture spot — flex the casing open and look for a cut, exposed threads, or a bulge. You said none visible, but flexing reveals what a static look misses.
  4. Check the rim tape on the rim:
     - Spoke holes fully covered, no splits, no peeling edges, no exposed spoke nipple poking through
     - Tape centered over the hole bed, not slid toward the sidewall
     - Valve hole clean (no tear radiating from it)
     This is the August failure mode. Spend 30 seconds here.
  5. Confirm the bead is seated evenly all the way around on both sides before inflating. Crooked bead = pinch-flat risk on first inflation.
  6. Patch the tube per the kit: rough the area, apply glue, wait until tacky (not wet), apply patch, press firmly 30+ sec.

PRESSURE-TEST CHECKLIST (after mounting, before riding):

  1. Inflate to near max sidewall pressure (e.g., 90–100 psi for a typical 700c road/hybrid; check the sidewall for the actual range). This stresses the patch and seating harder than riding pressure will.
  2. Wait 5 minutes. Should not drop audibly or by more than ~2 psi by feel.
  3. Spin wheel slowly, listen near the valve, patch location, and each spoke hole on the rim for hissing.
  4. Soap-bubble test if you have any dish soap handy: brush soapy water along the tire/rim seam, valve stem, and patch. Bubbles pinpoint any leak. This is the test that would have caught the August rim tape split immediately.
  5. If clean, deflate to riding pressure (most commuting tires 70–85 psi front/rear) and remount.
  6. Squeeze-test the tire all the way around — should feel uniformly firm, no soft spots.

ABANDON THE PATCH AND USE THE SPARE IF:
  - You find a second shard, a casing cut, exposed threads, or a bulge during inspection
  - The rim tape is split, peeling, or has an exposed spoke nipple
  - The patch loses more than ~2 psi in 5 minutes at max pressure, or the soap test bubbles anywhere on the rim seam

If the patch passes the pressure test, you're good to ride the errand. If it goes soft within a day or two after that, skip straight to "rim tape is suspect" — that's the pattern from August, and the spare tube alone won't fix it; you'll need the spare *plus* rim tape.

That sounds like a careful repair, and the hand-check inside the tire is the right move — most "patch failures" turn out to be residual debris in the casing rather than the patch itself, so feeling around by hand before inflating is exactly what the August saga taught.

A few practical notes:

  3 miles at 62 psi with no loss is encouraging but not definitive. A full commute is longer and more variable (cold casing, slower leaks show up over time). The re-check before your next ride is the smart gate.
  Visual + thumb-press on the tire before you leave is a quick sanity check; if it's still firm at 60+ psi, you're probably good.
  Keep the spare tube in your bag as planned. If it does go soft on the road, that's the casing signal again — same playbook as 8/31 (shop inspection, not another patch on top of debris).
  If the next ride is a time-pressured commute and you want zero risk, rideshare from the start stays on the table.

Otherwise the sequence you're running — patch, short test, re-check before commute, spare in reserve — is the conservative one. Hope it holds.

For a dry cold-press card with lifted fibers along an edge, the safest play is to keep the shadow wash *away* from the rough strip rather than try to fix the strip. Three options, ranked by how little they touch the existing work:

1. **Re-mask just inside the damage.** Lay a fresh strip of clean masking tape (or washi) so the lifted fibers fall *outside* the new paint zone. Run your shadow wash up to that line and stop. The rough strip becomes the border, the wash never touches it, and the existing paint is untouched. Zero risk to what's already dry. This is the move I'd default to.

2. **Trim it.** If the lifted strip is along the border anyway, put the card face-down on a cutting mat and slice 2–3 mm off that edge with a fresh blade — one pass, no sawing. On a 5x7 a clean crop that small reads as intentional, and you get a fresh edge for the wash to terminate at. The cold-press tooth stays intact on the rest of the card.

3. **Coax the fibers down with a barely-damp brush.** Soft round, size 6 or 8, almost dry. Drag *along* the strip in one direction, not into the wash. Let it dry flat before you do anything else. This is the riskiest of the three because cold-press loses its tooth the moment you press on it, and if the brush is too wet the existing wash will lift. Only worth it if you really need the full 5x7.

What I'd skip: pressing the fibers back with a finger or bone folder (crushes the tooth into a shiny smear), rewetting to "settle" them (the wash will bleed), or painting over the rough strip to hide it (cold-press will give you a tide line exactly where the damage is).

If it were my card, I'd re-mask. It's reversible, it leaves the wash alone, and the lifted fibers just become the frame.

The 62 → 37 psi overnight drop confirms another slow leak source in the tire/tube interface, not the patch itself failing — same pattern as August. Treat the casing as suspect until you have eyes and fingers on the inside surface.

INSPECTION SEQUENCE (do these in order — skipping ahead is what punctures the spare)

1.  Before dismounting, with the 37 psi still in the tire:
    - Spin the wheel slowly against a bright light (headlamp or phone flashlight) and look at the tread from at least three angles. You've already found two shards in different parts of the tread — assume there's a third.
    - Flex the tread with your thumbs over the area where each shard was embedded; cuts in the casing sometimes close up when the tire is at rest and only open under flex.
    - Squeeze the sidewalls and look for any soft spots or bulges that aren't there on the opposite side.

2.  Pull the valve core or press the valve to dump the remaining air fully. Mark the valve position on the tire with a chalk mark or scratch so you can match it to the rim hole on reassembly.

3.  Unseat one bead only — start opposite the valve, use two plastic tire levers, lever the second one along as you go. Don't run a metal lever across the rim bed.

4.  Before pulling the tube out, note where the valve exits the rim and slide the tube around inside the tire so you can pull it out without dragging it across the casing. Pull the tube out, then set it aside.

5.  Find the leak on the old tube:
    - Inflate it and listen, or submerge section-by-section in a basin of water and watch for bubbles.
    - Mark the hole location on the tube with a pen. The matching spot on the tire casing is your highest-priority inspection zone — that is almost certainly where the offending shard entered.

6.  Inner-casing inspection (this is the step that prevents puncturing the spare):
    - Fold the unseated bead back so you can see and reach the inside of the tread across the full circumference.
    - With a clean fingertip or a thin glove, sweep slowly around the inside — every millimeter. Embedded glass often protrudes inward as a hard point you can feel even when it's hard to see.
    - Sweep twice around, once lightly (for glass), once with a firmer press (for any embedded metal wire or thorn tip).
    - Use the flashlight aimed nearly parallel to the casing — raking light catches glass slivers that direct light misses.
    - Pay extra attention to the area matching the tube's hole.

7.  Rim inspection (with the tire fully off):
    - Rim tape: confirm it fully covers every spoke hole edge-to-edge with no splits, no gaps at the valve hole, no frayed edges. This was your August failure mode — check it first.
    - Spoke nipples: run a fingertip across the rim bed. Any nipple protruding above the rim bed surface is a guaranteed tube-killer.
    - Rim bed itself: feel for burrs, dents, cracks, corrosion pits. Anything you can snag a fingernail on will snag a tube.
    - Bead seat (the two small lips the tire bead hooks onto at the rim edges): look for sharp edges, corrosion, debris. Wipe with a clean rag.

8.  Exterior tire check you may not have caught the first time:
    - With the bead unseated, run a finger inside each sidewall too — sidewall glass is rare but possible.
    - Look at the bead wire all the way around: any kink, broken strand, or section that won't sit round.

9.  Reinstall in this order to protect the spare:
    - Partially inflate the spare tube just enough to hold its shape (no wrinkles, not firm).
    - Insert the valve straight through the rim hole first, then work the tube into the tire all the way around. Make sure the tube isn't twisted.
    - Seat the bead back onto the rim by hand as far as you can, finishing the last bit with the lever near the valve — never lever near the valve.
    - Before you inflate past 10 psi, do a tube-tuck: squeeze the tire wall all the way around and push the tube up into the tire so it's not pinched between bead and rim.
    - Inflate to ~20 psi first and check the bead is seated evenly all the way around on both sides. Then go to riding pressure.

TIRE IS UNSAFE TO REUSE — REPLACE INSTEAD OF JUST REPAIRING IF ANY OF THESE ARE TRUE

  - Cut or gouge reaches the casing ply — i.e., you can see threads, cords, or a discolored line through the rubber. Hairline cuts that don't reach the casing are usually OK; anything that exposes casing is not.
  - Any bulge, blister, or soft spot when inflated at riding pressure, especially on the sidewall. That means a broken casing ply and a blowout is coming.
  - Bead damage: kink, broken strand in a folding bead, exposed wire core, any section that won't sit round in the rim hook. A damaged bead won't stay seated under hard cornering or braking.
  - Sidewall gash deeper than a couple of mm, or any sidewall cut that flexes open when you squeeze the tire.
  - Casing ply separation or delamination — looks like a bubble under the rubber, or the rubber lifts away from the fabric when probed.
  - You find a third embedded shard, or the casing is so pitted with old glass scars that you can't be confident the inside is clean. Two punctures in different tread zones in one season is a tire that's telling you its casing is full of debris paths.

ONE PRACTICAL NOTE

Given two shards in different parts of the tread and a patch-then-repatch-then-patch pattern, this tire is probably at end of life even if the inside currently looks clean. If you'd rather not gamble on the Tuesday office commute, a ~$30–50 replacement tire now is cheaper than a roadside rideshare or a worse-case bead failure under load. If you do replace, match the size printed on the sidewall (e.g., 700x28c or 700x32c) and, if you ride in winter, consider a harder compound or a tire with a more cut-resistant casing.
