Quick read: rapid clicking + hard light dim with nothing else going on is almost always a battery that can't deliver cranking amps. At 4.75 years old and in January cold, "end of life" is the leading guess. You won't actually know if it's the battery or the charging system until it starts - the plan below is built around two crank attempts and a 10-minute verdict, not more.

BEFORE YOU CONNECT
- Parking brake on. Transmission in Park (auto) or Neutral (manual).
- Headlights, climate, radio, chargers, dome lights all OFF.
- Key out of the ignition until both clamps are on.
- Quick look at the battery: no swelling, no wet residue, no rotten-egg smell, no heavy crust. If any of those appear, do not jump - it's a tow.
- Safety glasses if you have them. Lead-acid can crack under a heavy crank.

CONNECTION ORDER (do this in order, do not start the car yet)
1. Red clamp to battery + (positive) terminal.
2. Black clamp to a clean, unpainted metal ground on the engine block or chassis bracket - NOT the battery - terminal. This puts any spark away from the battery.
3. Power on the jump pack. Set it to 12V / "start" / "engine" mode if it has a mode switch.

CRANK ATTEMPTS - TWO TOTAL, NO MORE

Attempt 1: Turn the key to START for 3-5 seconds, then release.
- Engine cranks and starts -> let it idle, go to "AFTER START" below. Do not disconnect the jump pack yet.
- Still rapid clicking or no crank -> STOP cranking. Wait 60 seconds with the jump pack still connected so it can recover.

Attempt 2 (only if attempt 1 didn't start it): same 3-5 second crank.
- Starts -> go to "AFTER START."
- Still rapid clicking -> stop. Two attempts is the diagnostic cap. A third won't teach you anything new; it just cooks the jump pack and the battery.

STOP CONDITIONS - disconnect the jump pack and stop work if ANY of these happen at any point:
- Smoke, hissing, bubbling, or a hot-to-touch battery
- Battery starts swelling, even slightly
- Jump pack shuts off, flashes an error, or its case gets hot
- Burning or "electrical" smell
- A loud pop or crack from the battery
- Both crank attempts used and engine still hasn't fired

AFTER THE ENGINE STARTS
Leave it idling. Do NOT disconnect the jump pack for at least 30 seconds - the alternator needs a moment to take over load. Then disconnect in REVERSE order: black ground clamp first, then red + clamp.

THE SMALLEST POST-START CHECK SET

Three checks, in this order. Enough to separate "old battery" from "charging system" in most cases.

Check 1 - Does it stay running on its own?
- Let it idle 2-3 minutes after you remove the jump pack.
- Stays running -> charging system is at least keeping the engine alive.
- Dies, stalls, or runs rough with dash lights flickering -> charging system problem. Stop here, call for service.

Check 2 - Charging voltage at the battery, engine idling, no big loads on (no headlights, no A/C, no rear defrost).
- 13.8 - 14.7 V -> alternator is charging normally.
- Below ~13.5 V -> alternator is not charging (or not enough). Charging system problem.
- Above ~14.9 V -> regulator is overcharging. Stop the engine if it climbs much above 15 V; it's cooking the battery.

Check 3 - Resting battery voltage, 5-10 minutes after you shut the engine off.
Same meter, engine off, doors closed, no lights on. Wait for surface charge to settle.
- 12.6 V or higher -> battery is holding charge. The "dead" event was probably a one-off (sat too long, cold snap, something left on). Battery is at end of life given its age, but it isn't failed.
- 12.2 - 12.5 V -> battery is weak / partially discharged. Likely end-of-life - it started today, it'll leave you stranded again.
- Below 12.0 V -> battery is bad (likely a dead cell). Replace it.

WHAT THE PATTERNS MEAN
- Started, stays running, idle voltage 13.8-14.7 V, resting voltage 12.6+ -> alternator fine. Battery just aged out; replace it within the next week or two so this doesn't repeat on a colder morning.
- Started, stays running, idle voltage good, resting voltage below 12.3 V -> battery is dead, not the alternator. Replace the battery.
- Engine won't stay running without the jump pack, OR idle voltage is outside 13.5-14.9 V -> charging system (alternator / regulator / belt). Don't keep driving it; get it to a shop. A good battery can't run a car indefinitely without the alternator.
- Battery hot, swollen, or wet after the attempt -> battery is gone. Don't keep driving it; replace.

ONE-SECOND TELL IF YOU DON'T HAVE A METER
With engine idling, watch the headlights. Rev slightly to ~2000 rpm.
- Headlights clearly brighten when you rev and dim at idle -> alternator is producing but weak. Still a charging-system concern.
- Steady and reasonably bright at idle -> alternator is fine.

BOTTOM LINE
- Two crank attempts max, 3-5 seconds each, 60 seconds of recovery between them.
- Stop on any of the listed warning signs, no exceptions.
- The three post-start checks above are the minimum set; everything else is optional.
- Most likely outcome is a 4.75-year-old battery that finally gave up in the cold. You'll know for sure inside ~10 minutes, and you'll have your answer before you commit to either a battery swap or a shop visit.

Your read is right — it's a hierarchy problem, not a damage problem, and the mud risk from adding pigment to dry paper is real. The instinct to keep layering is the wrong instinct here.

Order, lowest-risk first:

  1. CROP TEST. Before any brush touches the paper. Two L-cards, scraps of paper, or your thumbs on the four edges — try each crop. If one crop alone resolves the competition, you're done and the painting is untouched. If it doesn't fully resolve, you've still learned which mass needs to go quiet and which can stay loud. Zero risk, decision-only.

  2. SOFTEN ONE EDGE. Pick the tree mass nearest the path bend and soften just its far edge — the side AWAY from the focal point. Damp (not wet) brush, blotted first on a paper towel, one light pass. Edge softening reads as recession without changing value, so it can't muddy. Let it dry ~60 seconds, then evaluate.

  3. LIFT A BIT OF VALUE on one of the remaining two. Smallest mass, or the one whose body sits behind the focal point. Damp brush, lift, blot. You're not trying to lighten dramatically — just breaking the value-tie. Target hierarchy: path-bend > one anchor mass > two quieter masses.

  4. CONNECTING SHADOW only if 1–3 don't get you there. Thin, cool shadow tying two of the masses to a shared ground line (not all three). This is the only move that ADDS pigment, so it's also the move most likely to tip into mud — which is why it's last.

Stop rule — pick whichever version you'll actually honor:

  - Stop the moment the bend in the path reads FIRST on a fresh look, even if the three trees still feel slightly imperfect. A painting that asks the eye to work is broken; a painting where the eye lands and then wanders is done.
  - Between any two steps, let the paper dry fully, then either squint or look from across the room. Squint collapses values to midtones — if the three masses still merge into one shape under squint, you need more separation; if they read as separate but the focal point still wins, stop.
  - One move per evaluation. If you've softened one edge and you're tempted to also lift AND add a shadow in the same sitting, don't. Next Sunday's fresh eyes are cheaper than this Sunday's mud.

This is a draft review for the 1/22 collaborator-invite reminder test. Top-line read: the hypothesis is +8pp on a broad population (all paid accounts 30-90 days old), the decision rule is "stop and ship when p<.05," and exclusions/guardrails are missing. The prior readout in the September renewal cohort showed +0.7pp retained (p<.05), single-cohort first read, with the October cohort named as the stabilization gate. The pattern that came out of that work was: narrow scope, gate on replication, hold until the second cohort reads. This draft goes the opposite direction.

GAPS YOU LISTED

1. Existing reminder exposure.
   The population needs to be filtered by what other reminders these accounts already receive. If a cohort is already getting a setup tip, an integration nudge, or a renewal-window reminder, a day-5 collaborator-invite reminder stacks on top, and the lift (or the complaint rate) cannot be attributed cleanly. Filter to accounts with no collaborator-invite reminder in the prior 30 days, and identify what other reminder categories they are in.

2. Adoption-plan and recent-support states.
   Per Ines's standing concern, accounts with open CS adoption work or recent support contacts should be excluded. A reminder sent to an account mid-adoption reads as pressure rather than guidance. Suppress for accounts with an open adoption plan or a support contact in the prior 7 days. The admin_proof_attested = true exclusion from the prior proposal still applies.

3. Time remaining until renewal.
   Accounts 30-90 days old are not comparable on time-to-renewal. Stratify by renewal-window bucket (e.g., 60-90 days to renewal, 30-60 days to renewal) or restrict the test to a single bucket. Otherwise treatment and control will differ on baseline renewal probability before the reminder does anything.

4. Unsubscribe outcomes.
   No guardrail for unsubscribe or complaint rate. Add one: pause if the unsubscribe rate in treatment exceeds control by more than a stated basis-point threshold, or if complaint-tagged support contacts from treatment cross a floor. This is also a deliverability safeguard, not just a metric.

5. Support contacts.
   Beyond using recent support contacts as an exclusion, the design needs a support-mix read during the test: count permissions, billing, import, and ordinary-setup questions from treatment vs. control. The September readout showed permissions/admin-ownership ticked up under heavier outreach; that should be a guardrail here too.

6. Stabilization cohort.
   The design needs a second cohort as the gate. The September readout explicitly held October as the stabilization gate before any lifecycle change. This draft should follow the same shape: first cohort is directional only, second cohort replicates before ship. "Stop and ship when p<.05" should become "stop and consider only if the first cohort reads at p<.05 with mechanism checks holding AND the second cohort replicates at similar magnitude."

STRUCTURAL CONCERNS BEYOND THE LISTED GAPS

Cohort scope. "All paid accounts between 30 and 90 days old" is much wider than the mid-segment (75-200 seats) the prior readout came from. There is no basis given for widening the segment, and the prior proposal explicitly capped at mid-segment only — no top-of-funnel, no expansion. The right scope for a first read here is mid-segment, restricted by time-to-renewal, with the exclusions above. A wider cohort is a separate, later test.

Effect-size estimate. +8pp is roughly 10x the +0.7pp observed in the prior single-cohort readout. What is the basis for that estimate? If it is directional, the decision rule needs a minimum effect (e.g., +2pp retained on a directional first read, with the second cohort as gate) rather than a pure p-value cut. Otherwise the design risks shipping a tiny but significant effect or rejecting a real one.

Decision rule. A p-value cut alone is the third take-home concern from the prior review — it does not bound a lifecycle change. The rule needs:
    a minimum effect floor,
    a support-load guardrail (permissions, billing, complaint-tagged),
    an unsubscribe / complaint-rate guardrail,
    mechanism checks (teammate-invite rate and integration-connect rate inside the window) so the lift is not borrowed from an unrelated behavior change that week.

Exclusions. Mirror the prior proposal: suppress for accounts with an admin login in the last 3 days (recently active, does not need the reminder), suppress for admin_proof_attested = true, suppress for open CS adoption work, suppress for recent support contact.

Secondary metric floor. "At least two collaborator invites within 14 days" — is two the right floor? The prior readout looked at teammate-by-day-10 as the mechanism. Align the secondary metric to the mechanism check that has been used before, or justify a new floor with evidence.

WHAT THIS SHOULD LOOK LIKE BEFORE IT GOES ANYWHERE

Narrow the population to mid-segment (75-200 seats), restrict to a single time-to-renewal bucket (e.g., 60-90 days), apply the four exclusions above, and revise the decision rule to require first-cohort plus second-cohort replication with mechanism checks and guardrails. The +8pp hypothesis should be replaced with a directional expectation tied to the prior readout magnitude, and "stop and ship when p<.05" should be replaced with a multi-criterion decision rule. Direct answer first: do not run this as a renewal-rate A/B. Logging it anyway is the move I'd push back on hardest — running at ~17% power and treating "no significant difference" as a real read is worse than not running, because it produces an artifact (a null) that will be cited as evidence later. The design wants 446/arm (you have 56/arm). That's an 8x shortfall, not a marginal one.

Power check (worked by hand to confirm the 892/446 figure):

  z(alpha/2, two-sided 5%)  = 1.96
  z(beta, 80% power)        = 0.84
  p1 = 0.72, p2 = 0.80, pbar = 0.76

  n_per_arm = ( 1.96*sqrt(2*0.76*0.24) + 0.84*sqrt(0.72*0.28 + 0.80*0.20) )^2 / (0.08)^2
            = ( 1.184 + 0.505 )^2 / 0.0064
            = 2.852 / 0.0064  ~  446 per arm.

  Owen's 892 / 446-per-arm is correct.

  At n = 56/arm (112 eligible, ~50/50):
    SE under H1 = sqrt(0.2016/56 + 0.16/56) = 0.0804
    noncentrality z = 0.08 / 0.0804 = 0.996
    power = Phi(0.996 - 1.96) + Phi(-0.996 - 1.96)
          ~ 0.167 + 0.0016
          ~ 0.169, so ~17%.

  Minimum detectable effect at n=56/arm, 80% power, 5% two-sided:
    solve (p2 - 0.72)/sqrt(0.2016/56 + p2(1-p2)/56) ~ 2.80
    -> p2 ~ 0.915, i.e. MDE ~ +19.5 pp absolute.

Read that carefully: at 56/arm the experiment could only formally distinguish a ~91.5% renewal rate from a 72% control at 80% power. A real reminder email doesn't move a number that big. The +8pp aspiration would be detectable at full power (~89% at n=446/arm), but at 56/arm you'd only declare significance ~17% of the time — and that's assuming the +8pp is real.

One more tension worth naming: the September read you're already sitting on was +0.7pp (control 79.8% vs treated 82.1%), an order of magnitude below the +8pp this design is powered for. Either the September read was noise, or +8pp is the wrong target. The new audit doesn't tell us which — and running underpowered doesn't resolve it.

Why a faster invite-rate secondary does not rescue the underpowered renewal claim:

  Power is a property of the primary endpoint and its variance at the chosen n. A faster secondary signal doesn't transfer statistical certainty onto a different, slower metric.

  The questions are also different. Invite-rate-at-day-10 answers "did the reminder move a teammate invite?" Renewal-rate answers "did the reminder change the renewal?" Even if both move in the same direction, an unpowered renewal test still can't tell you whether the renewal movement is real or which share of it is confounded by the invite behavior you just measured. A leading indicator that agrees with a noisy primary is not validation; it's correlated noise.

  The contamination risk runs the other way too. Ines's open-CS-adoption concern lives on the invite-rate metric as much as on the renewal metric. Bolting a powered invite-rate read onto an underpowered renewal test, then claiming the renewal result is "supported," inverts the discipline — you'd be using a softer signal to certify a harder one.

Why first significance still needs a stabilization cohort:

  One cohort is one draw. Whatever the September read shows — and the new audit doesn't change what the September read showed — it carries seasonal variance, cohort-mix variance, regression-to-the-mean, and noise from the open dependencies you've already named (permissions, imports, billing, support-mix). The +0.7pp you wrote up is the kind of effect that size-of-third-thing can easily produce.

  Replicating in October is the pre-registered half of the evidence the design claims to require. Skipping it because "September already moved" compounds Type I error across what becomes two implicit looks (a "directional" September and a "confirms" October) — and the cost of being wrong is a send-config committed to mid-segment renewal traffic that's hard to walk back without a churn signal of its own.

  The new audit doesn't relax the replication gate. It confirms the population frame, which is useful and worth keeping — but the gate stays.

What I'd actually do:

  1. Hold the renewal-rate test. Don't run it at 56/arm. Don't log it as if it were a test.

  2. Keep the operational readiness intact — copy with Ines, scope sign-off with Marcus, send-config drafted. If a future cohort reaches the 446/arm threshold, you should be able to run without rebuilding.

  3. If something has to happen in this window, frame it as a single-arm directional observation on this population: record rates, no significance claim, no "test passed/failed" framing. Honest, doesn't lock you in, doesn't get cited later as evidence.

  4. If the team wants a powered read at this population size, invite-rate is the candidate — but as its own experiment with invite-rate as primary, pre-registered, not as a sidecar on an underpowered renewal test.

Why the W-2 does not need a correction:

The IRS and SSA match W-2s to returns by SSN (and check the EIN, name control, wages, and withholding). The mailing address printed on the employee copy of the W-2 is not part of that match — it is essentially a delivery artifact for the employee's records. Form W-2c is reserved for substantive tax-data errors: wrong SSN, wrong wages, wrong federal/state withholding, name mismatch, or incorrect taxable amounts. You confirmed name, SSN, wages, and withholding all check out against the final paystub, so there is nothing to "correct." Filing your return with a current address while Sam's W-2 carries the old Austin one is normal — the IRS will not flag it as a mismatch.

One thing that would have mattered but doesn't here: Sam works in Texas, which has no state income tax, so there is no state withholding box (Box 17) in play. If he had moved between two states with income tax, the answer about which state return to file would depend on when wages were earned and where he lived when earned — but that is a separate question from the W-2 address and is not an issue for Texas wages.

Even though it does not affect this filing, ask Sam's restaurant to update the address on file so that:
- Next year's W-2 (and any 1099s, if applicable) goes to the right place.
- Future employment verifications, wage corrections, or unemployment claims route correctly.
- The employer's records reflect Sam's actual current residence.

A short email or a quick update in the payroll/HR portal is enough — not urgent, just hygiene.

Bottom line: file with your current address, skip the W-2c, and have Sam ping payroll to fix the address for next year.

Good news on your read of the lights: power, downstream, and upstream solid + online blinking is the classic "modem is bonded to the cable plant but cannot finish registration" pattern. Downstream/upstream solid only tells you the physical layer is up; it does not tell you signal quality is in spec. Online blinking after a full power-cycle is what points the suspicion firmly upstream rather than at your router. The amber router light is consistent with that — most routers show amber when they have no WAN IP to hand off.

Here is a low-risk sequence, ordered by what each step tells you. None of these touch settings.

1.  Note the cadence of the modem's online blink.
    Slow blink (about one per second) = trying to register with the CMTS.
    Fast blink / flicker = still scanning for a downstream frequency.
    Off entirely = no downstream lock at all.
    The cadence narrows whether this is "modem can't see plant" vs "modem sees plant but cannot register."

2.  The single most decisive test: bypass the router entirely.
    Unplug the router's ethernet from the modem. Power the router off.
    Plug your laptop directly into the modem with an ethernet cable.
    Power-cycle only the modem (unplug 30 seconds, plug back in).
    Wait a full 3 minutes — modems often sit on a step for 60-90 seconds before timing out and retrying.
    Watch the online light. Try to load a page.

    What this tells you:
    - Online light goes solid + you reach the internet from the laptop = the modem and line are fine; the problem is the router's hand-off (WAN negotiation, MTU, or a stuck session). You have not reset anything.
    - Online light still blinking, no internet from the laptop = the line or account is the problem. Stop here; nothing on your side will fix it.

3.  While the modem is rebooting in step 2, inspect the coax chain end-to-end.
    Look behind the wall plate, behind any TV, behind any MoCA adapter, at the ground block if there is one. Splitters are the usual silent killer — a forgotten splitter behind a TV you haven't watched in months, or one added for a recent device, will drop return-path signal enough to break registration while leaving the bonded-channel lights lit. Fittings should be hand-tight + quarter turn with a wrench; push-on fittings and kinked cable are common.

4.  If you can reach the modem's diagnostic page, capture the signal numbers.
    With the laptop directly connected to the modem (still in step 2 setup), try http://192.168.100.1 in a browser. Many modems will only respond on this address when nothing else is connected, so this works best right after step 2.

    The numbers you want, with rough healthy ranges:
    - Downstream power:  -7 to +7 dBmV per channel
    - Downstream SNR:    35 dB or higher (some plant uses 30)
    - Upstream power:    35 to 49 dBmV
    - Upstream SNR:      30 dB or higher
    Anything in the 50s on upstream power, or SNR below the floor, is plant trouble even if the lights look healthy.

5.  From the same direct-connected laptop, run a continuous ping to capture packet behavior.
    In Terminal (mac) or PowerShell (Windows):
      ping -i 2 8.8.8.8   (mac)
      ping -t 8.8.8.8     (windows)
    Let it run for 3-5 minutes. Save the output. If the modem ever comes online during this window, the output tells you whether you are seeing full drops vs. partial packet loss vs. latency spikes — very useful for the ISP ticket.

If step 2 shows the modem cannot register on its own, here is what to capture before you call. Having this ready cuts the back-and-forth dramatically.

For the ISP call / ticket:
- Modem make, model, and MAC address (sticker on the bottom of the unit)
- Account phone number or service address on the account
- The exact online-light cadence from step 1 and whether it changes over 3+ minutes of watching
- Signal readings from step 4 (downstream power, downstream SNR per channel, upstream power, upstream SNR) — screenshot or photo
- Output of the ping from step 5
- A traceroute to 8.8.8.8 the moment you see any connectivity at all:
    traceroute 8.8.8.8     (mac)
    tracert 8.8.8.8        (windows)
- Time the trouble started (you said this afternoon; be specific)
- Any weather event in your area — heavy rain, wind, ice — even if it has cleared
- Anything new on the coax chain in the last few weeks: a new splitter, a new TV, a MoCA adapter, a moved cable, anything an installer touched
- Confirmation that multiple devices are affected simultaneously and that a direct laptop-to-modem test failed

A useful framing for the call: "My modem has solid downstream, upstream, and power lights but the online light is blinking after a full power-cycle, and a laptop plugged directly into the modem also has no internet. I would like you to check the CMTS and my modem's provisioning status on the line." That tells the tier-1 rep exactly which path to send the ticket down instead of walking you through another reboot.

One last note on the timing: Sunday-afternoon CMTS maintenance windows are common, and a temporary provisioning blip can clear on its own within 30-90 minutes. If step 2 fails but the modem eventually comes online on its own, keep the ping and traceroute outputs anyway and run the same test again next time it happens — pattern data on a single ticket is much more persuasive than pattern data on a single occurrence.

────────────────────────────────────────
1. SUMMARY OF THE RISK
────────────────────────────────────────

The shape of the fix is: dual-write shadow before the cutover, dual-read after, retire only after Owen and Ines sign off on equivalence.

2. MIGRATION PHASES
────────────────────────────────────────
Phase A — Inventory + map (now → Feb 5)

3. DUAL-READ FORMULA
────────────────────────────────────────

Here's the assessment and a script you can send, kept tight and in the warm-but-grounded tone you've used with her before.

PHISHING SIGNS — what you've already noticed, plus the usual tells:
  - Carrier name misspelled or stretched (USSP, FedX, UPS-Delivery, etc.)
  - Link domain does NOT end in the carrier's real domain (real USPS is usps.com; UPS is ups.com; FedEx is fedex.com; Amazon is amazon.com)

  - Urgency: "confirm within 24 hours or return to sender"
  - Shortened URL (bit.ly, t.co, tinyurl)
  - Slightly off grammar or weird punctuation
  - The fact that you don't recognize a real incoming package
  - All major US carriers (USPS especially) have stated publicly: they do NOT send tracking texts with clickable links

TEXT TO SEND MOM (two short parts — the first is reassurance, the second is the steps):

  Reassurance (send first, on its own):
  ---
  Hey Mom — really good instincts not clicking. These "package on the way"
  texts are one of the most common scams going right now, and the vast
  majority of them are fake. You did nothing wrong. Don't reply, don't
  click, don't feel like you have to deal with it today. Sending you a
  couple of calm steps in a second message.
  ---

  Steps (send right after, numbered so she can ignore what she doesn't need):
  ---
  If you ever want to check whether a real package is actually on the way:

  1. Don't use the link in the text. Open the app or website yourself —
     Amazon app, USPS.com, UPS.com, FedEx.com — whatever you actually use.
  2. If you didn't order anything recently, it is almost certainly fake.
     A real carrier will leave a paper slip in your mailbox, not a text.
  3. If you're still unsure, call the carrier using the number on their
     website (not a number from the text). They can look up any real
     package by your address or name.

  To clear the message off your phone:
  - Forward the text to 7726 (that's SPAM on the keypad — your carrier

  - Then delete it.
  - No need to report it anywhere else unless you want to.
  ---

IF SHE DID CLICK (only relevant if it turns out she tapped before reading this — don't send this proactively, just have it ready):

  - If she did not enter any info: nothing to do beyond the steps above. Phone is fine.
  - If she entered an account login (Amazon, bank, email, etc.): change that password from a different device, right now. Turn on two-factor if it isn't on.
  - If she entered payment info: call the card company's number on the back of the card. Ask to flag the card and issue a new one. Don't wait for a charge to appear.

That's a smishing text — classic USPS impersonation. A few tells:

- USPS does not collect redelivery fees via SMS, does not threaten return inside 12 hours, and does not ask you to "Reply Y, reopen the message, then open a link." That three-step dance is the social-engineering part: getting you to confirm the number is live, then re-engage.
- The domain `usps-redelivery-track[.]com` is not USPS. Real USPS domains are `usps.com` and `usps.gov`. Anything with hyphens chaining "usps" + action words ("redelivery," "track," "confirm") on a different TLD is a phish.
- The bracketed dots `[.]` are a security-research notation that defangs the link so a paste doesn't render as clickable — handy if you're logging samples, but it's also a hint you already suspected this wasn't legit.

Recommended handling:

1. Do not reply Y, do not open the link, do not call any number in it.
2. Forward the text to 7726 (SPAM) — that reports to your carrier and the FCC pipeline, and costs nothing.
3. Optionally forward a screenshot to USPS Inspection Service at `spam@uspis.gov`, then delete the message.
4. If you're expecting an actual package, check status directly at `usps.com` (type it, don't follow a link) or the Informed Delivery app.

Nothing to do on the workspace side — this is inbound personal SMS, not your email program or product surfaces. If you've been getting a wave of these, that's normal; carriers cycle smishing campaigns in bursts and they taper.

**Trim the bruises generously.** Cut away every soft spot plus about 1/4 inch of firm-looking flesh around it — bruised pear tissue oxidizes and tastes winey/off faster than you'd think, and the soft zone goes deeper than it looks from the outside. If the bruise is only skin-deep (a dark mark, still firm underneath), a shallow slice is fine. If it's gone mushy or weeping, cut deeper. Sound flesh goes in a bowl; the trimmings go in the trash, not the compost yet (they'll attract fruit flies overnight).

**Skip the stovetop pre-cook.** Instead, peel, core, and slice the pears about 1/2 inch thick, toss with 1 tbsp lemon juice, 2 tbsp brown sugar, 1/4 tsp cinnamon, and a pinch of salt, then let them sit 10–15 minutes. Drain off the pooled liquid before you top them. That's the forgiveness move — it draws out excess juice so the bottom doesn't go soupy, concentrates flavor, and skips a pan to wash. Only pre-cook on the stove if your pears are so ripe they turn to sauce when you look at them; in that case, 3–4 minutes in a skillet to evaporate some moisture.

**Topping (no eggs needed — eggs would make this a cake, not a crisp).**
- 5 tbsp cold butter, cubed
- 1/2 cup rolled oats
- 1/3 cup flour
- 1/3 cup packed brown sugar
- 1/2 tsp cinnamon
- 1/4 tsp salt

Work the butter into the dry ingredients with your fingers or a fork until you have a mix of crumbs and clumps — some pea-sized, some the size of a nickel. Don't overmix; you want texture, not paste.

**Assemble and bake.** Butter a small baking dish — an 8x8 square, a 9-inch pie plate, or two individual gratins all work. Pile in the drained pears, scatter the topping over the surface (don't press it down — keep it loose so it crisps). 

**Oven: 375°F for 30–40 minutes.** Start checking at 30. If the topping edges are browning fast but the center is still pale, lay a strip of foil over just the edges and give it another 5–10 minutes.

**Doneness cues that aren't just color:**
- Bubbling. This is the main one. Look for fruit juice simmering at the edges of the dish or venting up through the topping. If nothing is bubbling, the fruit is still raw and the topping is just browning on top of cold fruit.
- Skewer test. Push a thin knife or skewer through the topping into the fruit — it should slide in with almost no resistance. You want the pears tender, not al dente.
- Smell. The kitchen should smell like toasted oats and caramelized sugar, not just warm butter. That shift happens around the same time the bubbles appear.
- Topping texture. Tap a clump with your finger — it should feel set and crisp on top, not doughy or gummy underneath. If you're unsure, lift a corner of the topping with a fork and look at the underside; it should be golden, not pale and pasty.
- Internal temp if you have an instant-read thermometer: 195–200°F in the fruit layer is the safe "done" zone.

**Leftovers.** Cool completely, cover, refrigerate up to 3 days. Reheat at 350°F for 10–12 minutes to bring the topping back; the microwave softens it. A small splosh of cream or a spoon of yogurt on top is the right move if you have it.

Quick read: heel lift on the left plus a hot spot that showed up on run two is almost always a heel-cup/lacing mismatch, not a "needs more miles" situation. The skin is intact, which means you caught it early — treat it tonight, fix the fit before the next run, and use a hard return line below.

TONIGHT — protect the skin
- Wash with mild soap and lukewarm water, pat dry. No alcohol, no hydrogen peroxide — both slow healing on intact skin.
- Apply a thin layer of plain petrolatum (Vaseline) or a skin balm like Body Glide / Squirrel's Nut Butter over the pink area. This is friction barrier, not medicine.
- Cover with a hydrocolloid patch (Compeed, Band-Aid Hydro Seal, 2nd Skin). These are designed for pre-blister hot spots and stay put overnight better than fabric tape. Leave it on until it falls off or ~24h.
- No sock friction on it tonight — let it air when you're not moving. Don't pick at it, don't "check" it.
- Tomorrow: re-evaluate. If the redness has faded and there's no fluid under the skin, you're fine. If a clear blister forms, do not pop it — dress it and skip the next run.

BEFORE THE NEXT RUN — lowest-risk fixes, in order
Only change one thing per test run, keep the run short (1–2 mi), and walk the first 5 min so you can feel the heel before loading it.

1. Heel-lock lacing ("runner's loop"). Use the extra top eyelet on each side: lace through the eyelet away from the tongue, then down through the same-side eyelet on the other side, creating a small lock above the heel counter. This is the single most common fix for heel lift + posterior hot spot. Try this first.
2. Sock swap. Switch to a synthetic or merino running sock with a bit of heel padding (e.g., Balega Hidden Comfort, Darn Strong, Feetures). If you used cotton or a very thin racing sock, that's a friction trap. One pair change only.
3. Sock height. A micro/mini sock exposes bare skin to the heel counter. A quarter or crew sock puts fabric between skin and counter.
4. Try the second-from-top eyelet instead of the top one. If the top eyelet is pulling the heel upward at an angle, skipping it often kills the lift.
5. As a last pre-test, tape the heel. Leukotape or even strong medical tape over the hot-spot zone, plus a thin layer of balm underneath. This is diagnostic — if taping eliminates the hot spot, the shoe is the problem, not your skin.

If you go through 1, 2, and 3 on three short test runs and the hot spot returns in the same spot, stop testing the shoe.

WHEN TO RETURN, NOT BREAK IN
"Breaking in" a shoe means the shoe's foam and upper conform to your foot over 20–40 miles. It does NOT mean friction stops damaging your skin. Return the shoes if any of the following after you've applied fixes 1–3:

- Same hot spot recurs on the next short test run, in the same spot, with the same character (pink + tender, not just a vague awareness).
- The hot spot progresses to a fluid blister despite protection.
- Heel lift on the left is still detectable at walking pace after heel-lock lacing.
- The right heel starts showing the same pattern (bilateral = structural, not lacing).
- Anything changes your gait — currently you have none, which is good, and you want to keep it that way.

Two runs is still well inside any 30–60 day return window at most running shops. Most will take them back for fit issues even after a few runs if the store specializes in running. If you bought from a dedicated run shop, go back with the shoes on, show them the hot-spot location and the heel lift — they'll often exchange or credit without argument.

THE DISH

Buttered sourdough toast piled with wilted spinach and soft-scrambled eggs, strawberries on the side, coffee. One small skillet, one spatula, two plates — nothing else to wash.

NIGHT BEFORE (about 10 minutes)

  Wash and dry the strawberries; halve or quarter into a small bowl, cover, fridge.
  Wash and thoroughly dry the spinach — salad spinner is fastest, or roll in a clean towel and squeeze. Store in a container with a paper towel in the fridge so it's not wet in the morning.
  Set the butter out to soften, or leave it cold if you prefer it that way.
  Set the table: 2 plates, 2 forks, 2 mugs, butter dish, salt, pepper, the strawberry bowl, a small empty bowl for spinach.
  Stage at the stove: cutting board + bread knife, small nonstick skillet, silicone spatula, toaster cleared.
  Stage at the coffee maker: grounds measured into the filter, water in the reservoir. (If yours has a timer, set it for 9:25.)
  Put a fresh roll of paper towels at the sink.

  Do not pre-crack the eggs, and do not pre-toast the bread.

MORNING (9:25 to 10:05)

  9:25  Hit brew. Pull strawberries and spinach to the counter.
  9:30  Sam sits down; pour his coffee.
  9:32  Skillet on medium-low, a generous knob of butter, all the spinach in with a pinch of salt. Toss until just wilted — about 2 minutes. Tip into the small bowl, off the heat.
  9:35  Drop 4 slices of sourdough in the toaster.
  9:36  Same skillet, medium-low, another knob of butter. Crack in 2 eggs straight into the pan — no bowl, no whisk. Stir constantly with the spatula, low and slow, about 75 seconds. Pull off the heat while the curds still look glossy; they'll finish from the pan's residual heat. Salt.
  9:38  Build Sam's plate: buttered toast, eggs, a handful of spinach, strawberries on the side. Hand it over.
  9:39  Skelet back on the burner, butter, the last 2 eggs, same soft-scramble — about 75 seconds.
  9:41  Build your plate the same way.
  9:42  Both of you eating. Strawberries are already on the plate, no extra dish.
  9:55  While Sam finishes his coffee, clear the table. Run hot tap water into the still-warm skillet — the butter film lifts in about 15 seconds with the spatula, no scrubbing.
 10:00  Wash the skillet, spatula, two plates, two forks, two mugs. Wipe the counter.
 10:05  Sam's sink is empty. He can shower and walk out the door with nothing hanging over him.

WHY THIS STAYS LOW-MESS

  One pan, one spatula, two plates, two forks, two mugs.
  No bowl for the eggs — they go straight into the skillet.
  Toaster handles the bread; no pan for toasting.
  Hot water in a still-warm buttered pan does the work for you. A nonstick wiped with a paper towel at the end is honestly fine if you don't want to wash up at all.

ONE SOFT-SCRAMBLE NOTE

  Low heat and constant stirring is the whole trick. Off the heat while the curds still look wet and glossy. If they look dry in the pan, they'll be dry on the plate. First round is your calibration round — the second round will be perfect.

A SMALL THING

The point of this morning is that it's a held quiet thing — real food, a real mug of coffee, and out the door without either of you cleaning up after the other. It's not the lead-in to a long talk or a Valentine's debrief. Save that energy for a night when he's not on hour eleven.

TONIGHT'S BASELINE
What you're describing — sleepier than usual, mildly sore turning toward the injection side, ate dinner, drank, walked normally, no swelling, no systemic signs at ~2h45m post-vaccine — is the textbook mild response to a leptospirosis booster. The soreness is from the injection (often given in the shoulder/scapula area). The sleepiness is the immune system ramping up. Both are expected, not alarming.

WHAT'S NORMAL OVER THE NEXT 24–48 HOURS
  • Sleepier than usual; sleeping more
  • Mild soreness when touched or when turning toward the injection side
  • A small lump or slight swelling at the injection site (peanut-sized or smaller)
  • Slight warming over the site (low-grade fever — you won't see it, just feel it)
  • Eating slightly less, but still eating and drinking
  • Mild favoring of the side for 24–36 hours
  • Wanting to be near you / seeking comfort (normal, not a worry sign)

OVERNIGHT COMFORT PLAN
  • His usual sleeping spot — nothing new
  • Soft bedding within reach; water nearby if you want it
  • No need to confine or restrict; let him self-regulate
  • A slow pre-bed walk if he wants one; don't force if he's sleepy
  • The den / calming wrap / soft white noise routine from storm nights is fine to use if it helps him settle — same setup as usual
  • One quick check-in when you go to bed: look at the injection site, watch him get up to drink/pee, look at his gums (lift the lip — pink is good)

URGENT VET / EMERGENCY CLINIC — CALL NOW IF ANY OF THESE APPEAR
  • Facial swelling — eyes, muzzle, lips (even mild)
  • Hives or raised welts anywhere on the body
  • Vomiting (especially repeated)
  • Diarrhea
  • Breathing changes — faster, labored, noisy, panting at rest with no relief
  • Collapse, weakness in legs, or marked distress
  • Pale, white, gray, or blue gums
  • Trembling/shaking that doesn't stop
  • Restlessness that progresses — pacing, won't lie down, can't get comfortable
  • Injection-site swelling that grows rapidly, is hot to the touch, or spreads
  • Inability to urinate or no urination for 12+ hours
  • Any "this isn't him" feeling you can't shake — trust that

Serious vaccine reactions usually happen in the first 30–60 minutes (Type I / anaphylaxis), but delayed hypersensitivity can occur up to 24 hours later, so tonight's checks are worth doing. The window of greatest risk is the first 12 hours; after that the odds drop fast.

CALL REGULAR VET IN THE MORNING IF
  • Soreness isn't improving by 48 hours
  • Limp worsens instead of easing
  • Lump at the injection site grows past walnut-size or keeps getting bigger
  • Lethargy hasn't improved by tomorrow midday
  • Appetite is still low past 24 hours
  • Anything else that worries you but isn't an emergency

MORNING PLAN (FEB 15)
  • Daylight recheck of the injection site — look, gently feel
  • Note whether he's still favoring the side or soreness has shifted
  • Normal breakfast and normal walk if he's up for it
  • Most lepto-vaccine reactions resolve within 24–48 hours

OPTIONAL IF YOU WANT A DATA POINT
Rectal temp — normal dog is 101–102.5°F. Slightly elevated is fine and explains the sleepiness. Above 103°F warrants a call to your regular vet's advice line (most have a 24-hour nurse line). Skip it if it would stress him more than it's worth.

You know him. He's behaving like himself with two soft caveats (sleepy, sore), and he's past the early-reaction window without any red flags. That's a good place to be.

DIRECT CALL: Do not ride it. Not even 3 miles. Not even downhill. Walk it, drive it, or rideshare it — but do not put your weight on that wheel.

Why this is different from your previous flats:
- All your prior incidents were tread-area pinholes from glass — patchable, rideable with caution.
- This is a sidewall cut with visible casing threads. The sidewall is the thinnest, most flexed part of the tire. Every wheel rotation bends that cut open and closed. The casing is the structure; once you can see threads, the structure is gone.
- "Tube still holding air" is the slow-leak phase, not the safe phase. The failure mode you are trying to avoid is the tube ballooning into the cut under load and rupturing — that's a sudden blowout at speed, not a gentle flat. February cold rubber makes it worse: stiffer sidewall = sharper stress concentration at the cut.
- Your own framing is correct: the goal is keeping a repairable tire problem from becoming a crash.

Safest way to get it to the shop (in order of preference):
1. Walk it. 3 miles is 30–45 minutes on foot, zero risk. Boring and slow, which is the point.
2. Drive it. If you have a vehicle, throw it in the back tonight and drive to the shop in the morning.
3. Rideshare. Uber XL / similar — call ahead, some drivers accept bikes. Cheaper than a tow, no risk.
4. If 1–3 are truly impossible: push the bike, do not ride it. Hands on bars, feet on ground, scoot. Still some risk if you hit a bump that compresses the sidewall, but orders of magnitude safer than riding. Do not ride slowly. Do not "boot it from the inside and limp there." An inside boot on a sidewall cut does not restore casing strength; it just buys you a slightly slower blowout.

What to ask the mechanic:

2. Replace the tube. Even if it's holding air tonight, it's been pressed against the cut edges and almost certainly micro-damaged. Don't reuse it with the new tire.
3. Inspect the rim in that area. Look for impact marks, a dented rim bed, or recessed spoke nipples — anything the cut tire may have been hammering on.

5. Confirm the wheel is still true and dished. It looks true to the eye; the stand check costs them nothing.
6. Ask what caused the cut — glass, curb strike, pothole pinch, debris. The cause tells you how to avoid the next one.
7. Ask them to look at the front tire's tread depth and sidewall condition while it's on the stand. You've had multiple tire issues over the past year; if the front is also nearing end-of-life, replacing both at once is cheaper than paying the labor twice.

THE LIKELY EXPLANATION (PLAIN LANGUAGE)

Most US provider billing systems work in two stages, and the gap between them is almost certainly what your mom is seeing.

1. The provider sends the insurer a claim for the full charge — here, $184.
2. The insurer reviews it, applies their contracted rate and her cost-sharing rules, and sends back an Explanation of Benefits (EOB) that says: "Allowed amount was $X. We paid $Y. Patient owes $36.80."

Until the provider's office actually receives the insurer's payment (or its electronic equivalent) and posts it to her account, her patient statement keeps showing the original $184. The EOB isn't contradicting the statement; the statement just hasn't been updated yet.

So the EOB is most likely correct, and the statement is most likely just behind. She should NOT pay $184. If she pays before the insurer payment posts, she'll likely end up overpaying and waiting weeks for a refund check.

OTHER THINGS THE CALL SHOULD RULE OUT

  - The claim hasn't been filed yet, so the EOB is interim.
  - The EOB and the statement cover different dates of service (different visits on different documents).
  - The claim was denied or is pending appeal, and the provider is billing the full amount pending resolution.
  - A second insurance is involved and coordination of benefits hasn't been applied yet.
  - The provider is out-of-network and is balance billing beyond the insurer's allowed amount — this is the one case where $184 might genuinely be a fight, not just a timing issue.

NEUTRAL CALL SCRIPT

"Hi, I'm calling on behalf of my mom, [her full name], date of birth [DOB]. She got a statement dated [statement date] showing a balance of $184 for a visit on [date of service] at [provider or practice name]. She also received an Explanation of Benefits from [insurer name] showing $36.80 in patient responsibility for what looks like the same visit, claim number [from the EOB].

Before she pays anything, I'd like to understand how those two numbers reconcile.

  1. Has the insurance payment for this claim been received and posted to her account yet?
  2. If yes, what does her balance show on your system — $184 or $36.80?
  3. If it's still $184 on your side, is the claim pending, denied, or just not yet adjudicated on your end?
  4. Could you send an itemized statement that shows the billed charge, the insurer's adjustment, the insurer's payment, and the remaining patient balance? That makes any discrepancy easy to see at a glance.
  5. If the insurer has paid and the balance is still $184, can you put the difference in writing so we know what to dispute, and with whom?

If they push her to just pay the $184:

  "I'd rather not pay until the insurance payment is posted. Could you call me back once it's posted, or send an updated statement? I'll pay the patient-responsibility amount once it reflects on your side."

That keeps the call factual and doesn't require anyone to admit a document is wrong.

ONE EXTRA TIP

Have her also call the insurer (number on the back of the card) and confirm the EOB claim number is a real, fully processed claim — not a "this is not a bill" interim notice. If the insurer confirms the claim is finalized at $36.80 patient responsibility, that's strong leverage on the provider call.

Here's the plan, kept tight to your three asks.

Immediate cleaning (already pulled the thorn - now just close out the wound):

  - Cool water rinse over the paw for 30-60 seconds, working between the pads and around the puncture site. Plain water only.
  - No hydrogen peroxide, no alcohol, no Neosporin. Peroxide damages healing tissue; Neosporin isn't worth the lick-risk on a paw he can reach.
  - Pat dry with a clean cloth - dampness between pads is its own irritation source.
  - Apply a thin smear of plain dog paw balm if you have it, otherwise a thin film of plain Vaseline over the puncture. Both are pet-safe and lick-tolerant in small amounts.
  - While you're down there, quickly check the other three paws and all four interdigital spaces - thorns and grass awns from one patch usually travel in pairs.

Keeping him from over-licking (in order of escalation):

  - First line: a loose kid's crew sock over the paw, taped above the wrist with one strip of paper tape or self-adhering vet wrap. Loose enough that you can slip a fingertip past the top edge. This is the gentlest option and usually wins the first hour.
  - If he licks through it or wriggles it off in 10-15 minutes, switch to a soft inflatable "donut" collar. Lower stress than a hard cone and it reliably blocks paw reach.
  - Don't preemptively use a hard plastic cone - skip straight to the donut if the sock fails.
  - Distraction buys real time: a frozen stuffed Kong, a lick mat with wet food, or scatter five kibbles across the kitchen floor. Licking the mat is fine and gives the paw 20-30 minutes of rest.

Monitoring tonight - what's fine vs what's a flag:

  - Fine over the next 1-2 hours: intermittent licking that tapers, brief favoring that resolves, normal water/food intake, settling near you.
  - Flag tonight (call your vet / go in): swelling anywhere on the paw or spreading up the leg, bleeding that doesn't stop with gentle pressure in a few minutes, sudden refusal to bear weight, yelping when the paw is touched, lethargy, vomiting, or noticeably warm ears/paws.

Same-day vet triggers (don't wait):

  - Any of the flag signs above.
  - You can still see or feel a fragment in the puncture - don't dig, just go in.
  - The paw is clearly worse, not better, 2-3 hours from now.
  - He's clearly painful in a way the small wound doesn't explain.

Next-day vet is the right call if (this is the routine, same-day appointment tier, not the ER):

  - Licking is still happening at the morning daylight recheck, before breakfast.
  - A mild limp persists a few minutes into a short morning potty walk.
  - Redness is spreading around the puncture, or any discharge appears - cloudy, yellow, or smelly.
  - You're on the fence: call your regular vet and describe it; they triage by phone and will tell you which slot fits.

Why this line: a 4 mm thorn puncture looks clean the moment the fragment is out, but paw-pad punctures are the classic "quiet abscess in 24-72 hours" wound if a sliver stayed behind or bacteria was carried in. So the real observation window is the next 24 hours, not the next 5 minutes. Tonight is for catching the obvious flags; tomorrow morning is the daylight recheck that decides routine vs urgent.

But it only works if:

- Bounded. Pending has a TTL. After N minutes, records go to a review queue — not auto-eligible, not silent drop. Otherwise the guard becomes a way to lose records.
- Visible. Owen's HS dashboard should show a "pending — awaiting both states" state, with retry-gap duration surfaced. If pending is invisible, you've moved the uncertainty underground where Owen's read of activation/support-load gets distorted.
- No silent reclassification on timeout. Timeouts escalate; they don't infer.

Q: Who is Helio Start for?

Helio Start is for straightforward teams under 50 with clean admin ownership, supported billing, and a first integration that can be connected in the first week. Eligibility is checked before setup so a simple workspace doesn't get dropped into avoidable handoffs — workspace permissions, billing path, and a connectable integration all need to hold up. If you're not sure whether you qualify, "Check eligibility" will route you to the right next step.

Q: Can I import or migrate data into Helio Start?

Helio Start is set up around a clean workspace — data imports and migrations from another tool are handled on a separate, assisted track. If you're bringing data over from a different system, reply to your invite and we'll route you to the right team. Trying to land that work inside Start setup tends to slow first-week progress more than it helps.

Q: What billing options does Helio Start support?

Helio Start runs on Helio's standard supported billing — card on file, or standard invoicing for accounts that qualify. Workspaces that use manual invoicing, run billing through an agency or third party, or have custom payment terms are handled on a separate track so setup doesn't get blocked on billing details that aren't covered here. If that's your situation, let us know in your reply and we'll route it.

Q: What if Helio Start isn't the right fit for my workspace?

That's a setup decision, not a judgement about you — Helio Start is intentionally narrow so simple accounts don't end up in avoidable handoffs. If eligibility checks rule your workspace out, your invite routes you to a sales-assisted onboarding track that's built for workspaces with permissions, billing, or migration needs that Start isn't designed to cover. Reply to the invite and we'll move it to the right team.

You did two things right: rubber pickup (not a finger), and waiting until the wash was dry. The damage isn't from your removal technique — it's that masking fluid left to fully cure bonds into the surface fibers of cotton paper, and when it releases it brings fibers with it. That's the roughened strip.

Salvage, in order of how restrained they are:

1. Lift the loose pigment sitting in the roughened strip with a clean, barely-damp soft mop or hake. The dried wash underneath is bonded to the paper and won't release, but the pigment caught on top of the raised fibers usually will. Stroke very lightly, parallel to the edge, with the brush almost dry. This often softens the dark catch without disturbing the wash around it. Lowest-risk move.

2. Read it as part of the sky. A slight soft variation along a pale sky edge frequently reads as a wisp or atmospheric softness rather than damage once the rest of the painting is around it. If your eye stops catching on it after you finish other areas, leave it.

3. Re-mask just inside the damaged strip with low-tack tape if you still have sky work to do. Any further wash stops at the fresh edge, and the roughened strip becomes the "outside" of the painted area.

What not to do: don't scrub, don't re-wet the strip heavily (it'll lift the existing sky wash), don't paint over it (the dark catch will just compound), and don't press the fibers down with a finger or tool — pushing them back into the wet wash makes the damage more permanent.

For next time, the changes that matter most:

  Apply the masking fluid thinner — two thin passes instead of one thick one. Thick fluid penetrates deeper into cotton fibers and bonds harder.

  Remove the masking fluid the same session, ideally within an hour or two of applying it. Fully cured fluid (24+ hours, especially in dry air) is what does most of the fiber-lifting damage. Some watercolorists deliberately remove fluid while the wash is still slightly damp at the edges.

  Peel slowly at a low angle, rolling it off rather than pulling straight up.

  If you know an area will eventually need a soft gradient or pale wash, consider low-tack tape or frisket film instead of fluid — they're gentler on cotton fibers.

  Test on a scrap of the same sheet before using fluid on the painting. Different cotton papers behave differently with fluid, and a 30-second test will tell you whether to expect fiber lift.

The rubber pickup stays. That's the right tool.

Short answer: with the doors held closed for 2h 35m and the thermometer now reading 41°F, you are inside the standard food-safety window. The four categories you listed can all be kept. Here is the breakdown.

REFRIGERATED — KEEP

Milk, eggs, and the general leftovers: safe to keep. Closed-door fridges typically hold below 40°F for about 4 hours (full) or ~2 hours (half full). You went 2h 35m, the doors never opened, and the warmest spot is only 1°F over the threshold — that means the bulk of the outage was below 40°F. These items are fine. Put everything back in the coldest part (back shelf, bottom) right away.

WATCH CLOSELY

Cooked rice is the one item I would not be casual about. Bacillus cereus spores survive cooking and germinate in the 40–140°F range; the toxin they produce is heat-stable, so reheating will not rescue bad rice. The FDA's strict line is "discard if held between 40–140°F for more than 2 hours"; USDA's broader perishable rule is 4 hours. You are under both right now, but if the fridge climbs further, rice is the first thing I would throw.

Also worth a closer look: any leftovers that are dense, starchy, or dairy-heavy (cream sauces, custards, soups with milk, cooked pasta with cream). These cool slowly and warm slowly — currently fine, but they're the next-most-risky tier after rice.

FROZEN — KEEP

If items are still hard or still show visible ice crystals, they stayed below about 32°F. At that temperature bacterial growth is essentially stopped. You can:

  – refreeze them (safe; quality loss only — expect some texture change on meat, bread, vegetables), or
  – cook them now and refrigerate the cooked result (best option for meat and seafood).

If any package is soft throughout with no ice crystals at all but still feels refrigerator-cold, treat it as refrigerated: keep it in the fridge now, cook within 24 hours, and do not refreeze raw meat or fish raw.

DISCARD TRIGGERS — the conditions that flip an item from "keep" to "throw"

  1. Cumulative time above 40°F exceeds 4 hours. The clock started during the outage and keeps running if the fridge cannot recover. At 41°F now you have roughly 1.5–2 hours of budget left before anything refrigerated becomes questionable; once it climbs to 45°F, that budget shrinks fast.
  2. Any food feels room-temperature to the touch, not just "cool." Touch is reliable for the inside of a sealed fridge.
  3. Ice crystals are gone from a frozen item AND that item is soft all the way through AND it has been above 40°F for any meaningful time.
  4. Liquid has pooled under raw meat, fish, or poultry packages in the fridge.
  5. Anything that smells off or looks slimy — but you already ruled out relying on smell as the primary check, and that's the right call for the borderline cases.

MONITORING FOR THE NEXT FEW HOURS

  – Put the thermometer on the middle shelf (it's usually the warmest spot) so the next reading reflects reality rather than the cold back wall.
  – Recheck at the 1-hour and 2-hour marks. If it is at or below 40°F by then, you are fully clear.
  – If it holds at 41–43°F, the items above are still safe, but plan to cook the rice and the dairy-heavy leftovers within 24 hours rather than treating them as week-of-meals.
  – If it climbs to 45°F or above, start the discard clock: anything raw (meat, fish, poultry, eggs in shell borderline, milk, soft cheese, cooked grains/starches) that has been above 40°F for a cumulative 4 hours goes out.

Three cases, three classifications. The sorting question at the front door is: who holds admin on the connected marketing tool, and can that person act today? The answer routes cleanly into one of the three below.

CASE 1 — User who can add a verified admin the same day
Classification: PENDING ELIGIBILITY (not route-out, not setup support)

Runbook wording:

  Trigger — Customer is the primary contact but is not yet a verified admin on the connected marketing tool, and can add one today.

  Action — Pend eligibility. Continue pre-workspace intake; do not create the workspace yet. Once the verified admin is added and admin proof is in, resume normal setup.

  Why — Admin proof is a pre-workspace gate. Holding until it clears is not a refusal; it keeps the workspace from being created with an unverified owner.

  Boundary — If the admin lives with an agency, IT, or a contractor and can't be added today, that is not this case — see Case 2.


CASE 2 — Agency administrator applying for a client's workspace
Classification: ROUTE-OUT (assisted setup)

Runbook wording:

  Trigger — Admin on the connected marketing tool is held by an outside agency. This covers both shapes: the agency is the applicant acting on behalf of a client, and the customer applying on behalf of a workspace where the agency holds tool-side admin.

  Action — Route to assisted setup. Name the person who holds admin on the connected tool — that is who must accept the workspace invite before workspace creation. The customer's team stays the primary contact on the account; the agency just holds tool-side admin.

  Why — Admin ownership must be clear from day one. Split ownership between workspace owner and tool admin is the support handoff this gate is designed to prevent. Assisted path is the practical route, not a penalty.

  Boundary — Do not create the workspace first and confirm agency admin later. "Set it up and have the agency step in once onboarded" is not a workaround — it produces the exact handoff we're trying to avoid. If the agency admin can be named and accept the invite today, proceed under the assisted path; if they can't, hold open, do not improvise.


CASE 3 — Admitted verified admin who only needs help connecting a supported integration
Classification: ADMITTED SETUP SUPPORT (not pending, not route-out)

Runbook wording:

  Trigger — Admin proof is in. Customer is an admitted verified admin asking for help connecting a supported integration in week 1.

  Action — Stay in self-serve setup. Help with the integration connection — docs-first, then a hand if they're stuck. This is ordinary setup support.

  Why — Eligibility is decided before setup. Once admin proof clears, supported-integration setup help is exactly what first-week HS support is for. It is not a refusal signal and does not count as a route-out or eligibility failure.

  Boundary — If the integration is not on the supported list, or the ask expands into migration, imports, manual billing, or unsupported permissions, that is a different conversation — flag it, do not conflate with this case. Setup support load tracks separately; do not let ordinary help reclassify as an eligibility failure.


THE LOAD-BEARING DISTINCTION

Do not collapse these three. The refusal boundaries stay intact when each case is held to its own trigger; they erode the moment an admitted admin's setup question is read as an eligibility question. CS rule of thumb: if admin proof is satisfied, the answer to "is this HS-eligible?" is already yes — what remains is setup, not screening.

One thing worth pulling into the runbook header above all three cases: the triage question itself, stated as the first line a CS rep reads on a routed-before-setup session. That keeps the three cases from re-lumping under pressure, since the sorting happens before the rep reaches the case-specific wording.

Two named beneficiaries on a brokerage beneficiary form. Plain-language explanation, kept neutral.

Per stirpes ("by the roots")
Each named beneficiary is treated as a separate branch. If a beneficiary dies before the account owner, that beneficiary's share passes to their own descendants (children, then grandchildren) and stays within that branch. The other named beneficiary's share is unaffected.

Per capita ("by the head")
The account is divided equally among the named beneficiaries who are alive when the account owner dies. If a beneficiary dies first, their share is reallocated to the surviving named beneficiary(ies). It does not pass to that beneficiary's children unless they are also named on the form.

Hypothetical for each (assume a 50/50 split between Beneficiary A and Beneficiary B):

Per stirpes:
Mom dies. Beneficiary A died two years earlier. A has two children.
  - Beneficiary B receives 50%.
  - A's two children split A's 50%, so each gets 25%.
  Result: B = 50%, A's kids = 25% each.

Per capita:
Same situation. Mom dies, A died two years earlier, A has two children.
  - Beneficiary B receives 100%.
  - A's children receive nothing, since they are not named on the form.
  Result: B = 100%, A's kids = 0.

The practical question this turns on:
Does she want a deceased beneficiary's share to stay in that family line (per stirpes), or pass entirely to the surviving named beneficiary (per capita)?

A third option to watch for:
Some forms offer a hybrid phrasing like "per capita at each generation." If she sees that on the form, it is worth pausing to ask the brokerage what it means in their specific document — it is not the same as either of the two above.

When to confirm with the brokerage or an estate attorney:
- If the form has its own definition, footnote, or asterisk for these terms. The form's wording controls, and brokerages sometimes use slightly different mechanics.
- If any named beneficiary is deceased, incapacitated, or a minor.
- If there are grandchildren, stepchildren, adopted children, or children from a prior relationship she wants included or excluded.
- If she has a will, trust, or other estate documents. The beneficiary form should be consistent with those, since beneficiary designations usually override a will for the named account.
- If she wants unequal percentages rather than an even split. Both methods still apply, but the math gets more layered.
- If she wants contingent or secondary beneficiaries named. The form's structure matters here.
- For tax consequences, blended family situations, special-needs planning, or any state-specific rules, an estate attorney is the right call.

I am staying neutral on which to choose. That is an estate-planning decision for her, and possibly her attorney, not a call I should make for her or frame as a recommendation.

Quick reading on the form before you tick a box:

The two options do different things if one of you dies before the person whose plan this is (parent? grandparent? — you didn't say whose document this is, and that matters for context).

Per stirpes — each beneficiary's share passes to that person's own descendants by representation. So if Riley predeceases, Riley's 50% flows down to Riley's children (split equally among them); if Marcus predeceases, Marcus's 50% flows to his children. The deceased beneficiary's line continues through their kids.

Per capita — the deceased beneficiary's share is simply re-pooled and divided equally among the *surviving* primary beneficiaries. So if Riley predeceases, Marcus takes the full 100%; if Marcus predeceases, Riley takes the full 100%. If both predecease, the contingent class kicks in (whatever is named after).

A few things I'd want to know before picking:

  Whose estate/plan is this? You've listed yourself and your brother as the two primary beneficiaries, which is the right shape if this is, say, a parent's life insurance or retirement-account beneficiary form, or a family trust. But it would be wrong shape if you're naming your own beneficiaries — you wouldn't be on your own form.

  Do either of you have children (or are likely to before this would ever pay out)? That's the decisive question for per stirpes vs per capita:
    - If yes to either side, and the intent is "keep the share in that branch of the family even if the named person dies first," pick per stirpes.
    - If neither side has kids and the intent is "just go to whichever of us is alive," pick per capita.

  Does the document define what happens if both primary beneficiaries predecease? That's the contingent beneficiary section, which usually follows the primary block — worth checking it's filled in, since per stirpes vs per capita only governs the primary class.

If you can tell me whose plan this is and whether either of you has kids, I'll point you at the right box. Otherwise the safer default for two adult siblings with no kids (or whose kids you're not trying to ring-fence) is per capita — simpler, and it does what most people mean when they name siblings 50/50.

1. The pending account is in the denominator but not in the numerator. Pending is an undecided future state, not a nonrenewal. Counting it as not-renewed silently pulls the rate down by ~2.4 points. 2. Expansion and contraction are folded into "renewed" without labeling. A logo-only readout should isolate who is still a customer versus who churned; scope changes (the +2 expansion, the -1 contraction) are a revenue-movement line, not part of the renewal-rate numerator. Mixing them makes the headline unreproducible — a reader can't tell whether 95% means "kept the logo" or "kept the logo or changed scope."

A few framing risks worth surfacing before this gets quoted as a headline:

1. Logo vs ARR-weighted. "Renewal rate 95%" is a logo metric. The 1 churned account and the 1 contraction could be large or small. Without dollar weighting you can't tell whether revenue was retained at ~95% or whether a single big contraction is masking meaningful net ARR erosion. If the pulse is for a board/leadership read, an ARR-weighted version should sit alongside the logo number (or replace it).

2. Pending is doing real work. 1 pending in a 42-account cohort moves the headline 2.38pp. Today the rate is 40/42 = 95.2%. If pending renews → 41/42 = 97.6%. If pending churns → still 40/42 = 95.2% (already in denom). The headline is therefore *floor-flavored* — it can't get worse from pending, but it can look meaningfully better. Worth saying "logo renewal rate 95%; 1 renewal pending (2.4pp at stake)."

3. Cohort size. n=42 is small. Q4 closed mid-segment was 384 accounts (89.7% active-admin / 82.4% no-active-admin per memory). On 42 accounts, 1 churn is 2.4pp; on 384, 1 churn is 0.26pp. The 95% is genuinely strong if the population is comparable, but the noise band on a 42-account pulse is wide enough that the rate should be quoted with the n attached, not as a clean point estimate.

4. Expansion/contraction mix. 2 expansions vs 1 contraction = +1 net expansion logo. If the read is "renewals are healthy," that's worth calling out separately rather than letting it hide inside "95%."

5. Comparison anchor. Memory shows Q4 closed mid-segment 89.7% (active-admin subset). If the March mid-segment definition is the same slice, 95% is a real jump worth explaining (timing? active-admin share? cohort composition?). If the definition is different (e.g., only accounts up for renewal in mid-March rather than the full mid-segment stock), the comparison is apples-to-oranges and shouldn't be drawn.

Suggested wording, if this is going outside the team:

  "March mid-segment renewal rate (logo): 40 of 42 accounts renewed = 95% (95.2%). 1 renewal pending; outcomes not yet reflected. 2 renewals included expansion, 1 included contraction. n=42 — single-account volatility is 2.4pp. ARR-weighted view not included in this pulse."

That preserves the headline, makes the pending and n visible, and leaves room to add the ARR-weighted version without re-litigating the number.

    - Audiences are nested, not parallel. Day-5's 594 = Day-2 non-completers minus suppressions. Day-9's 281 = Day-5 non-completers minus suppressions. Each later row is a more-stuck subgroup.
    - "Activated within 7 days of signup" is window-of-signup, not window-of-message. Some of the 326 in the Day-2 row activated after seeing the Day-5 send, which makes row-level attribution murky even descriptively.
    - Day-9 sits past the activation window, so its activated column is N/A by design.
    - Sanity check on the nesting: 326 (Day-2 activated) + 594 (still eligible for Day-5) = 920 (Day-2 eligible). Confirms the audiences are strictly nested as the notes imply.

  Headline pattern
    - Click rate drifts down with message number: 33.8% (Day-2) → 33.4% (Day-5) → 26.6% (Day-9).
    - Reply rate drifts up sharply: 2.2% → 5.2% → 16.2%.
    - Support-route rate drifts up even more sharply: 1.4% → 3.8% → 12.7%.
    - Activation rates per row look similar (40.2% vs 41.9%), but on different denominators that are progressively more stuck. Treating them as comparable is a trap.
    - Suppression share of eligible rises through the sequence: ~12% (Day-2) → ~15% (Day-5) → ~19% (Day-9). Likely cumulative unsubscribes / recent-support contacts accumulating as users sit longer in-funnel.

  What we can say
    - Engagement shape is stable at the top of the funnel and bends hard toward escalation at Day-9. The Day-9 audience is clicking less, replying more, and routing to support ~9x more often than Day-2 recipients.
    - That pattern argues for a different channel at Day-9 (CSM touch, in-app help, setup call offer) rather than another reminder email — but that's a design hypothesis, not a result.
    - Day-5's 41.9% activation on a more-stuck subgroup is descriptively notable (activation in the last 2 days of the window after a setup-help send), but without a holdout it is suggestive at best.

  What we cannot say from this table
    - Whether Day-2, Day-5, or Day-9 caused any activation lift.
    - Marginal effect of Day-5 on top of Day-2, or of Day-9 on top of Day-2+Day-5.
    - Whether the three-send sequence outperforms a single Day-2 send.
    - Whether Day-2 is doing work at all, or whether activation in that row is just the natural curve.

  If you want causal signal
    - A randomized holdout (or step-up randomization across the three sends) before any of this is treated as rollout evidence. Per the standing readout rules, this is mechanism-mix descriptive, not experiment-grade — and the Day-9 escalation shape is the thing worth a controlled read before changing treatment.

Practical effect of the four answers

1. Computers, bicycles, art supplies = personal property.

2. Theft away from the residence is covered on both quotes, with two qualifiers.
   It is subject to the policy terms (most policies apply a sublimit for off-premises theft, often a percentage of the personal-property cap, sometimes a category cap on bikes or electronics) and subject to the deductible. Net: a stolen bike from a trailhead or coffee shop is a claimable event on either quote, but the payout is reduced by the deductible and possibly by a sublimit that wasn't covered in the insurer's reply.

3. The replacement-cost quote does not pay replacement cost up front.
   The first payment is actual cash value (depreciated). The recoverable depreciation is held back and paid only after you buy a replacement and submit receipts. If you don't replace the item, you keep only the ACV portion. This is standard, but it means "replacement cost" is conditional on your replacement behavior, not automatic.

  Deductible:           $1,000 -> $500 (only matters when a claim is filed)
  Liability limit:      the cheaper quote's level (likely $100,000 to meet the portal minimum) -> $300,000
  Water-backup:         not included -> included

Subject: Helio Start setup — confirming admin ownership

INTERIM LIGHTING PLAN (Tue evening → Thu)

Primary rear light: clip-on backup, not the broken-bracket light. Mount on the seat post (best — stable, points rearward naturally) or clipped to a backpack strap if your bag is between you and traffic. Belt-loop clipping works for short hops but bounces on rough pavement.

Add a leash either way. Wrap a small rubber band or zip-tie through the clip and around the seat post or strap so if the clip pops off on a bump, the light doesn't go into the rear wheel or onto the road. A loose light bouncing into the spokes is a worse outcome than no light.

Redundancy: reflective vest you already own stays on. If you have a second small LED (front light, Knog, or even a steady-on phone in a jersey pocket) tuck it on as a backup so one failure doesn't leave you unlit.

Pre-ride check, every time, takes 30 seconds:
  - Tug the clip hard enough to simulate a bump
  - Walk around behind the bike and look — confirm it points rearward, not at the ground or sky
  - Check the angle again after the first 100 m of real road

Fallback: if the clip fails or you forget it, do not ride that leg in the dark. Transit, rideshare, or a lift — same pattern that's worked for you before. No dark commute is worth saving a 15-minute wait.

THURSDAY INSPECTION — REPAIR BRACKET vs REPLACE WHOLE LIGHT

Take the light off the bike and look at three things before talking to the shop:

1. The light body — housing, lens, switch feel.
2. The battery — full charge cycle after the cracked bracket was discovered; does it hold, flicker, or cut early.
3. The mount interface on the light itself — is the boss/slot that the clamp grips still intact, or is that part damaged too.

Repair the bracket only if all of these are true:
  - Housing and lens undamaged, switch positive
  - Battery holds a full charge normally
  - The light's mount interface is intact AND a replacement bracket/compatible aftermarket mount exists (bring the model number)
  - Bracket cost is clearly less than a comparable new light (rule of thumb: bracket under ~half the price of a new equivalent unit, or the light is high-end where replacement is expensive)

Replace the whole light if any of these are true:
  - Battery is aging — short runtime, flickering, or won't take a full charge. A new bracket on a dying battery just delays this conversation by a month.
  - Housing or lens is cracked, even if it still lights up. Water ingress will finish it.
  - The mount interface on the light is stripped, cracked, or deformed — no clamp will hold reliably no matter what you bolt on.
  - The light is a basic/cheap model and a replacement bracket costs nearly as much as a new one. Repair economics don't pencil out.
  - No compatible bracket is available for that model.

Quick frame to use at the shop: "Is the light the strong part or the weak part?" If the light is sound and only the clamp failed, spend $10–20 on a bracket/mount. If the light is the weak link — age, battery, housing, or a broken mount boss — put the bracket money toward a new unit and start fresh.
