This is a different location than the calf concerns you've been tracking, so I'll frame this for the lateral ankle specifically. The pattern — onset in the final mile with no twist, fall, pop, or sudden pain, weight-bearing normal, no visible swelling or bruising, 2/10 pain descending stairs — is reassuring but worth treating conservatively rather than pushing through.

CONSERVATIVE SELF-CARE (next 24 to 72 hours)

- Stop running today. Normal walking and stairs are fine; don't avoid stairs just because they twinge slightly.
- Ice 15 to 20 minutes on/off over the tender spot for the first 24 to 48 hours, especially after any activity that bothers it.
- Light compression: an ankle sleeve or a light ACE wrap if it's comfortable. Don't cinch it.
- Elevate when you're sitting.
- NSAIDs only if you need them for pain, and take them with food. They can mask the signal you're using to gate return-to-run.
- Avoid aggressive stretching. Passive inversion pulls (rolling the sole inward) on a hot lateral ankle can irritate the peroneals and the anterior talofibular ligament region. Skip the calf-and-ankble stretches today.
- Gentle pain-free mobility only: ankle alphabet (drawing letters with your big toe), circles both directions, slow controlled eversion and inversion through a small range.
- Hydrate and sleep. Both matter for soft-tissue recovery.
- Worth checking: new or recently changed shoes, a different surface today, or any camber/slope to the road. Lateral ankle aches in the final mile of an easy run often show up when one of those changes quietly compounded.

SHOULD YOU SKIP YOUR NEXT RUN

Yes. Today is a Step 0 day. Use the same stepwise protocol you've been using, but with ankle-appropriate gates between steps:

  Step 0  Walking only — pain-free walking and stairs (your current state
          qualifies, with stairs at 2/10 — keep monitoring; goal is 0/10
          on stairs before you move on).
  Step 1  Self-check the next morning before any run: single-leg balance
          on the right foot 3 x 30 seconds, 3 x 10 slow double-leg calf
          raises, and 3 x 10 controlled eversions against a light band
          — all pain-free. If any of those twinge, stay at Step 0.
  Step 2  Brisk 15 to 20 minute walk ending with 4 to 6 easy 30-second
          strides on flat soft surface.
  Step 3  Easy 1.5 to 2 miles at a noticeably slower pace, flat soft.
  Step 4  Easy 3 miles at the same conservative pace.
  Step 5  Resume your normal easy pace.

Advance only when each step is silent during the run and the next morning. If anything lights up at any step, drop back one step for at least a day and try again.

SIGNS THAT JUSTIFY PROMPT MEDICAL EVALUATION (within 24 to 48 hours, not "watch and wait")

  - Any swelling develops, especially rapid or asymmetric against the
    other ankle.
  - Any bruising or ecchymosis around the lateral malleolus, heel, or
    along the outer foot — even a small patch suggests a ligament
    fiber gave way even without a twist you noticed.
  - Inability to bear weight, or a new limp you're compensating for.
  - Pain at rest, not just on movement.
  - Pain that worsens over 3 to 5 days rather than improving with rest.
  - Pain above the lateral malleolus, up the fibula, or between the
    tibia and fibula — high ankle / syndesmotic concern, which behaves
    differently and is easy to miss early.
  - Numbness, tingling, or burning along the outer leg or top of the
    foot — peroneal nerve irritation.
  - Clicking, catching, locking, or a feeling of the ankle giving way.
  - Visible deformity.
  - Calf swelling, warmth, tenderness, or a palpable cord on the same
    side — DVT risk is low here, but the lateral ankle and calf share
    territory and any of those signs should be checked the same day.
  - Fever or any systemic symptoms.

Non-urgent but worth scheduling (clinic, not urgent care): soreness on stairs or single-leg balance that persists beyond 7 to 10 days, any recurrence on the first test run, or a second similar episode within a few weeks — that's the point where a podiatrist or sports-med clinician is more useful than another rest cycle.

If everything stays quiet, the typical return window for a Grade I lateral ankle irritation is 3 to 7 days, similar to the calf protocol. Worth logging shoes and surface so you have it if this recurs.

That plan tracks well. A few things worth adding, in case useful:

Quantify "well below four miles" — for a first walk-jog back, 1.5 to 2 miles total is plenty. A simple structure: 5 min easy walk warm-up, then 4–6 cycles of (1–2 min easy jog / 2 min walk), finishing with a few minutes walking to cool down. Jog pace should feel conversational — if you can't speak in short sentences, slow down. Flat, soft surface (track or grass) is easier on the ankle than pavement.

Don't run two days in a row to start. If Saturday's walk-jog is clean during the run and clean the next morning (Sunday), the natural next step is one continuous easy run of about 1.5–2 miles at a conversational pace — not jumping straight to 3 miles. Build to 3 only after that holds.

On the strength side, banded eversion and inversion are the right priority for a lateral ankle issue — that line of work targets the peroneals, which is where the original ache lived. Single-leg calf raises are fine to add later, but they're not the main limiter here, so don't rush them.

Two red flags I'd add to your list, because they're easy to miss:

  - any sense of "giving way" or a momentary catch of trust in the ankle, even without true mechanical instability
  - pain that doesn't fully settle within an hour or two after the run (mild soreness that lingers or worsens into the evening is a signal, not just post-workout fatigue)

If Saturday produces even a 1/10 ache that wasn't there before, or any of the above, drop back to another day or two of walking only and retry — don't push into it. If it's fully clean through Sunday, you're essentially back to baseline by next week.

Short answer: Mom does not owe the $185. The EOB's remark N20 means the post-procedure follow-up is bundled with another service on the same date — the insurer has determined it is not separately payable, and patient responsibility is $0. The provider's statement is wrong: there is no patient balance.

What's happening

The EOB says:
  Allowed $0 (bundled)
  Plan paid $0
  Patient responsibility $0
  N20 — "Service not payable with another service rendered on the same date"

The provider's statement shows:
  Insurance adjustment $0
  Patient balance $185
  Due May 23

The provider's "$0 insurance adjustment" actually matches the EOB's $0 allowed, so they correctly received the denial. Where they went wrong is assigning the full $185 to patient responsibility. Under the EOB, that $185 is the provider's bundled write-off, not a patient balance. Balance-billing a patient for a service the insurer has denied as bundled (N20) is not permitted under standard payer contracts.

How this is different from the $40 copay issue

The April dispute was a posting error (unapplied payment). This one is a billing-interpretation error: the provider is treating a bundled denial as patient-billable. Same response shape — don't pay, call billing, push for correction — but the lever is different. She will need to point specifically to remark N20 and ask for the line to be written off as bundled, not for a payment to be applied.

What Mom should do

1. Do not pay the $185 before the May 23 due date. There is still time.

2. Call provider billing, not the front desk. Have the EOB in front of her.

3. Roughly: "I'm calling about a statement dated May 13 showing a $185 patient balance for the post-procedure follow-up on [date]. Our insurer's EOB shows $0 allowed, $0 paid, and $0 patient responsibility, with remark code N20 — service not payable with another service rendered on the same date. That means this is a bundled service and the $185 should be written off as a contractual adjustment, not billed to the patient. Can you confirm you'll adjust the balance to $0 and send a corrected statement?"

4. Ask for the corrected statement in writing (portal message or letter) so there is a record.

5. If billing pushes back ("you owe this"), the next moves are:
   - Ask them to file a provider appeal with the insurer on the bundling edit. Until/unless that appeal is decided in their favor, the $185 is not a patient balance.
   - Ask which other service on the same date they believe the follow-up is bundled with — they'll need to justify keeping the line open if they want to pursue it.
   - If they still insist, ask them to put the dispute in writing with the contractual basis. Mom can also call the insurer to confirm the N20 reasoning and ask whether the patient has any appeal rights (on bundling edits, the appeal is usually provider-side).

Draft message she can send through the patient portal or as a letter:

  Re: Account [number], date of service [date of follow-up]. The statement dated May 13, 2024 shows a $185 patient balance for the post-procedure follow-up visit. Our insurer's EOB for this claim shows $0 allowed, $0 paid, and $0 patient responsibility, with remark code N20 — "Service not payable with another service rendered on the same date." This indicates the follow-up is bundled with the primary procedure on the same date and is not separately payable to the patient. Please adjust the balance to $0 as a bundled/contractual write-off and issue a corrected statement. Claim number [X]. Patient [Mom's name], DOB [X]. Thank you.

If you want, I can tighten that draft once you give me:
  - provider/clinic name
  - date of the follow-up (and ideally the date of the original procedure on the same day, if you have it)
  - claim number
  - Mom's name and DOB
  - insurer name

Timing note: May 23 is ten days out, so there is room. If the provider doesn't respond before then, Mom should not pay. The EOB governs patient responsibility. If the account goes into a pending status while the bundling dispute is worked out, that is the provider's problem to resolve, not hers — and the corrected statement should still arrive showing $0 due.

General rule of thumb you can apply right now (works for either episode):

  Pause payment if the statement balance does not equal (patient responsibility from EOB) minus (any copays or payments already made at or after the visit) minus (any patient payments already posted by the provider). Pay only the difference, and only after the statement reconciles to that math.

If the math doesn't reconcile, the safe move is to hold payment, ask the provider's billing office (not the front desk) for an itemized walk-through, and pay the corrected amount once they confirm in writing.

Checklist for the call or portal message to the provider (use this regardless of which episode, then fill in the numbers):

  Facts to have ready, in this order:
    1. Patient full name and date of birth on the account
    2. Date(s) of service on the statement
    3. Statement date and statement number / account number
    4. Insurer name, member ID, and claim number from the EOB
    5. EOB line items: billed, plan allowed, plan paid, patient responsibility
    6. Provider statement line items: facility/professional charges, contractual adjustment, insurance payment posted, patient responsibility, amount due
    7. Any payments already made (copay at check-in, prior patient payments) with date, method, and last 4 of card if relevant
    8. Portal balance, if it differs from the paper statement

  Questions to ask billing, in this order:
    1. Can you confirm the EOB payment of [insurer paid amount] has been posted to this account for [date of service]?
    2. If posted, on what date and under what reference number?
    3. If not posted, why, and what is the expected posting date?
    4. Can you walk me through how the amount due of [$X] was calculated from billed, allowed, insurer paid, and contractual adjustment?
    5. Is the $40 copay payment from [date] reflected on this statement? If not, where is it?
    6. Does the portal balance match the statement balance? If they differ, which is authoritative?
    7. Is there any prior balance, other service date, or separate claim rolled into this statement?
    8. Can you send a corrected itemized statement showing each line and the resulting patient balance?
    9. In writing (portal message or letter), can you confirm the corrected amount due before I pay?

  Things to record from the call:
    - Rep name, reference/ticket number, date and time of call
    - Exact figures they read back for each line item
    - Any commitment to issue a corrected statement and by when

  Do not pay the statement as-is if:
    - The insurer payment line shows $0.00 on the statement but the EOB shows the insurer paid
    - A copay or prior patient payment is missing from the statement
    - The portal balance and statement balance disagree
    - The amount due is greater than (EOB patient responsibility minus payments already made)

If you paste the current two documents' line items, I'll do the exact arithmetic, flag which lines disagree, and tell you whether the gap looks like a posting lag, a missing copay line, a contractual-adjustment misapplication, or something else — without claiming any specific cause I can't verify.

  - Gait changes — any limp, favoring, or shortened stride

  - Pain does not settle to baseline within ~10 minutes of stopping

    -   `EA-eligibility-loss` — locked out before exposure (churn / dropped out of retained-mid); stays in ITT denominator per the existing rule
    -   `EA-competing-event` — sales-led expansion conversation before exposure; not silently removed, per the existing rule
    -   Plus one guardrail label that rides on all 30 + reserve from launch through end of pilot: `EA-do-not-commercially-prompt`. This is the part that fixes Owen's specific concern. 3.  Where the guardrail label surfaces

    -   Reserve list randomized separately, reported separately

    -   No prompts being sent — this is design

    -   CS can still vary handling based on observed account attributes (size, segment, admin activity) within a wave. I don't have a code-execution tool exposed in this session, so I'll work the arithmetic by hand and double-check each line.

**Given**
- Sales (38 plates @ $19): $722.00
- Food cost (all 44 prepared plates): $244.80
- Incremental labor: 3 hours @ $28/hr loaded = $84.00
- Repeat-decision threshold: $450 contribution

**Arithmetic check**

Post-food contribution: $722.00 − $244.80 = $477.20 ✓
Post-labor contribution: $477.20 − $84.00 = $393.20 ✓

Gap to $450 threshold: $393.20 − $450 = −$56.80 (short by $56.80)

**Maximum labor the same sales/food cost can support**

$477.20 − $450 = $27.20 of labor
$27.20 ÷ $28/hr = 0.971 hr ≈ 58.3 minutes

So the same $477.20 food-contribution can carry only ~0.97 incremental hours, not the 3.0 hours actually used. The run is ~2.03 hours ($56.80) over the labor cap that the threshold would allow.

**The six unsold portions in view**

- 44 prepared, 38 sold, 6 unsold.
- Per-plate food cost = $244.80 ÷ 44 = $5.5636/plate.
- Sunk food cost in the 6 unsold plates = 6 × $5.5636 = $33.38.
- Those 6 portions also represent $6 × $19 = $114 of unrealized revenue.
- If they had sold at the same $19, post-labor would have been ($722 + $114) − $244.80 − $84 = $507.20 — clearing the $450 threshold by $57.20. So the threshold is reachable on this menu price, but only with full sell-through; at 38/44 it falls short.

**Food-cost contribution is not full profit**

$477.20 still has to absorb: the $84 incremental labor above, plus its share of fixed overhead (rent, utilities, base salaried labor, disposables beyond the recipe, etc.). Calling it "profit" would overstate the run by at minimum the labor gap and likely more.

**Verdict on repeat at unchanged parameters**

The completed run does not support an unchanged repeat against the $450 threshold.

- Post-labor contribution: $393.20
- Threshold: $450.00
- Shortfall: $56.80

The shortfall is fully explained by two factors, and either one alone could close it:
1. Sell-through. The 6 unsold plates represent $114 of forgone revenue at $33.38 of additional food cost — a $80.62 net contribution that would have pushed post-labor to $473.82 (above $450). Even selling 3 more plates ($57 sales, ~$16.69 food) would add ~$40.31 net and clear the bar.
2. Labor load. Three incremental hours at $28 are $84; the same food contribution only justifies ~$27 of labor (≈ 58 min) at the $450 bar. If a repeat can be done in ~1 hour of incremental staff time, it would clear the threshold on 38/44 sell-through.

A repeat is supportable if one of these is true going in: expected sell-through ≥ ~41/44, or incremental labor can be held to ~1 hour, or the menu price moves up (each $1 added to the price across the 38 sold plates adds $38 to post-labor, taking it to $431.20 at +$1 and $469.20 at +$2 — $469.20 clears $450). Leaving menu price and prep yield unchanged and expecting 38/44 again, three hours of labor is too much for the $450 bar.

Bottom line for the chef-owner: do not repeat unchanged. The repeat decision needs one of the three levers — tighter labor, fuller sell-through, or a modest price increase — to clear the $450 threshold.

Good timing on reserving the 2 Tbsp before the chicken goes in — that step is what keeps the glaze safe. Quick answers:

1. Safe internal temperature: 165°F (USDA standard for all poultry). Pull the thighs at 160–162°F and tent loosely; carryover heat will coast them to 165°F while the juices settle, which keeps the meat juicier than cooking straight to 165°F on the burner. If you're using an instant-read, it takes ~10 seconds; leave the door closed between checks.

2. Where to place the thermometer:
   - Bone-in thighs: probe into the thickest part of the thigh, alongside the bone but not touching it. A bone-touching reading will run high and mislead you. Slide the tip in from the side so it bypasses the bone entirely.
   - Boneless thighs: center of the thickest piece, about midway through.
   - Aim for the meatiest section — for thighs, that's the inner side near the body of the piece, not the thin tapered edge.

3. Avoiding contamination from the used marinade:
   - The reserved 2 Tbsp never touched raw chicken, so it's safe to brush on as-is during the last few minutes — exactly what Mom's recipe intends.
   - The marinade the chicken soaked in is now contaminated. Don't baste with it, don't pour it over the finished dish, and don't return a used brush to the reserved sauce.
   - Use one utensil/brush for the reserved clean sauce only, and a separate one if you handle the raw or used marinade. Wash hands, brush, and any plate that held the raw marinated chicken before they touch the cooked meat or the glaze.
   - If you want a saucier finish, you can pour the used marinade into a small saucepan and bring it to a full rolling boil for at least 1 minute (some sources say 3+ for thicker, sugar-loaded sauces) — but with Mom's recipe you already have the clean 2 Tbsp, so the boil step isn't necessary.

Below is a cautious next-week plan plus the three rule sets you asked for.

NEXT WEEK — THREE WALK-JOG SESSIONS, ~48 h APART, FLAT SOFT SURFACE

Session 1 — Tue 5/28
  Repeat today exactly: 24 min total, 2 walk / 1 easy jog for the first 12 min, then 1 walk / 1 easy jog for the second 12 min. ~10 min jogging, ~1.5–1.7 mi. Treat it as a confirmation run.

Session 2 — Thu 5/30
  Hold the 1:1 walk-jog ratio, extend total time to 26 min. ~13 min jogging, ~1.7–1.8 mi. Same easy pace.

Session 3 — Sat 6/1
  Extend to 28–30 min total, 1:1 walk-jog throughout. ~14–15 min jogging, ~1.9–2.1 mi. Still flat, still easy.

Rest days: pain-free walking or easy cycling is fine. No back-to-back run days. Each session is gated by the next-morning check.

The Sunday 5/26 morning check is what opens Tuesday. If Tue + Wed AM are silent, take Thu as planned; if Thu + Fri AM are silent, take Sat as planned. If all three are clean, the week after can start lengthening jog intervals (e.g., shift the second half to 1 walk / 2 jog) and work toward a continuous 1.5–2 mi easy jog by mid-to-late week 2. The jump from there to 4 continuous miles is still a separate, slower step — not a single leap.

REPEAT-A-LEVEL RULES
  - Any symptom during or after a session — even a 1/10 ache, mild tightness, or fatigue that lingers past 30 min — repeat the SAME session next time. Same time, same ratio, same pace. No advancement.
  - Only advance when BOTH the repeat run and the next-morning check are silent.
  - If two consecutive repeats both produce symptoms, step back to the previous easier level and hold there an extra cycle.
  - Never increase pace and distance in the same session — one variable at a time.

STOP RULES — DURING OR RIGHT AFTER A RUN
  Stop the session, walk home, and skip the next planned run if any of these appear:
  - Pain rises above mild, becomes sharp, or becomes focal
  - Gait changes — limping, shortened stride, guarded foot placement
  - Pain doesn't settle within 1–2 min of returning to walking
  - New swelling, warmth, or bruising around the ankle or lower leg
  - Instability, clicking, catching, or a sense of giving way
  - Pain at rest, or pain that wakes you overnight

  Treat the post-session window the same way. If something appears in the first 8–24 h after a run that wasn't there before, hold the next session and use only pain-free walking or easy cycling until the next-morning check is clean.

SEEK EVALUATION (RED FLAGS) — DON'T WAIT FOR THE NEXT SCHEDULED RUN
  Same-day or urgent care / ER as appropriate for any of these:
  - Visible swelling, redness, or warmth in the ankle or calf
  - Focal bony tenderness over a specific spot (medial or lateral malleolus, talus, navicular, fifth metatarsal base)
  - Bruising that wasn't there before
  - Inability to bear weight, true instability, or a sense the ankle is giving way
  - Pain at rest, or pain that is worsening rather than improving over 24–48 h
  - Calf pain with swelling, redness, or warmth — needs urgent assessment for a blood clot, not a wait-and-see
  - New mechanical symptom (locking, catching, persistent clicking) that wasn't there before the injury

  Non-emergency but worth scheduling, not grinding through:
  - Persistent mild symptoms across two consecutive sessions
  - Stuck repeating the same level for three weeks in a row
  - Any return of instability, even mild

Closing notes for this phase:
  - Keep every session on a flat, soft surface at the same easy jog pace until you've cleared the next-morning gate three times at a new level. Don't speed up while lengthening.
  - Today's ~10 min of jogging is the new floor — don't go below it on future sessions, only equal or above.
  - If sleep, hydration, or shoes slip, it's fine to repeat a level even with no symptoms.

SESAME-ALLERGY MEAL — JUNE 1 PRIVATE DINNER (20 guests)
For: Sam + chef-owner

BLUF
The garnish is the least of it. The standard entrée's glaze contains sesame oil, and sesame oil carries sesame protein. Removing only the toasted seeds does not make the entrée safe for a sesame-allergic guest. A conservative plan treats this as a fully separate meal from start to finish: different oil, different pan, different tools, different cook window, different plating hand, different server.

WHAT CANNOT BE GUARANTEED JUST BY LEAVING OFF THE GARNISH
- The chicken is glazed with sesame oil; removing seeds does nothing about the oil.
- Cross-contact from the same sheet pan, tongs, brush, sauce pot, or cutting board used for the regular batch.
- Cross-contact from any shared cooking surface that night (grill, flat-top, oven rack).
- Shared fryer oil, if sesame items have been fried in it earlier in service.
- Hand transfer from a server or expeditor who just handled the regular entrée or its platter.
- Aerosolized sesame protein from toasting seeds or hot sesame oil nearby during the allergy meal's cook.
- Plate or garnish residue: seed crumbs in a garnish bowl, on a wiped-down plate, on a cloth, on stacked plate bottoms.
- Every bottled ingredient being sesame-free without reading the label — some chili oils, hoisin blends, oyster sauce derivatives, "Asian" seasoning mixes, flavored salt rubs, and a small number of commercial soy sauces carry sesame or are made in shared facilities.

WHAT TO RECONFIRM WITH THE GUEST (call, ideally before prep day)
- Severity: is the allergy anaphylactic? Past reaction? Symptoms to watch for?
- Triggers: seed only, oil only, or both? Any cross-reactive triggers (mustard, other seeds, tree nuts)?
- EpiPen: do they carry one; will they have it at the table; are they comfortable with the kitchen's plan if it's used?
- Other allergens or restrictions, in case a second concern needs the same protocol.
- Walk them through what the kitchen will actually do (sub oil, separate pan, plated first); let them accept or pass.
- Confirm they want chef-owner to lead the prep, not a line cook.

WHAT TO RECONFIRM WITH THE CHEF-OWNER (before the menu is finalized)
- Willingness to prepare a fully separate allergen meal, not a modified standard entrée.
- Substitute oil agreed on (canola, grapeseed, or rice bran are neutral; olive oil is too flavor-forward for this glaze) and that the bottle is stored away from any sesame product.
- A dedicated set of tools available that night: cutting board, knife, sheet pan or sauté pan, tongs, small sauce pot, brush, probe thermometer, and a clean plating plate — none of them in the regular service rotation that evening.
- Timing: allergen meal cooked first, on cleaned equipment, while the line is calm and no sesame is in the air.
- Ingredient verification: chef-owner reads every label — soy sauce, any chili or finishing sauce, salt blends, spice rubs, even the brown sugar if it's a flavored blend.
- Plating and pass: who plates the allergy meal (chef-owner or designated lead), with a fresh glove change, on a plate wiped clean and not stacked near the regular plates.
- Service handoff: which server carries it, that they know the table and seat, and the symptoms-to-action plan (call chef-owner, call 911, do not move the guest).
- Whether the restaurant carries an unexpired EpiPen on premises; if not, the guest is the source.

PREP SEQUENCE
T-72h or earlier
- Guest reconfirmation call.
- Chef-owner walk-through; lock in sub oil and the dedicated equipment list.
- Menu-side substitution: same ginger-soy glaze, sesame oil swapped 1:1 for the agreed neutral oil in both the marinade and the reserved glaze; no seeds on the plate or in the sauce; finish with sliced scallions and a citrus wedge.

T-24h
- Ingredient pull from sealed stock where possible. Wipe down bottles.
- Confirm labels are sesame-free on every item that touches the plate.
- Pre-stage dedicated tools on a separate shelf or marked section of the line.
- Brief the front-of-house: which guest, which seat if known, who the allergen server is, what to say ("separate prep" is fine) and what not to volunteer.

Day-of pre-service
- Clean and sanitize the prep area, then cover with clean sheet pans or a dedicated board.
- Lay out the dedicated tools; chef-owner confirms visually before service starts.
- Make the allergy glaze in a clean pot with the substitute oil; reserve a portion for brushing.
- Prep the allergy chicken on the dedicated board; do not season or marinate alongside the regular batch.
- Label the allergy container clearly (colored tape, written lid, flagged hotel pan) — visible from across the line.

SERVICE SEQUENCE
Before the regular batch
- Cook the allergy chicken first, on cleaned equipment, while the line is calm.
- Probe to temp; rest on a clean plate; brush with the reserved allergy glaze.
- Plate: scallions and citrus, no seeds, on a wiped plate. No shared garnish bowls touch this plate.
- Plated by chef-owner or designated lead with a fresh glove change; ticket and plate flagged (colored pick or an "S" sticker); verbal handoff to the allergen server.

At pass and delivery
- Allergen server carries the plate directly to the table; minimizes handling other plates on the way.
- Server confirms the guest verbally before setting the plate.
- If anything feels off — wrong plate, glove slip, a question about prep — pull the plate and start over; do not serve.

During service
- If the guest shows a reaction: stop, call chef-owner, call 911, do not move the guest. Stay with them.
- Front-of-house has the guest's seat number and the chef-owner's name on a card at the pass.

POST-SERVICE
- Allergy pan, tools, and containers go through a separate wash cycle, not the same bus tub as the regular service.
- Debrief with Sam and chef-owner: did the guest flag anything? Was the timing right? Note for the next dinner in the summer run.

ONE-LINE SUMMARY FOR SAM
The garnish is the visible risk; the glaze and the cross-contact are the real ones. Separate oil, separate pan, separate cook window, separate hand, separate plate, separate server — that's the whole plan.

1. Outcomes I materially influenced in H1

On Helio Start, the March continuation decision held as a bounded operating plan because the evidence boundaries were framed up front: refusal rules were part of the decision, the connector-access check was a separate descriptive cohort rather than a routing claim, and post-admission support was kept distinct from connector-intake assistance. That framing is also why paid acquisition and a Q3 pipeline target were declined as separate questions rather than folded into the continuation answer. For the May evidence review, I wrote the decision worksheet and the opening so reviewers had a common shape to argue from without the framework becoming a centralized approval template. The August first beta read stayed a working session because the agenda was scoped to activation shape, support load, lifecycle risk, instrumentation confidence, and the keep-capped-vs-widen-later boundary rather than a launch readout.

2. Where my judgment changed the team's direction

I corrected the November framing when it started to drift toward GA, pricing-page exposure, or revenue credit — Helio Start's evidence at that point supported January readiness questions only, and that correction is the same reason the $24K Q1 envelope went to lifecycle QA and ops contractor capacity rather than a paid-acq reserve that would have inverted the agreed sequence. Inside the evidence itself, I separated the connector-access check from activation (descriptive cohort, its own denominators, not a routing claim) and kept post-admission support distinct from connector-intake assistance so support load would not get read as activation friction. And I held first-paid and day-90 retention as the gating evidence before any reconsideration of paid acquisition or pipeline — those questions did not move earlier just because activation was workable.

3. One operating edge to improve in H2

The edge I want to fix is upstream-of-the-audit discipline on two seams. Timestamp semantics — what an activation timestamp actually means and what window it bounds — should be on the table at framing time, not surfaced as an audit exception after the cohort is already built. Finance dependencies are the same shape: any Helio Start language that touches paid acquisition, pipeline, forecastable revenue, or a Sales-ready framing should be flagged at the proposal stage so it does not have to be unwound after the fact. Both are about catching the boundary at the front of the work rather than at the audit, and I expect that to make the next evidence review materially cleaner.

Diagnosis

The dashboard is double‑counting because it treats Helio Start events as a flat log and then groups by `state` without applying the event taxonomy Owen and Daniela agreed on. The taxonomy distinguishes:

  - provisional events (in‑flight signal — emitted while a submission is still pending a final routing)
  - final events (terminal routing — `final_admitted`, `final_assisted`, `final_ineligible`)

The reporting layer must be mutually exclusive on **final state per submission** (one row per applicant/workspace), with provisional events preserved as evidence but kept out of the headline counts. The mock is violating both rules:

  1. A‑117: 08:03 `provisional_pending` → 08:22 `final_assisted`. A‑117 has had its final routing for 19 minutes. The dashboard is currently including the 08:03 provisional row alongside the 08:22 final row and counting it as "pending." That is the original 3/19 reporting overlap — a provisional eligibility event shown next to a final route‑out, inflating the pending tile and risking double‑count of A‑117.
  2. A‑219: 10:01 `provisional_admitted` → 10:19 `final_ineligible`. A‑219's final state is `final_ineligible`. The dashboard is still showing the 10:01 provisional row as "admitted," which would (a) inflate the admitted count by 1, (b) put a non‑admitted submission into the admitted‑workspace denominator, and (c) violate the long‑standing guardrail that no workspace is admitted while its answer is No or Not sure (and a `final_ineligible` row is by definition not admitted).

In both cases the error is structural: the view is taking **every event** as a current‑state observation instead of taking the **latest final event per submission** as the current state. That is the same class of bug as the March 19 first‑live‑export overlap, and it is exactly the failure mode the instrumentation‑quality table was built to prevent.

Corrected aggregation logic (keep history, fix the view)

Two derived views, both built from the same untouched event log:

  1. `hs_current_state` (mutually exclusive, one row per submission)
     - Grain: one row per `submission_id` (A‑117, A‑204, A‑219, …).
     - Rule: take the row's terminal `final_*` event by timestamp; if no `final_*` exists, the submission is `provisional_pending` and is excluded from the current‑state headline tile (shown only in the intake‑support / exception view).
     - Output for the five mock rows:
       - A‑117 → `final_assisted` (the 08:22 event). The 08:03 `provisional_pending` does not assign current state.
       - A‑204 → `final_admitted` (the 09:14 event). No provisional precedes it; it is also the current state.
       - A‑219 → `final_ineligible` (the 10:19 event). The 10:01 `provisional_admitted` does not assign current state.

  2. `hs_event_audit` (preserves every event, used for instrumentation review)
     - Grain: one row per event, unchanged.
     - Columns: `submission_id`, `event_ts`, `event_type` (provisional/final), `state`, `lag_from_provisional_min` (for events that follow a provisional of the same submission).
     - This is the table Owen already owns per the 3/27 sprint and the 4/10 backfill; the dashboard should read from it for the "provisional events observed" exception tile, not from `hs_current_state`.

Headline tile rollups (apply `final_only = true`):

  - Admitted: 1 (A‑204). A‑219 is excluded — its `provisional_admitted` is not a `final_admitted` event.
  - Assisted: 1 (A‑117).
  - Ineligible: 1 (A‑219).
  - Total resolved: 3, mutually exclusive. No submission appears in more than one tile.

Exception / intake‑support view (do not delete the provisional events; surface them separately):

  - Provisional events observed: 2 (A‑117 08:03, A‑219 10:01).
  - Provisional→final same‑submission pairs: 2 (both pairs reconcile, both final states match the taxonomy: provisional `pending` → final `assisted`; provisional `admitted` → final `ineligible`).
  - Median lag provisional→final: 19 min (A‑117) and 18 min (A‑219).
  - These rows belong in the instrumentation‑quality / pre‑admission‑assistance cut, **not** in the admitted‑workspace support denominator and **not** in the activation numerator. That preserves the 3/19 acceptance test (mutually exclusive final states, provisionals visible in the audit table, admitted denominator untouched) and the 4/29 reporting spec (pre‑admission assistance in its own section, separated from admitted‑workspace support).

Caveats Owen should keep on the tile while the seven‑day activation window is still immature

  - The admitted count (1) is not yet an activation rate; the day‑7 window has not closed for any submission in this window. Do not publish an activation percentage from this export.
  - The exception view is descriptive, not causal — provisional→final pairs show event‑order evidence, not a conversion claim.
  - Pre‑admission assistance (the 2 provisional events, the assisted intake path) is reported separately from admitted‑workspace support and does not enter the admitted‑workspace support denominator.
  - No workspace was admitted while its answer was No or Not sure; A‑219's `final_ineligible` confirms that guardrail held.

Why this is the right fix (not just "remove the duplicate rows")

The duplicate rows are not a data‑entry error — they are a schema error in the dashboard query. Deleting or hiding the provisional events would lose the evidence Owen and Daniela explicitly preserved in the instrumentation‑quality table automation (3/27 sprint, 4/10 backfill, 5/20 closed‑cohort validation). The fix is to read current state from `hs_current_state` (final‑only, one row per submission) and keep the provisional events visible in `hs_event_audit` for the exception view, which is the structure the 3/19 acceptance test, the 3/29 retro rewrite, and the 4/29 reporting spec all already require.

  ───────────────────────── ──────────────── ─────────────────────────────────
  Chicken thighs            12 lb            13.2 lb (13 lb 3.2 oz)
  Soy sauce                 2.5 c            2.75 c  (2 c + 12 Tbsp / 660 mL)
  Brown sugar               1.25 c           1.375 c (1 c + 6 Tbsp  / 330 mL)
  Rice vinegar              0.75 c           0.825 c (~13 Tbsp + 1 tsp / 198 mL)

  Grated ginger             0.5 c            0.55 c  (8 Tbsp + 2 tsp + ½ tsp / 132 mL)

  garnish. It is NOT safe for the allergic guest under any circumstance.

  0.25 c soy sauce
  2 Tbsp brown sugar
  1 Tbsp rice vinegar

       Cover, refrigerate 2 hr.

  5. STORE both batches on different cooler shelves, in labeled Cambros,

COOK ORDER — allergen FIRST

  6. Re-sanitize allergen station. Hand-wash again. Stage dedicated

Calculations based on the June 1 delivery (standard batch only — the sealed allergy-safe 1.5 lb package is held aside as instructed):

STEP 1 — Expected cooked yield from 13.8 lb raw at 68%
  13.8 lb × 16 oz/lb = 220.8 oz raw
  220.8 oz × 0.68 = 150.144 oz cooked ≈ 9.384 lb cooked

STEP 2 — Target for 22 portions at 7 oz each
  22 × 7 oz = 154 oz cooked ≈ 9.625 lb cooked needed

STEP 3 — Shortfall
  Cooked shortfall: 154 − 150.144 = 3.856 oz cooked
  Portion shortfall: 3.856 oz ÷ 7 oz/portion ≈ 0.55 portions
  (Equivalently, 13.8 lb at 68% yields 21.45 portions, not 22.)

STEP 4 — Minimum additional raw chicken (standard batch only)
  Raw needed to replace the 3.856 oz cooked shortfall at 68% yield:
      3.856 oz ÷ 0.68 = 5.67 oz raw
      5.67 oz ÷ 16 oz/lb ≈ 0.35 lb raw

SUMMARY
  Standard-batch cooked yield:     150.1 oz (9.38 lb) → 21.45 portions
  Portion shortfall:               ~0.55 portions (≈ 3.9 oz cooked)
  Min. additional raw chicken:     ~5.7 oz raw (≈ 0.35 lb), outside the 1.5 lb allergy-safe package

Practical note: the 0.35 lb figure is the clean math minimum. Realistically you would round up to whatever the supplier will sell — if the smallest purchase increment is 1 lb raw, plan on ordering ~1 lb additional rather than 0.35 lb. And as flagged previously, the 68% yield assumption for chicken thighs is on the generous side — if actual yield comes in at 65%, the shortfall widens to about 1.6 portions and you'd want closer to ~0.55 lb additional raw.

Short answer: this is a soft, delayed signal — not an alarm — but it does mean you should not repeat today's 30-minute session yet and you should not push to longer continuous running. Wait for the next-morning gate (Sunday morning, 6/2) before deciding anything.

INTERPRETATION OF TODAY'S SESSION
- 30 min, ~12 min of easy jogging (≈20% jump in jogging volume from the 5/25 pain-free 24-min session).
- No pain during the session, no swelling, no limp, no instability, no focal tenderness, no bruising.
- A faint 1/10 outer-right-ankle ache appeared ~2 h later on first stairs, resolved within an hour.
- A delayed, transient, stair-only, sub-2/10 ache without any alarm sign reads as a load-tolerance signal, not an acute injury. It does, however, mean the ankle registered the new volume, so the right move is to consolidate, not to repeat or progress.

NEXT-MORNING GATE (Sun 6/2, on first steps and again 30 min later)
- GREEN — ankle fully at baseline: no pain, no stiffness, no swelling, no focal tenderness, stairs feel normal, the 1/10 outer-ankle awareness has not returned. → see branch below.
- YELLOW — faint outer-ankle awareness, mild morning stiffness that lasts >30 min, or the ankle simply feels "present" on stairs. → hold, do not jog today.
- RED — any alarm sign (swelling, bruising, focal bony tenderness, limp, instability, giving-way, pain at rest, or the 5/11-type ache returning with ordinary walking). → evaluation.

DECISION BY GATE
- GREEN → repeat a trimmed version of today, not the full 30 min. Two clean options, pick one:
    (a) 28 min: keep the structure, drop 2 min from the cool-down walk (4 jog + 2 walk × 3, with 5-min warm-up and 5-min cool-down).
    (b) 30 min with the jogging trimmed by ~1 min: 4 + 3 + 4 jog blocks separated by 2-min walks, 6-min warm-up and cool-down (≈11 min jogging).
  Do not progress to 32+ min continuous running until one of these is silent during the session AND clean on the next-morning check.
- YELLOW → step back to the 5/25 24-min session (the 2/1 then 1/1 pattern) for the next attempt. Re-try the 30-min level only after a clean 24-min repeat and a clean next morning.
- RED → arrange evaluation before any further jogging.

SYMPTOM AND RECURRENCE THRESHOLDS THAT SHOULD PROMPT EVALUATION
Stop self-managing and arrange a formal assessment if any of the following appear, even if each individual episode is mild:
- Any "alarm" finding on its own: visible swelling, bruising, focal bony tenderness over the lateral malleolus or peroneal tendons, limp, instability or giving-way, inability to bear weight, pain at rest, or pain that wakes you at night.
- Pain that occurs during the session rather than delayed afterward (suggests active tissue irritation, not just post-load soreness).
- Ache that persists >24 h, or recurs with ordinary walking or stairs the next day.
- Ache that intensifies session-to-session at the same load, or that requires you to alter gait.
- Two consecutive sessions at the same level produce a delayed ache — that pattern points to a load-tolerance mismatch worth formal assessment rather than another self-managed step-back.
- Three or more episodes of outer-ankle ache with running within ~6 weeks, even if each resolves quickly.
- New features: numbness, tingling, color change, or temperature change in the foot; pain that radiates up the lateral calf or into the heel/sinuses-of-the-foot region.

In short: today's session earned a hold and a next-morning check, not a repeat. Treat the 30-min level as gated — repeat only after a clean green morning, and step back to the 24-min session if the morning is yellow. Use the thresholds above as the line between "consolidate and self-manage" and "arrange an evaluation before longer continuous running."

For the corner where the lifted strip reaches about 1/8 inch into the mat opening, the key fact is that the wash itself is intact - so the pigment is fine. The lifted fibers are a surface texture issue, not a paint issue. Conservative handling:

1. Do not add water. A damp brush risks pulling the existing wash up with the fibers and disturbing pigment that is currently fine.
2. Do not press with a finger or tool. That crushes the loose fibers into the wash surface and tends to make the damage more visible, not less.
3. Use a clean, completely dry, soft mop or quill (a 1/2-inch or larger natural-hair brush). With very light pressure, stroke parallel to the lifted edge - in the direction the fibers were originally laid down - coaxing them back toward the paper. Do not stroke across the strip. Work under raking light so you can see what the fibers are doing.
4. A kneaded eraser, lightly dabbed (not rubbed) against the strip, can sometimes persuade fibers to settle. Try it first on the part that sits outside the mat opening, where any mistake is hidden.
5. Once matted to 8x10, a 1/8-inch corner intrusion reads as paper character rather than damage at normal viewing distance. If it still bothers you, shift the mat opening slightly so that corner sits under the mat, or rotate the sheet a hair when you register it.

The strip outside the 8x10 mat opening needs nothing - it will be hidden by the mat.

For future sheets, two refinements make tape removal much less likely to lift fibers:

A. Pull angle matters more than tape brand. Pull the tape back over itself at a very low angle - almost flat against the paper, not straight up. Support the sheet with your free hand near the line. Slow, steady tension. A 90-degree pull is what grabs fibers; a low-angle pull shears them free instead.

B. Consider skipping tape altogether for clean borders on 300 gsm sheets. Paint right to the edge, let the wash dry fully, then place a fresh #11 blade and a metal ruler along the intended border and trim. The cut edge is crisper than any tape line, and there is nothing to lift off. Reserve tape for situations where you need a hard mask mid-sheet (a sky line, a window edge) rather than a perimeter border.

If tape is unavoidable mid-sheet, burnish only the edge you intend to keep as the paint boundary; leave the outer edge of the tape unburnished so it lifts more freely. And always test the specific tape on a scrap of the same paper before committing a finished sheet.

NEAR-MISS → REMAINING-DINNER SERVICE PROTOCOL
Cause: garnish tray was placed adjacent to allergy plates at the pass; visual separation failed; Sam caught it before contact. No reaction, no known contact. The protocol held on prep; it broke on handoff. The fix keeps sesame garnish and allergy plates from ever sharing pass space, and locks the handoff with a single owner and a script.

For any number of allergy meals (1, 2, or more) — the count per dinner is reconfirmed at pre-service with the chef-owner.

PLATE PLACEMENT
  - Allergy plates go on a dedicated mat at one end of the pass, marked with a red boundary (chef-owner's call). Minimum 18 inches from any other plate, garnish, or hand traffic.
  - Toasted sesame garnish tray does not live at the pass. Garnish is added to standard plates at the standard garnish station, before they reach the pass. Allergy plates therefore never share pass real estate with sesame.
  - If garnish must briefly pass through the pass for any reason, it travels in a lidded container; lid stays on; container returns to the standard side immediately.
  - Allergy plates go down first, before any standard plate is set at the pass. The allergy plates are spaced ~4 inches apart so a server can lift one without brushing the other.
  - Allergy plates are delivered last within the course, so the server is not running two plate streams at once.

LABELS
  Three layers, all written or placed by Sam or the chef-owner only:
    1. Bright allergen pick in the protein — red, "ALLERGY — SESAME".
    2. Rim or under-plate label, visible to the server at pickup.
    3. Label on the pickup spot of the pass itself.
  Allergy plates arrive at the pass finished — no scallion, no citrus, no finishing sprinkle. The plate looks deliberately under-garnished next to the standard plates, so no one is tempted to "finish" it for visual consistency.
  Runners do not write, place, move, or replace any allergen label. If a label is missing or falls off, the plate does not leave the pass until Sam resets it.

WHO MAY GARNISH
  Sam (or the chef-owner, if Sam is off the line) is the only person who may touch, move, garnish, label, or hand off an allergy plate.
  Runners may not touch allergy plates for any reason — not to tidy, not to deliver, not to wipe the rim. If asked, the answer is "ask Sam."
  Standard plates are still garnished by runners, but at the standard garnish station, before they reach the pass. Garnish is never applied at the pass.
  Sam runs a 60-second pre-service reminder at the start of each remaining dinner with the line and runners: allergy zone location, runner hands-off rule, handoff script.

FINAL VERBAL HANDOFF
  Scripted, at the pass, server to Sam (or designated expo lead):
    Sam: "Allergy plate. Table [X]. Guest [Y]. Sesame. No garnish, no mods. Do not co-carry with another plate. Read it back."
    Server reads the same line back. If the server hesitates or paraphrases, Sam restates and waits for the verbatim read-back.
  Once read back, that server owns the plate from pass to table. No plate-to-plate handoff in the hallway. If the server is bumped or unsure mid-walk, the plate comes back to the pass and Sam walks it.
  The same server who took the read-back places the plate in front of the named guest. No final placement by a different server or runner.

PER-DINNER CHECKS
  Pre-service: Sam confirms the allergy count and guest names with the chef-owner; the dedicated mat and red boundary are in place before the first plate hits the pass.
  During service: Sam stays at or near the allergy zone until every allergy plate is out.
  Post-service: Sam debriefs with the chef-owner — what went right, what almost went wrong — even on a clean dinner. Same five-question debrief, every dinner.

If any part of this sequence can't be done at a given dinner (different line, different expo layout, Sam off), Sam and the chef-owner decide together whether to run the dinner with the protocol intact or reschedule. The protocol does not bend for convenience.

      - energy: stays alert/curious
      - breathing: easy at rest, not elevated

FOOD AND WATER HANDLING

  - Tonight: water as above, no food.
  - Tomorrow morning (7-9 AM), if no more vomiting and he looks normal: offer a small bland meal — plain boiled skinless chicken + plain white rice, in 1-2 tablespoon portions. Wait 60-90 minutes. URGENT VET — GO NOW (ER, do not wait for morning)

Any one of these:

  - Blood in vomit — red streaks, or coffee-ground appearance

  - Refusing water for more than 12 hours, or any signs of dehydration (skin tenting, dry gums)

  - Mild belly tenderness when you press gently
  - Any new symptom you're unsure about

PANCREATITIS WATCH — the 24-72 hour concern

Chicken skin is the classic trigger. Pancreatitis doesn't always show up the same night. Over the next 2-3 days, watch for:

  - Repeated vomiting (not just the one)
  - Hunched back or "praying position," guarding the belly
  - Refusing food completely
  - Severe lethargy
  - Diarrhea, especially if it looks greasy or yellow

If any of those emerge, don't wait — call the vet the same day. Pancreatitis is treatable but not something to monitor through at home.

  - Single vomit tonight, no more
  - Pink moist gums, soft belly, alert demeanor through the night
  - Keeps down small water sips
  - Eats and keeps down the morning bland meal
  - Normal stool within 24-36 hours
  - Energy and appetite normal by tomorrow afternoon

UPS watt rating - a small honest answer: residential UPS units don't really come in 40 W sizes; they come in standard VA/W buckets, and the smallest commonly sold units are:
  - 300 VA / 180 W
  - 450 VA / 280 W
  - 600 VA / 360 W

Any of those will run your 33-42 W load with massive headroom, which is what you want. A 300 VA / 180 W unit is the right pick here (smallest, cheapest, plenty of capacity for two wall-wart-class devices). Going to 450 VA gives you longer runtime on the same internal battery and more margin if you ever add a small switch or phone.

Watt-hour range for ~90 minutes:
At the design load of ~42 W, 90 min = 63 Wh drawn from the inverter. Accounting for ~85% inverter efficiency and ~50% usable depth on a lead-acid battery (the chemistry in basically every sub-1 kVA UPS), that's roughly:
  63 Wh / 0.85 / 0.50  ~  148 Wh of battery
  i.e. about a 12 V / 12 Ah internal pack.

At realistic actual draw (~20 W), the same UPS will run well over 2-3 hours on a 12 V / 7-9 Ah pack, so 90 min is an easy target.

Practical recommendation:
  - UPS size: 300 VA / 180 W (a 450 VA / 280 W is also fine and a touch roomier).
  - Look for a unit whose spec sheet lists a 12 V / 7-9 Ah internal battery; that gives ~60-80 Wh usable and ~90+ min at your real load.

No. One labor-compliant test with a one-portion yield loss is not enough evidence to propose another sale run. Sam should require a repeatability test first, for three independent reasons.

WHY ONE TEST IS INSUFFICIENT

1. Labor result is a single observation with a thin margin.
58 min vs the 60-min ceiling is roughly a 3% buffer. A single timed run cannot tell you whether the new method reliably hits the ceiling or merely happened to this time. The test was almost certainly run by Sam under favorable conditions; a real production cook will face service interruptions, timing pressure, and a different pair of hands. A second execution that lands at 64 min puts the whole proposal back to where it started. Better to confirm repeatability on labor BEFORE pitching the chef-owner, not after.

2. Yield moved the wrong direction, and one observation cannot diagnose why.

- This run: 19.1 cooked lb from 30 raw = 63.7% retention
- Chef-owner's expected: 68%

The revised method is producing 8 oz LESS cooked chicken than the old method. The "one-portion loss" is the visible symptom; the underlying signal is a yield drift that needs an explanation. Possibilities include longer marinade contact, altered tray geometry changing heat transfer, or just noise. One cook cannot separate those. Two more cooks will tell Sam whether 63.7% is the new normal or an outlier.

There is also a hard math consequence: at 63.7% retention, a 30-lb raw case mathematically cannot deliver 44 complete 7-oz portions — 44 × 7 = 308 oz cooked requires 30.2 lb raw, and that is before any safety margin. (b) A yield distribution across all three cooks. The chef-owner needs to see the proposal work at the yield the kitchen actually delivers, not the 68% that was originally assumed.

(c) A documented prep procedure — marinade pre-stage timing, tray sequence, oven temp/time — so the next cook follows a recipe rather than improvising from memory.

(d) Only then, a single sale run with a defined sell-through gate (e.g., "≥38 of 42 portions sold at $X clears the food-cost and labor test"). A real service is the only way to complete the evidence chain.

SEQUENCING
Kitchen repeatability → documented procedure → recalibrated portion and cost plan at actual yield → sale run with a sell-through gate. Smishing — the text is fraudulent. Here's the assessment and the safe path.

SCAM INDICATORS

- The math kills it first. Corrected statement = $0 due. Mom never paid the removed balance. There is no refund owed. A real refund notice would match a real credit on a real account; this one matches nothing.
- Unsolicited "refund ready" claim. Providers credit accounts or mail checks — they don't push bank-detail collection by SMS.
- Urgency cue ("today"). Classic pressure tactic.
- bit.ly short link to "confirm bank details." Legitimate providers never collect bank info through a shortened URL in a text. Real portals live on the provider's own domain.
- Generic sender ("Provider Billing"). No provider name, no account/visit/claim reference. Real billing messages identify the practice.
- "Reply STOP to opt out." A fake opt-out. Replying confirms the number is live and resells it to other scammers. Don't reply — even to stop.

VERIFICATION (provider's known channels only — never the text)

1. Don't tap the link. Don't reply. Don't delete yet.
2. Screenshot the full message, including the sender number and timestamp.
3. Verify independently using one of these — both come from outside the text:
   a. Provider's official patient portal. Log in the way Mom normally does (bookmarked site or app, not a link). Look for a "refunds," "credits," or "payments" section. Expected result: nothing pending.
   b. Provider's billing phone number printed on her actual paper statement or a previous legitimate bill/EOB. Ask: "Are you issuing me a $185 refund, or do you have any refund pending in my name?" Expected answer: no.
4. If the portal or the billing office confirms zero refund pending, the text is confirmed fraudulent. Nothing further is owed from Mom's side.

REPORTING

- Forward the screenshot/text to 7726 (SPAM). That's the carrier-side reporting shortcode used in the US.
- File at reportfraud.ftc.gov — category: impersonator / unsolicited refund text. Include the sender number, the bit.ly URL, and the $185 amount.
- Block the sender number on Mom's phone.
- Delete the message after the reports are filed.
- Optional but useful: tell Mom's carrier if she uses a carrier-branded spam-reporting tool (AT&T ActiveArmor, Verizon Call Filter, T-Mobile Scam Shield). It helps flag the same campaign for other subscribers on that number range.

WHAT MOM DOES NOT NEED TO DO

She didn't tap, didn't reply, didn't enter anything. So:
- No bank action. Nothing was disclosed.
- No password changes.
- No credit freeze or fraud alert — those are warranted only if personal or financial info was entered.
- No mobile scan or factory reset — nothing was downloaded.

A short note for next time, if useful: any future "refund," "delivery fee," "account suspension," or "verify your info" text — same protocol. Verify on the portal or call the number on the actual statement. Real providers don't collect bank or card details through SMS links.

Question

At what point does preferring the cleaner artifact stop being a private aesthetic choice and start being a quiet act of editing other people out — and is the brother, shouting beyond the frame, the first thing the narrator has decided not to hear?

Interpretive angle

The word "cleaner" is doing double work in this passage. It praises the photograph (quieter, sharper, easier to hold) and at the same time names exactly what's been removed: the mosquitoes, the sour bank, and a brother's voice. The narrator isn't failing to remember — the artifact is winning. The swap isn't neutral; it edits people out, not just sensations. So the deeper question isn't whether the narrator can still tell memory from photograph — it's what the cleanness was protecting them from, and what (or who) it cost.

A few things are probably stacking on top of each other: the orange is reading "pasted on" because the edge is too crisp and the chroma is too high next to your diluted shadow, and the mud risk is real because burnt sienna and ultramarine are near-complements — when they meet wet they optically mix into a muted brown right where you want the softest transition.

The fix is to break the meeting line into stages so the orange never sits directly against raw ultramarine.

Sequence:

  1.  Soften the warm-facing edge of the dry shadow wash before you add any color. Take a damp (not wet) brush — just water — and trace along the boundary where the rim will sit. Lift, don't scrub. You're feathering the pigment outward into a damp halo, then stop and let it dry. That gives you a pre-softened edge so the warm paint doesn't have to do all the softening itself.

  2.  Pre-tone the burnt sienna on the palette. Your scrap test is telling you the pure orange is too loud. Push the mixture toward coral, not toward red:

      -  2 parts burnt sienna
      -  1 small dab quinacridone rose
      -  enough water that it flows but still has body

      The rose is a violet-red rather than an orange, so it warms the sienna without pushing it deeper into the complement zone. Test again on scrap — same hue, about one step lower in chroma.

  3.  First warm glaze, wet-on-dry, only on the warm side of the line. Paint the rim on dry paper, staying just inside the warm half of the transition. Use a small brush and broken strokes rather than a continuous line — backlit Kibo's rim is fuzzy and discontinuous anyway, and broken strokes give you free soft edges. Let this dry completely.

  4.  Bridge glaze at the boundary only. Re-wet a thin strip right along the transition with clean water — a brush-width wide, no more. While it's damp (not puddling), drop in a touch of quinacridone rose, very thin. Rose is warm, but it's a violet-red that sits comfortably next to ultramarine's violet undertone. It bridges the two zones without neutralizing either. This is the layer that does most of the edge-softening work — it carries a little into the cool side and a little back into the warm side, and neither reads as mud because no burnt sienna is present in the meeting strip.

  5.  Optional second warm pass. Once everything is dry, deepen the rim with another very thin burnt sienna glaze — but only in the brightest part of the rim, not at the edge. The first pass already broke the hard line, so the second can go a bit stronger without looking pasted on.

What to leave alone:

  -  The deepest, most saturated part of the cool shadow. Don't glaze over it. The luminosity is the white paper glowing through transparent blue — anything you add on top costs you that glow.
  -  The brightest specular spot on the rim. Either leave it as paper or lift it now while the wash is dry; don't try to paint white over color.

If the first test still reads orange-on-blue rather than warm-rim-into-cool-shadow, the usual culprit is pigment load. Try the same sequence with about a third more water in the warm mix. Transparent warm over transparent cool reads as luminous; opaque warm over transparent cool always looks stuck on.

UPS Comparison — Cherrywood Modem + Wired AP

Load recap (from your labels):
  Modem:       12 V × 1.5 A  =  18.0 W
  AP injector: 48 V × 0.32 A =  15.4 W
  Combined label-max: ~33.4 W

Sizing
Both options have comfortable headroom on max wattage (33 W against 225 W or 450 W limits), so neither will overload or run hot. On sizing alone they both fit the load; Option B is just oversized, which is fine.

Runtime at your ~33 W load
Published numbers are at 30 W, so de-rate slightly for the extra 3 W:

  Option A:  ~45 min  (from published 50)
  Option B:  ~91 min  (from published 100)

That alone rules out Option A for a 90-minute target — even on day one, brand new, it falls 40+ minutes short. Only Option B is in the right ballpark, and only just.

Confidence in the published runtime
Treat the published figure as a best-case ceiling, not a guarantee. Real-world runtime is typically 65–80% of published because of:

  - Conversion loss: the inverter is ~85–90% efficient, so a 33 W load pulls ~37–39 W from the battery
  - Battery aging: SLA commonly drops to ~70–80% of original capacity by year 2, ~60% by year 3–4; lithium is better but still degrades
  - Temperature: a hot closet or cold garage both reduce usable capacity
  - State of charge: a UPS topped up minutes before an outage gives more runtime than one that has been float-cycling

Applied to your two options:

  Option B (100 min published):
    New, derated:    ~70–85 min
    Aged 2–3 yr:     ~55–70 min
    -> 90 min is plausible early in life with mild derating, but NOT guaranteed as the unit ages.

  Option A (50 min published):
    New, derated:    ~35–40 min
    Aged 2–3 yr:     ~25–30 min
    -> Cannot plausibly cover 90 min at any age.

Recommendation
Option B. It is the only one that plausibly supports 90 minutes, and only with modest margin — best fit for the stated target, not overkill.

Two practical notes:

  1. If 90 min must be reliable across the battery's life (not just month one), step up one more size (roughly 1000–1500 VA class). Same published-at-30 W number, larger battery, derated runtime stays above 90 min even at year 3.
  2. The user-replaceable battery on Option B is a real long-term win. Sealed non-replaceable (Option A) becomes e-waste when the cell dies, usually 3–5 years in. Option B can stay in service 7–10 years with a $20–40 battery swap.

If "good enough" means covering the typical outage (most are under 30 min) with cushion, Option B new is comfortably sufficient. If "good enough" means a true 90-minute floor across years of service, either plan on a year-3 battery swap for Option B or step up one size class.

Quick read on what happened, then the plan.

WHAT THIS EPISODE IS TELLING YOU

This is your second delayed lateral-ankle response after a jogging-volume increase. The first (6/1, 3x4 min jog, 12 min total) produced a faint 1/10 on stairs that faded within an hour. This one (3x5 min, 15 min total) produced a slightly stronger 2/10 that lingered about four hours on stairs. Same location, same ~2-hour delay, same "no pain during running" pattern, still no swelling, bruising, focal tenderness, limp, instability, or rest pain.

That picture (delayed lateral-ankle ache, worse on descending stairs, provoked by added load, no acute findings) most often reflects early peroneal tendon overload rather than a ligament or bone issue. The good news: nothing here suggests acute structural damage. The caution: the response is dose-dependent and trending upward, which means 15 min of continuous jogging is currently above your tendon's load tolerance, and adding more on top of it would likely keep producing these episodes or escalate them.

NEAR-TERM (NEXT 24-48 HOURS)

  - No jogging today or tomorrow.
  - Pain-free walking and easy cycling are fine; stop either if they reproduce the ache.
  - Gentle, pain-free mobility only: ankle circles, ankle alphabet, light eversion/inversion. No stretching, no foam-rolling the lateral ankle, no calf stretching yet.
  - Optional: ice 10-15 min after any activity that produces awareness; light sleeve if stairs feel irritable.
  - Re-check yourself tomorrow morning against the same closeout criteria you have been using: comfortable walking and stairs, ten pain-free double-leg calf raises, no swelling, no bruising, no focal tenderness, no instability, no rest pain.

NEXT-MORNING GATE (SUNDAY 6/16)

GREEN — ankle fully back to baseline, stairs clean, no morning awareness:
  Step back to your last SILENT session, not the failed progression. The cleanest recent reference is the 24-minute walk-jog format from 6/8 (alternating 1-2 min jogging with 1-2 min walking on the flat). Do not retry 3x5 min today and do not retry the 30-minute 3x4 min session either, since that one also produced a faint delayed stair ache. The 24-minute 1-2 min jog format is the volume your lateral ankle has actually tolerated cleanly.

YELLOW — faint outer-ankle awareness, mild stiffness on stairs, or any ache lasting more than ~30 minutes in the morning:
  Take another 24-48 hours off jogging, return to pain-free walking and easy cycling only, then re-check against the closeout criteria before attempting anything. Do not retry the 24-minute session until you have a clean GREEN morning.

RED — any of: new swelling, bruising, focal bony tenderness over the lateral malleolus or sinus tarsi, limp, instability, catch/giving-way, inability to bear weight, pain at rest, or an ache that does not fully resolve within 24-48 hours:
  Stop running and arrange a clinical evaluation before the next walk-jog. A physical therapist or sports-med clinician familiar with running can confirm whether this is peroneal tendinopathy, sinus tarsi irritation, or something else, and give you a graded loading program rather than one you are calibrating by feel alone.

HOW TO REBUILD MORE GRADUALLY (ONCE YOU HAVE A CLEAN GREEN)

The lesson from today is that a single jump from ~12 min to 15 min of total jogging was too steep. Smaller increments, held longer:

  1. Repeat the 24-minute 1-2 min jog format at least twice on separate days with a clean next-morning gate between each before changing anything.
  2. Add total jogging time in roughly 1-2 minute increments per week, not 3 minutes at once. For example: extend one jog interval from 2 to 3 minutes, hold for two clean sessions, then extend a second interval.
  3. Keep every session flat and easy pace until the new volume is silent during the run AND silent on stairs the next morning.
  4. Keep a simple log: total jogging minutes, any post-run stair awareness, and next-morning status. Two clean sessions at a new volume is your gate to the next bump; one symptomatic response means that volume is your current ceiling.

THRESHOLDS FOR CLINICAL EVALUATION (BEFORE THE NEXT PROGRESSION)

Arrange a formal evaluation, even if you feel "fine," if any of the following apply:

  - This lateral-ankle pattern recurs a third time after a progression, even at a lower dose. Two failed progressions with the same location and character is a meaningful signal that self-calibration is not enough.
  - The delayed ache lasts longer than the previous episode, or the intensity creeps above ~3/10, or it begins to appear during the run rather than only afterward.
  - Any new finding shows up: swelling, bruising, focal tenderness over the lateral malleolus, sinus tarsi, or peroneal tendons, a limp, a feeling of instability or giving-way, pain at rest, or pain that persists into the next day rather than resolving within hours.
  - You reach a point where the volume you can run without symptoms is so far below your goals that a structured rehab plan would clearly help more than another self-guided progression.

A sports physical therapist or sports-medicine physician can confirm the diagnosis, rule out anything that needs imaging, and give you a graded peroneal and lateral-ankle loading program (isometrics, slow heavy calf work, controlled eversion progressions) that usually lets runners return to their prior volume within a few weeks once the right dose is identified.

BOTTOM LINE FOR TOMORROW MORNING

  - If you wake up fully baseline: run the 24-minute walk-jog format, not 3x5 min.
  - If there is any stair awareness or lingering ache: another rest day, re-check Monday.
  - If anything new appears (swelling, focal tenderness, instability, rest pain, persistent ache): clinical evaluation before the next jog.

The 24-minute walk-jog is your current proven ceiling. Build from there in 1-2 minute increments, hold each new volume for two clean sessions, and bring in a clinician if this pattern repeats a third time or any alarm sign shows up.

A backrun that has dried into a concentrated bead is one of the easier marks to soften, because the pigment is sitting on the surface rather than soaked deep — but only if you go in lightly.

Before anything: confirm the paper is bone-dry, not just dry to touch. Press a clean tissue to the spot for a few seconds; any coolness means wait longer. Rewetting damp paper spreads the dark pigment into the surrounding sky, which is the opposite of what you want.

1. Test on a scrap of the same paper if you have one. A backrun on a fresh sheet behaves very differently from one on a sheet that already has washes.

2. Mask the roof and a margin of sky around the mark. A loose sheet of copy paper held flat over the painting, or low-tack tape along the roof edge, keeps a stray rinse from bleeding down into the wash below. The roof is the priority — it will catch any pigment you lift.

3. Use a small round brush, damp not wet. Shake or blot it so the bristles hold moisture without dripping. You want the bead to dissolve, not flood.

4. Lay the brush flat on the backrun for 3–5 seconds, lift straight off, blot the brush on a clean tissue, repeat with a freshly dampened brush. Each pass should pull a little less pigment. Stop when the mark is still visible but its edge has gone from a hard ring to a faint halo.

5. Do not rinse the area, do not flood, do not scrub. If you rewet the surrounding sky, the bead migrates into exactly the zone you said should stay airy.

If after two or three passes the bloom still reads hard, the practical move is to stop lifting and integrate. Two restrained options:

  - Local glaze only. Mix a very thin wash of the same pale ultramarine, diluted to barely-tinted water. With the sky bone-dry, lay one thin pass over the bloom and a small margin around it, feathering the edges so it blends into the surrounding wash. This pulls the mark's value up toward the sky rather than erasing it. One pass; do not rewet.

  - Reinterpret as a soft cloud edge or distant treeline. A faint, low-contrast smudge sitting just above a roof reads as atmosphere if its edges are soft and it has no hard ring. You can nudge it that direction by adding one slightly cooler, slightly larger wisp nearby, so the eye groups the backrun with the new shape rather than reading it as a mistake.

What to avoid: lifting through tape, kneaded eraser, palette knife, scrubbing, rewetting a wide area, glazing the whole sky to "match." The first three roughen or scar the surface; the last two undo the airy quality you're trying to keep.

If after the scrap test the mark doesn't respond to gentle lifting, leave it overnight and decide with fresh eyes. Backruns often look harder in the moment than they do the next morning.
