Setup and controlled runtime-test for the new 900 VA / 540 W UPS on the Cherrywood modem + wired AP only.

==========================================================================
1. INITIAL CHARGE (do this BEFORE any runtime test)
==========================================================================

Why first: SLA batteries ship partially charged and need a full conditioning charge for accurate runtime readings. Skipping this can understate real capacity by 15-30%.

- Plug the UPS into a wall outlet
- Connect NOTHING to its battery-backed outlets yet
- Leave it charging for at least 12 hours, ideally 24 hours
- Confirm "battery full" or 100% on the front panel before proceeding
- During charge: UPS may show ~80% for several hours near the end - that is normal absorption charging, not a fault

==========================================================================
2. PRE-TEST CHECKLIST - prevent accidental laptop connection
==========================================================================

The single biggest risk is plugging the wrong thing into the UPS and getting a misleading test (a laptop at 30-65 W would roughly double the load and cut runtime in half).

Cable routing:
- Use a dedicated, labeled power strip for the UPS outlets
- Plug ONLY the modem PSU and the AP injector PSU into that strip
- Run that strip's cables physically away from your laptop area
- Plug your laptop charger into a DIFFERENT wall outlet entirely - not the UPS, not the same strip

Before starting the test, look at the UPS load display and confirm it reads roughly 30-40 W (modem 18 W + AP injector 15.4 W, plus small inverter overhead). If it shows 60+ W, something extra is plugged in - stop and investigate.

Schedule the test:
- Pick a window with NO work calls (a weekend morning or evening is ideal)
- Tell Sam the network will go down briefly during the test
- Avoid peak heat if the UPS is in a warm spot - SLA capacity drops noticeably above ~30 C

==========================================================================
3. WHAT TO RECORD
==========================================================================

Keep a simple log (paper or note file). Record at minimum:

- Date and time you pull the wall plug (test start)
- UPS-reported load in watts (sanity check)
- UPS-reported estimated runtime (if displayed)
- Battery percentage at start (should be 100%)
- Time at each checkpoint (every 15 minutes is fine)
- Time of any audible alarm (low-battery warning)
- Battery percentage when you stop
- Ambient temperature near the UPS
- Wall plug reconnect time (test end)

Optional but useful:
- Voltage reading at the UPS input/output if it has a display
- Any LED state changes (some units flash or change color on battery)

==========================================================================
4. TEST SEQUENCE
==========================================================================

Step A - Full charge confirmed (from section 1)

Step B - With mains still connected, plug modem and AP into the UPS
         Verify network is working normally
         Record the steady-state wattage the UPS displays
         Confirm laptop is NOT on the UPS

Step C - Pull the wall plug to start the test
         Record exact start time
         Confirm modem and AP stay up (link lights steady, Wi-Fi SSID visible on phone)

Step D - Check at 15-minute intervals:
           - 15 min: still up? battery %?
           - 30 min: still up? battery %?
           - 45 min: still up? battery %?
           - 60 min: still up? battery %?
           - 75 min: still up? battery %?
         If at any point the low-battery alarm sounds, jump to Step E immediately.

Step E - STOP THE TEST. Do not run to auto-shutdown.
         Reconnect the wall plug
         Confirm network restored
         Record end time and final battery %

Step F - Recharge fully before any future use or second test
         (8-12 hours minimum)

==========================================================================
5. WHEN TO STOP - the stopping rule
==========================================================================

This is the most important part. Do NOT let the UPS auto-shut down on this first test. Reasons:
- A full deep discharge to cutoff stresses the SLA battery unnecessarily
- You lose the ability to observe what "low battery" looks like for future reference
- Aging units can fail to restart after a deep discharge

Stop the test in either of these conditions, whichever comes first:

a) The UPS low-battery alarm sounds
   - Most units beep steadily or flash when battery reaches ~20-30% remaining
   - This is the natural, safe stop signal

b) A planned time cutoff of 75-80 minutes
   - Your design target was ~90 minutes
   - Stopping at 75-80 minutes preserves battery health AND still validates that you meet the 90-min target with reasonable margin (new-battery runtime at 33-40 W load should be 85-95 minutes; if you reach 75-80 minutes still running, you have confirmed the target)
   - If the alarm fires before 75 minutes, the unit is underperforming - record that data point but stop anyway

c) Any abnormal behavior (clicking repeatedly, smell, hot casing, modem rebooting) - stop immediately regardless of timing

==========================================================================
6. INTERPRETING THE RESULTS
==========================================================================

After one full recharge post-test, here's how to read what you got:

Runtime reached | What it means
----------------|-------------------------------------------------
85-95 min       | Matches published spec, healthy new battery. You have the ~90 min target with margin.
70-85 min       | Normal new-unit result after derating (real-world 75-85% of published). Target met. Plan a battery replacement in 3-4 years.
55-70 min       | Underperforming but serviceable. Worth re-testing once after a full 24-hour charge to rule out incomplete initial conditioning. If still low, contact the seller.
< 55 min        | Defective unit or wrong load. Stop using as primary backup, contact manufacturer for warranty replacement.

Temperature note: if the room was warm (>28 C / 82 F), expect 5-10% less runtime than the same unit would deliver at 20-25 C. Not a defect, just chemistry.

==========================================================================
7. AFTER THE TEST
==========================================================================

- Recharge fully (8-12 hours) before relying on it for backup duty
- One characterization test like this is enough - don't repeat it
- For ongoing confidence, do a brief 5-minute "is-it-still-working" check quarterly: pull the plug, confirm modem+AP stay up, plug back in
- Note the test date on a label on the UPS so you know when the battery is aging (replace at year 3-4, or sooner if quarterly checks show shorter-than-expected runtime)

The point of this exercise is to know what you have on day one, not to wear the battery down confirming it. One good test, then leave it plugged in and mostly forget it until the quarterly check.

Here's a plan that follows the same conservative playbook you've used before, adapted for a superficial scrape rather than a thorn or burr.

CLEAN AND PROTECT TODAY

  - Rinse the pad with plain saline (or cool clean tap water) for 30-60 seconds. Gentle, low pressure.
  - Pat dry with a clean cloth. Don't rub; the skin is already abraded.
  - Check all four pads and the webbing between them in good light. Gravel, glass, and tiny thorns hide here.
  - Skip hydrogen peroxide, alcohol, and essential oils — they sting and slow healing.
  - No ointments unless a vet directs it. Many dogs lick them off, and some (Neosporin, etc.) irritate dogs.
  - If you want a barrier for the next walk, a thin smear of plain dog paw balm or a light breathable dog sock worn only outdoors and supervised is fine. Take it off at home so he doesn't chew it.
  - Right after cleaning, redirect with a food toy or a short scatter so he settles and stops re-licking.

SHORTEN WALKS

  - Yes. Today and tomorrow, cut to roughly a third to half the usual distance.
  - Stay on soft surfaces — grass, shaded dirt, the cool end of the lake trail. Skip the second outing or make it a brief sniff-walk.
  - Avoid pavement that's still warm to the back of your hand. June heat plus an open scrape is a bad combo.
  - Brief favoring in the first minute is fine; favoring that returns mid-walk or at the end means head home.

VET-CALL TRIGGERS

Call your regular vet if any of these appear:

  - Limping that lasts more than a few minutes, returns on tomorrow's walk, or gets worse instead of better.
  - Swelling, spreading redness, or warmth around the pad.
  - Discharge, odor, or crusting.
  - Bleeding that restarts or won't stop with gentle pressure within a couple of minutes.
  - A fragment surfacing in the wound that won't slide out with clean tweezers.
  - Yelping or pulling away when you touch the paw.
  - Nonstop licking that won't break with redirection.
  - Lethargy, reduced appetite, or fever.

Acceptable in the next 24-48 hours without a call:

  - Light licking for 30-60 minutes, then settles.
  - Brief favoring at the start of a walk, then normal gait.
  - Pad looks slightly pinker than usual but not red, swollen, or warm.
  - Normal eating, drinking, sleep, and mood.

Do a daylight recheck tomorrow before the walk. If the scrape looks smaller and drier, work back to normal distance over a day or two. If it's unchanged or any of the triggers above show up, place the call.

Setup before touching anything more

Work in a dry, ventilated room with a clean table. Put on nitrile gloves and an N95 mask — mold disturbance is the main health risk here, and your lungs are the priority over the prints. Have plain paper, a soft pencil, a phone or camera, and clean paper envelopes or glassine sleeves ready. Lay down a clean sheet of paper as a work surface; never set a photo directly on a kitchen counter where food residue lives.

First look, before any moves

Photograph every print in the box exactly as you found it, including the stuck cluster and the fuzzy edge spots. These phone photos are your "before" record — useful both for tracking loss and for any conservator you consult. Note which prints touch which.

Then sort by condition into three piles:

  Pile A — clean and dry (most of the box)
  Pile B — the six stuck glossy prints
  Pile C — the two prints with fuzzy edge spots

Keep each pile in its own paper enclosure and label them. Do not return any photo to the original cardboard box until you have decided what to do with the box itself — if it sat near the leak, it is probably a spore reservoir.

What "fuzzy spots" usually mean

Small fuzzy spots along the edges of prints that lived near a leak are almost certainly mold colonies. The question is whether they are active or inactive. Active mold looks soft, possibly colored (white, green, gray, black), and may feel damp or smell musty. Inactive mold looks dry, powdery, sometimes flaky, and does not smell. Even inactive mold sheds spores when disturbed, so the PPE and isolation are the same either way.

Do not brush, vacuum, wipe, or blow on the spots. Do not apply bleach, vinegar, alcohol, or any household cleaner. Any of these drives spores into the air and may permanently damage the emulsion.

Pile C — the two prints with fuzzy spots

If the spots are small, dry-looking, and confined to the edges, isolation alone is a reasonable short-term step: sleeve each print in clean glassine or a clean white paper envelope, label, and set aside. Do not try to clean them yourself. A photograph conservator can evaluate whether the colonies are active or dormant and what is happening to the paper and emulsion beneath them. For two prints, an in-person or mail-in evaluation is usually inexpensive relative to the irreplaceable value.

Pile B — the six stuck glossy prints

These need a conservator. Stuck photographs cannot be pulled apart dry — the gelatin emulsion will tear off one print and adhere to the other, destroying images on both sides. Professional separation methods (humidity chamber, controlled warming, sometimes solvents matched to the specific emulsion) require equipment and training that cannot be replicated at home. Your instinct not to pull them apart is the correct one.

While you wait to deliver them:

  - Keep them exactly as they are, stuck together, dry.
  - Store flat in a clean paper envelope labeled "stuck — do not separate."
  - Do not refrigerate or freeze them at this stage — freezing is a useful later transport step once a conservator advises it, but introducing fridge-moisture first can reactivate dormant mold.

Pile A — the rest of the box

Assuming they are dry to the touch with no visible fuzzy growth, handle with clean dry gloves, sleeve each in clean paper or glassine, and store in a dry room (below about 50 percent relative humidity if you have a hygrometer; a dehumidifier is fine in the room, not aimed at the prints). If any of them smell musty or feel cool or damp, treat them as suspect and isolate them too — mold can be present without visible spots. If you can, write the family notes you want preserved onto a separate index card rather than directly on the prints, since ballpoint or marker on old emulsions is fragile.

The original box

Once the photos are out, decide whether to discard the cardboard box or store it separately. Do not put clean photos back into a contaminated enclosure.

When a photograph conservator is strongly recommended (basically: here)

  - Any prints that are stuck together.
  - Any prints with fuzzy spots, even small ones, if these are family photographs you cannot replace.
  - Any print that is curling, buckling, has a tide line, or shows a white crystalline bloom on the surface.

How to find one

The American Institute for Conservation (culturalheritage.org) maintains a "Find a Conservator" directory with a photographs specialty filter. Many regional paper or photo conservators will do a free or low-cost initial phone or email review if you send clear photos of the condition. Mail-in evaluation is standard; expect a written condition report and a treatment estimate before any work is done. Ask specifically for a photo conservator rather than a general paper one — gelatin and silver-image chemistry have their own rules.

One short note for Mom, if you want one

"Thank you for trusting me with these — I'm going to have them properly looked at before I do anything to them, so we don't lose anything we can't get back." That lands cleanly and gives you the days a conservator may need without anyone feeling rushed.

If it would help, I can sketch the isolation workflow as a one-page printed checklist you can keep on the table while you work through the box.

Scaling 24 → 30 servings is a factor of 1.25.

SCALED PREP SHEET — 30 servings
- 15 English cucumbers (whole; clean number, +3 over the 24-batch)
- 1 quart (32 oz) plain yogurt — buy a single quart container; measure out 3 3/4 cups, hold back 1/4 cup
- 2 cups chopped herbs (1.875 cups scaled → round up; hold back 2 Tbsp for finishing)
- 3/4 cup + 3 Tbsp lemon juice (≈15/16 cup; hold back 1 Tbsp for finishing)
- 1/2 cup + 2 Tbsp olive oil (5/8 cup; hold back 1 Tbsp for finishing)
- 2 Tbsp + 1 1/2 tsp kosher salt (hold back the 1 1/2 tsp for finishing)

MIXING SEQUENCE
1. Cucumbers first. Halve lengthwise, scoop seeds if you want a drier salad (English cukes are usually fine seeded in), then slice. Aim for a uniform 1/4–3/8 inch thickness so dressing clings evenly. Toss the cut cucumbers with 1 tsp of the salt (2/3 of the scaled amount goes to the cukes; this draws out a little water and seasons the cucumbers directly, which is where most of the salt should land for a cucumber salad). Rest 10–15 min, then drain off any liquid that pools.
2. Build the dressing in a separate large bowl — not on the cucumbers yet. Whisk together: 3 3/4 cups yogurt, 3/4 cup + 2 Tbsp lemon juice, 1/2 cup + 1 Tbsp olive oil, and 1 Tbsp + 1 tsp salt. Whisk until smooth, then taste on a leaf of cucumber. Yogurt-based dressings read flat until they hit acid and salt; correct with the reserved 1 Tbsp lemon first, then salt if it still needs lift.
3. Add 1 7/8 cups herbs (reserve the last 2 Tbsp) to the dressing. Whisk again — herbs go into the dressing, not on top, so every slice is seasoned.
4. Combine. Add the drained cucumbers to the dressing and fold gently until every slice is coated. Do not dress and walk away — at 1.25× the original volume the cucumbers will release more water into the yogurt than at 24 servings, and the bowl can go soupy fast. Fold, then let it sit 2–3 minutes and look for pooling.
5. Final adjustment (this is the part the reserves are for):
   - If the bowl looks wet at the bottom: stop. Don't add more dressing. Either drain briefly or fold in a handful of extra sliced cucumber.
   - If it looks tight/dry or the yogurt tastes flat: add the reserved 1/4 cup yogurt in splashes until it loosens.
   - If it tastes flat or one-note: add the reserved 1 Tbsp lemon a little at a time.
   - If the cucumbers taste under-seasoned: add the reserved 1 1/2 tsp salt, sprinkled across the surface, then fold once more.
   - Stir in the reserved 2 Tbsp herbs at the very end so they read bright and green on the plate.
6. Hold cold. Cover and refrigerate until service. Give one final fold right before plating so the dressing hasn't all settled to the bottom of the bowl.

A note on why the reserves are split this way: salt mostly belongs on the cucumbers (step 1), not in the dressing — at 30 servings an over-salted yogurt base will read harsh on the finished plate even after dilution. Holding the lemon and oil back as finishing reserves means the last adjustment happens on the actual dressed salad, not in the bowl, which is the only place you can really judge it.

Short answer: **yes, this supports trying the repair first** — the diagnostics all line up with the failure mode the repair targets, and the contractor has put a real backstop on the table.

Why the diagnostics point to the repair

- An 18°F supply-to-return split is the textbook target (commonly 16–20°F on a properly charged system in cooling mode). Combined with normal compressor amperage and no detected refrigerant leak, the sealed system and compressor are behaving normally right now. That's not consistent with a bad compressor, low charge, or a metering-device failure — which are the things a replacement would actually fix.
- The two parts called out — a capacitor out of spec and a pitted contactor — are the classic cause of exactly the symptom described: intermittent shutdown under heat load, then a restart that holds. A weak capacitor drops torque under high head pressure (hot afternoons), and a pitted contactor causes voltage drop and chattering at the same moment. Both are wear items, not system-end failures.
- The 30-day credit is the key. It ties the two options together in a way that lets Mom capture most of the value of the repair *and* the optionality of the replacement. Worst case if the same fault recurs, she pays roughly the labor/diagnostic portion only and goes straight to replacement — she isn't punished for trying.

The material risk that remains

The repair only addresses the two parts that were measured and visually flagged. It does **not** address what else might be aging inside an 11-year-old system. The honest residual risks are:

1. **A different next failure, not the same one.** The credit is explicitly conditioned on "the same intermittent shutdown" recurring. If a different component fails within 30 days — say the condenser fan motor, the reversing valve if it's a heat pump, the TXV, or a relay — Mom eats the $468 and still faces the replacement decision. That risk is small but real, and it's the part contractors don't usually volunteer.
2. **The contactor pit was a symptom of something.** Pitted contacts usually mean the contactor has been arcing — sometimes just from age and load cycling, sometimes because the capacitor was weak and forcing the contactor to make/break under loaded conditions. With a new capacitor *and* a new contactor installed together, this is unlikely to recur, but it's worth asking the technician directly whether the pit pattern suggests a one-time event or a chronic condition.
3. **Short warranty horizon on a 11-year-old system.** A 90-day labor warranty means that if anything related to the repair workmanship surfaces after day 90, it's on Mom. On a system this age, the expected next failure (independently of this repair) is probably 1–3 years out. So the repair is best understood as "buy 1–3 years of runway at $468," not as a fix that returns the system to like-new reliability.
4. **No refrigerant leak detected is not the same as no leak.** Detection at one visit with electronic sniffer or soap doesn't rule out a slow leak that won't show until the system runs hard for hours. If the same shutdown recurs and the cause turns out to be low charge rather than the capacitor/contactor, the credit still applies (same symptom), but Mom should know that's a possibility.

Questions worth asking before authorizing the repair (so the backstop is enforceable)

- Get the 30-day credit **in writing on the invoice**, with the exact wording "same intermittent shutdown" defined — and ask whether credit applies if a *different* failure surfaces in that window.
- Ask whether the new capacitor and contactor are name-brand with the rated microfarad and voltage on the invoice (so warranty paperwork is unambiguous).
- Ask the technician point-blank whether the contactor pit pattern looked like age-only or like the capacitor was forcing it. His answer tells you whether the repair is two independent fixes or one cause-and-effect fix.

Bottom line for Mom

The math is straightforward: $468 buys a targeted fix with a credible diagnostic basis and a contractor-backed credit if the symptom returns. $9,240 buys a sealed-system reset with long warranty coverage but addresses problems the technician did not actually find. The repair is the rational first move. The replacement becomes the right call only if (a) the same shutdown recurs inside 30 days and she uses the credit, or (b) she decides that on an 11-year-old system she'd rather pay now to avoid an unscheduled failure on a 95° afternoon next summer — which is a peace-of-mind choice, not a diagnostic one.

Short answer: no — not as a way to reach the 90-minute target. There's a narrow scenario where the exchange isn't actively harmful, but it doesn't move you any closer to 90 minutes. The refund is the defensible choice.

Why the exchange doesn't help:

1.  The manufacturer just told you, in effect, that 73 minutes at 31 W is inside their acceptable range for this model. That concedes the published ~100-minute figure is a ceiling, not a guarantee. A replacement is drawn from the same population as the unit you already have, so there's no reason to expect it to do materially better in your test conditions — and no recourse if it doesn't.

2.  The problem isn't this specific unit, it's the product class. From the earlier analysis, this size UPS realistically delivers 65–80% of published runtime when new (inverter conversion loss + the headroom manufacturers bake into their charts), so even a "good" unit of this same model lands around 70–85 minutes, not 90. An exchange rolls the dice inside a distribution whose mean is below your target.

3.  If you take the exchange and the replacement also comes in at ~73 minutes, you have no leverage for a second return — the manufacturer has already pre-declared that outcome acceptable. And if you can't re-test before the return window closes, you're stuck with a unit you've now learned cannot meet your requirement.

The only scenarios where the exchange is defensible:
    - You genuinely can't use the refund (store credit you can't route elsewhere) AND you've already decided to accept ~70 minutes as the real target.
    - You're going to size up regardless, and just want a free spare while you wait — knowing the spare is a ~70-minute unit, not a 90-minute one.
    - You can re-test the replacement within the return window and have a fallback purchase ready if it also misses.

What I'd actually do:
    - Take the refund with the prepaid label.
    - Then either size up to a 1000–1500 VA class unit (published 130–140 min at 30 W de-rates to 90+ min real-world for the first couple of years), or explicitly downgrade the requirement to ~70 minutes and keep whatever you buy with eyes open about what it will actually deliver.

The one thing the exchange definitely is not: a path to a reliable 90 minutes on this product.

Short answer:
1. The repeated-hop result does not yet meet the clinician's gate.
2. Easy cycling is still reasonable.

Why the hop result doesn't clear the gate yet

The clinician's condition was specifically that stair descent AND repeated single-leg hops be pain-free for at least 48 hours. Walking and stairs are clean — three days running. The hop result is the part that fails: two pain-free reps and a reproducible faint 1/10 on the third. "Repeated" doesn't mean only the first rep — it means the tendon has to tolerate repeated loading without symptoms. Reproducibility is actually more informative than a one-off twinge, because it shows the tendon is reacting at a load threshold below what the gate allows.

That said, this is not a setback in any concerning sense. Faint 1/10, no swelling, no instability, no pain at rest, walking and stairs all clean — that's a tendon that is load-sensitive but not injured. You are learning where the threshold sits, which is exactly what the test is for.

Easy cycling

Yes, still reasonable. The 25-minute ride was pain-free during the ride and the following morning — both checks the clinician asked for. Stay at easy pace, flat terrain, no hills or out-of-saddle efforts, and keep applying the same gating: pain-free during and pain-free the next morning, otherwise back off.

Running

Wait for the July 2 PT intake. Three reasons:
- The hop test is the gate the clinician set, and it isn't clearing yet. Running on top of a gate that's failing is inconsistent with the medical advice.
- Running is a higher cumulative peroneal/tendon load than single-leg hops in several respects (rebound forces, sustained stance, fatigue). If three hops reproduce a faint ache, a 20-minute jog is more likely to reproduce or escalate it.
- PT is in three days. The cost of waiting is small; the value of a clinician re-testing the hop, watching your mechanics, and giving you a graded return-to-run plan is high.

Between now and 7/2

- Keep walking, stairs, and easy cycling as currently tolerated.
- Continue the rehab you've been doing within pain-free range — ankle circles, slow double-leg calf raises, banded eversion/inversion.
- Avoid the things that load the peroneal tendon: lateral moves, single-leg hopping, jumping, hills, uneven ground.
- I'd stop re-testing the hops every day. Re-testing can re-irritate the tendon and effectively resets the 48-hour clock. If you want a data point, one more check Tuesday or Wednesday is fine; it's not necessary, because the PT will test on 7/2.
- Keep the red-flag list in mind: any swelling, bruising, limp, instability, pain at rest, or pain during ordinary walking = call the clinic rather than wait for PT.

The reversible test that gives you the most honest preview is an actual 8x10 mat laid on top of the painting. Buy or borrow a pre-cut 8x10 mat with a window — a standard off-the-shelf mat is fine, you are not committing it yet. Set the painting flat, lay the mat on it, and step back. A good fallback if you do not have a mat handy: cut four L-shaped strips of card stock or mat board to frame an 8x10 window and slide them around on the painting. Same idea, easier to source.

The conservator's findings put you in a favorable window, not a desperate one. The detail that matters most is "early and contained" — adhesion only at corners, mold only at edges, no image-layer loss yet. That is exactly the state where professional treatment has the lowest risk and the highest chance of clean results, and it is also exactly the state that quietly degrades if you wait.

Here is the concrete risk balance for the two groups:

  Six stuck glossy prints
    - Bonding is currently limited to corners. That is the least-damaged stage of emulsion-to-emulsion adhesion and the easiest stage to reverse. The longer they sit, the more surface area is likely to bond, and the more likely separation will pull image layer with it.
    - Professional humidification in a controlled chamber is a standard photograph-conservation technique. The expected failure modes are minor — slight cockling after separation, occasionally a faint tide-line — and the conservator will already plan for flattening and post-treatment drying. The reason this is in a conservator's hands and not yours is precisely because the variables (humidity ramp time, dwell, separation mechanics) are tuned per print.
    - Deferring doesn't preserve the prints as-is. It just lets the bond strengthen and the eventual separation become riskier.

  Two fuzzy-edge prints
    - "Localized surface mold, not spread into central images" means the colonies are on the binder or surface coating, not yet digesting the image. Surface mold at the edge is the most treatable stage.
    - Treatment here is mechanical/chemical under microscope — the conservator will not be rubbing the print. Stabilization consolidates what's there and stops further growth.
    - The non-treatment path is not "leave it dormant." Even currently inactive mold reactivates with humidity swings, and once it reaches the gelatin binder it can pit the image layer in a way no later treatment can undo.

The asymmetry is the part worth holding onto: treatment risk is bounded and known; non-treatment risk grows over time and is currently zero-day reversible. The earlier you treat, the smaller both the cost and the consequence.

The decision the three of you actually need to make is narrow:

  1. Approve the bundled $420 treatment (humidification + separation for the six, surface treatment + stabilization for the two) at the conservator's shop, with a 4–5 week turnaround, OR
  2. Defer treatment and continue isolation, accepting that conditions will worsen and the eventual treatment will be either more expensive, more invasive, or both.

There is no third option that preserves the prints unchanged. Inaction is also a choice, and it has a cost.

For the conversation with Marcus specifically, the condition summary he needs is short:

  - Eight prints affected, no others at risk from these.
  - Six stuck glossy: bonded at corners only, no image loss yet. Treatment = humidification + separation. Reversible now; less reversible later.
  - Two fuzzy-edge: localized surface mold, contained at edges, central images intact. Treatment = surface treatment + stabilization.
  - Combined fixed estimate $420 ($95 assessment already credited). Turnaround 4–5 weeks.
  - Conservator's recommendation: treat now.

If Marcus's instinct is to ask "what if we wait," the honest answer is: you can wait, but every month the window narrows. Adhesion strengthens, mold can spread, and a print that separates cleanly today may not in a year. The $420 is buying the early-stage window, not just the procedure.

If his instinct is to ask whether treatment is necessary at all, the answer is that neither condition is cosmetic — both are active deterioration, and both are progressing slowly even in isolation.

Things to confirm together, since three of you are deciding:

  - The $420 is acceptable to all three.
  - No one objects to the prints being out of the house for 4–5 weeks.
  - No one wants a second opinion before authorizing — reasonable if anyone does, but the assessment was already in-person and the findings are concrete.
  - Post-treatment storage (sleeves, RH, flat files) is something the conservator will likely recommend at pickup. Worth deciding now whether Marcus wants to be looped in on that or whether you and Mom will handle it.

One thing to keep explicit among the three of you: there is no safe home-DIY path between where you are and the conservator's shop. Anything you could safely do at home, you have already done — isolation, no pulling, no cleaning, no moisture. The next step either is professional treatment or is choosing to defer professional treatment. There is no middle move that reduces risk without professional work.

Bottom line: use the indoor ride this Friday, not the commute. The commute isn't unsafe on its own, but it's the wrong setting to discover how your ankle handles the new loading exercises plus cycling on the same day.

Why indoor this week

  Three reasons, in order of weight:
  
  1. Same-day test not yet run. You haven't done the loading exercises and cycling back-to-back. Indoor lets you run that experiment with a kill switch — resistance down, feet on the floor, done. The commute has no kill switch that doesn't cost you the rest of the day.
  2. The commute stacks variables you don't control. Two short rises are not nothing for a peroneal tendon recovering from irritation — even a short rise loads plantarflexion and eversion more than flats. Wind, traffic stops, and a 50-minute total (there and back) double the dose compared to one indoor session. Indoor keeps resistance and duration constant.
  3. Your own framing. "Preserve pain-free cycling, not turn the commute into a running substitute I have to complete" is the right instinct. Indoor lets you preserve; the commute risks turning Friday into something you white-knuckle through because work is on the other end.

During-session rule (apply Friday on the indoor ride)

  Start at the same easy effort as the prior pain-free ride. Then watch for three signals in this order:
  
  - Any ankle awareness — a sense of "it's there," a faint warmth behind the lateral malleolus, anything that isn't true silence. Stop the interval, drop resistance, pedal easy. If it doesn't clear in 60 seconds, end the session and switch to walking or rest.
  - Effort creep. If your breathing leaves conversational, you're no longer doing the test that earned you the green light. Back off until it's easy again. The rule is pain-free cycling, not a workout.
  - Pushing to "finish." If you find yourself rationalizing the last five minutes because the timer is running, that is the running-substitute mindset you're trying to avoid. Stop.

  Document the session in two lines: duration, perceived effort, any awareness (yes/no, where). That's what the next-morning check references.

Next-morning rule (Saturday, this is the gate that matters)

  Do a real test, not a passive "I woke up and felt fine."

  - Baseline on all three + loading exercises yesterday felt normal = you may repeat the same indoor ride (same duration, same resistance, not more). No commute yet.
  - Any one of the three off-baseline = rest day. Pain-free walking only. No indoor ride, no commute. The next session begins only after a symptom-free repeat of Friday's session plus a clean next-morning check.
  - Worse than baseline, or any swelling, instability, or pain at rest = stop the experiment and call the PT office about the referral already on the calendar.

  - One clean same-day loading-plus-indoor ride session, with a clean next-morning check.
  - A second clean repeat at the same dose, with another clean next-morning check.
  - Then one commute day, treated as a test: same gates, same kill-switch mindset (turn around if the first rise registers, walk the bike the rest of the way home if needed, accept being late). A clean next-morning check after the commute is what unlocks commute as a default.
  
  Two short rises are the part to watch on the commute day, not the flats. If the first rise is silent, the second is data; if the second is silent, the ride home is a confirmation, not a push.

The peroneal tendon doesn't punish you during the session — it punishes you the next morning if you let effort creep during the session. Short answer: take Option 1. The 1/8" overlap is exactly right, and the $46 saving on Option 2 isn't worth losing the composition you built.

Mat overlap — why 1/8" works
  - The math is 9 - 8.75 = 0.25" total vertical, 12 - 11.75 = 0.25" total horizontal; half of each goes to each edge, so you get 1/8" on all four sides.
  - 1/8" is the textbook archival overlap for watercolors: it covers the paper edge so no white sliver can ever show, and it gives enough margin to absorb slight sheet irregularities or any future paper movement without exposing the edge.
  - It's also wide enough that, if you ever get a tiny surface nick on the painted side near an edge, the mat will likely hide it. Anything tighter (1/16") starts to look risky on a hand-pulled sheet; anything wider (3/16"+) starts eating into the image noticeably.

Option 1 vs. Option 2 — the real trade-off
  - Option 1 (12x16, archival mat + backing, $74) presents the full 9x12 sheet. The 8.75x11.75 window is not a crop — it's the full sheet minus the 1/8" mat bite, which reads as the complete painting. Composition, including that ~1.25" of pale right-side wash you staged for diagonal-shadow breathing room and the off-center plant, stays intact. The work is also reversible: a future you (or a future framer) can re-window the mat without touching the sheet.
  - Option 2 (8x10 stock, $28) is irreversible. To fit the stock frame you have to physically cut the sheet. You already know what gets sacrificed: most of that pale right wash and the spatial counterweight it gives the plant. What remains is a tighter, more centered composition that you didn't paint. You also lose the archival backing the quote mentions for Option 1 — watercolors on 300 gsm cotton should sit against archival materials, not whatever foam board a stock frame ships with.
  - Price: $46 difference. That's meaningful but small relative to a one-of-a-kind sheet you spent a Sunday block composing, and small relative to the framing market in general (custom archival 12x16 often runs $120+; $74 with mat and backing is a fair price).

One small thing worth doing before you commit
  - Ask the framer to confirm the mat opening dimensions are 8.75 x 11.75 (not 8.5 x 11.5 or any other near neighbor) and that the backing is archival (acid-free, lignin-free) rather than standard foam core. Both should be in writing on the work order. If the framer can mat it with a 4-ply rag board rather than a 2-ply, that's a modest upgrade worth asking about for a piece you intend to keep.

Recommendation: Option 1, with the 1/8" overlap confirmed in writing. Don't cut the sheet.

The cleanest approach is to log by **task × person**, not by shift, and define "incremental labor" as **net added minutes** (additive trial work minus trial work that displaces a normal task). That keeps the 60-minute threshold and the June 28 comparison intact.

RECOMMENDED LOGGING METHOD FOR JULY 26

One row per trial task performed by one person. Sam fills it in during/right after the shift; chef-owner can scan it without a calculator.

Columns:

  Time start | Time end | Person | Trial task | Displaces a normal task? | Minutes
  -----------|----------|--------|------------|---------------------------|---------
  14:00      | 14:12    | Prep A | Stage sheet pans            | No (purely additive)      | 12
  14:05      | 14:18    | Sam    | Truss 30 lb of chickens     | Yes — replaces veg trim   | 13
  14:20      | 14:28    | Sam    | Load/rotate pans in oven    | No                         | 8
  14:25      | 14:31    | Prep A | Portion & plate chickens    | No                         | 6

Footer (three numbers, in this order):

  1. Total additive trial minutes (rows marked "No"):   26
  2. Total displaced normal-task minutes (rows marked "Yes"): 13
  3. NET INCREMENTAL LABOR = (1) − (2):               13

Only line 3 compares to the 60-minute ceiling and to June 28's 57 minutes. The 60-minute threshold does not change.

WHY THIS HANDLES THE THREE CONSTRAINTS

- "Records added task minutes by person": each row is one person on one trial task, with its own duration. The prep cook's full scheduled shift is never summed.
- "Overlapping trial tasks without double-counting clock time": overlapping rows are kept separate by person. Two people working at the same wall-clock moment produce two rows, both counted, because each is a distinct worker doing distinct work. Within one person, rows cannot overlap by construction (one task at a time).
- "Preserves comparison with the June 28 baseline": June 28's 57 minutes was net incremental labor under the same definition. Using the same definition here means a direct comparison. If you instead totaled person-minutes, you would silently change the metric and the threshold would no longer mean the same thing.
- "Doesn't change the 60-minute threshold": the threshold is on net incremental labor, not on person-minutes and not on wall-clock elapsed time. It is unchanged.

TWO EDGE CASES WORTH FLAGGING ON JULY 26

- Trial task that *partially* displaces a normal task (e.g., 10 minutes of staging eats into 20 minutes of scheduled prep, leaving 10 minutes of real prep). Log the full 10 minutes of trial work as a row, and log a separate "displacement" row for 10 minutes so the offset is honest. Net contribution = 0, which is correct.
- Trial task that *adds* work but the same person would have been idle anyway (slow patch in service). Log as additive — it is still labor that would not have happened without the trial. The decision about whether to count "downtime" is the chef-owner's call, not Sam's; flag it in the Notes column and let the chef-owner rule.

  - Header: July 26, 2024 — Roasted-chicken repeat trial

  - Time-log block (columns above), filled during the shift

OVERNIGHT PRECAUTIONS

- Keep the dishwasher's local shutoff CLOSED. That valve is your main control for the night; you already confirmed it stops the drip.
- With that valve closed, the rest of your home's cold water is unaffected. Kitchen sink cold side, bathrooms, etc. all still work normally.
- Open the under-sink cabinet doors and leave them open. Airflow finishes drying the cabinet and lets you see or hear anything new.
- Move anything stored in the cabinet (cleaners, trash bags, pans, anything cardboard) up onto the counter for the night so it isn't damaged if water returns.
- Lay a clean, dry towel on the cabinet floor directly under the supply connection. Lay a second dry towel or paper towels at the back of the cabinet floor where water would flow first.
- Optional but useful: set a shallow pan, rimmed baking sheet, or a small plastic container under the supply connection in case of a slow residual drip.
- Have a flashlight and a couple of extra dry towels within reach.
- Note the time of the original observation and the amount (~2 tablespoons) - useful for the plumber and for the property record.
- Locate your home's main shutoff tonight (meter, garage, where the main enters the house). You almost certainly will not need it, but knowing its location before bed is a small precaution.
- Do NOT run the dishwasher overnight. Reasons: a running cycle can reflood the cabinet if the drain side is also compromised, and vibration/pressure could worsen a loose supply fitting.

DIAGNOSING SUPPLY FITTING vs. DRAIN LEAK WITHOUT DISMANTLING

Strongest clue you already have: the drip stopped the moment you closed the dishwasher's local shutoff. That is consistent with a supply-side leak (the angle stop, the tee, the supply-line nut, or the braided line itself). A drain-side leak would NOT respond to the supply shutoff at all - it would only show during or right after a drain cycle. So tonight's evidence leans heavily toward supply-side, and you are already in good shape to keep it controlled.

To localize further without running a cycle:

1. With the supply valve still CLOSED, dry the cabinet completely and lay fresh dry paper towels in three spots:
   (a) Under the supply valve / connection under the sink where you saw water tonight.
   (b) At the bottom-front of the dishwasher where the supply line enters the unit (pull the dishwasher out a few inches if needed, or shine a flashlight along the side).
   (c) At the drain hose connection - usually where the corrugated dishwasher drain hose clamps to the top or side of the garbage disposal, or to a sink tailpiece, or to an air gap on the counter.

2. Open the dishwasher supply shutoff. Do NOT start a cycle.

3. Wait 20-30 minutes.

4. Recheck the three towels:
   - Only (a) wet: leak is at the under-sink supply connection (angle stop, tee, or supply-line nut).
   - Only (b) wet: leak is at the dishwasher inlet valve or the supply line inside the unit.
   - Only (c) wet: drain-side issue dripping without a cycle (gravity leak from trapped water or a damaged hose) - uncommon but worth ruling out.
   - Multiple towels wet: water has migrated; the highest/wettest towel is closest to the source.

This isolates the leak without taking anything apart.

A second pass that DOES need a running cycle (do this tomorrow during the day, supervised - never overnight):
- Dry all three towels again.
- Start a SHORT cycle (rinse-only if your model has it; otherwise a normal cycle is fine since you'll be watching).
- Have someone watch the cabinet, especially during the drain phase (last 10-15 minutes of a typical cycle, when the pump empties).
- New water during FILL (early): still supply-side, possibly pressure-related (fitting holds static but not dynamic flow).
- New water during WASH or DRAIN: drain-side.

WHEN TO CALL URGENTLY vs. WAIT

Call urgently tonight or first thing in the morning (do not wait for a normal appointment) if any of the following happen:

- Drip resumes with the dishwasher's supply shutoff CLOSED. The shutoff has failed or there is an upstream leak - you no longer have local control and the situation can grow.
- Cabinet wetness is INCREASING rather than drying overnight, especially if more than a few tablespoons accumulate.
- Water reaches or approaches any electrical outlet, the dishwasher's power cord or junction box, or any other plug-in appliance in or near the cabinet.
- Cabinet floor starts to swell, soften, or delaminate visibly.
- You hear continuous running water or hissing in the cabinet.
- A sewage or rotten-egg smell appears (different problem - main drain or trap; not safe to wait).
- You lose water service elsewhere in the home (could indicate a larger supply issue).
- Water appears in multiple cabinets, on the kitchen floor, or anywhere outside the sink cabinet.

Wait for a scheduled plumber (this is the path tonight's evidence supports) if:

- The cabinet is drying and towels stay dry overnight.
- The drip reliably stops with the dishwasher's supply shutoff closed.
- No water anywhere near electrical.
- Cabinet floor stays dry with no swelling.
- You can avoid using the dishwasher until a normal appointment.

Given what you reported, the leak is under control and a standard plumber visit within a day or two is reasonable. The overnight precautions above are your safety net. Most likely culprit based on the evidence: a loose supply-line compression fitting, a worn ferrule, or a failing braided supply line - all common, all quick fixes for a plumber.

Reading the situation before touching the sheet:

The bloom is a classic backrun: a wet edge dried into a hard cauliflower line in the exact place you did not want one — the soft transition between shadowed cheek and pale muzzle. Because your shadow mix almost certainly includes burnt sienna (and probably ultramarine), the pigment in that line is partly granulating and partly staining, so you are working against a ceiling, not an open field. The good news: the bloom sits in a zone that is *supposed* to be soft. A faint halo there reads as fur; a hard line there reads as a mistake. Your stopping point is therefore a soft gradient, not a clean lift.

Pre-flight (do these before the brush goes near Kibo):

  1. Photograph the painting now, straight-on, in the same light you are working in. This is your "before" — you will judge progress against it, not against memory.
  2. Confirm bone-dry by cheek (back of hand near the sheet, not on it). Cool spots mean residual moisture, which will feed new blooms the moment you rewet.
  3. Mix the same dark you used for the shadow on a scrap of the same paper (or a corner of the test sheet). Let it dry. That is your calibration swatch — it tells you how much lift is actually possible before the stain sets.

Sequence (least to most aggressive — stop and reassess at each step):

  A. Dry brush, no water. Take a clean, dry small round (00 or 0), soft synthetic or kolinsky. Lightly sweep across the bloom in one direction, no pressure. This alone sometimes knocks the hardest granulation off the surface tooth. Blot with a clean tissue.

  B. Barely-damp brush. Dampen the brush, then blot it on a tissue until it feels almost dry — the bristles should not drip, and a touch on the back of your hand should leave no visible bead. Touch the bloom edge for 2–3 seconds, lift, blot immediately with a clean tissue (press, don't rub). One pass only.

  C. Redry wait. Set a timer for 8–10 minutes and do not touch that area until it is fully dry again. Working into damp paper is what created the original bloom and will compound it.

  D. Repeat B and C, moving the work inward from the outer edge of the bloom toward the muzzle by only a millimeter or two per pass. Never flood the whole zone — keep the damp footprint smaller than a fingernail.

  E. If the bloom edge softens but the body of it stays dark, you have hit the staining floor of the burnt sienna. That is your signal to reinterpret, not to keep scrubbing.

Stopping point (the part you asked me to be explicit about):

  Stop when the hard cauliflower edge has become a soft, slightly cool transition that you would not notice from across the room, and *before* the muzzle pigment begins to look chalky or uniformly pale. The cotton tooth of the paper should still be visible through the area — that texture is what makes the muzzle read as fur rather than as paper. A pass that leaves the grain showing is a good pass. A pass that leaves the area looking slick or rubbed is a pass too far. Plan on three to five passes total across the whole bloom, not three to five passes in one spot.

What that stopping point looks like in practice: the boundary between cheek and muzzle is now a gentle gradient instead of a dark notch. Some pigment remains in the paper tooth — that is correct, and it is what protects the area from going mud-colored if you later add anything nearby.

If you reach the staining floor (step E) without the edge softening enough:

  Reinterpret the remaining softness as a darker patch of cheek fur overlapping the muzzle edge. In a backlit study, that read is actually plausible — light through ear and cheek does cast a soft local shadow there. Adding a thin glaze of the *same* shadow color in one controlled pass can unify the zone, but only if the surrounding area is bone-dry and you do the glaze in a single stroke without going back into it. Do not glaze the muzzle itself.

Things to keep out of this:

  - Kneaded eraser, palette knife, razor, scrubber of any kind. Cotton cold-press pills and stains under abrasion, and you cannot undo it.
  - Tape over the bloom to "pull" pigment. You have had tape lift fibers twice already this year (March 10, June 2). The bloom is not worth that risk on a Kibo study.
  - Wide rewetting to "blend it out." That is how the original bloom happened.
  - Working the eye and nose at all. They are intact because they are dry and untouched. Leave them that way — your brush footprint stays in the transition zone and nowhere else.

One small judgment call: if the bloom sits within a millimeter or two of the eye or nose, mask those features first with a tiny piece of low-tack tape (just over the shape, not pressing into the wash) before you start step B. The protection is cheap and reversible; a stray damp footprint on the eye is not.

Proper treatment for this specific case, in order:

**1. May ordinary commercial follow-up begin? — Yes, but only as a direct response to the customer's own ask.**

The account is asking, on its own initiative, for pricing on "the two options you showed us" with effective dates. That is a customer-initiated commercial inquiry, not CS-initiated selling. CS may answer it: send the two price points and the earliest effective dates as requested. This is responsive service to an inbound ask, which is different in kind from CS proactively pitching options off the back of the help-path handoff. The help-path → handoff rule (help is a CS handling item, not a sales lead) is not violated, because the next commercial step is being driven by the customer's own message, not by CS's outreach.

Guardrails that still hold:
- CS responds only to what was asked (two options + earliest effective dates). No re-pitching, no bundled upsell, no "while we're at it" language.
- If the account wants to proceed, that creates a normal commercial opportunity opened through the standard path — not a pre-existing pipeline item from the pilot.
- CS does not describe this to the account as "Expansion Assist pricing" or anything that ties the conversation back to the pilot's prompt.

**2. Handoff and reporting treatment.**

- **CS side:** log the inbound pricing request as a customer-initiated commercial inquiry that originated from an EA-exposed account. Respond with pricing + earliest effective dates. If the account moves forward, the resulting opportunity/opportunity-amount is commercial-attributed (the account asked, we answered) — not EA-attributed.
- **Owen / readout side:** the exposure event for this account is unchanged (it was exposed in W1, used the help path, and has now self-initiated a pricing inquiry). Owen's per-account log records the sequence: exposure → help-path handoff → inbound pricing request. None of these events, individually or together, generate pilot pipeline or forecast credit under the wave's no-credit rule.
- **Reporting boundary:** the pilot still does not produce pipeline, weighted pipeline, or forecast contribution from this engagement. If anything commercial materializes, it lives in the standard CS/Sales pipeline, separate from the EA measurement file.

**3. Why the pilot itself still receives no automatic pipeline or forecast credit.**

Three reasons, all already baked into the design:

- **Separate-measure boundary.** The EA pilot's purpose is to measure the bounded help-or-options exposure against its holdout/comparison, not to generate commercial pipeline. Auto-credit on any expansion that emerges from an exposed account would conflate the exposure event with later, separately-caused commercial behavior — including behavior the customer would have taken on its own. That destroys the comparison the pilot is designed to support.
- **Help-path ≠ pipeline.** The original handoff for this account was explicitly logged as a CS handling item, not a sales lead. The customer returning on their own with a pricing request changes the *trigger* for the commercial conversation, but it doesn't retroactively re-classify the help-path handoff as pipeline creation, and it doesn't make the EA exposure the cause of the customer's later inquiry.
- **No outcome/forecast claim, by design.** This is the same rule that governed the refusal of Marcus's earlier forecast-credit ask and the HS invite-path "early pipeline lift" framing. Bounded pilot exposures get described in terms of exposure, eligibility, and observed behavior — not in terms of pipeline produced. Once a customer self-initiates a commercial conversation, the commercial motion gets normal attribution; the pilot does not also get to claim it.

**4. What to tell Marcus.**

Same answer as the prior forecast-credit conversation: the customer's commercial behavior, however encouraging, is not EA pipeline. If the opportunity converts, it shows up in the regular CS/Sales pipeline with standard attribution. The EA pilot's readout continues to describe what the exposure produced in observable terms (account returned, used help path, self-initiated pricing inquiry, responded to pricing) — and stops short of any pipeline, weighted-pipeline, or forecast claim from the pilot itself. That keeps the measurement clean for any future rollout decision and avoids the same over-claim problem that came up around the HS invite path.

Quick read: the asymmetry you're describing — Safari `signup_start` down, backend session-create flat — is the classic tracking-loss signature, not a real decline. Real signup drops almost always drag backend session-create down with them. That doesn't mean you can stop at "probably tracking," but it does mean your first job is to *prove* the front-end signal is the only thing that moved.

Diagnostic sequence, ordered by what kills the hypothesis fastest:

1.  Sanity-check the headline (15 min)
    - Confirm the Safari `signup_start` drop is real on the raw event count, not a dashboard change. Re-run the count for the investigation window vs. the prior comparable window (same weekday, same hour-of-day mix). Same for the whole signup funnel top-of-funnel, not just pricing.
    - Confirm backend application-session creation is genuinely flat at the *hour* level, not just daily. A flat daily can hide a 6-hour hole. If daily backend is flat *and* hourly is flat, that's strong.
    - Quick scope check on "Safari": split by Safari-on-iOS vs. Safari-on-macOS, and by major version (Safari 16 vs. 17 vs. 18). The shape of the drop tells you a lot — ITP/version issues cluster by version; a real-UX bug usually doesn't.

2.  Browser / client-side (cheap, parallelizable — Owen + Daniela)
    - Reproduce in real Safari on a real device against prod. Open Web Inspector, watch the network panel and the console while clicking the CTA that fires `signup_start`. Does the event actually fire, or does it fire and fail to deliver?
    - Check CSP, CORS, and the analytics endpoint's response headers as seen from Safari. Safari is strict — a Content-Type mismatch, a missing CORS header, or a new `frame-ancestors` directive can silently break `navigator.sendBeacon` / `fetch` keepalive.
    - Check whether the pricing page picked up a deploy in the affected window (any JS/CSS change, even unrelated). A stale module reference, a renamed event-binding selector, or a hydration-order regression can kill one event without touching anything else. Roll back forward-deploys in staging and re-test.
    - Check the analytics SDK bundle itself — was it re-served? Did the CDN return a stale or wrong-versioned file to Safari (MIME / brotli edge cases hit Safari harder than Chrome/Firefox)?
    - Check ITP state: any new third-party iframe or cross-site resource added to the pricing page this week? New SDK init touching `document.cookie` or localStorage that Safari 17's "click-to-load" / storage partitioning now blocks?

3.  Analytics pipeline (medium-cost — Owen)
    - Pull raw ingest from PostHog/Segment for Safari UA in the window. Are events arriving at all? Are they arriving but failing validation (e.g., missing `distinct_id` because referrer got stripped by ITP)? Are they arriving but routed to a dead-letter queue?
    - Check bot-detection / sampling filters — a bot-rule update this week would land on mobile Safari harder than desktop. Mobile Safari UA strings trip aggressive filters.
    - Check feature-flag SDK cookie logic on Safari. ITP blocks many first-party cookies set via JS on cross-site contexts. If any flag the pricing page reads has a different code path for control vs. treatment and the cookie is missing, the page could behave differently on Safari. (Not `pricing_page_v3` — that flag has no traffic and no rollout rule, so it's a non-cause unless diagnostics say otherwise. But check *other* flags the pricing page touches.)

4.  Backend confirmation (load-bearing — Owen, this is the one that decides the answer)
    - Pricing-page-view → application-session-create conversion rate, by browser, by hour, for the window vs. baseline. If Safari's backend conversion is unchanged, the front-end event is the only thing that moved. If Safari's backend conversion is also down, you have a real decline and the diagnostic above becomes UX-investigation, not tracking-investigation.
    - Backend attribution on the surviving Safari sessions in the window: campaign source / referrer / UTM should still be intact on the `session_create` event. If attribution made it through to the backend but didn't make it onto `signup_start`, that localizes the loss to the frontend event specifically (and tells you ITP / referrer-policy is the prime suspect).

5.  Decision rule
    - *Backend flat, only `signup_start` down on Safari → tracking failure.* Don't change the funnel chart, don't blame pricing. Fix the instrumentation, annotate the metric as broken for the window, and move on. Owen writes the closure note.
    - *Backend also down on Safari → real decline.* Switch to pricing-page UX diff for Safari in the window (CSS, viewport, button hit-area, payment-iframe sandbox attribute, anything that hits Safari differently). Now the question is "what changed for Safari users," not "what broke in our pipe."
    - *Both flat → dashboard artifact.* Re-run, re-check query.

Two things to actively *not* do:

- Don't waste time on `pricing_page_v3`. It's stale, has no rollout, no traffic split. Unless a diagnostic step above lands on it, treat as irrelevant to this incident. Flag-cleanup work is separate hygiene.
- Don't ship a "fix" before step 4. The instinct on a sharp drop is to revert something; if you revert the wrong thing (e.g., a flag that wasn't actually causing this), you'll mask the real cause and break a baseline.

Here's a calm, step-by-step plan based on where things stand — one small, attached tick behind the left ear, no symptoms yet, fine-tipped tweezers ready, no home remedies applied. Good to act quickly but not urgently.

SAFEST REMOVAL (do this first)

1. Settle Kibo where he can't shake his head and dislodge the tick into his face/eye or yours. A helper holding his collar/chest, or his side against your body, works well. A small treat helps.
2. Part the fur so you can see the mouthparts clearly. Good light matters more than magnification.
3. With fine-tipped tweezers, grasp the tick as close to the skin as possible — aim to grip the head/mouthparts, not the body.
4. Pull straight up with slow, steady, even pressure. No twisting, no jerking, no "rocking." Twisting can leave mouthparts behind or cause the tick to regurgitate into the bite.
5. If a tiny dark fragment stays embedded in the skin: don't dig for it. The body will wall it off like a splinter. Only dig if it's clearly loose and superficial.
6. Do NOT use any of the folk methods — no oil, petroleum jelly, nail polish, heat, alcohol, or soap. They make the tick salivate/regurgitate, which increases the chance of transmitting infection.

AFTERCARE OF THE BITE SITE

- Clean the spot with plain soap and water, then a dab of rubbing alcohol or chlorhexidine if you have it.
- A small red bump or scab for 1–3 days is normal and expected.
- No antibiotic ointment needed unless it looks irritated later.
- Don't bandage — keep the area dry and open to air.

WHAT TO DO WITH THE TICK

Best option: save it.

- Put the live or just-removed tick in a small sealed zip-top bag or a tight jar with a slightly damp paper towel or a bit of rubbing alcohol.
- Label it: date (7/27/2024), location on Kibo (behind left ear), and "Cherrywood yard."
- Keep it for 2–4 weeks at room temperature or in the fridge. If Kibo develops any symptoms later, your vet can identify the species, which narrows the disease risk meaningfully (different ticks carry different diseases — blacklegged/deer vs. American dog vs. Lone Star vs. others).
- If you'd rather just be done with it: drop it in rubbing alcohol, seal in a bag, or flush. Don't crush with bare fingers.

MONITORING — TWO TIMELINES

Same-day / next 24–48 hours — these mean call the vet or go in promptly:

- Rapidly spreading redness or swelling at the bite site, or the area becomes hot, painful, or oozing
- New facial swelling or hives anywhere
- Vomiting, diarrhea, or refusal of water
- Breathing changes (fast, shallow, noisy, panting at rest)
- Pale, blue, or tacky gums
- Sudden weakness, wobbliness, or collapse
- Unusual quietness or hiding that feels "not him"
- Any sign of tick paralysis: ascending weakness starting in the hind legs, gait that looks drunk, change in bark, trouble swallowing, drooling — this is uncommon but can come on within hours to a couple of days of certain bites and is a true emergency
- You can't get the tick out cleanly, or a large piece is clearly broken off and the area is bleeding/painful

Next 2–4 weeks — these mean a routine vet call (don't wait for them to worsen):

- Lethargy, low appetite, or weight loss
- Fever signs: warm ears and paws, panting at rest, restlessness at night
- Lameness, joint pain, or "walking on eggshells" — especially if it shifts from leg to leg
- Swollen joints or a new limp with no obvious injury
- Unusual bruising, nosebleeds, or bleeding that doesn't stop
- Changes in urination (much more, much less, or dark/bloody)
- A bull's-eye or expanding rash at the bite site (less common in dogs than humans, but worth noting)

GENERAL REASSURANCE

Most single, brief tick attachments do not transmit disease. The biggest risk-reduction step is the one you've already taken: removing it cleanly and soon after discovery, without using heat or chemicals. Watch for the signs above, save the tick just in case, and you've done the right things.

FOR THE CHERRYWOOD YARD GOING FORWARD (when you have a moment, not tonight)

- Walk the edges: tall grass, leaf piles, and brushy borders are the high-risk zones. Keeping a clear mowed buffer reduces the population locally.
- A quick post-yard tick check (ears, neck, armpits, groin, between toes, under tail) each time is the highest-yield habit.
- If Kibo isn't already on a veterinarian-recommended tick preventive (topical or oral), mention today's find at his next checkup so you can pick one suited to your area and his size. The vet can also tell you whether a baseline 4-week Lyme/anaplasma titer makes sense in your region.

Pre-flight
- Photograph first. Confirm bone-dry (back of the sheet cool to the touch, not just the face).
- On a scrap, mix your warm glaze recipe and test a 2-second lift and a thin cool overlay. Know how far the pigment gives before you touch the painting, and lay a swatch of the warm with the cool glaze dried over it so you can see whether granulation survives a thin coat.

Phase 1 — lift only the heaviest mass
- Dry brush sweep first across the most solid patch. Single transparent glazes often release surprising pigment dry.
- Where it holds, small round, barely damp, 2–3 seconds, blot immediately. Wait 8–10 minutes. Repeat, working inward 1–2 mm per pass.
- Stop with a clean dry margin — a torn-paper mask along the horizon helps — and never let lift water cross into the reserved light. Three to five passes is usually the ceiling before the glaze hits its staining floor.

Phase 2 — cooler glaze to tie it back to the violet sky
- Tone the same violet mix you used above (ultramarine + a touch of quinacridone rose) thin — clear tea, not milk. Cobalt is a stand-in if you want a cleaner cool without the rose influence.
- Apply wet-on-dry, only on the warm bank, in broken strokes rather than a flat wash, so the existing granulation keeps reading through the glaze. A flat overlay fills in the tooth and kills the texture.
- At the boundary with the horizon light, pre-wet a narrow strip with clean water and drop a thin line of the violet mix, letting it feather to nothing — softens the bank's lower edge without touching the reserved opening.

Stopping points
- Horizon opening stays clean and untouched.
- Some warmth remains — storm underbellies are legitimately warm. The goal is to make the bank support the sky, not neutralize it.
- Granulation still visible in the bank after the glaze dries.
- If the warm now reads as part of the same air as the violet rather than a separate mass, stop.

Avoid
- Glazing the violet sky above, and any wide rewetting on the sheet — a fresh backrun in the dry sky would be a worse problem than the warm bank ever was.
- Kneaded eraser, palette knife, scrubbing. One transparent glaze on cotton lifts with patience; force burnishes the paper and locks the warm in.

Yes — what you're describing at the site five days out fits a typical minor local reaction to a tick bite. Here's the read on it and how to handle it.

WHAT IT LIKELY IS
A ~4 mm pink, slightly raised bump with a dry center, stable in size, not hot, draining, or markedly tender, with normal energy and appetite, is consistent with the normal local inflammatory/granulomatous response to the bite puncture. These commonly persist 1–3 weeks and slowly flatten as they resolve. A tiny retained mouthpart fragment can also keep a mild, non-infectious bump going a bit longer without causing trouble.

CARE THAT WON'T IRRITATE
- Leave it alone as much as possible. Don't pick, squeeze, or scrub at it.
- If it gets dirty, gently clean with plain lukewarm water and a mild dog-safe soap, then pat dry. Don't soak the ear.
- Avoid hydrogen peroxide and alcohol on the site — both can slow healing and irritate.
- No antibiotic ointment needed unless irritation appears or he's scratching at it. If he does scratch, a thin smear of chlorhexidine is fine; most of these do best dry and uncovered.
- No bandage needed; the ear is well-aerated and easy to leave alone.
- Keep up tick prevention so this doesn't recur.

ROUTINE (NON-URGENT) VET CALL IF YOU NOTICE
- Bump still present and unchanged at 3–4 weeks, or slowly enlarging over many days.
- Persistent scratching or head-shaking directed at the ear.
- A small scab that keeps reforming, or a firm pea-sized nodule that isn't shrinking.
- New mild lameness, joint stiffness, or low-grade reluctance to move, especially 2–6 weeks from now (Lyme and other tick-borne illnesses can present this way).
- Subtle drop in energy or appetite that lasts more than a day or two.

URGENT / SAME-DAY VET CARE IF YOU NOTICE
- Rapid enlargement, increasing heat, marked tenderness, pus or oozing, or red streaks spreading from the site.
- Facial swelling, hives, or sudden itching anywhere on the body.
- Vomiting, diarrhea, refusal of water.
- Breathing changes, coughing, pale or blue gums.
- Sudden weakness, wobbliness, collapse, or marked lethargy.
- Tick paralysis signs: ascending weakness, "drunk" gait, voice/bark change, trouble swallowing, drooling.
- Sudden lameness with joint pain or feverish behavior (can be Lyme or another tick-borne illness).
- Any overall condition that just feels unlike his normal self.

A NOTE ON TICK-BORNE DISEASE
The bite site itself isn't where tick-borne illness shows up. If something was transmitted at the original bite, signs (lethargy, fever, lameness, joint pain, inappetence, sometimes shifting leg stiffness) typically appear 2–6 weeks later for the common tick-borne diseases. Your current picture has none of those — Kibo is acting like himself. Just keep the next several weeks on your normal radar; a routine call is reasonable if anything low-grade shows up rather than waiting for it to become obvious.

If the bump doesn't resolve over the next 2–3 weeks, or if anything in the urgent list appears, a vet visit is warranted. Otherwise this is the kind of thing that quietly fades on its own.

Hallway wall is safest. It avoids both the direct light and the cooking humidity, and the indirect-light / steady-humidity combination is exactly what archival framing is built for. The farther viewing distance is solvable with placement and lighting (below).

Living-room west wall — why I'd skip it
Two hours of direct west sun daily, 3-5pm, hits the paper with the full visible spectrum and heat. UV-filtering acrylic blocks most UV (typically 95-99% depending on product) but does not block visible-light fading or thermal effects on paper and pigment. Watercolors on paper are among the most light-sensitive media; daily afternoon sun will visibly shift the pale wash within a few years even with the acrylic doing its job. The acrylic is necessary protection, not sufficient.

Kitchen — why I'd skip it
Cooking produces cycling humidity and grease aerosols. Acrylic glazing is not a humidity seal — moisture and airborne particles reach the paper at the edges, the back, and any micro-gaps. Grease film on the glazing also attracts dust and gradually dulls the wash. Good exhaust helps but doesn't eliminate the exposure.

If you use the hallway
  Hang on an interior partition wall, not an exterior wall — exterior walls transfer outdoor humidity and temperature swings into the back of the frame.
  Keep it clear of HVAC supply/return registers and any spot above a radiator or near a bathroom door (humidity spikes).
  Sightline: hang at the natural eye level for the position you'll actually view from. Standing in a hallway is typically 56-60" to center; lower if you'll view it seated from a chair at the end.
  Lighting: a low-UV, low-heat LED picture light, ~2700-3000K, aimed to graze the painting at roughly 30° so it washes out acrylic glare rather than bouncing back at the viewer. Put it on a timer or photoswitch so it isn't on when no one is looking.
  Quarterly: peek at the back of the frame for dust or moisture signs; inspect the glazing for film or fine scratches.

If you pick a non-hallway spot anyway
  Living-room west wall: the danger is the direct beam, not the acrylic. Rotate the piece off the wall into a closet 3-5pm daily, or close west blinds during peak hours, or move it to a wall outside the beam. Hanging it in the beam and trusting the acrylic to handle it will fade the painting.
  Kitchen: hang on the wall farthest from the cooktop, run exhaust whenever cooking, and never near a window that steams up. Paper art and kitchens rarely mix well even with precautions.

Acrylic-care reminders
  Mild soap and water, or an acrylic-safe cleaner, on a clean microfiber cloth. Never ammonia-based glass cleaner, never paper towels — both scratch and degrade the coating.
  Spray the cloth, not the glazing.
  Avoid finger contact with the acrylic; skin oils attract dust that then shows as a film.

If you tell me which stretch of hallway wall you have in mind, I can suggest a sightline and lighting setup that makes the viewing distance a non-issue.

Here's the proposed neutral convention. It keeps both P023 attributions on the record with sources, leaves P028 explicitly unknown, and uses the album/envelope as the authority rather than memory confidence.

PRINCIPLE
Memory is a clue, not proof. The original physical artifact (the album page, envelope, sleeve, or written note) is the verification step. When two sources disagree, neither attribution is promoted to "fact"; both are kept as candidate hypotheses tied to their source, and resolution is deferred until the artifact is checked. When nobody is confident, the field stays open rather than being filled with a guess.

PROPOSED INVENTORY FIELDS (per record)
- P### (temporary ID, never replaced by a guessed name)
- scan_file (scan_P###_front.jpg, scan_P###_back.jpg)
- estimated_date_range (your prior estimate, kept as an estimate, not a fact)
- estimated_location_context (same, kept as estimate)
- identified_people (only if someone is identified by the artifact itself, e.g. a written caption)
- condition (dry, loose)
- attribution_status (one of: confirmed_by_artifact / single_source_memory / multi_source_memory_conflicting / unknown)
- attribution_notes (the actual attributions, each with source, never collapsed)
- verification_source (what physical item would resolve it: album page, envelope, sleeve note, caption, etc.)
- verification_status (pending / checked-no-match / checked-confirmed)
- open_questions

HOW P023 IS RECORDED
- attribution_status: multi_source_memory_conflicting
- attribution_notes:
    - Mom: Austin gathering, ~2002 (memory, low-to-medium confidence per Mom)
    - Marcus: San Antonio gathering, ~2004 (memory, low-to-medium confidence per Marcus)
- verification_source: original family album page / envelope in which the print was filed before it came loose
- verification_status: pending
- estimated_date_range and estimated_location_context are left as your prior estimate or marked unresolved; they are NOT updated to either 2002/Austin or 2004/San Antonio until the album or envelope confirms one.

HOW P028 IS RECORDED
- attribution_status: unknown
- attribution_notes: neither Mom nor Marcus supplied a date or occasion; no artifact-based caption present
- verification_source: original family album / envelope (check for a sleeve caption, album date, or contextual photos on facing pages)
- verification_status: pending
- estimated_date_range and estimated_location_context left blank or marked "unknown"

RESOLUTION RULE (when the album or envelope is checked)
- If the album page or envelope has a written date/place that matches one of the memories, that source is logged as verified_by_artifact and attribution_status becomes confirmed_by_artifact; the other memory is recorded as not_confirmed but preserved in the notes.
- If the album/envelope has a written date/place that matches neither memory, both memories are recorded as not_confirmed and the artifact caption becomes the record.
- If the album/envelope has no relevant caption and no contextual match, attribution_status stays unknown and both memories (or the absence of memory, for P028) are preserved as-is; the case is not closed by elimination.

REJECTED ALTERNATIVE (for the record, so it's explicit)
Choosing the more confident-sounding memory (Austin 2002 over San Antonio 2004) is rejected. Confidence level is not evidence; it is a bias risk. Two equally-weighted memories plus an available physical verification step means the verification step runs before any commitment.
