Short answer: yes, contact them Monday — but a brief portal message or phone call is enough, not necessarily an in‑person visit. The picture isn't alarm‑level, but two consecutive runs (9/8 and 9/11) reproduced the same lateral‑ankle ache at a lower dose (34 → 30 min), and the tenderness is now lingering four days later with a brief return after a 25‑min walk. That's the kind of pattern a PT who already knows you can triage in five minutes, and the cost of one more "try again next Sunday" cycle is higher than the cost of asking.

Why this rises above "just keep resting":

  - 6/26 dx was peroneal tendon irritation, and the current symptom map (lateral, no swelling, no instability, load‑reproducible) still fits that. Good — same problem, not a new one.
  - But the bar the 6/26 clinician set ("pain‑free stair descent and repeated single‑leg hops for 48 h") is not fully met: stair descent is clean, but the focal tenderness on palpation hasn't cleared, and a 25‑min walk is now briefly re‑provoking it. That's a lower threshold than running, which means the tendon isn't yet tolerating your normal walking volume cleanly.
  - You've already done the right conservative moves: held Sunday, no substitute session, kept easy cycling separate. The fact that it still isn't fully quiet after several days is the signal to loop a clinician back in, not to push harder.

What to send the PT (concise, in this order — they can read it in 60 seconds):

  1. One line of context: "peroneal tendon irritation diagnosed 6/26/24 at [clinic name]; completed PT course with you; re‑presenting with recurrent symptoms."
  2. Timeline:
       - 9/8 Sun — 34 min easy run; normal first 28 min, then 2/10 lateral ankle ache; persisted ~30 min during walk home, then faded. No swelling, limp, instability, sharp pain.
       - 9/11 Wed — 30 min easy run (reduced); normal first 24 min, then 2/10 ache same spot; stopped at 26 min; faded after ~45 min walking + breakfast. Same negatives.
       - 9/12 Thu — held Sun's planned run; faint 1/10 tenderness on palpation; no pain with walking or stairs.
       - 9/15 Sun — held recovery check, no run, no substitute session.
  3. Current findings today:
       - Pain‑free ordinary walking and stair descent.
       - No swelling, limp, instability, rest pain, first‑step stiffness.
       - Focal tenderness 1/10 on palpation of the same lateral spot.
       - Tenderness briefly returns after a 25‑min walk, then settles.
  4. Two or three focused questions:
       - Is the recurrence after a 25‑min walk (not just running) concerning, or expected for an under‑recovered peroneal?
       - Should I stay paused on running, and for how long before a graded re‑introduction?
       - Any change to the home program (isometrics, heavy slow resistance, eccentrics, calf/banded work) given this pattern, and is easy cycling still fine as long as it stays symptom‑free during and the next day?
       - Optional: do you want to see me in person, or is this manageable over message?

Practical notes on the contact itself:

  - "Former PT" usually means discharged, not unreachable. Most clinics will answer a re‑check question from a prior patient via the patient portal or a front‑desk phone message routed back to the therapist; call the clinic Monday morning and ask.
  - If you can't reach your prior PT quickly, the fallback is a portal message to the 6/26 sports‑med clinician — same clinic, same chart, same dx — asking the same two questions. Either route is reasonable; the PT is just the faster one because they already have your loading history.
  - Don't ask for imaging or escalate to urgency yourself — leave that to them to decide based on the pattern you're describing.

What to keep doing between now and Monday:

  - No run, no substitute running session — you're already doing this; stay the course.
  - Walking is fine, but treat the 25‑min re‑provocation as useful information: if you have a longer walk planned (errands, commute), break it up or shorten it until you hear back, so you don't keep poking the tendon and muddying the signal.
  - Easy cycling: keep it only if it's symptom‑free during the ride and the next morning, and keep it separate from any running question (no "cycling in place of running" framing yet).
  - No new exercises. Don't add heavier calf raises or banded work on top of an unresolved focal tenderness — that's a Monday question, not a Sunday experiment.

One thing not to do: don't skip the contact because the symptoms are "only 1/10." Low‑grade persistent tendon irritability is exactly the stage where a PT can keep you out of a longer layoff. The threshold for reaching out isn't pain severity; it's failure to clear over a sensible rest window, which is where you are.

REPEAT-CONTACT RULE — HS HIGH-EFFORT DIAGNOSTIC

This rule defines what counts as a contact, what is excluded as an automated acknowledgement, and when a contact becomes a repeat. 1) CONTACT EVENT (counted)
A record in the post-admission product-support file qualifies as a contact event if it meets ALL of:
  - Substantive content (more than a one-line template)
  - Initiated by a customer, or by an agent responding to a customer action
  - Sender identity is a human or human team (not platform / bot / system)
  - Internal CS notes are excluded entirely

2) AUTOMATED ACKNOWLEDGEMENT (excluded)
A record is treated as an automated acknowledgement and dropped from contact counts if ANY of:
  - Sender identity is a platform, automation, or system account
  - Body is a templated status notification (ticket-received, status change, SLA notice, "we'll be in touch")
  - One-direction only (no two-way exchange follows)
  - Time-stamped within seconds of the prior event with no new information

3) REPEAT CONTACT (counted as a repeat within a workspace)
A repeat contact is a contact event that is the second or later customer-initiated contact in a workspace's post-admission record:
  - First customer-initiated contact: 0 repeats
  - Second customer-initiated contact: 1st repeat

Goal: feel how long the bead survives without intervention, and see which brush state produces a bloom on a sheet whose sheen has dulled.

Setup
- 11x15 quarter sheet, fresh
- Single pigment, mid-value (burnt sienna or ultramarine — one pigment so the bead reads cleanly)
- Two water cups (pigment and rinse)
- #10 or #12 round
- Board tilted around 20 degrees
- Paper towel

Exercise A — bead longevity, no brush (5 min)
- Load the brush fully and lay one continuous stroke top to bottom
- Do not touch the sheet again
- Mentally mark every five seconds: where is the bead, where is the sheen, when does the sheen dull, when does the bead stall
- This calibrates your internal clock — what 30, 45, 60 seconds of bead life actually looks like

Exercise B — three re-entry states on a fresh sheet (10 min)
- Tape three vertical strips on a new quarter sheet
- Lay the same wash down each strip, top to bottom
- At about two-thirds down each strip, re-enter with a different brush state:
  - Strip 1: brush loaded to MATCH the bead wetness — should flow in seamlessly
  - Strip 2: brush WETTER than the bead — the clinic state, this is the bloom condition
  - Strip 3: brush genuinely DRY — almost no water, just enough to move pigment
- One re-entry per strip, then leave the sheet alone
- After dry, set the three strips side by side and read the spectrum

What this isolates: Exercise A isolates time only. Exercise B isolates brush moisture only. Same wash, same paper, same motion in each case — only the variable changes.

STUDY 2 — Edge timing ladder (about 12 minutes)
Goal: see the full spectrum from soft to hard edge produced purely by timing the softening pass.

Setup
- 11x15 quarter sheet, fresh
- Tape it into five vertical cells (about 2.25 wide each, quarter-inch tape dividers between)
- Same single pigment, same mix as Study 1
- Same brush
- Board nearly flat
- Phone timer visible

Procedure
- Mix a generous puddle — same mix used for all five cells
- Load the brush the same way each time
- For each cell: lay the wash, then make one softening pass along one edge at the target time. T+0 is the moment the brush leaves the paper after laying the wash.
  - Cell 1: softening pass at T+10s
  - Cell 2: softening pass at T+20s
  - Cell 3: softening pass at T+30s
  - Cell 4: softening pass at T+45s
  - Cell 5: softening pass at T+60s
- The softening pass is the same brush, lightly damp, drawn once along the wet edge

After the sheet dries, write the time next to each cell. Likely outcome you can use as a reference: T+10s too wet (halo or mush), T+20 to 30s clean soft edge, T+45s hardening, T+60s hard edge matching what you got on the second cylinder.

What this isolates: only timing changes. Brush state, brush motion, pigment load, paper, board angle — all constant across the five cells.

How to use the dried sheets
The sheets themselves are the study notes. Study 1 Exercise A is a clock reference, Exercise B is a brush-state reference. Study 2 is a timing reference. Once dry, label each cell or strip with the condition that produced it. Before the next clinic, glance at the sheets and pick the cell or strip that matches the state you are walking into — bead alive or dull, edge fresh or late — and your hand will remember what to do.

Both studies leave the paper alone after the one intentional pass. No scrubbing, no repainting finished work, no corrective gymnastics on drying paper.

Two questions, both deliberately constructed to argue rather than recap.

Q1 (opening — ambition inside intimacy):
Does the novel finally believe artistic ambition and intimacy can coexist in these friendships — or is one of them always being quietly fed to the other?

What it's doing: forces a stance on compatibility vs. cannibalism before anyone can drift into "well, Tova is… / Seamus does…". The phrase "fed to the other" is meant to be provocative enough that someone pushes back, which is where the conversation starts.

Q2 (ending's effect on sympathy):
Does the ending ask you to revise your sympathy for anyone — and whose earlier behavior now reads most differently to you?

What it's doing: a diagnostic question. It forces each reader to commit to a specific revision (or to defend why they wouldn't change anything), which is how disagreement surfaces. Works even if members started the book with very different sympathies — the question is "did anything shift," not "did everyone arrive at the same place."

A practical note on using them: lead with Q1, let it run until the room repeats itself, then move to Q2 once someone has volunteered a specific example. If Q2 goes flat ("no, I still feel the same"), the productive follow-up is "what would have had to happen at the end for you to revise?" — that gets the group back to arguing about craft rather than plot.

Here's the framework for the next 12 to 24 hours.

SIGNS THIS IS ORDINARY STRESS (consistent with what you saw)
  Panting, drooling, restlessness in the car
  Alert and responsive, tracks you, takes treats, soft eyes
  Pink gums; pressed gum color returns in under 2 seconds
  Drinks water within an hour of getting home
  Begins to settle on his bed within 30 to 90 minutes of being home
  Tired or sleepy later in the day (rebound from adrenaline)
  Mild appetite dip for a few hours

SIGNS TO CALL THE REGULAR CLINIC (non-urgent, same day or next day)
  Stress symptoms still strong 2 to 3 hours after getting home
  Won't drink water at all within 4 to 6 hours
  Refuses food for more than 12 to 18 hours
  One episode of vomiting or a single soft stool with no blood and no other symptoms — call if it repeats or doesn't resolve overnight
  Continued pacing or inability to settle tonight
  Mild limp or favoring a paw that was handled — observe, call if it persists past tomorrow
  Anything that just "feels off" but isn't dramatic — your read on him is reliable, trust it

SIGNS THAT NEED URGENT OR EMERGENCY VET (call the ER or go now)
  Collapse, fainting, or sudden weakness
  Pale, white, blue, or gray gums
  Difficulty breathing — belly heaving, neck extended, open-mouth breathing at rest, tongue or gum color change
  Facial swelling, hives, sudden itching or scratching
  Repeated vomiting (more than 2 to 3 times in an hour) or any blood in vomit
  Profuse watery diarrhea, bloody stool, or black tarry stool
  Bloated, distended, or hard abdomen, especially if also retching without producing anything
  Inability to stand or walk normally

  Symptoms that get worse rather than better over 1 to 2 hours

Bottom line: the estimate covers the math but the floor is too thin to commit to 26 confidently, so ask the supplier for a guaranteed minimum before sending any confirmation.

The math, plain:
- Need to produce: 24 plated + 2 kitchen contingency = 26 complete portions
- Supplier estimate: 27-30 per case (low-high), not guaranteed
- Buffer at low end (27): exactly 1 portion above the 26 you want to produce
- Buffer at high end (30): up to 4 portions spare

Why that's not enough commitment to act on:
- 24 plated is the only firm guest-facing number and is safe even at the low estimate (27 - 24 = 3 spare)
- The 2-portion contingency depends on the case landing at or above 26 after trim
- We've seen real variance already — the Sept 12 case came in at 33 against a 34 projection, a ~3% shortfall
- A similar-sized slip from the 27 estimate floor puts you at 25-26, which collapses one of the two contingency portions and leaves no margin
- The 2-portions contingent is internal-only by design (no seconds advertised, no open batch, no recurring signal), so it doesn't need to be in the host confirmation — but Sam still needs to be able to produce them in the kitchen

What to do before promising anything to the host:
1. Go back to the supplier and ask for a guaranteed minimum per case after trim, in writing, for the Oct 19 lot. A floor of at least 27 lets the plan hold with one portion to spare; a floor of 26 means contingency could disappear on a low-yield case.
2. Until that minimum is in hand, do not lock the 26-production number internally either. Stage the count as "plan to produce 26, contingent on case yield meeting the agreed minimum."
3. To the host, only confirm 24 roasted-chicken meals and 4 vegetarian meals for the 28 adults. Do not mention a 2-portion contingency in any host-facing message — it has never been advertised, and a private-dinner cushion is not an open-ended weekly batch.
4. Keep the tested pre-staging sequence as the production method. No change there.
5. Once the supplier minimum is confirmed, lock the production count internally and proceed. If the minimum comes in below 26, fall back to 24 plated and a smaller or zero kitchen contingency, and tell Sam not to open a second case.

So: yes, the estimate makes 26 physically possible, but the estimate is not a commitment and the buffer is one portion. Get the supplier's guaranteed minimum first, confirm 24 plated to the host now (or once you have the minimum), and hold the 2-portion contingency as a kitchen-side decision that depends on the guaranteed floor.

Operationally, the two options trade different costs. Both keep the contingency boundary intact — the extra portions stay kitchen-only and are not advertised or offered as seconds — so the comparison is about which other cost is more material.

Service split alignment with the host
- Option A (one case, 23 chicken / 5 vegetarian) moves the host-requested 24/4 split by one seat in each direction. The host asked for 24 chicken meals, so this needs re-confirmation before the count is locked, and any guest-side communication that referenced 24 chicken would need to be updated.
- Option B (two cases, 24/4) preserves the host's request exactly. No guest-side coordination is required.

Chef-owner production preference
- Chef-owner wanted 26 produced with 2 portions held as kitchen-only contingency. Option A produces 25 (23 plated + 2 contingency), one short of that preference. Option B produces 26 (24 plated + 2 contingency), matching it exactly.

Yield and waste exposure
- Option A stays inside the supplier's guaranteed 25-portion yield for one case. There is no second-case uncertainty, and trim/waste is limited to the normal single-case footprint.
- Option B opens a second case whose post-trim yield has not been stated for this event. Same supplier and same process suggest a yield close to the first case, so the production risk is mainly overproduction rather than underproduction. Against a 26-portion need, the second case pushes total usable portions into the high forties or low fifties; roughly 20–25 portions sit outside the plated and contingency boundary and have to be absorbed as staff meals, next-day use, or trim/waste.

Service-day buffer
- Option A holds the 2-portion kitchen contingency entirely inside the guarantee. If any portion is lost during prep or plating — the Sept 13 platter-drop precedent — the buffer drops to one and there is no headroom above that. The contingency boundary is preserved, but it is a tighter contingency.
- Option B carries the same 2-portion kitchen contingency on the plated-count side, with the second case functioning as an unspoken upper buffer. A single drop or trim loss is absorbed without touching contingency, but that same buffer is the source of the overproduction noted above.

Production labor and pre-staging
- Both options use the tested pre-staging sequence; production method is unchanged.
- Option B roughly doubles raw prep, trim, and roast labor for one service, even though only 26 portions are formally allocated.

Communication and document cost
- Option A requires a written update to the host (and possibly to the service captain) plus an internal note that the plated count moved by one seat.
- Option B leaves the host communication unchanged; opening the second case is an internal production decision and does not need to reach the guest side.

Net shape of the tradeoff
- Option A's cost is one chicken seat shifted to vegetarian and a re-confirmation with the host, in exchange for clean single-case production, no second-case yield question, and a tighter (but still present) 2-portion contingency.
- Option B's cost is roughly 20–25 portions of overproduction and a doubled prep workload, in exchange for keeping the host-requested split and the chef-owner's 26/2 production count intact.

Neither option is locked. The choice turns on how the host-flexibility cost in Option A weighs against the waste-exposure and labor cost in Option B, and on whether the chef-owner is comfortable absorbing the excess from a second case or would rather see the plated count shift by one seat.

Take the bus now. Leave the bike at the covered rack and retrieve it tomorrow morning. That is the safest of the three options by a wide margin, and it's also the best call for Kibo.

Why riding now is off the table
- Lightning is a hard stop. NWS guidance: if you can hear thunder, you're within striking distance and need to be indoors. You are two hours into the lightning window right now. A bicycle leaves you exposed and elevated — not where you want to be in an active thunderstorm.
- 35 mph gusts are a real control-loss risk on a bike, not just discomfort. Crosswinds can push you into a lane, sudden gusts can pitch the bike, and storm debris plus wet leaves on the road compounds it.
- Wet roads lengthen braking, and painted markings, manhole covers, and tram tracks get slick. Driver visibility is also reduced, so you're harder to see.
- "Leaving early" doesn't help here — the 4–7 pm window is already underway. The storm isn't going to get safer in the next 20 minutes.

Why waiting isn't the right play either
- Waiting means about two more hours at the office, then a ride home at or after dusk on wet, leaf-strewn roads with possible debris down. Safer than riding through the lightning, but still an avoidable exposure.
- More importantly for your house: Kibo would be home alone through the peak of the storm. You can short-circuit that.

Why the bus wins
- Zero exposure to lightning and gusts. An enclosed vehicle is the safe place during a thunderstorm.
- The bike stays where it already is — covered, locked, no moving it in the rain.
- You're home well before peak intensity (6–7 pm), which is what Kibo actually needs.
- Tomorrow's commute is a solved problem: bus or transit to the office in the morning, bike is sitting there waiting for the ride home. The rack is covered and accessible in the morning, so retrieval is clean.

Go catch the bus.

FOOD
- Hold food for the rest of tonight. Skip dinner entirely.
- Tomorrow morning (~7 AM), if he has been quiet all night with no further vomiting and is still alert: offer a bland breakfast — 1–2 tablespoons plain boiled skinless chicken + white rice, no seasoning, no fat.
- If he holds that for 30–60 minutes, a second small portion is fine.
- Return to normal food at his next regular meal after that if bland is held down.

ACTIVITY
- Leash-only potty breaks, 3–5 minutes, yard or very nearby. No walks, no fetch, no stairs to chase.
- Settle him in his usual sleeping spot. Quiet, dim lights.
- If he's a "den + fan + white noise" dog (fireworks-night setup), that routine helps here too.

MONITORING — quick checks every 2–3 hours, plus once overnight (e.g., ~3 AM)
- Gums: still pink = good. Pale, gray, blue, or tacky = not good.
- Belly: soft and non-painful = good. Hard, swollen, or "praying position" (front down, rear up, reluctant to move) = not good.
- Energy: alert when you check in = good. Profound lethargy OR sudden restlessness = not good.
- Breathing: easy at rest = good. Elevated rate or effort at rest = not good.
- Vomit, stool, water intake — any changes.

CALL THE REGULAR VET (within 24 hours, non-urgent)
- A second vomit at any point tonight or in the morning.
- Won't drink water for more than 12 hours.
- Diarrhea starting overnight (any kind).
- Refuses the bland breakfast but otherwise seems "off."
- Mild lethargy or appetite loss that hasn't resolved by tomorrow afternoon.
- You just want reassurance — that's a valid reason to call in the morning.

SEEK URGENT / EMERGENCY CARE NOW
- More than one vomit tonight, or vomiting that keeps recurring.
- Blood in vomit (fresh red or coffee-ground looking).
- Hard, swollen, or painful belly; "praying" posture; won't let you touch the abdomen.
- Pale, gray, blue, or sticky/tacky gums.
- Collapse, profound lethargy, or sudden unresponsiveness.
- Labored or rapid breathing at rest.
- Bloated-looking abdomen with dry heaving and no production (GDV/bloat — time-critical).
- Refusing water >12 hours plus dehydration signs (skin tenting, sunken eyes).
- Bloody or black/tarry diarrhea.
- Anything that just feels "wrong" and you can't explain.

- One vomit, kept water sips down.
- Sleeps normally; alert when you check.
- Pink gums, soft belly, easy breathing all night.
- Eats bland breakfast, holds it; stool normal by tomorrow.
- Back to normal routine by tomorrow afternoon/evening.

Study 3 — moisture × timing at fixed T+20s

Setup
- Same quarter sheet (11 × 15), fresh, taped into 3 vertical bands (~5" wide each).
- Same pigment and brush as 10/5. Tilt ~20°, two water cups, paper towel.
- Phone timer. Lock T+20s as the sole timing variable — do not vary it across bands.

Protocol
1. Band A (control). Lay the wash, wait exactly 20 s, re-enter with matched-wetness brush (your normal softening-pass load). Set the brush down. Walk away from the band — no return, no matter what the sheen does after.
2. Band B (wetter). Lay the same wash, wait exactly 20 s, re-enter with the same load plus one quick dip in clean water and a single light towel touch (drip off, not pulled). Set the brush down. Leave it.
3. Band C (drier). Same wash, wait exactly 20 s, re-enter with the same load plus one firm pass on the paper towel (pulls ~10% moisture). Set the brush down. Leave it.

Cap at ~12 minutes. Three bands, single pass each, zero reworking.

What you're reading
- Band A is the sanity check. If it doesn't match your 10/5 T+20s result, your brush load drifted and the comparison breaks — note it and repeat before trusting B and C.
- Band B: a softer edge, possibly a faint halo. Compare directly to your 10/5 T+18s band.
- Band C: a narrower softening with a hint of seam. Compare to your 10/5 T+22s band.

If wetter mimics earlier and drier mimics later, timing and brush moisture are interchangeable levers. That gives you a 2D safety margin instead of a 2-second window: if you land at T+19s, a slightly drier brush pulls the result back toward controlled; if you land at T+21s, a slightly wetter one does the same.

Why this stays a study
Three identical bands, no subject, no composition, single pass per band, no return after dulling — same rules as Study 2. The deliverable is a comparison sheet, not a painting.

One thing to keep from 10/5: don't go back to "fix" any band once the sheen dulls. If a band blooms or seams, that's data, not a problem to scrub out.

This is a drain-side issue, separate from the supply-side drip we dealt with before. The dishwasher pumps into the same drain line as the sink, so when that line is partially blocked, dishwasher discharge has nowhere to go and comes back up into the basin. The good signs: no sewage smell, no cabinet water, and no other fixtures affected — that points to a local clog (P-trap, dishwasher air gap, or the wall lateral just past the trap) rather than a main-line backup.

IMMEDIATE CONTAINMENT
  1. Leave the dishwasher off. Do not start another cycle. Every cycle pumps more water into a drain that can't take it, and the next one will reproduce the backup.
  2. Minimize sink use. The cold tap is fine for drinking water — that's supply-side and unrelated — but anything that goes down the drain should be the smallest practical amount, and you should bail the basin afterward rather than relying on it to drain.
  3. Bail the standing water now by hand into a bucket or the toilet, not back into the same drain. This prevents overflow, lets you see whether new water drains at all, and makes any further step safer.
  4. Leave the under-sink cabinet doors open and put a dry towel on the cabinet floor for the next few hours so any new moisture shows up immediately.
  5. Supply valves don't matter for this issue — it's a drain problem — so leave the cold-water shutoff in whatever position it was. Don't touch the dishwasher's local supply shutoff either; that's only relevant to supply-side leaks like the July 17 one.

WHAT NOT TO POUR DOWN THE DRAIN
  - No chemical drain cleaners (Drano, Liquid-Plumr, similar). With standing water in the trap the chemical just sits there, can splash back at you when you plunge or open the trap, corrodes the metal slip nuts, and is a hazard for whoever services the line.
  - No boiling water on top of standing water in a porcelain basin — thermal shock can crack the sink, and the water won't reach the clog anyway since it's just adding to what's already pooled. Boiling water is only useful once the basin is empty and you suspect a grease clog near the trap.
  - No baking-soda-then-vinegar "miracle" combo. The fizz is mostly CO2 happening inside the trap; it doesn't generate enough force or heat to clear a real clog, and it can push water back at you when you remove the trap.
  - No "flush it through with more water" instinct. If the line is slow, extra water just pools.

SAFE DIY, IN ORDER, ONLY IF YOU WANT TO TRY
  1. Check the dishwasher air gap first — that's the small chrome cylinder on the countertop near the sink, if your kitchen has one. Unscrew the cap, lift out the cap and the small plastic piece inside, and clear any gunk. This is the single most common cause of dishwasher-into-sink backup and takes about 30 seconds.
  2. If there's no air gap or it's clear, try a cup plunger (flat-bottom orange kind, not the flanged toilet kind) on the slow basin, with the other basin sealed with a wet towel and the sink overflow taped shut with a damp cloth. Six to eight firm plunges, break the seal, repeat up to 3 times. If you feel no resistance or the water rushes back, stop — the clog is past the trap arm.
  3. If plunging doesn't help, clean the P-trap: bucket underneath, hand-loosen the two slip nuts (channel locks only if needed), drop the trap, clear gunk, check that you can see open pipe past the trap arm into the wall, reassemble with the same rubber washers hand-tight plus a quarter turn. Run hot water and check for drips before walking away.
  4. If the trap is clear and the basin still drains slowly after a minute, the clog is in the wall lateral. Stop DIY and let maintenance handle it as a drain-line issue.

STOP DIY AND CALL MAINTENANCE / EMERGENCY LINE IF
  - Sewage smell appears at any point.
  - Other fixtures start backing up (tub, toilet, washing machine drain).
  - Water appears under the dishwasher or anywhere in the cabinet.
  - Slip nuts on the trap are corroded, cracked, or won't budge.
  - You see standing water past the trap arm when you remove the trap — that means the clog is downstream and the bucket under the trap won't catch it.

WHILE YOU WAIT FOR MAINTENANCE
  - Dishwasher: stay off. This is the most important rule for the next 24 hours.
  - Kitchen sink: minimal use; bail rather than drain when you can.
  - Washing machine and bathroom: fine to use — they're on separate drains. If the washing machine drain slows or you hear gurgling in the bathroom, that's a bigger-line issue and the emergency line is warranted.

She handled it correctly. Closing a blank page on a current iPhone with nothing typed is the safe outcome — there's nothing on the device beyond routine Safari hygiene.

Why this is low-risk
  The blank page means the kit didn't render its credential or card prompt before she closed. Nothing was typed, so nothing was stolen. A drive-by compromise of a current iPhone through Safari isn't a realistic threat. The only thing a blank render can leave behind is a passive cookie or fingerprint, which is harmless on its own.

Device (~1 minute)
  1. Settings → Safari → Clear History and Website Data.
  2. Settings → Safari → confirm Fraudulent Website Warning is on.
  3. Settings → General → VPN & Device Management — should be empty; remove anything unfamiliar.
  4. Settings → General → Software Update — confirm up to date.
  No reset, no antivirus. iOS doesn't need either.

Accounts (verify, don't churn)
  1. No password changes needed — she typed nothing.
  2. If she has a USPS Informed Delivery account, sign in at usps.com (typed, not clicked) and rotate that password. Smishing kits cycle, and the background threat is password reuse, not the tap itself.
  3. Apple ID sanity check: Settings → [her name] — confirm only her devices appear.

Reporting (~3 minutes)
  1. Screenshot the message with the sender number and timestamp visible.
  2. Forward the text/screenshot to 7726 (SPAM).
  3. Email the screenshot to spam@uspis.gov.
  4. File a brief report at reportfraud.ftc.gov.
  5. Block the sender number, then delete the message.

Monitoring (light habit, 30 days)
  1. Watch for any "new sign-in" or "password reset" emails she didn't initiate — that's the only signal that matters.
  2. Glance at bank/card statements weekly for unfamiliar small charges.
  3. Optional: a free fraud alert via any one of the three credit bureaus — only if she wants extra cushion.

Bottom line: she did the right thing. The steps above are hygiene, not remediation.

  - "Once per crank revolution" is the signature of a single bad or stiff link, not generalized wear
  - After overnight rain, the most common cause is water washing lube out of one link or getting into cable housing near the bottom bracket

IF YOU RIDE HOME
  - Stay out of the two affected gears; ride one gear higher or lower instead
  - No hard pedaling at any point — cruise effort only
  - Take the flattest line home; avoid headwinds and hills
  - If the skip becomes audible under cruising (not just hard pedaling), pull over and bus the rest of the way

IF YOU TAKE THE BUS
  - Bike is fine at the covered rack overnight; or bring it inside the office and bus with it
  - Best play: bus home, inspect tonight in good light with the bike flipped or on a stand

OFFICE INSPECTION (eyes and hands only, no tools)
  1. Hand-rotate pedals BACKWARD slowly through the whole cassette — listen for clicks, feel for a link that doesn't flex smoothly
  2. Slow-rotate specifically in each of the two affected gears and one gear on either side; a bad link usually shows up as a tight spot you can feel
  3. Eyeball the cable housing entry at the bottom bracket and the derailleur — water pooled there after rain causes exactly this pattern
  4. Look at your most-used cassette cogs for hooked or shark-fin teeth — you'll recognize them from May

SHOP-REPORTING SEQUENCE (in order)
  1. "Chain skips once per crank revolution under hard pedaling in the two middle rear gears. Silent under light pedaling. Developed after the bike sat covered overnight in rain. Other gears clean, shifting crisp, brakes fine."
  2. "Cassette and chain were replaced May 2024 — roughly five months and [your mileage estimate] ago."
  3. "Please check for a stiff or damaged chain link first — that's the most likely cause given the rain and the once-per-revolution rhythm."
  4. "If that's not it: cable housing for water ingress, derailleur hanger alignment, cassette wear on those specific gears, chain wear with a gauge."
  5. "Tell me what you find before any work. I want to approve the repair and the cost."

ONE CONSTRAINT WORTH FLAGGING: even if the ride home goes fine, do NOT ride the bike to work again until a shop has actually looked at it. This kind of skip can become sudden loss of drive under stop-and-go traffic, and you've now had it happen across two replacement cycles — that pattern deserves a real diagnostic, not a workaround.

ASSESSMENT — IS THE ENZYMATIC CLEANER SENSIBLE?

Yes, with realistic expectations. Enzymatic/bacterial drain cleaners use live cultures plus enzymes (lipase, protease, amylase) to digest organic buildup — exactly the kind of grease + food residue that dishwasher discharge leaves in the line. They are safe for PVC, copper, and cast iron; safe with municipal sewer and septic; and they do not preclude a chemical opener later if maintenance chooses to use one. They do not clear solid obstructions, inorganic scale, or a fully blocked line, and they work on hours-to-days timescales, not minutes.

Fit for your situation:
- Likely clog = organic buildup downstream where the dishwasher drain tees into the line, which fits "drains slowly alone, backs up on dishwasher discharge."
- Enzymes target that directly, but a slow drain that actively backflows on appliance discharge is on the edge of what overnight enzymatic treatment can resolve in 3 days.
- Bottom line: enzymes are a sensible, low-risk best-effort interim measure — not a substitute for the Tuesday visit. Expect incremental softening at best; the maintenance tech is still the fix.

PRODUCT-LABEL CONDITIONS THAT MATTER

1. Product type. Pick a true enzymatic/bacterial product, not a hybrid with caustic. Reliable options: BIO-CLEAN, Green Gobbler, InVade Bio Drain, Drain Gel, EcoLogic. The label should list bacterial strains and/or enzymes (lipase, protease, amylase). Avoid products where sodium hydroxide or sulfuric acid is in the first three ingredients — that is a chemical opener with a marketing coat of "plus enzymes."

2. Contact time. Most labels specify 6–8 hours or "overnight when the drain will not be used." This is the binding constraint with a dishwasher in the picture. You cannot get a real contact window if anything is running into the drain for hours after dosing.

3. Standing water. Labels typically tell you to bail out standing water first so the bacteria sit in the line, not float on top of sink water. If the label is silent, this is still the right practice.

4. Activation temperature. Warm — not hot, not boiling. Boiling kills the bacteria. Many labels say "follow with ~1 cup of warm water." Anything close to boiling partially or fully neutralizes the dose.

5. Dose and frequency. Most call for a measured amount (typically 2–4 oz liquid, or 1–2 tablespoons powder) per treatment, repeated nightly for up to a week. One dose rarely clears a developed clog.

6. Compatibility. Do not mix with chemical drain opener, bleach, ammonia, or acidic cleaners (some bathroom/kitchen sprays) — any of these will kill the culture. Since you have not used chemical opener, you are starting clean; keep it that way.

7. Pipe and sewer. Universally safe for all pipe materials and for municipal sewer (your building). No label concern, but worth confirming on the bottle.

8. Shelf life. Bacterial products expire. Check the bottle is in date; dead culture is useless culture.

INTERIM GUIDANCE THROUGH TUE OCT 15 (9:00–11:00)

Dishwasher — leave it OFF through the visit.
This is the single most important call. Every cycle adds warm soapy, food-laden water that both worsens the clog and washes out any enzyme dose before it can act. One dishwasher run between now and Tuesday can effectively undo a night of enzyme treatment.

Sink — minimal, careful use.
- Cold or lukewarm water only. No hot/boiling (kills enzyme if dosed; also already on your do-not-pour list).
- Bail standing water into the toilet before each enzyme dose.
- Skip the garbage disposal if you have one — extra mechanical agitation and water flow work against the treatment.
- Nothing greasy, no coffee grounds, no food scraps, no starches (rice, pasta water) down the drain.
- Hand-wash in a basin, then bail the wash water into the toilet, not the drain. Paper plates are a reasonable 3-day workaround.

Enzyme protocol (if you go ahead).
1. Pick a true enzymatic product (above).
2. Each evening through Mon Oct 14: bail standing water, dose per label, follow with ~1 cup of warm (not hot) tap water, leave the drain unused overnight.
3. In the morning, run only a brief cold trickle to clear the line, then resume minimal sink use.
4. Repeat nightly. Realistic expectation: incremental improvement, not full clearance, before Tuesday.

Watch-items — call maintenance / the emergency line if any of these appear.
- Sewage smell from any drain (kitchen, bathroom, washing-machine standpipe) — clog has moved to a shared downstream line.
- Any other fixture backing up (bathroom sink, tub, washing machine) — main-line signal.
- Water under the dishwasher, under the sink cabinet, or around any supply/drain connection.
- Standing water visible past the trap arm when you peek with a flashlight — confirms the clog is in the wall lateral, not the local trap, and is exactly where the dishwasher ties in.
- Slow drain getting worse despite overnight treatments.

Prep for the Tue Oct 15 visit.
- Clear under-sink storage so the tech can reach the P-trap and supply lines.
- Keep the cabinet dry; doors can stay cracked open overnight if you want to monitor.
- Note the pattern for the tech: does the sink back up immediately when the dishwasher discharges, or only after a few minutes? That timing helps localize the clog for them.
- Confirm building access / entry instructions if you will not be home the whole window.

One last thing: the maintenance tech may have a preferred product or treatment. When they arrive Tuesday, it is fine to ask whether the enzyme you used is compatible with whatever they plan to do — most enzymatic residues are, but a one-line confirmation costs nothing.

SAFER TEMPORARY SETUP: use Kibo's flat collar for the walk.

The harness clasp is the failure point, not the rest of the harness. A hairline crack that opens under hand pressure will fail under sudden load (leash lunge, squirrel, startled turn) — and a failed clasp means a loose dog mid-walk, which is the actual hazard. A small carabiner does not solve this; it adds a second load-bearing part with its own failure mode (gate opening under force, metal-on-plastic leverage that can worsen the crack). For a short, calm neighborhood walk the collar is the right call: it is a separate, undamaged system that you have already confirmed fits.

QUICK COLLAR-FIT CHECK (do this in 30 seconds before you clip the leash):
  • Two-finger test: you should be able to slide two fingers flat between the collar and the back/sides of Kibo's neck. One finger = too tight. Three+ = too loose and a backer can slip it.
  • Position: sits high on the neck, just behind the ears, not sliding down toward the trachea. A flat collar rides correctly when the ID tags hang at the chest, not under the chin.
  • Hardware: slide the buckle with your thumb — same hand-press test you just did on the harness clasp. If the collar's buckle has any flex, cracking, or clicks loose under thumb pressure, stop and use a different collar (a backup martingale, a slip lead held by hand for one walk, etc.).
  • Tags: confirm the ID tag and rabies tag are on the collar, not just the harness. If his tags live on the harness only, transfer them now or split between collar and harness before the walk.
  • Clip the leash to the collar's D-ring, not a tag ring — tag rings are not load-rated.

HARDWARE ASSESSMENT OF THE DAMAGED HARNESS (decide now whether it is repairable or trash):
  • If the clasp is a snap-buckle (the two halves click together): a hairline crack in the housing is retire-now. These are not user-serviceable; the spring/latch geometry depends on the housing being intact, and plastic fatigue cracks grow with each flex cycle. Do not reuse, even with a carabiner backup.
  • If the clasp is a side-release buckle (the kind you pinch to open): check whether the crack is in the male tab, the female housing, or the bridge between them. A crack across the bridge is also retire-now. A small crack confined to the tab itself is theoretically patchable with a wrap, but on a load-bearing part this is still not worth the risk for a dog that pulls even occasionally.
  • Either way: park the harness. Do not put it back on Kibo even for a "quick" trip until it is replaced.

REPLACEMENT CHECKLIST (when you shop, whether in-store or online):
  • Closure type: a metal side-release buckle (like a heavy-duty backpack clasp) is more durable and field-repairable than a plastic snap-buckle. If you stay with plastic, look for acetal or metal-reinforced plastic, not standard ABS.
  • Connection point: a welded D-ring on the back, not a stitched-on webbing loop, for the leash attachment.
  • Webbing: check the chest and girth straps for fraying at the adjustment slides — that is where harnesses usually fail before buckles do.
  • Fit test on Kibo: two-finger snug at the chest strap (it should not slide over his shoulders when he steps back), four-finger room at the neck opening so he can lower his head without choking, and the back D-ring should sit centered between his shoulder blades, not off to one side.
  • Consider a backup option: if you walk at dawn or in low light often, a harness with reflective trim or a small clip-on light on the collar is worth adding now.

FOR THIS AFTERNOON:
  1. Transfer tags to collar if they live on the harness.
  2. Two-finger fit check on collar.
  3. Thumb-press the collar buckle to confirm it is solid.
  4. Short calm walk on collar only, leash to the D-ring.
  5. Order or pick up a replacement harness tonight — do not delay past a couple of days; the cracked harness goes in the recycling, not the "maybe still good" drawer.

If anything about the collar feels off when you do the thumb-press test, tell me what you see (brand, buckle type, where it flexes) and I will tell you whether it is safe for one walk or whether to use a hand-held slip lead as the backup instead.

Here's the framework. Three parts: (1) what the two documents mean and how they relate, (2) what to keep on file, (3) what to ask billing.

1. RECONCILIATION

The EOB is the authoritative source for what the contract says you owe. Your patient responsibility per the EOB is $35.00, not $95.00.

The portal's "insurance pending" status is the key clue: the clinic's ledger has not yet applied the insurer's 10/09/2024 payment. The $95 is a pre-posting balance and should drop to $35 (or lower if a copay was collected at the visit) once the EOB is posted.

The $60 gap between portal ($95) and EOB ($35) is almost always one of three things:

  a. The clinic has applied the insurer's $110 payment but not yet the contractual write-off (the difference between what they billed and the $145 allowed). If the billed charge was, say, $205, the math is: $205 billed - $110 paid = $95 portal; once they apply the write-off ($205 - $145 = $60 adjustment), the balance drops to $35.

  b. The clinic has not applied the $110 payment at all yet, and the $95 is an interim figure. Less common, but possible if they posted an estimated allowed amount before the EOB arrived.

  c. A copay was collected at the visit and is sitting in an unapplied batch — same pattern as your Mom's $40 Visa payment in April. In that case the corrected balance after posting would actually be lower than $35.

In every scenario the action is the same: do not pay the $95, and do not pay $35 either, until the portal reconciles to the EOB and you have written confirmation of the corrected figure.

2. IDENTIFIERS AND RECORDS TO COMPARE AND RETAIN

Keep all of the following side by side before you call:

  - EOB (the document itself): save the PDF or photo. You need the claim number, date processed (10/09/2024), allowed amount ($145), plan paid ($110), patient responsibility ($35), and any remark codes.
  - Clinic portal screenshot: balance ($95), "insurance pending" status, and the date you captured it. The status and date matter — if it changes after you call, you want a record of what it showed.
  - Service line: date of service 10/02/2024, "ankle reassessment," and the CPT code if the EOB shows one. You'll match this to the clinic's itemized statement.
  - Insurer identifiers: member ID, group number, claim number, payer name and customer-service phone (on the EOB).
  - Provider identifiers: clinic name, billing entity name (often different from the clinic), provider NPI or tax ID if listed on either document.
  - Date-of-visit receipt: anything you were given on 10/02/2024 — copay receipt, card slip, or visit summary listing what was collected at check-in. This catches scenario (c).
  - Call log: date, time, billing rep's name, reference or ticket number for the call.

If you don't yet have the billed (gross) amount — the charge before the $145 allowed figure — request it from billing. It's the missing piece that lets you see scenario (a) directly.

3. QUESTIONS TO ASK BILLING

Call the clinic's billing department, not the front desk. Have the EOB and portal screenshot in front of you. Specific questions, in order:

  1. Has the insurer's EOB for date of service 10/02/2024, processed 10/09/2024, been received and posted to the ledger? If yes, on what date and under what reference or trace number?
  2. If not posted, when do you expect it to post, and why is the portal balance still showing $95 with status "insurance pending"?
  3. What is the billed (gross) charge for the 10/02/2024 visit, and what CPT code was billed? (This lets you see the contractual adjustment.)
  4. Walk me through how you got from billed charge to the $95 patient balance — line by line: billed, contractual adjustment, insurance payment, any copay applied, prior balance.
  5. Was a copay or any patient payment collected at the 10/02/2024 visit? If yes, has it been posted, and is it sitting in an unapplied batch?
  6. Per the EOB, my patient responsibility is $35.00, not $95. Please reconcile and tell me what the corrected balance will be and the date it will post.
  7. Are there any other services, prior balances, or separate claims on this account included in the $95?
  8. Please send me an itemized statement showing the CPT code, billed amount, contractual adjustment, insurance payment, and patient balance for 10/02/2024.
  9. Please provide written confirmation (patient portal message or letter) of the corrected balance before I make any payment.
  10. What is your reference or ticket number for this call?

If they say they haven't received the EOB: give them the claim number from the EOB and ask them to re-claim or trace it via the payer ID. Do not pay $95 in the meantime.

If they insist the $95 is correct and won't walk through the math: ask for the billed amount and contractual adjustment. If those don't reconcile to the EOB's $35, ask for a supervisor or escalate in writing through the patient portal.

After the call, save the itemized statement, the corrected-balance confirmation, and the reference number. Pay only after the portal shows the EOB-based balance and you have written confirmation of the figure.

Everything else that could mimic or mask the symptom has been checked and ruled out (derailleur in tolerance, hanger straight, wheels seated, brakes clear), so the skip can be attributed to the chain/cassette pair rather than to adjustment. Doing chain-only would repeat the false-economy call the shop warned about back in May — a fresh chain on hooked sprockets typically just skips differently.

One side note worth filing: 0.75% chain wear in roughly five months since the May replacement is on the aggressive side. It's not wrong, but if it shows up this fast again, the culprits are usually a damp/gritty commute without routine wipe-and-lube, or a chain that arrived slightly stretched from the factory. Worth drying and re-lubing the new chain on a tighter cadence this time.

Pickup test before you commute (5–8 minutes, parking lot or quiet block):

1. Static indexing — with the bike on a stand or being walked, click through every rear cog up and back down. Each shift should land in one click with no hesitation, grinding, or extra click. Specifically stop on the middle sprockets where the skip was; they should hold cleanly under hand-spin.
2. Standing load — on each of those middle sprockets, stand and put firm (not max) force through 15–20 pedal strokes. Listen for any tick, slip, or sudden forward jerk of the cranks. Quiet and round is a pass.
3. Launch — from a near-stop in a middle sprocket, accelerate firmly as if at a traffic light. The drivetrain should engage instantly with no ratcheting.
4. Brake sanity — at low speed, pull each lever firmly. Lever should feel solid, no rubbing, no pull-to-bar.
5. Loaded loop — one lap around the block at normal commuting cadence, including one short hill or a simulated climb in a middle gear.

Pass criteria: all shifts land in one click, no tick/skip under standing or launch load, brakes firm. If any gear ticks or slips under load in step 2 or 3, do not commute on it — back to the shop. The road test the shop ran is good evidence, but doing steps 2–3 yourself with your own effort is what confirms the fix holds for your pedaling style.

Quick read on what's in front of you: the rotation toward the left armpit is a meaningful signal, not just cosmetic. A chest strap is supposed to sit centered on the sternum, about 2–3 inches behind the front legs, and ride slightly UP toward the throat when leash pressure is applied. When it slides sideways into the armpit, it stops doing that job and starts doing a different one — pressing into soft tissue under sustained load. The 10-minute calm indoor test is far less demanding than an outdoor walk (no distractions, no pulling, no lateral movement, less duration), so what you saw is likely a floor, not a ceiling. The flattened fur line without redness tells you the strap was pressing hard enough to displace fur, just not long enough to inflame skin yet.

Two possibilities, and you can distinguish them indoors before any outdoor exposure:

Possibility A — adjustable-fit problem (fixable):
  - The chest strap had too much slack at the buckle, so it found the path of least resistance (the armpit gap)
  - Tightening so it sits "just-snug" (two fingers, not loose, not compressing) keeps it centered
  - Repositioning the slider on the chest webbing puts it in the right zone for Kibo's 25.5" frame
  - At 25.5" on a 24–32" rated harness, you may simply need the strap near its tightest setting

Possibility B — shape mismatch (return):
  - No amount of strap shortening keeps it centered on the sternum
  - It migrates back toward the armpit on every test regardless of tension
  - The harness's chest-strap geometry doesn't match Kibo's chest taper
  - Common when a harness is "one-shape-fits-most" with broad adjustability but a deep or narrow chest

Safe indoor fit test (10 minutes, calm conditions):

  1. Re-fit from scratch. With Kibo standing squarely (not sitting or slumping), slide the chest strap so the buckle sits centered on the sternum, 2–3 inches behind the front legs. Adjust so two fingers fit flat under the strap at the chest with light leash tension — not loose, not compressive.

  2. Mark the starting position. Put a small piece of masking tape or a fabric-safe dot on the webbing where it crosses the centerline of his chest. This is your reference point.

  3. Lift test. With Kibo standing still, apply gentle forward leash pressure (mimicking a walk). The chest strap should rise slightly toward the base of the throat. If it pulls backward toward the armpits or twists on its axis, that is already a fail — stop the test, do not proceed outdoors.

  4. Walk test (5 minutes, indoors). Normal pace, mild turns, one or two sit/down transitions. No pulling, no distractions. Watch the tape marker.

  5. Re-check at 5 and 10 minutes:
       - Marker stayed within ~1 inch of the sternum centerline → adjustable fit, keep this harness
       - Marker drifted toward the armpit even at the tightest non-riding-up setting → shape mismatch, return
       - Chest strap is now lying in or touching the armpit fold → return regardless of cause

  6. Fur and skin check at the end:
       - No fur line, no flattening in the armpit zone → continue to next step
       - Flattened fur line anywhere on the chest or sternum → harness geometry is wrong for Kibo, return
       - Any flattening specifically under the armpit → return, do not retry

  7. Slower follow-up (only if step 5 passed): a second indoor session of 15 minutes with mild leash resistance (a gentle "come" pull a few times). If the strap holds center through this, the harness is safe to introduce outdoors on a short, low-distraction walk. If it migrates under real leash tension, return.

Decision rule, stated flatly:
  - Fix and keep: strap holds center under both lift test and walk test, no fur flattening, two-finger snug throughout
  - Return before any outdoor use: strap migrates to armpit regardless of adjustment, fur flattens in soft-tissue zones, strap twists on its axis, or chest strap pulls backward instead of upward under leash pressure

A note on the previous cracked-clasp episode: since this is the replacement harness and you haven't confirmed the buckle type, do the buckle thumb-press and twist check on this one too before the fit test — press the closed clasp firmly with your thumb and twist 90° in each direction. If there's any flex, creaking, or partial opening, that is independent grounds for return regardless of how the fit test goes.

Short version: the rotation is not yet a return verdict, but it is not yet an outdoor-walk pass either. Run the test above. If the strap holds center with two-finger snug tension, you have an adjustable fit. If it migrates on its own, the shape is wrong for Kibo and you want this resolved before any outdoor exposure, not after.

STUDY 4 — Two-wash sky, wash-angle ladder

Goal: hold the one-firm-blot, T+20s, one-touch controls fixed; vary only the wash angle (interpreted as board tilt, since that is the standard lever — the brush stroke itself stays horizontal along the horizon line in both panels).

Format: two adjacent sky panels on a single fresh 11x15 quarter sheet, divided by a vertical tape line. Each panel ~7.5x5 or so.

Materials
- Fresh 11x15 quarter sheet, taped vertically into two panels
- One primary sky pigment (ultramarine reads cleanly; cobalt if you want softer)
- Optional horizon wash: a tiny amount of dilute burnt sienna or quinacridone gold, kept on a SEPARATE brush and cup so the sky color stays clean
- Two water cups (one per pigment if using two)
- #10 or #12 round brush (or one per cup)
- Paper towel
- Phone timer
- Board with adjustable tilt (books, foam wedge, etc.)

Conditions (only difference between panels)
- Panel A: shallow tilt, ~8 to 10 degrees
- Panel B: steeper tilt, ~18 to 22 degrees

Procedure (identical for both panels except tilt)
1. Tape sheet to board. Set board to the panel's assigned tilt.
2. Load brush fully with sky pigment.
3. Lay a continuous graded wash from the top of the panel down to about two-thirds. Heavier at top, fading downward. Keep moving so a bead carries without flooding.
4. While the upper wash is still wet (within the bead window), lay a horizon band along the bottom third — either a dilute second sky-color wash or the dilute burnt sienna on a clean brush. This is the second wash.
5. Mark T=0 the moment the horizon band finishes.
6. At T+20s: rinse the softening brush, then ONE FIRM blot on the towel. Pick it up and go immediately.
7. ONE TOUCH ONLY: a single horizontal sweep along the line where the upper sky meets the horizon band. Do not retrace.
8. Do not return to the panel after the sheen dulls. No fixing, no scrubbing.
9. Photograph when fully dry. Note the actual tilt you used.

Held constant (the controls from the prior exercise)
- T+20s timing
- One firm blot on the towel before the touch
- Single touch, no return strokes
- Same brush, same pigment ratio, same water ratio, same load size
- No rework after sheen dulls

Vary only
- Board tilt between Panel A and Panel B

What to record per panel
- Bead-loss time after the horizon wash was laid
- Whether the horizon band crept upward, pooled at the tape edge, or stayed put
- Whether the one-touch produced a controlled transition, feathered too broadly, or left a visible seam
- Any blooms (should be zero if the no-return rule held)
- The actual tilt angle you used
- A side-by-side photo of the dried panels

Predicted outcomes
- Shallow tilt (~10°): bead lives longer; horizon band may creep further up into the sky wash; the one-touch softening likely produces a narrower, more controlled gradient.
- Steeper tilt (~20°): wash pulls down faster; bead disappears sooner; horizon band stays more localized; the one-touch softening likely produces a slightly broader gradient with more natural haze — but if too steep, the wash may run and pool at the bottom edge.

Why this design
- It is a study, not a painting — comparison is the goal, product is not.
- The two-wash structure gives the one-touch a real meeting line to soften, not a synthetic test stroke.
- Holding every other variable constant means any difference between the panels traces cleanly to tilt.

Two fields, reported separately, never merged or substituted:

1. Summed human agent-minutes = 49 minutes
   - Agent A: 09:18–09:38 = 20 min, plus 09:48–10:02 = 14 min → 34 min
   - Agent B: 09:30–09:45 = 15 min
   - Total: 34 + 15 = 49 min
   - The 09:30–09:38 overlap (8 min) is counted for both agents. Concurrent work means two people are laboring in parallel, so each agent's minutes are summed independently. The overlap is not a double-counting artifact — it reflects that during those 8 minutes two human agents were actively working the case.

2. Elapsed customer-blocked time = 52 minutes
   - 09:10 (customer reports blocker) → 10:02 (customer confirms cleared) = 52 min wall-clock
   - This is the duration the customer was blocked from progressing, regardless of how many agents were working, whether they overlapped, or whether any work happened at all during the interval.

Why the automated acknowledgement at 09:10 contributes zero to both:
- Summed human agent-minutes measures human labor only. An automated ack is system-generated; no human agent minute is expended.
- Elapsed customer-blocked time measures wall-clock duration of the blocking interval. The ack is instantaneous and does not shorten or lengthen the interval; including it would conflate "time we noticed" with "time the customer was blocked."

Overlap treatment is asymmetric on purpose:
- In agent-minutes, overlap is additive (each agent's labor counted separately) — this is a labor measure, not a customer-experience measure.
- In elapsed customer-blocked time, overlap is invisible — the customer's clock runs at wall-clock speed whether one or three agents are on the case; counting agent overlap into customer-blocked time would conflate staffing with the customer's actual wait.

The two fields answer different questions and are reported in separate columns. They will not sum, average, or substitute for each other in any downstream analysis or brief.

Short answer: the fit is largely working, but the belly-strap position is a real gap that may or may not be fixable by adjustment. Here's the read on why, then a focused indoor test that gives a clean keep/return signal.

Why the belly strap is the only open question
The two-finger rule at neck and chest, the clasp under pressure, the no-rotation result over ten minutes, and the absence of redness or abrasion all line up — this is a meaningfully better shape than the last harness on every axis you tested. What's left is geometric, not comfort. The fit card's two-inch clearance puts the strap behind the shoulder/leg crease where forward leg swing won't ride up into the armpit. At one finger-width (~½ inch) the strap is sitting right at the leading edge of the leg fold. On a calm indoor walk that's fine; once you add pace, leash tension, or a turn, that's where rotation and fur-line flattening start.

What adjustment can and can't fix
You cannot slide the belly strap backwards on the dog by loosening it — its position is set by where the side panels meet it (the Y-front geometry). Loosening only lets the strap hang lower; it can drop a little further from the armpit but it can't move behind the leg crease on its own. What can shift the strap rearward is slightly shortening the chest/neck straps so the whole harness sits a touch higher and the join point pulls back. There's a narrow window where this works before the chest/neck become too tight and you trade one problem for another.

Indoor test — keep or return
  1. Refit from scratch: chest strap centered on the sternum, two-finger snug at neck and chest, belly strap at its current hole.
  2. Loosen the belly strap by roughly one inch of webbing and let it settle for a minute. Note the new position relative to the front-leg crease.
  3. If loosening alone drops the strap to ~2 inches of clearance, you're done with this step. If it doesn't, shorten the chest strap by about half an inch and re-check — this is the move that can pull the join point back.
  4. Place a small piece of tape on the strap at the leg-crease reference line.
  5. Ten-minute indoor walk at normal pace, including two mild leash tugs (forward and a gentle left turn). No outdoor yet.
  6. Re-check at 5 and 10 minutes. Look at the tape and at the leg crease.

Decision rule
Keep the harness if, after step 3, the strap sits at ~2 inches of clearance at rest AND the tape holds within roughly half an inch of that position through the walk with no ride-up into the armpit and no fur flattening. Return it if clearance stays at one finger-width even after the chest-strap shortening, if the strap migrates forward into the armpit during the walk, or if you had to crank the chest strap tight enough to break the two-finger rule. The harness shape is wrong in any of those cases, and outdoor forces will only magnify it.

STUDY 5 — Lower-bead wicking frequency at 35°

Context
  Prior run: 15° wash was even; 35° wash produced cauliflower because the lower bead grew heavy enough to feed back into the drying wash during the T+20s softening pass. Instructor guidance: isolate wicking frequency, do not change brush moisture again.

Question
  At 35° tilt, how often must the lower bead be lifted to prevent cauliflower feed-back, while the brush condition, T+20s, and one-touch softening pass stay fixed?

Held constant across all cells
  - Board tilt: 35°
  - Brush prep: one firm blot on a clean towel before laying
  - Same brush, pigment, water ratio, load size
  - Laying pass: one continuous stroke top→bottom, ~15s
  - Softening pass: one touch at T+20s, no rework
  - No contact after the softening pass; no return after sheen dulls

Variable (the only thing that changes between cells)
  - How often the lower bead is wicked during the 0–18s window
  - Note: wicks are NOT counted as the "one-touch" — that one-touch refers only to the T+20s softening pass

Wick method (same in every wicking cell)
  - Fold a fresh paper towel into a clean corner
  - Touch the corner to the very bottom of the bead for ~1s, lift straight down
  - Do not drag into the working wash; rotate to a clean corner if it loads up

Cells — 4 horizontal strips on one 11×15 quarter sheet, same session

  A — control: never wick                         (replicates instructor's failure)
  B — wick every 15s: one wick near T+15s         (just before softening pass)
  C — wick every 10s: two wicks ~T+8s and ~T+16s
  D — wick every 5s:  three wicks ~T+5/10/15s

Pre-flight
  - Photograph the sheet before starting
  - Confirm 35° with a protractor or pre-marked wedge
  - One calibration swatch on scrap to confirm pigment/water/load matches the prior 35° run

Reading the cells (after full dry, side-by-side)
  - Lower edge: clean / soft gradient / cauliflower bloom
  - Mid-wash evenness: matches the laying pass, or disrupted
  - Compare Cell A to instructor's cauliflower reference
  - Compare Cell D to the 15° even reference

Expected direction (for design only, not for confirmation)
  - A → cauliflower (replicates the 35° failure)
  - B → bead may still build enough to feed back at T+20s
  - C → bead stays moderate; lower edge likely clean
  - D → bead stays light; cleanest lower edge; check that wicking did not streak the working wash

Stopping rules
  - Stop a cell if a wick lifts a visible streak into the working wash (touch was too high or too long)
  - Stop if any cell goes chalky at the lower edge (over-wicking pulled pigment out of the wash)
  - If Cell C is clean, you have your answer; Cell D then asks "is more wicking necessary, or just more frequent than C?"

What this answers
  - The minimum wick frequency at 35° that prevents cauliflower without disturbing the wash
  - Whether wicking frequency alone — no brush-moisture change — fixes the 35° failure

What this does NOT answer (deferred to later)
  - Whether a different bead-removal method (dry-brush pickup, absorbent strip at the lower edge, etc.) is cleaner
  - Whether 35° is worth keeping at all once wicking is dialed in — separate decision once frequency is known

Here is a safe sequence. Goal: ≥27 GB free (need +8 GB minimum; target +10–12 GB for buffer). Order matters — verify the backup before deleting anything, and never move company Helio data into a personal account.

PHASE 0 — BACKUP VERIFICATION + PRE-UPDATE SNAPSHOT (~15 min)
  Do this first. A backup from Oct 19 is only "successful" if you can actually read the files back.

  1. Verify the Oct 19 backup is reachable and complete
     - Open it via Time Machine / your endpoint backup client
     - Confirm the timestamp is Oct 19 and the set is marked complete (no failed/partial indicators)
  2. Take a fresh pre-update snapshot of what you're about to touch
     - Either a new full backup if time permits, or at minimum: copy Desktop + Downloads + cache dirs to a snapshot folder on the backup drive, e.g. pre_update_2024-10-26/
  3. Build a checksum manifest of the Helio Desktop exports
     - mac: shasum -a 256 ~/Desktop/* > manifest_desktop_2024-10-26.txt
     - win: Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 (Get-ChildItem $env:USERPROFILE\Desktop\*) | Out-File manifest_desktop_2024-10-26.txt
     - Save the manifest on the BACKUP DRIVE, not on the laptop you're about to clean
  4. Spot-check: pick 2–3 Helio files, confirm the backup's copies have matching checksums. If anything mismatches, stop and refresh that file in the backup before proceeding.

PHASE 1 — RELOCATE INACTIVE HELIO DESKTOP EXPORTS (~15 min)
  Active analyses stay on the laptop. Only move what is truly archive-eligible.

  1. In Helio, for each Desktop export, confirm status:
     - Active / in-progress / being edited → KEEP on Desktop, do not touch
     - Completed, exported, shared, or stale → eligible to archive
  2. For archive-eligible files:
     - Copy to the backup drive into Helio_archive_2024-10-26/
     - Verify the copy with a checksum comparison
     - Only after checksums match: delete from Desktop
  3. Update the manifest with the new archive location for each moved file
  Expected gain: depends on how much of the 9 GB is stale. If most of it is inactive, you can reclaim most of it.

PHASE 2 — CLEAR VIDEO-CALL CACHES (~5 min)
  These are regenerable; canonical recordings live on the company Zoom/Teams/Meet servers.

  Quit the apps first, then delete:
    - Zoom (mac):   ~/Library/Application Support/zoom.us/
    - Zoom (win):   %AppData%\Zoom\
    - Teams (mac):  ~/Library/Caches/com.microsoft.teams/  and  ~/Library/Application Support/Microsoft/Teams/
    - Teams (win):  %LocalAppData%\Microsoft\Teams\
    - Chrome/Meet:  clear site data for meet.google.com in Chrome settings
  Reopen each app, confirm sign-in and a quick test call; caches rebuild automatically.
  Expected gain: ~6 GB.

PHASE 3 — PROCESS DOWNLOADS (~10 min)
  Sort by date. Anything ≥30 days old that isn't an active work artifact is a candidate.

  1. Flag files still in active use (opened in the last 30 days, referenced by current projects)
  2. Move the rest into Downloads_archive_2024-10-26/ on the backup drive
  3. Verify non-reproducible files with checksums
  4. Delete from Downloads
  Expected gain: ~4 GB if nothing is in active use.

PHASE 4 — TOP-UP IF STILL SHORT (~5 min)
  Use only if you haven't crossed 27 GB yet.

  - Empty Trash / Recycle Bin (often holds what you've already "deleted")
  - System temp: mac → ~/Library/Caches/   win → %TEMP% and C:\Windows\Temp
  - Browser caches for non-work profiles
  - Old app caches (Spotify offline, etc.) — only if not actively used
  - Mail caches and large attachments (not the messages themselves)
  - mac: thin local Time Machine snapshots: tmutil thinlocalsnapshots / 1g 1
  - win: Disk Cleanup → "Clean up system files"

PHASE 5 — VERIFY AND UPDATE
  1. Re-check free space: must be ≥27 GB
  2. Quick sanity:
     - Helio opens one active analysis cleanly
     - One video-call app starts and signs in
     - A file copied into the new archive folder opens from the backup drive
  3. Then run the OS update

GUARDRAILS — DO NOT
  - Run the OS update before Phase 0 is complete
  - Delete any Desktop file before its checksum is confirmed against the backup
  - Move company Helio exports to a personal cloud account (personal Dropbox/Google Drive/iCloud) or unencrypted personal USB stick
  - Move files into a OneDrive/iCloud/Dropbox-synced folder unless that sync target is the company-managed one
  - Pause or kill the backup client mid-write during Phase 0
  - Clear caches of an actively-running call app — quit first

RECOVERY FALLBACKS
  - If any Phase 1 file looks uncertain, leave it on Desktop and reclaim space elsewhere first — you can always return to it
  - If backup verification fails, stop the cleanup and fix the backup before continuing. Running an OS update with a broken backup is the worst ordering
  - If a Helio export on Desktop turns out to be active after you archived it, restore from pre_update_2024-10-26/ and re-derive the working copy

EXPECTED RECLAIM IF ALL PHASES RUN
  Phase 1 (partial — only inactive): 4–8 GB
  Phase 2 (full):                    6 GB
  Phase 3 (full):                    4 GB
  Phase 4 (top-up):                  1–3 GB
  Total:                            15–21 GB above the current 19 GB free, well past the 27 GB threshold.
