HALLOWEEN EVENING SETUP FOR KIBO
================================

PHASE 1 — BEFORE 5:30 PM (DO THIS NOW)
---------------------------------------

Leashed potty walk
  - Keep it brief: out, potty, high-value treat on return, back inside
  - Goal is to empty his bladder so he's not restless later, NOT exercise
  - Use the back/side yard if you have one; avoid the front porch entirely
    so he doesn't associate the front area with the upcoming doorbell noise

Pre-stage the candy handoff so the doorbell never rings
  - Place a large bowl of candy on the porch step (visible from the walkway)
  - Painter's tape sign facing the path: "TAKE ONE — HELP YOURSELF"
  - Porch light ON so trick-or-treaters see it's a participating house
  - Front entry / hallway lights OFF so the house looks like nobody's home
  - If your doorbell has a chime volume control or smart "quiet hours" mode,
    silence the indoor chime now. Even one chime through the walls can
    re-trigger him.

You should not need to answer the door once between 5:30 and 9:30.


PHASE 2 — KIBO'S ZONE (REAR BEDROOM, BY 5:30 PM)
-----------------------------------------------

Setup the room before you bring him in:
  - Curtains drawn
  - White noise on before he enters (fan on low-medium is fine, or a
    white-noise app at a steady volume — not classical music yet, just
    neutral masking sound)
  - His normal bed in a corner away from the door, with one familiar
    soft item (a blanket or shirt that smells like Sam or you)
  - Water bowl within reach but not where he'll knock it over
  - Room slightly cool if you can
  - Door closed (or baby-gated, depending on whether his stress calms
    faster with you visible or fully separated — you know which)

Bring him in with a high-value treat and a calm voice. No fuss. Treat on
the bed, settle him, stay in the room with him.

Lights: dim in this room only. Rest of house can stay normal.


PHASE 3 — DURING THE WINDOW (5:30–9:30 PM)
-----------------------------------------

Your job is to be a calm, present anchor. Not active, just present.

Every 20–30 minutes
  - Glance at him, confirm he's resting or calmly alert
  - Note breathing rate, lip-licking, whale-eye, posture
  - Don't force interaction; a quiet "good boy" is fine

Every 15–20 minutes
  - Offer 1–2 tbsp of water. Don't push if he refuses once.

Calming tools, in order of escalation only
  1. Your presence + low voice + room setup (the baseline)
  2. A scatter of high-value treats on his bed — sniffing and licking
     are self-soothing
  3. Long-lasting food toy (frozen Kong, lick mat with peanut butter or
     wet food) — best deployed during the peak 6:30–8:00 rush so he has
     an active outlet
  4. Calming wrap if you have one and he's tolerated it before — ONLY
     if he escalates past steps 1–3. Not preemptive.

Do NOT
  - Force him onto his bed
  - Grab his paws, pick him up, or restrain
  - Coddle in a way that telegraphs your own anxiety (fast voice, hovering)
  - Take him outside during peak doorbell traffic

If a stray knock gets through (it shouldn't, with the bowl)
  - Soft voice, treat tossed near him, slow pet on the chest — not over
    the head. Keep the room the same; don't react as if it's an event.


PHASE 4 — POST-WINDOW (9:30 PM ONWARD)
--------------------------------------

  - Wait an extra 30 minutes past 9:30 for stragglers, then bring the
    candy bowl inside
  - Kibo stays in the bedroom; don't move him yet
  - When Sam gets home, low-key homecoming — no doorbell, no excited
    greeting at the door (Sam can text you from the driveway and come
    in through the garage or side door)
  - Don't move Kibo to his normal spot until he's been calm for at
    least 20 minutes and the doorbell threat is fully gone
  - Optional: brief slow leashed walk if he wants it and he's decompressed.
    Skip if he's still clingy or shut down.


EMERGENCY VET — CALL RIGHT AWAY IF YOU SEE ANY OF THESE
=======================================================

These are action thresholds, not "wait and see." If in doubt, call your
emergency vet line and describe what you're seeing.

1. ESCAPE BEHAVIOR WITH INJURY RISK
   - Scratching at the door, window, or walls until you see blood
   - Chewing through a baby gate, crate, or door frame
   - Breaking teeth or nails trying to get out

2. SELF-INJURY
   - Broken nail (bleeding or hanging)
   - Cut or raw patch on paws, nose, or gums from frantic pawing/rubbing
   - Any bleeding you can't immediately stop with gentle pressure

3. VOMITING (not just drooling)
   - Especially repeated vomiting or vomiting with bile
   - He can't keep water down for more than 30 minutes

4. DIARRHEA WITH BLOOD OR SUSTAINED DIARRHEA
   - More than 2–3 episodes in an hour, or any visible blood

5. SUSTAINED PANTING THAT WON'T SLOW
   - Open-mouth, sides heaving, despite cool room + quiet + 30+ minutes
     of the full calming setup. This is heading toward heat-stress /
     dehydration territory.

6. TREMBLING OR SHAKING THAT DOES NOT STOP
   - Body-wide shaking that continues even when the room is quiet and
     he's in your lap / on his bed. Persistent, not just a startled jolt.

7. DISORIENTATION
   - Staring into space, not tracking you, eyes glazed
   - Doesn't recognize you or respond to his name
   - Bumping into furniture like he can't see

8. UNCOORDINATED MOVEMENT
   - Stumbling, falling, can't stand normally, swaying
   - "Walking" while lying down (paddling)

9. COLLAPSE OR LOSS OF CONSCIOUSNESS

10. SEIZURE ACTIVITY
    - Paddling legs, loss of bowel/bladder, rigid body, loss of awareness

11. SUDDEN AGGRESSION (PAIN/FEAR RESPONSE)
    - Snapping or biting when you approach or touch him, when he has
      never done this before. This is a panic-pain signal, not
      misbehavior.

What "calm but stressed" looks like (NOT vet triggers):
  - Pacing that eventually settles
  - Lip-licking, whale-eye, ears back
  - Panting at a moderate rate
  - Hiding behind furniture or under the bed
  - Refusing one or two water offers but accepting the next
  - Shaking briefly at a loud sound then recovering

These are expected for a noise-anxious dog and are what the setup is
designed to manage.


PRE-STAGE THESE NOW (BEFORE 5:30)
=================================

  - Regular vet's after-hours emergency line (in your phone, written
    down too in case phone dies)
  - Nearest 24-hour emergency vet clinic — name, address, phone, and
    driving route (you may not be at your sharpest later)
  - Kibo's carrier accessible, not buried under a pile
  - A towel or blanket you can wrap him in for the car (scent + calm)

When you call, tell them:
  - Halloween doorbell triggers
  - Known noise/storm anxiety history
  - No vet-prescribed situational medication (you ruled this out, which
    is the right call for tonight)
  - Specific symptom + when it started + what you've already done


ON THE MEDICATION DECISION
==========================

Your call to not improvise is the right one. OTC options (Benadryl,
melatonin, CBD) are not interchangeable with vet-prescribed situational
anxiolytics, and dosing errors or wrong formulations can make things
worse. If tonight's setup isn't enough and you're seeing the vet-trigger
signs above, the vet visit is the answer — not a guess at home dosing.

If this becomes a pattern (Halloween, July 4, storms), the right next
step for a future plan is a vet consult for a prescribed situational
med, ideally trialed on a calm day so you know how he responds. Not
tonight.


ONE LAST THING — YOUR STAMINA
=============================

Four hours alone in a dim room with a stressed dog is real work, even
when it's going well. Build in small comforts for yourself:
  - Water and a snack in the room
  - Phone on silent but charged
  - A book or something quiet — your boredom is Kibo's calm signal

You've done this protocol before (1/4/24 fireworks, the 11/17 storm).
Tonight is a known shape. The bowl on the porch does most of the heavy
lifting before you even start.

Here's how the two plans compare on what the Plan Finder pages actually show, plus what to pin down before Mom enrolls.

  The numbers, stripped to premiums vs. drugs

  Hill Country Rx Value
    Annual premium alone: $28.90 × 12 = $346.80
    Annual drug deductible: $590
    Stated annual estimate: $1,284
    Implied drugs + deductible in that estimate: $937.20
    Caveat: this $1,284 assumes preferred mail order. Her neighborhood pharmacy is standard under this plan, so filling locally will cost more than $1,284.

  Lone Star Saver Rx
    Annual premium alone: $36.40 × 12 = $436.80
    Annual drug deductible: $545
    Stated annual estimate: $1,236
    Implied drugs + deductible in that estimate: $799.20
    Caveat: this $1,236 is at her neighborhood pharmacy, which is preferred under this plan.

  The known annual difference

  On the published numbers, Lone Star Saver Rx is $48/year cheaper ($1,236 vs. $1,284). The mechanics: Lone Star's drug-and-deductible portion is $138 lower, which more than offsets its $90 higher annual premium. So the $48 advantage is real on paper, but it's conditional — Hill Country's $1,284 only holds if Mom moves routine refills to preferred mail order.

  The pharmacy tradeoff (the bigger story than $48)

  Hill Country rewards mail order. To hit $1,284, she'd need to send maintenance prescriptions to a preferred mail-order pharmacy. Her current neighborhood pharmacy is standard, so filling there will run higher than the estimate. Realistic options: switch refills to mail order and use her local pharmacy only for urgent or short-fill needs, or accept a higher-than-$1,284 annual cost at her current pharmacy.

  Lone Star keeps her current routine. Her neighborhood pharmacy is already preferred, so the $1,236 estimate reflects how she already fills. No behavior change required.

  Practical implications to weigh:
    - Mail order works well for stable, chronic meds on a fixed schedule. It works less well for as-needed meds, new prescriptions, and anyone who values walking into a pharmacy and talking to a pharmacist.
    - Same-day starts (a new antibiotic, a sudden need) typically require a local fill, which under Hill Country means paying standard rather than preferred pricing.
    - If she travels or spends time away from home, mail-order continuity helps; if she doesn't, the local-pharmacy convenience may matter more than $48.

  What to verify before enrolling (priority order)

  1. Formulary match for every medication Mom takes. Tier placement matters more than the headline premium. Pull each plan's 2025 formulary and look up each drug by exact name and dose. A medication moving from Tier 2 to Tier 3, or onto a prior-authorization requirement, can swing annual costs by hundreds — far more than the $48 difference.

  2. Vaccines. Part D covers ACIP-recommended adult vaccines (shingles, Tdap, RSV, etc.) at $0 when in formulary and in-network. The Plan Finder estimates generally include only the medications entered, not vaccines. Confirm coverage and the pharmacy it can be obtained at.

  3. As-needed medications. Often not in the estimate. Look each one up in the formulary by tier and add it in manually based on how often she actually refills it.

  4. Preferred-pharmacy network for 2025, for both plans. The 2025 ANOC already warned that Hill Country's preferred network is changing. Confirm her specific pharmacy's 2025 preferred status using each plan's 2025 pharmacy directory, not the third-party comparison page. A pharmacy that was preferred in 2024 may not be in 2025.

  5. Copays and coinsurance after the deductible. Get each plan's Summary of Benefits and look up the actual copay by tier (Tier 1 generics, Tier 2, etc.) at preferred retail and at mail order. The estimates are averages — actual copays could differ.

  6. Distance to the 2025 out-of-pocket cap. The 2025 Part D cap is $2,000. If Mom's actual drug spend approaches that, both estimates become irrelevant — once she hits $2,000, covered Part D drugs are $0 the rest of the year.

  7. Last 12 months of Explanation of Benefits statements. The best predictor of next year's spend is this year's actual spend. Pull her 2024 EOBs and total her drug costs, then compare that figure against each plan's estimate.

  8. Star ratings. CMS publishes star ratings for each plan. A 5-star plan has a special enrollment window outside Open Enrollment, which is useful as a fallback if she enrolls now and wants to switch later.

  9. Low-Income Subsidy (Extra Help). If Mom's income is limited, Extra Help can drop the premium and deductible substantially. Confirm eligibility before deciding — it can change the comparison entirely.

  10. Medicare Prescription Payment Plan. New for 2025; lets her spread out-of-pocket costs monthly. Doesn't reduce total cost, but helps cash flow if her drug costs are front-loaded early in the year.

  Bottom line

  On the published numbers, Lone Star Saver Rx is $48/year cheaper AND keeps her at her current preferred pharmacy with no behavior change. Hill Country Rx Value is cheaper only if she switches routine refills to mail order at a preferred pharmacy.

  Because $48 is small, the decision really hinges on items 1, 3, and 4 above: whether every medication is on each formulary at a reasonable tier, how her as-needed meds and vaccines are covered, and whether her neighborhood pharmacy's preferred status under each plan is actually accurate for 2025. Those should be verified before enrolling, not after.

STUDY 6 — Twenty-second wick interval, duration extension at 35°

Question
  With the 35° angle, one firm blot, T+20s one-touch softening, and one-touch boundary all locked from Study 5, does the 20-second lower-bead wicking interval keep producing a clean lower edge across a longer wash, or does it drift in later cycles?

Locked controls (carried from Study 5)
  - Board tilt: 35°
  - Brush prep: one firm blot on towel
  - Brush, pigment, water ratio, load size: same as Study 5
  - Softening pass: T+20s, single touch, no return
  - Lower-bead wick: dry brush tip touched once to the bead, lifted
  - No rework after sheen dulls

Variable
  Extension of the 20-second wick interval across multiple cycles in one longer wash.

Procedure
  1. Pre-flight, same as Study 5: photograph the sheet, confirm 35° tilt, lay a calibration swatch.
  2. Lay a single continuous wash, paced so the wash reaches roughly 80s before sheen dulls.
  3. At T+20s: one-touch softening pass, then wick #1 at the lower bead.
  4. At T+40s: wick #2. No softening pass this cycle.
  5. At T+60s: wick #3.
  6. At T+80s: wick #4.
  7. Stop the wash at the first sign of sheen dulling, or T+90s, whichever comes first.
  8. Photograph the sheet immediately after stopping.

Per-wick readings, recorded at each cycle
  - Bead position before the wick: lower edge / mid-paint / no bead visible.
  - Wick behavior: clean pull / streak / chalky pull / bead absent.
  - Lower edge condition after the wick.
  - Any backrun starting at the wick site.

End-of-wash readings
  - Lower edge condition.
  - Mid-wash evenness.
  - Seam or cauliflower anywhere on the sheet.

Stopping rules
  - Stop a wick if it streaks the working wash or leaves a chalky edge.
  - If a wick fails, note the cycle number (1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th) and continue the wash without that wick, so you can see whether the next interval still holds on its own.
  - Stop the whole wash at the first sign of premature seam.

Interval integrity rule
  Do not shorten or lengthen the wick interval during the study, even if a bead looks like it needs attention earlier or later than 20s. Record what you see; discuss afterward. This protects the test.

Comparison
  Hold Study 5's "one wick at T+20s, ~30s wash" reference strip on the table while you read the new sheet.
  - Success: every wick pulls like the Study 5 reference; lower edge stays even through T+80s.
  - Partial: first 1–2 cycles match, later cycles drift. Note which cycle broke first.
  - Failure: any wick streaks, chalks, or triggers a bloom. Note which cycle.

Predicted outcomes
  - Likely: interval holds for the first 2–3 cycles, then drifts by the 3rd or 4th wick — paper saturation or a thinning wash may make later wicks either chalky (brush picks up too little) or unnecessary (no bead at the lower edge to pull).
  - Possible: interval holds cleanly through all four cycles.
  - Risk: a later wick streaks because the bead has migrated mid-paint rather than sitting at the lower edge.

Short answer: DISCARD the cooked chicken and rice. RETURN everything else from the cooler to the refrigerator.

Why the chicken and rice cannot be returned, even now:

1. The 2-hour rule applies. Perishable food held at or above 40°F for more than 2 hours total is considered unsafe. Your chicken and rice sat in that refrigerator from 6:00 pm to 8:15 pm Sunday = 2 hours 15 minutes, and during that window the refrigerator was confirmed at 46°F (already above the 40°F danger-zone threshold). Because you do not know the temperature before that first 46°F reading, you cannot rule out the food being in the danger zone for the full 2 hours 15 minutes.

2. Cooked rice is specifically high-risk. Bacillus cereus spores survive cooking and germinate in the danger zone, producing a heat-stable emetic toxin that is NOT destroyed by reheating. No amount of rewarming can make held rice safe once it has spent that long above 40°F.

3. Smell and appearance are explicitly excluded from this decision. Even if the rice and chicken look and smell fine, the time-temperature history alone is enough to require discard under the conservative standard you set.

4. Subsequent safe cold holding does not reset the history. The fact that the chicken and rice have been at ≤38°F in the cooler since 8:15 pm Sunday does not undo what already happened. Pathogens and the B. cereus toxin that may have formed during the warm period are still present.

Why everything else in the cooler can go back to the refrigerator:

Those items (milk, raw meat, other leftovers) were moved into the cooler at the moment the 46°F reading was first taken, before they had accumulated 2 hours above 40°F. From that point on they have been held continuously at ≤38°F, which is verified. They never crossed the 2-hour danger-zone threshold, and their cold chain was preserved through the fan repair. The refrigerator is now verified at 37°F with the new fan cycling normally, so it is safe to receive them.

Recommended handling sequence:

1. Put the chicken and rice in a bag, tie it off, and place it in a lidded or lined trash bin. Do not dump it loose where an animal or child could reach it.

2. Wipe the inside of the cooler with hot soapy water, then sanitize with a fresh dilute bleach solution (about 1 tablespoon unscented liquid bleach per gallon of water). Let it air-dry.

3. Sanitize the refrigerator shelves, drawers, and door handles the same way. The interior was above 40°F for an extended period, so a wipe-down is worthwhile before restocking.

4. Return the remaining cooler contents (milk, meat, other leftovers) to the refrigerator. Put the most perishable items (raw meat, fish) on the coldest shelf, typically the lowest one.

5. Leave the thermometer on the middle shelf and confirm a 37–38°F reading now, then again in 1 hour and again in 4 hours. The freezer should hold near 0–1°F.

6. Use up the older leftovers first over the next 1–2 days; they have already had temperature stress in their history even if they stayed within the 2-hour window.

If you want a single written rule to follow: any food whose time above 40°F cannot be proven to be under 2 hours gets discarded; anything that has been held continuously at ≤38°F (cooler) or is now in a verified ≤38°F (refrigerator) is fine.

Reconciliation sequence for the one CSV whose Desktop mtime is 4 minutes later than its managed copy. Treat this as a controlled surgery, not a cleanup. Hold every prior guardrail: do not start the OS update, do not delete any copies, do not let the sync client re-overwrite the newer version.

Hard rules for this reconciliation
  - Do not delete the Desktop original yet. You will need it as the source of truth until the final gate passes.
  - Do not run the OS update yet. The 27 GB free-space gate still applies.
  - Do not let the sync client overwrite the newer CSV. If the client uses mtime-based or "managed wins" logic, a naive replace can be reverted on the next cycle.
  - Do not move the Desktop file out of its folder. Copy first; move only after checksum is verified in the managed folder.

R0. Quiesce the sync client (no writes happening)
  - Let the current sync cycle finish (status = idle / "Up to date").
  - Disable scheduled sync, or pause the client, so it cannot start a new cycle mid-reconcile. If your client has no clean pause, that is fine as long as it is idle and you do not touch the managed folder during the next few minutes.
  - Capture: client name, last sync timestamp, scheduled-sync state, and the folder path it is syncing.

R1. Capture pre-state (before you change anything)
  - Record for both copies of the diverging CSV:
      full path, byte size, mtime (with timezone), SHA-256.
  - Also record those three fields for every other file pair under Q4 exports. You are looking for any sibling divergence. The 4-minute one is the visible symptom; there may be more, and you need to find them before step R3, not after.
  - Open the Desktop CSV in Helio (or Excel, or read it with a script) and confirm it parses cleanly. Confirm the row count or a top-line value matches what you remember from the last save. This is your "I did not corrupt the file myself" check.

R2. Stage the newer copy in the managed folder without triggering a sync race
  Preferred path (sync client paused):
    - Copy Desktop CSV -> managed folder as a sibling staging file, e.g. `<name>.csv.new`.
    - SHA-256 the staging file. It must equal the Desktop original byte for byte.
  If you cannot pause the client:
    - Copy Desktop CSV -> managed folder as `<name>.csv.new`.
    - SHA-256 the staging file. It must equal the Desktop original.
    - Use `mv` (same volume) to atomically replace the older managed CSV with `<name>.csv.new`. On the same filesystem, `mv` is atomic at the inode level, so no reader ever sees a half-written file. Verify the staging file is gone after the rename.
  Either way: do not delete the older managed copy directly. The replace path goes staging -> atomic rename.

R3. Verify in place
  - SHA-256 the now-current managed CSV. It must equal the Desktop original.
  - mtime of the managed CSV should now be >= the Desktop original's mtime (rename updates mtime). Record both.
  - File size on both sides must match.

R4. Re-scan for other divergences
  - Walk the entire Q4 exports tree. For every file where managed mtime != Desktop mtime, decide:
      newer on Desktop  -> repeat R2-R3 for that file.
      newer in managed -> copy managed version back to Desktop (rare, but possible if someone edited in the managed location).
  - At the end of this scan, every file pair should have matching SHA-256. Anything that does not is unresolved; do not proceed past the gates until it is.

R5. Controlled sync re-run
  - Re-enable scheduled sync, or trigger one explicit sync.
  - After it reports idle / Up to date, re-SHA every file in Q4 exports. The set must still match what you recorded at the end of R4. If anything flipped back, sync is overriding your changes; stop, capture the discrepancy, and resolve before continuing.
  - Confirm the sync client's last-run timestamp is now later than R3 and shows no error.

R6. Write a reconciliation log
  Save somewhere persistent (the IT ticket, or a notes file outside both folders):
    - Which file diverged, by how many minutes, why you think it happened (saved during sync finalization is the most likely cause).
    - The SHA-256 of the Desktop original and the SHA-256 of the managed file after R3.
    - The timestamp of the post-R5 sync run.
    - The result of the R4 divergence scan (count of files checked, count of divergences found, count resolved).
  This log is what lets future-you trust that the managed folder is the real master.

Gate criteria — all six must be true before you delete Desktop copies and start the OS update
  1. SHA-256 of every file in Q4 exports matches between Desktop and managed. No unresolved pairs.
  2. The previously-newer CSV in the managed folder has the same SHA-256 as the Desktop original. Record both in the log.
  3. Sync client reports idle / Up to date, with a last-run timestamp later than R3, and no error for the folder.
  4. Free disk space is >= 27 GB.
  5. Reconciliation log from R6 is saved.
  6. IT ticket for the original backup-exclusion question is updated with the reconciliation result (whether it is now closed or still open). Do not silently drop this; if the ticket is still open, the OS update does not change that.

After all six gates pass, in this order:
  - Delete the Desktop originals.
  - Run the post-deletion sync and confirm it reports idle.
  - Then start the OS update.

If any gate fails, stop at that gate. Specifically:
  - If R5 shows sync is reverting your changes, do not delete the Desktop copies — they are still the master. Capture the failure in the log and the IT ticket.
  - If R4 finds a divergence you cannot explain (managed newer than Desktop with no obvious cause), do not overwrite. Keep both copies, log the pair, and surface it to IT before deleting anything.

Two pieces, both conservative because the wash held and that is the more valuable result.

SALVAGE FOR THE LIFTED EDGE (current sheet)

The wash is intact and fully dry, so the rule is: do not introduce water and do not press with a finger. Both will either reactivate pigment in the wash or embed the lifted fibers into the surface.

Step 1 — dry coaxing first. Take a clean, completely dry soft mop or 1/2-inch or larger natural-hair quill brush. With the sheet flat and supported on a clean board, stroke very lightly parallel to the lifted edge, working from the wash side outward, never across the edge. The goal is to lay the fibers back down without disturbing them, not to remove them. One or two passes only.

Step 2 — kneaded eraser pass if any rough nap remains. Dab (do not rub) a clean kneaded eraser along the strip, lifting straight up between dabs. This pulls loose fiber pills off without touching the wash.

Step 3 — decide based on the painting's future use.
  - If a final shadow or glaze wash is planned near this edge: re-mask just inside the damage line with fresh low-tack tape, so the new wash stops a hair short of the rough strip.
  - If the painting is essentially done: leave the strip alone and trim 2–3 mm off the lower edge with a fresh #11 blade and a metal ruler to create a clean border, OR rotate the sheet in the mat so the strip falls outside the mat opening.
  - Do not paint over the strip. The rough fibers will grab pigment unevenly and the damage will read more strongly than it does now.

Skip any "barely damp brush" coaxing this time. The 2023-12-03 protocol allowed it as an option because the card was small and the wash was simple. Here the longer steep-angle wash has more pigment in the lower edge, and any moisture will backrun into it.

TAPE-REMOVAL TEST (varies only tape handling, holds all wash controls fixed)

Setup — keep everything identical except the removal.
  - Substrate: three or four scraps cut from the same pad as the painting, same orientation of grain.
  - Wash: run the full protocol on each scrap — the longer steep-angle wash, 20-second bead-wicking interval, one firm brush blot, one-touch edge boundary. The wash has to be present because it changes the moisture and surface condition right next to the tape line.
  - Drying: let each sheet dry fully, same flat-dry time as the painting.
  - Tape: same brand, same roll, same width, applied the same way, same dwell time before removal.

Variables to test, one per sheet, applied only to the lower edge:

  Sheet A — control. Pull tape straight up at ~90 degrees, same speed as the failed pull. Expectation: replicate the fiber lift so you have a baseline.
  Sheet B — low-angle pull-back. Pin the sheet flat with one hand (or a clean weight at the corners, not over the wash). With the other hand, pull the tape back over itself at roughly 10–20 degrees from the paper surface, slow and steady, keeping the peel line advancing rather than yanking. Direction of pull: parallel to the edge, not across it.
  Sheet C — low-angle pull with rigid support. Same as B, but the sheet sits on a clean glass or smooth board so there is no flex at all during the pull.
  Sheet D (optional) — warm the tape briefly with a hairdryer on low or a warm palm for 20–30 seconds before the low-angle pull. Tests whether softening the adhesive reduces grab.

Evaluation, done blind if possible (label the backs only):
  - Run a clean dry fingertip lightly along the edge where the tape was. Any fibers that catch or lift are a fail.
  - Look at the edge raking light from a low angle. A clean release reads smooth; a lift reads as a fuzzy or rippled line.
  - Check the wash just inside the tape line for any dulling or backrun from handling.

Reading the results:
  - If only A lifts: low-angle pull is the fix. Switch to that and stop testing.
  - If A and B both lift but C is clean: rigid support is the missing variable — pull the painting off the table onto a board before removing its tape.
  - If B is clean but the wash dulls near the edge: the low-angle pull is good, but slow down the pull further or check that your supporting hand is not damping the paper.
  - If D is the only clean one: warmth is doing the work, and you have a pre-removal step to add.

Once you have the winning combination, retest it once on a fresh scrap before applying to a finished painting. The point of this test is to confirm the fix on your specific paper and tape, not just to trust the principle.

One note on the wash result: 20-second wicking holding steady across the longer steep-angle passage is the more important finding from this session, since the bead timing was the risk you were testing. File that as confirmed, keep the protocol, and isolate the tape failure separately so it does not contaminate future wash tests.

LOWEST-RISK OPTION: buy a small bag of his exact regular kibble locally
  Same food = no transition stress, no new GI variables, no prep. This is what I'd pick if any version of it is available, even at a small upcharge. The only "risk" is the very small chance of a formula tweak between batches within the same brand, but that's still vastly lower risk than introducing an unfamiliar protein, fiber source, or recipe.

Plan A — exact kibble found:
  Sunday evening: feed normally as usual
  Monday breakfast: last of the current bag (measure carefully so you don't run short earlier)
  Monday lunch onward: switch to the locally bought bag — same food, fresh bag, no transition
  Tuesday afternoon: shipment arrives; blend a little new-shipment kibble into the last of the local bag over 1-2 meals to ease between batches

Plan B — only same-brand or similar kibble available:
  Same brand, same protein is fine (chicken-to-chicken, for example)
  Avoid: novel proteins (salmon, lamb, duck), grain-free, "weight management" or high-fiber formulas, anything rich
  Pick the bag with the shortest, simplest ingredient list — chicken as first ingredient, minimal extras

Plan C — bland bridge (only if no acceptable kibble is findable):
  Plain boiled skinless chicken breast + plain white rice, ~1 part chicken to 2-3 parts rice
  No butter, oil, salt, or seasoning
  Portion size similar to his normal meal
  Keep the bridge as short as possible — ideally just 1-2 meals
  Resume kibble the moment the shipment arrives

WHAT TO COVER (Mon breakfast → Tue afternoon):
  Roughly Mon lunch, Mon dinner, Tue breakfast, and maybe Tue lunch — about 3-4 meals depending on exactly when Tuesday afternoon is. If the shipment arrives earlier in the afternoon, you may only need bridge food for Mon lunch through Tue breakfast.

VET CALL SIGNS during the bridge:
  - Vomiting, especially repeated or with blood
  - Diarrhea, especially bloody, black/tarry, or profuse/watery
  - Refusal of the bridge food for more than 12-24 hours, or refusal of water
  - Signs of dehydration (sticky gums, skin tenting when you lift the scruff)
  - Lethargy, hiding, or unusual quietness
  - Pale gums, hard or swollen belly, labored breathing
  - Anything suggesting he got into something he shouldn't have (food wrapper, toxin, foreign object)

Since he's healthy going into this and the gap is short and controlled, vet intervention is unlikely. The one realistic risk is a sensitive-stomach reaction to even a small formula change — if that happens, drop straight to the bland bridge and call the regular vet if symptoms don't resolve within 12-24 hours.

POST-VALVE-WORK FLUSHING — Tue 11/12, after the outage

What you are describing (cloudy cold tap, sputtering, no odor, no sediment, normal pressure, no advisory) is almost always entrained air from the valve work. Air is harmless but it has to be worked out of the lines before you trust appliances, ice, or the tap for drinking. Air clears fastest at high-flow fixtures with aerators removed.

1.  COLD SIDE FIRST. Do not push the hot side hard yet — running the tub or a long hot draw pulls from the water heater tank and can stir up sediment that has settled there. Clear cold first.

2.  OPEN VALVES SLOWLY. Crack each faucet to a steady moderate stream rather than full blast. A rapid reopen of a shut main sends a pressure surge through the lines, and through your older shutoffs — including the under-sink cold shutoff that was repaired May 6. Watch that paper towel.

3.  KITCHEN COLD TAP — the one that was cloudy.
    - Unscrew the aerator at the tip of the spout (hand-twist, or pliers wrapped in a rag). Set it aside.
    - Run cold at a moderate stream for 5–10 minutes. Run the sprayer hose too if you have one.
    - When the stream is fully clear with no bubbles and no spurting, rinse and reinstall the aerator.

4.  BATHROOM COLD TAPS — same drill: aerator off, 3–5 minutes each, reinstall.

5.  TOILETS — hold the handle down for a long flush once or twice at each toilet. The fill valve benefits from a couple of full refills to bleed trapped air.

6.  SHOWER(S) — remove the showerhead if you can (usually hand-twist). Run cold for several minutes. If you cannot remove it, run cold at full flow for several minutes and accept that some sediment may stay trapped in the head.

7.  TUB SPOUT — run cold for a couple of minutes.

8.  LAUNDRY OR MUDROOM COLD TAP, if you have one — same as a bathroom cold.

9.  OUTDOOR HOSE BIB, if accessible — run briefly. Outdoor runs often hold stagnant water.

THEN THE HOT SIDE — gently:

10. Brief hot flush at each fixture (1–2 minutes). You are clearing the short pipe run from the heater to that fixture, not the tank. Do not use the bathtub hot at full blast as a "flush."

APPLIANCES — only after the cold and hot lines run clear at the nearest fixture:

11. DISHWASHER — run empty on a rinse-only cycle (no detergent). Then normal use is fine; skip a heavy cycle for the first regular load.

12. WASHING MACHINE — run an empty rinse or "clean washer" cycle. Then normal use is fine.

13. REFRIGERATOR WATER AND ICE — discard the first 2–3 batches of ice. Run the water dispenser for 1–2 minutes. If the filter is near end of life, swap it now; post-work sediment commonly clogs filters.

14. INSTANT-HOT OR UNDER-SINK FILTER — bypass or don't use until the upstream cold is fully clear. A clogged filter after a main disturbance is common and is not your plumbing failing.

WHAT NOT TO RUN OR USE YET

-  No drinking or cooking from any tap until the kitchen cold runs clear.
-  No dishwasher on a normal cycle yet (step 11 covers this).
-  No washing machine on a normal cycle yet.
-  No ice or water from the fridge dispenser.
-  No filtered or instant-hot tap.
-  No refilling Kibo's bowl from the tap — keep using what you stored.
-  Do not pour the cloudy water down a drain you are already wary of (the Oct 9 slow-drain event). It's just water and air, but no reason to add volume to a marginal drain.
-  Do not crank the under-sink cold shutoff open and closed to "blow out" air. The May 6 repair should be checked, not exercised.

WHEN TO CALL MAINTENANCE OR STOP USING THE WATER

Call Cherrywood property management if any of the following appears:

-  Cloudiness does not clear after 15–20 minutes of real cold flushing. That is sediment, not air.
-  Visible sand, grit, flakes, or rust-colored water at any tap.
-  Yellow, brown, or reddish discoloration anywhere. Air looks white/milky; color means real material.
-  A strong chemical or solvent smell. A mild chlorine smell for a short window is normal after main work; sewer, sulfur, or solvent smell is not.
-  Pressure drops sharply, or pressure is suddenly much higher than normal. A surge can damage the under-sink shutoff you had repaired.
-  Water stops flowing at any fixture that was working.
-  The paper towel under the kitchen cold shutoff gets wet again, or you see any new moisture in that cabinet. The May 6 repair should still be dry.
-  Any new leak anywhere, or water appearing outside a sink cabinet.
-  The property manager issues a boil-water advisory at any point.

If you see sediment, discoloration, odor, or a sudden pressure change: stop using the tap for drinking, cooking, and Kibo; keep using stored water; skip the dishwasher and laundry until cleared. Toilets can keep being used once their refill runs clear — the refill itself is the test that the line is clean.

Quick check-in I'd suggest after you finish step 3: look at the paper towel under the kitchen cold shutoff. If it is still dry, the May 6 repair is holding through the disturbance. If it is wet, that is a separate ticket you already have grounds for — note it and include it when you next contact the property manager.

Short answer: do not ride it. This is the same situation as the February and August cuts — sidewall cut with visible casing and the slit opening under flex means the tire's structural layer is compromised. Even with the tube holding pressure, a sidewall failure can be sudden, and the casing threads you're seeing are the part that keeps the tire from deforming under load. Both prior times the shop confirmed the tire was unsafe and replaced it.

Sequence to get it home / to the shop

1. Mark the cut. Slide a small piece of painter's tape or a sticky note over the cut so it stays clean and easy to point at later. Avoid touching the exposed casing with bare fingers (oils contaminate it; the shop may want to look at it).
2. Deflate fully. Remove the valve cap, then depress the valve stem briefly in short bursts until air is out. If you have a valve core tool, unscrew the core for a faster, more complete dump — catches any chance of the tube unseating through the cut mid-transport.
3. Protect the cut for transport. Wrap the sidewall with a clean rag, paper towel, or a folded ziploc taped over it so the cut doesn't snag on straps, trunk carpet, or the rack.
4. Pick a transport mode:
   - Rideshare / car (easiest): put the whole bike in the back seat or trunk, drive side up or wheel-up. No need to remove the wheel.
   - Transit: roll the bike on, stand it where you can keep an eye on the cut side away from other riders' bikes.
   - If you want to remove the wheel: quick release = flip the lever and unscrew by hand; thru-axle = 6mm hex; axle nuts = 15mm wrench. Mind the rotor if disc brakes — don't let it flex or get bumped.
5. Drop it off or take it in. Same-day is fine since you're not riding on it.

Photos and details to send the shop

- One wide shot of the whole rear wheel so they can see where on the sidewall the cut sits (drive-side vs brake-side, near the shoulder vs mid-sidewall, distance from the bead).
- One close-up of the cut itself, in focus, with a coin or ruler in frame for scale (the ~8 mm reference). Take it with the tire un-squeezed first, then a second shot with a thumb pressing from the opposite side so the slit opens — that's the diagnostic image that shows casing exposure.
- A photo of the tire size and brand markings (look on the opposite sidewall: e.g. 700x32c, manufacturer, model).
- A photo of the rim strip / rim tape area if you can see it, just so they know whether to inspect the rim while it's in.

Short note to send with the photos:

"~8 mm sidewall cut on rear tire, casing threads visible inside the slit, slit opens under flex, tube still holding air as of [time today], wheel appears true, no bulge. Tire is a [size/brand/model] last replaced [date if known]. Tube is [butyl vs latex if you know]. Rim is [alloy/carbon, rim brake or disc]."

That gives them enough to quote a replacement tire (if they need to order) before you arrive, and confirms they should plan to inspect the tube and rim before reassembly.

This matches the familiar shallow-scrape pattern (2023-10, 2023-12, 2024-03, 2024-08), and your description — gravel rinsed free, bleeding stopped, weight-bearing, no swelling or embedded material — fits a wound that should heal cleanly with conservative care. Plan below.

CLEANING (tonight and once daily for 2–3 days)

- Lukewarm plain water or sterile saline rinse over the scrape for 30–60 seconds. The gravel is already out; this is just to flush any remaining grit from the pad edge and the interdigital web.
- Pat dry with a clean cloth or paper towel. Don't rub.
- Inspect all four pads and the webbing between toes — Kibo's previous scrapes have occasionally had a second tiny spot you don't notice until you look.
- AVOID on this wound: hydrogen peroxide, rubbing alcohol, chlorhexidine scrub, essential oils, Neosporin/generic antibiotic ointment, and any dog "antiseptic spray" unless a vet has directed it. These delay healing on pad tissue.
- A thin smear of plain dog paw balm or plain petroleum jelly on the scrape is fine and helps protect against re-licking.

PROTECTION

- A breathable dog sock over the affected paw for the next 24–48 hours is the easiest way to keep it clean and break the lick cycle. From your 2024-09-02 experience: a loose sock is the failure mode — he slipped out and reopened the spot. Make sure it stays on.
- No human Band-Aids, no tight wraps, no damp socks. No cone yet — but have the soft e-collar on hand in case the sock comes off and the licking restarts overnight.
- Indoors you can leave the sock off once the scrape has a dry surface and he's leaving it alone.

ACTIVITY (next 24–48 hours)

- Short on-leash walks on clean, dry pavement only.
- Avoid grass, sand, gravel, mulch, dirt trails, dog park, off-leash, fetch on rough ground, ice-melt/salt, and hot pavement.
- Indoor activity stays normal.

VET-CALL TRIGGERS — any one of these means a call today or tomorrow

- Bleeding that doesn't stop with 5–10 minutes of gentle, steady pressure, or bleeding that restarts after being quiet.
- New or worsening swelling, heat, or spreading redness around the pad or up the leg.
- Discharge (cloudy, yellow, green), foul odor, or increasing moisture from the scrape.
- The scrape gapes when his toes flex, or you can see deeper tissue (fat, fascia) in the wound bed.
- Persistent lameness, refusal to bear weight, or obvious pain when the paw is handled — whimpering, pulling away, snapping.
- Torn, cracked, or displaced nail on that foot, or any new injury to the adjacent pad.
- A fragment still embedded that you can't rinse free.
- Re-licking that reopens the wound despite the sock, or any bleeding through the sock.
- Systemic signs: lethargy, inappetence, fever-warm ears/trunk, vomiting.
- No improvement at all in 48 hours, or worsening at any point.

OVERNIGHT / MORNING CHECKS

- One quick look before bed: is the sock on, is the scrape dry, is he leaving it alone?
- Morning: brief paw inspection, fresh rinse only if he's walked through anything dirty. If the surface looks clean and dry and he's not favoring it, you can drop the sock during the day indoors and resume it for walks.

You're already doing the right things — the absence of swelling, embedded material, and lameness is genuinely reassuring. If tonight stays quiet and tomorrow morning looks unchanged, this should resolve on its own in a few days.

- Paid social: 42/90 = 46.67%

Short interpretation (evidence-safe):

Observed shape. Paid social sits clearly below the other two (46.7%) and below the pooled 60.0%. Organic (65.0%) and partner (73.3%) both sit above pooled, and their point estimates are separated by ~8.3 pp.

Unequal denominators. The eligible populations are 120 / 45 / 90 — organic is 2.7x partner and 1.3x paid social. Partner's rate is the most sample-sensitive (smallest n, widest uncertainty band) and its interval overlaps with organic's; paid social's separation from the other two is the only gap that holds up under that noise. Organic is also the volume backbone — 78 of 153 activations (~51%) and 120 of 255 eligible (~47%) — so its lower rate still drives most of the quarter's activation count.

Descriptive vs. causal. These are channel-of-acquisition cuts, not a randomized channel test. Users self-select into source, and the partner line in particular has previously been inflated by manually assisted accounts (manual setup assistance is not a channel property). The 73.3% partner rate should therefore be read as a descriptive mix of source and assistance, not as evidence that the partner channel produces higher-quality acquisitions than organic. Paid social's gap is the safest descriptive read, but a causal "paid social underperforms" claim needs a holdout or a step-up.

Suggested wording for the readout: report the three rates and the pooled 60.0% together, note organic's volume share, flag partner's small n and the manual-assist confounder, and stop short of ranking channels causally.

"The first sync worked; I'm not sure our lifecycle stages are mapped right."
Sync appears to have fired; the user's doubt is about correctness of mapping, not about whether activation occurred. Sits past v3 — activation has plausibly been met; the friction is downstream quality, not activation itself.

CAUTIOUS SYNTHESIS

The five comments sort cleanly into the three categories you named, and none of them challenge v3.

Authority (off-product, pre-activation). Theme 4 is the only one. The shape is identical to the workspace-admin case in the recent diagnostic (Salesforce-admin approval at 10:41) and to the "different ownership shape / non-standard billing path" shape the HS lifecycle copy already routes to an assisted track. v3 is not implicated — the activation gate is downstream of an org-internal access-policy decision. This is already accommodated in the existing copy architecture and does not require a v3 or message change.

Guidance (within self-serve path). Themes 1 and 2. Both come from users who have done something and don't know whether to keep going, change direction, or stop. Theme 1 is sequencing ("what's next"); Theme 2 is definition ("does this count"). Neither user has reached the connected-and-verified state v3 requires; both are on the path. The risk these surface is that activation is obscured by ambiguity *ahead* of it. A clearer next-action signal and a clearer "this is what counts as activated" signal would address guidance without redefining activation. Copy alone won't fix this — it's a product-surface question.

Product-state (instrument vs. reality). Themes 3 and 5. These are mirror issues on either side of the v3 line. Theme 3 is pre-activation: the checklist hasn't caught up to the team invite. Theme 5 is post-activation: the integration is connected, but the user has no surface that tells them whether the mapping is right. Both are about trust in the product's own status indicators — Theme 3 trust in the checklist, Theme 5 trust in the absence of a validation surface. Note Theme 5 is past v3 and bears on retention/quality, not activation.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT SHOW (explicit non-claims)

- Prevalence. Five signup-survey comments are not a rate. Nothing here supports a claim about how common any theme is in the funnel, in Helio Start, or in the broader base. The strongest defensible statement is "this shape of friction exists." Anything stronger overreads n=5.

- A v3 problem. None of the five comments describe a workspace that connected + verified an integration and was nevertheless treated as not activated, or the reverse. The comments live adjacent to the v3 boundary — three before, one after, one off-path — not on it. No case here justifies moving the line.

- A copy problem. The lifecycle copy architecture already accommodates Theme 4 via the "different onboarding track" branch. Themes 1–3 are self-serve UX issues that an email cannot resolve. Theme 5 is configuration quality, which is out of scope for activation-stage messaging.

- A funnel-failure signal. These are signup-survey comments, not activation-failure signals. Treating them as evidence that activation is broken would conflate survey sentiment with the activation gate and risk moving the goalposts without warrant.

DIAGNOSTIC QUESTIONS THESE THemes RAISE (not changes)

If you want to convert "this shape exists" into something more useful before any v3 or copy decision, three questions are worth answering with better data:

- For Themes 1 / 2: does the product surface a single unambiguous "next action" and a single unambiguous "activated" state, and do users who complete a connector actually encounter them? (Guidance surface.)
- For Theme 3: what is the lag between an action completing and the checklist reflecting it, and does that lag exceed the survey response window? (Instrument latency.)
- For Theme 5: is there a post-activation surface where users can validate mapping correctness, and is it being used? (Post-activation validation.)

Answers to those would inform any later change. None of those changes are implied or warranted by the five comments alone.

STUDY 7 — CLEAN LOW-ANGLE TAPE PULL AT 45° ON FULL DRY PASSAGE

Instructor's directive (verbatim): "Keep the wash exactly as it is. Test the clean low pull on a full passage; don't add heat, change the paper, or alter the bead timing yet."

This collapses the prior four-sheet plan (A control, B low-angle, C low-angle on glass, D heat) into one focused test per the instructor's guidance: the clean low pull alone, at ~45°, on the full successful wash, with heat, paper, and bead timing held for later if needed.

SINGLE VARIABLE
- Tape-removal direction: pull back over itself at ~45° from the paper surface.
- Everything else matches the 11/9 successful longer steep-angle wash.

LOCKED CONTROLS (held exactly as 11/9)
- Board tilt: 35° (as in Study 5/6).
- Brush: same #10 or #12 round used 11/9.
- Pigment: same single pigment.
- Water ratio, load size: same as 11/9.
- Lay: one continuous wash over the full passage (the full length used 11/9, not a strip).
- Brush prep: one firm blot on towel.
- Softening pass: T+20s, single touch only.
- Lower-bead wick: T+20s, dry brush tip, single touch only.
- After sheen dulls: no rework.
- Paper: same pad, do not substitute.
- Tape: same roll/brand as 11/9.
- Tape application: same hand pressure, same direction.
- Sheet support during pull: same as during wash (board, not lifted freehand).

EXPLICITLY EXCLUDED (per instructor — "yet")
- No heat on tape (no hair dryer, no warming by hand or lamp).
- No paper substitution.
- No alteration to bead timing (no extra wicks, no shift in the T+20s mark).

PRE-FLIGHT
- Photograph the full sheet before taping.
- Confirm 35° tilt.
- Confirm brush, pigment, water, and tape match the 11/9 reference.
- Optional calibration swatch on a scrap from the same pad (consistent with prior studies).

PROCEDURE
1. Tape the sheet using the same tape and application as 11/9.
2. Load the brush per the one-firm-blot protocol.
3. Lay one continuous wash over the full passage (full length, not a partial strip).
4. Softening pass at T+20s — single touch only.
5. Lower-bead wick at T+20s — single touch only.
6. No further contact; let the sheen dull on its own.
7. Allow the sheet to dry FULLY before the pull — lay flat in the same orientation; wait past touch-dry to true dry. Record the elapsed time as confirmation.
8. Tape pull (the only variable):
   - Lift a short corner of the tape by hand.
   - Pull the tape back over itself, keeping the peel line at ~45° from the paper surface (not 90° up, not flat along the surface).
   - Direction: low and back across the sheet, not straight up off it.
   - Speed: slow and steady, no jerk.
   - Support: sheet on the board, undisturbed from wash position.

EVALUATION
- Run a fingertip lightly along the lower edge under the wash — feel for any lifted fiber.
- Inspect the same edge under raking light (phone flashlight held at a low angle).
- Photograph the edge close-up after the pull.
- Inspect the wash surface for any dulling, scuff, or disturbance along the peel path.
- Note any adhesive residue left on the paper.

RECORD
- Estimated pull angle (~45° ± 5°).
- Drying time between wash completion and tape pull (to confirm "fully dry").
- Any fiber lift, edge tear, or wash disturbance.
- Side-by-side comparison to the 11/9 reference, where the ~90° straight-up pull lifted a narrow strip of fiber.

SUCCESS CRITERION
- Lower edge clean (no lifted fiber), wash undisturbed.

PREDICTED OUTCOME
- Likely: clean edge. At ~45° back-over-itself, the adhesive rolls along the paper rather than prying up at the line, so the fiber-lift mechanism from 11/9 should not engage.
- Risks to watch: angle drift during the pull (target ~45° ± 5°); wash dulling if the moving tape drags across the wash surface; adhesive residue if the tape is older than expected (out of scope — same tape as 11/9).

NEXT STEP AFTER THIS STUDY
- Clean edge and undisturbed wash → 45° back-over-itself becomes the tape-handling rule for the 35° longer wash.
- Fiber lift persists at 45° → report the result before changing anything else. Per instructor, heat, paper, and bead timing stay held for the next round, not introduced in this one.

The echo is doing real work — and "where anyone who knew me would look" is part of why. Mara didn't just pick a hiding place; she taught one whose whole structure was already an invitation: hidden in plain sight, at a spot anyone trusted could find. The narrator returning the key to that same spot reads as continuity, maybe even a small inheritance. I'd want to honor that before complicating it.

But the lock sits ahead of the placement in the sentence. The narrator locks the gate first, then puts the key back. That's a deliberate sequence: close, then leave the means of access where it can be found. So the gesture isn't "leave the key where Mara taught" — it's "lock the gate, then leave the key where Mara taught." The second half doesn't undo the first.

What I can't settle is whether these belong to the same tradition or two different ones. The text shows us what Mara taught — where to put the key, and the logic of the spot (known, findable, hidden in plain sight). It doesn't show us whether Mara would have locked the gate. So the ending either completes Mara's instruction as she taught it, or layers a deliberate boundary on top of something Mara left more open. *Same surface, but not the same gesture.*

Does the group read the locked gate as part of what Mara taught, or as something the narrator has added on top of it?

A few notes on the choices, in case you want to tighten:

— Opening with the engagement on "where anyone who knew me would look" does two things at once: it honors the other member's reading by treating the invitation as already present in Mara's teaching, and it sets up the complication, because Mara's teaching is about the placement, and the lock is something extra in the ending.
— "I'd want to honor that before complicating it" mirrors the Brixton register — it announces the move so the room doesn't read the complication as a flat counter.
— The sequencing point (lock first, then key) is the load-bearing move. It reframes the ending as a two-step gesture rather than a single one, which is what creates the structural room for both readings.
— "The text shows us what Mara taught… It doesn't show us whether Mara would have locked the gate" is the move that keeps the ambiguity alive. The text supplies half of Mara's practice (placement and the logic of the spot) and is silent on the other half (whether she locked). Naming that silence is what holds the question open.
— *Same surface, but not the same gesture* is meant to clarify the structure without resolving it — the two readings overlap on the literal action but diverge on whether the lock is inherited or added.
— The closing question offers two formulations ("part of what Mara taught" vs "added on top of it") rather than asking which is correct. The structure of the question preserves the tension instead of asking the room to choose.
— If you want it shorter, the most cuttable line is "continuity, maybe even a small inheritance" — it could become just "continuity" and the opening still works. The closing sentence of paragraph 2 ("The second half doesn't undo the first") also restates the sequencing point and could be dropped without losing the argument.

GROUND RULE — DO NOT INFER FOOD TIME FROM THE AIR READING
- The air log (38°F at 10:30, 46°F at 11:15) describes ambient air behavior. It does NOT tell you:
  - When the food crossed 41°F (food lags air; mass, container, location on shelf all change the lag)
  - How long the food stayed above 41°F
  - Whether the food peaked higher than its current probe reading and is now cooling
- For each item, use the PROBE READING as the food temperature at the moment it was measured. Without other evidence, work from the assumption that the food may have been at or above 41°F for some unknown duration up to a conservative ceiling of 4 cumulative hours (the FDA Food Code danger-zone limit). That ceiling is a planning assumption, not an inference about this incident.
- Document, do not estimate. If a time-in-zone is not directly known, write "UNKNOWN" and proceed conservatively.

1. FOOD-HOLDING PLAN

1a. RAW CHICKEN (probe 40°F at unknown time before 11:20, now in walk-in)
- Treat as potentially time-in-danger-zone. Cannot be served raw. Cannot be held to tomorrow's service.
- Path A — use today: cook in the smallest practical batches to a verified 165°F internal in the thickest part (calibrated probe, not touch-test). Hold hot at ≥135°F until plated, OR cool rapidly (135→70°F in 2 hrs, 70→41°F in 4 hrs) and use within 24 hrs of cook time.
- Path B — do not use: discard into a lined, labeled waste bin. Log the discard with weight/quantity.
- Do NOT: rinse and re-use; partially cook and finish later; hold raw for a later service; rely on a future reheat to "fix" it; rely on smell or appearance.

1b. PREPARED VEGETABLE SAUCE, COVERED (probe 42°F at unknown time before 11:20, now in walk-in)
- 42°F probe is above the 41°F threshold. Time-above-unknown. pH/salt/acid unknown.
- Path A — use today: bring to a sustained rolling boil (≥212°F) for ≥1 minute, then hold hot at ≥135°F or cool rapidly and use within 24 hrs.
- Path B — do not use: discard. Log.
- Any fresh garnish or herbs added after the boil must come from a verified-safe source — NOT from the failed reach-in.

1c. FAILED REACH-IN — ALL OTHER CONTENTS (not just the two probed items)
- Every item in the unit at failure is "exposure-unknown." Treat all as quarantine.
- Probe each item with a calibrated thermometer. Group by reading:
  - ≤40°F probe AND a known short exposure (≤2 hrs ambient door-open/closed): may move to the walk-in, segregated, and resume normal hold. Re-probe at 30 min and 60 min to confirm stability.
  - 41°F+ probe OR exposure unknown: same logic as chicken/sauce — cook-to-temp-or-discard per category.
- High-risk categories (conservative — discard unless cooked today to a verified safe internal temp):
  raw poultry, raw ground meat, raw fish, raw shellfish, dairy, cooked starches (rice, pasta), cooked vegetables, cut leafy greens, cut melons, sprouts, raw eggs, soft cheeses.
- Lower-risk categories (probe-verify, then move to walk-in with date/use-first mark):
  whole intact fruits, whole uncut firm vegetables, sealed shelf-stable items, sealed condiments with pH <4.6, hard cheeses.
- NEVER return any item to the failed reach-in until the unit has been cleared for return to service (Section 5).

2. SEGREGATION

- Designate a QUARANTINE shelf/zone inside the working walk-in. Lowest shelf. Away from ready-to-eat foods. Below any raw items that could drip.
- Use a single color of container (red or orange) for ALL quarantined items. Label every container with:
  "QUARANTINE — REACH-IN FAILURE 11/27/2024"
  item name
  probe reading at segregation
  time placed in walk-in
  disposition decision (COOK TODAY / REHEAT TO BOIL / DISCARD)
- Quarantined items physically separated from in-service inventory. No shared utensils or pans. Anyone handling quarantined items must wash hands and change gloves before returning to normal prep.
- Quarantine waste goes to a separate lined bin, labeled "FOOD SAFETY HOLD — DO NOT CONSUME," removed from prep area at end of service and recorded.
- Tag the failed reach-in itself: "DO NOT USE — PENDING REPAIR." Door closed. Plug/breaker left ON only if needed to keep the unit cold during the repair window; otherwise powered down per tech instruction.

3. LOGGING

Use a single sheet (paper or digital) titled "REACH-IN TEMPERATURE FAILURE — 11/27/2024." Capture:

- Header
  - Date, time of discovery, staff name who discovered
  - Reach-in unit ID / location
  - Reason for failure (UNKNOWN — pending investigation)
- Air temperature log
  - All retrievable entries (10:30 = 38°F; 11:15 = 46°F; plus any prior readings from the data logger)
- Food probe log (one row per item)
  - Item name, time probed, probe reading, thermometer ID + last calibration date, action taken
- Movement log
  - Item, time moved, destination shelf/zone, staff initials
- Decisions
  - Per item: cook-to-temp / reheat-to-boil / discard / hold-and-recheck
  - Decision-maker name and time
- Disposition
  - Per item: used in service (with cook/reheat and final verified internal temp) OR discarded (weight/quantity, waste vendor run)
- Repair and verification
  - Tech arrival time, diagnosis, parts replaced, repair-complete time
  - Post-repair temperature log (per Section 5)
- Sign-off
  - Kitchen manager + general manager initials at end of day
- Retain the log per local health code (commonly 90 days minimum for temp logs; longer for any incident with discard or potential service impact).

4. ESCALATION

In order, same day, in real time:

- Now: on-shift kitchen manager / chef de cuisine — in person. Confirm segregation, quarantine zone, and stop-use on the failed reach-in.
- Within 30 min: general manager / owner-on-duty — verbal or phone. They decide whether to bring in a service tech today.
- Same day: refrigeration service tech. Describe the failure mode (air rising from 38→46°F in 45 min, no obvious cause yet) and request checks on compressor, evaporator fan, door gasket, condenser coil, refrigerant charge/level, and any controller/datalogger fault codes.
- Same day: food vendor. If a delivery hit this unit earlier today, pull the receiving log and confirm delivery temperature was in spec. Cold-chain failure on their side is a separate cause to rule out.
- Within 24 hrs: review whether health-department notification is required. Triggers that typically require notification in many US jurisdictions:
  food at internal temp >41°F was served AND consumption is reasonably recent
  a suspect foodborne-illness case linked to the establishment
  extended loss of refrigeration with documented service impact
  If unclear, call the local health department's after-hours line for guidance — a phone call now is better than a written complaint later.
- Within 48 hrs: insurance broker (commercial property / business interruption) if equipment failure with food loss is covered.
- Communications discipline: one designated spokesperson (GM or owner) handles external calls. No social media, no press, no customer-facing discussion beyond what's needed to run service.

5. RETURN TO SERVICE — DO NOT RUSH

The failed reach-in stays out of service until ALL of the following are true:

- Refrigeration tech has diagnosed the root cause and signed off the repair in writing.
- Unit interior cleaned and sanitized (hot soapy water → fresh dilute bleach OR quat sanitizer per label dwell time → rinse if required → dry).
- NEW or freshly calibrated thermometer placed on the middle shelf.
- Unit run empty for ≥4 hours with door openings kept to a minimum. Log temperature every 30 min:
  Acceptable: every reading ≤41°F, no single spike above 41°F, no upward drift across shelf levels.
  Not acceptable: any reading >41°F, any upward drift, or inconsistent readings across shelf levels.
- After empty verification passes: restock minimally; log every hour for the first 8 hours of use; then resume normal logging cadence per house HACCP plan.

If the tech cannot get to the unit today, the unit stays empty and tagged "DO NOT USE" until verified.

ONE-LINE SUMMARY YOU CAN GIVE SAM: don't read time off the air log — work off the probe readings; segregate everything from the failed reach-in in a labeled, color-coded quarantine zone on the lowest walk-in shelf; cook the chicken to 165°F today, boil the sauce for 1 minute, discard anything else that probed above 41°F or has unknown exposure; log everything on one incident sheet; call the kitchen manager now, the GM within 30 min, and a refrigeration tech today; do not put the reach-in back into service until it holds ≤41°F empty for 4 hours after a written tech sign-off.

Bottom line: no need to call poison control or rush to a vet. The actual allium dose Kibo got is well below any documented toxicity threshold, and he's asymptomatic.

Why this is low-risk

Onion and garlic both contain organosulfur compounds (notably N-propyl disulfide) that cause oxidative damage to red blood cells → Heinz body hemolytic anemia. Cooking does NOT destroy these compounds, so cooked alliums count fully. The relevant toxic thresholds in dogs:

- Garlic: ~5 g/kg of body weight to cause hematologic changes; smaller doses (~1 g/kg) can cause GI upset
- Onion: ~15–30 g/kg of fresh weight; some sensitive individuals react lower

For Kibo (~19 kg / 42 lb), that's roughly:
- ~95 g of fresh garlic to threaten his red blood cells
- ~285 g of fresh onion for the same

What he actually got: less than 1 teaspoon (~5 mL) of finished gravy. Even assuming a generous recipe where onion+garlic make up ~10% of the gravy by weight, that's on the order of 0.5 g of allium — roughly 0.025 g/kg. That's about 200× below the hematologic threshold and well below the GI-upset threshold. A taste of gravy is not the exposure profile seen in published Heinz body cases; those typically involve a dog eating a meaningful portion of allium food (several cloves of garlic, several rings of onion, a bowl of allium broth).

What allium toxicity actually looks like (so you know what you'd be watching for)

The hallmark is delayed hemolytic anemia. Mechanism is cumulative oxidative damage, so clinical signs lag the exposure:

- Typical onset of clinical signs: 1–5 days after ingestion if a toxic dose was reached
- Lab abnormalities (Heinz bodies on blood smear, falling PCV/HCT) can be detected earlier, often within 24 hours

Delayed signs to monitor over the next 5–7 days

Watch for these — any single one warrants a vet visit, because a CBC can pick up Heinz bodies and anemia before things get serious:

- Lethargy or noticeably reduced exercise tolerance (often the earliest subtle sign of anemia)
- Pale, gray, or tacky gums instead of normal pink
- Loss of appetite over coming days
- Dark or reddish-brown urine (hemoglobinuria from RBC breakdown — this is the most specific sign)
- Yellowing of gums, inner ear pinnae, or sclera (icterus from bilirubin spillover)
- Rapid or labored breathing at rest
- Vomiting or diarrhea starting days later

Practical guidance for tonight

- Continue normal feeding and routine.
- No need to induce vomiting, give activated charcoal, or change anything.
- If you want an easy daily check: glance at his gum color and watch his energy level on walks for the next 5 days. That's a sensitive, cheap proxy for early anemia.
- If any of the delayed signs above appear, a vet can run a CBC and check for Heinz bodies — treatment is straightforward if caught early.

Realistic expectation: at this dose, the probability of clinical illness is essentially nil. The monitoring is a low-cost insurance habit, not a likely outcome.

Best move: carve the breast off now, cool it fast, and reheat at service time. Keep the thighs/drumsticks in the roaster at 200°F, since dark meat tolerates that for three hours without much quality loss. This avoids both the "3 hours at room temp" problem and the "breast turns to leather" problem at the same time.

Why split the bird:

- Breast at 165°F sitting in a 200°F roaster for ~3 more hours will keep climbing toward 180°F+ and dry out noticeably. Breast meat is the part you cannot afford to overcook.
- Thighs/drumsticks are already at 173°F and have more fat and connective tissue. Three hours at 200°F is essentially harmless to them — they're not going to get meaningfully drier, and the temperature stays well above the 140°F safe-holding floor the whole time.

Steps, in order:

1. Right now (~11:10–11:20am): Carve the breast off the bone while it's hot — hot turkey slices cleanly. Leave thighs and drumsticks on the bone, return them to the covered roaster at 200°F. They are done; this is now a holding move, not a cooking move.

2. Slice the breast meat against the grain into roughly 1/4-inch pieces. Spread in a single layer on a rimmed sheet pan (or two if needed). Don't cover yet — you want steam to escape so the meat cools fast. A light brush of melted butter or warm broth on the surface helps keep it from forming a dry skin.

3. Cool quickly. Set the sheet pan on a wire rack on the counter for about 15–20 minutes until the slices stop steaming and feel like they're approaching room temp. Faster option: set the pan over a shallow ice bath in the sink for 10–15 minutes, stirring/rotating once.

4. Move to the fridge by ~12:00pm in shallow containers, loosely covered or with foil tented so heat can still escape. Don't stack deep in a bowl — it'll stay in the danger zone too long. You're aiming to be under 40°F well before 1:00pm.

5. At about 1:30pm, reheat the breast. The countertop oven is spoken for (stuffing 1:15–1:50, rolls 1:50–2:00), so use the stovetop or microwave:
   - Skillet method (best): warm 2–3 Tbsp turkey broth (or chicken broth + a knob of butter) in a covered skillet over low heat. Add the sliced breast, cover, warm gently 5–7 minutes, turning once. Target 165°F internal.
   - Microwave method: arrange slices in a single layer in a shallow dish, add 2 Tbsp broth, cover with a damp paper towel or vented plastic, heat at 50–60% power in 60–90 second bursts, rotating between bursts, until 165°F. Lower power prevents the edges from turning rubbery.

6. At 1:55–2:00pm, pull thighs/drumsticks from the roaster and tent loosely with foil for 5 minutes to settle the juices, then plate. They can go straight to the table.

Food-safety sanity check, end to end:
- Breast: out of roaster ~11:20am → room-temp brief cool → fridge by ~12:00pm → reheat to 165°F at ~1:30pm. No segment of that is in the 40–140°F danger zone for more than about 30–45 minutes total, and the reheat is verifiable with a thermometer.
- Thighs: stay continuously at ≥173°F in the roaster until ~2:00pm. Safe holding, no break in the hot chain.
- Neither piece of meat spends any meaningful time at room temperature, and nothing gets blasted with 200°F dry heat for hours.

One small note on the roaster: if the lid seal isn't tight, a tablespoon or two of broth or water in the bottom under a rack (not touching the meat) keeps the thigh skin from toughening. Don't bother tenting the thighs with foil inside the roaster — it'll just trap steam and make the skin soggy.

Stopping the memory attempts and answering the user. The Study 7 finding (45° vs 90°) is mechanically meaningful but n=1 on a single edge, so one 45°/45° confirmation is the right next step before committing it to a real painting.

INTERPRETATION

This is a within-sheet paired comparison — the strongest single-trial design you can do at the workbench. Same paper, same wash, same tape, same contact time, same drying; the only manipulated variable is removal angle. The contrast is clean: ~45° back over itself left the edge clean; ~90° straight up lifted a narrow strip of paper fibers in two places.

Why it works: at ~90° the peel force concentrates along a narrow line directly above the tape edge, and peak tensile force on the surface fiber network exceeds fiber cohesion at the two weak spots, so fibers tear away with the adhesive. At ~45° back over itself, the peel front propagates gradually and a larger share of the force vector acts in-plane (releasing the adhesive progressively) rather than perpendicular to the paper. Peak force on the surface drops, and the bond releases before the fiber network fails.

That is the textbook result for pressure-sensitive tape on paper.

What the design controls and what it doesn't:
  - Controls: paper variation, wash variation, tape batch, contact time, drying, paper-handling.
  - Does NOT control: edge-specific effects. From this trial alone you can't tell whether the right edge's lift came from direction alone, or whether that edge also had a subtle uncontrolled difference — marginally heavier tape burnish, slightly wider overlap, a hair more wash wicking under the tape at that spot — that made it prone to lift regardless of angle.

RECOMMENDATION: RUN ONE MINIMAL CONFIRMATION FIRST

The within-sheet control is strong and the mechanism is exactly what tape-peel physics predicts. But 90° was tested on a single edge, n=1. A confirmation costs one scrap sheet plus the locked protocol (about 20 minutes active plus drying). The cost of being wrong on a finished painting is the painting. Confirm first.

The confirmation should hold direction constant and vary only the edge. That is what separates "removal direction" from "unnoticed edge difference," as you asked.

MINIMAL CONFIRMATION DESIGN

  - One scrap sheet from the same pad.
  - Lock the full wash protocol: longer steep-angle wash, one firm blot, 20 s bead-wicking interval, one-touch edge boundary, board tilt 35°, same brush, same pigment ratio, same tape, same roll.
  - Mask two opposite edges (top/bottom or left/right — pick the pair you did not use in Study 7 if you want broader coverage, or repeat the same pair if you want a direct replication).
  - Let dry fully.
  - Pull BOTH edges at ~45° back over itself, same slow motion you used on the Study 7 left edge.
  - No heat on either edge.

DECISION RULE

  - Both edges clean → direction is the operative variable. The Study 7 lift was the 90° angle, not an edge quirk. Use 45° back over itself as your standard on the next painting.
  - Both edges lift → direction is NOT the operative variable. Something about the edge (tape adhesion, paper-surface variation, wash wicking depth) dominates. Revisit before risking a painting.
  - One clean, one lifts → edge-specific effect dominates. The Study 7 clean edge was either lucky or the lifted edge had a real difference. Don't generalize yet — characterize what differs between the two edges of the confirmation sheet before the next painting.

AFTER THE CONFIRMATION

Two sheets supporting 45° is enough to make it your standard on the next painting. Treat any future deviation — different paper pad, different tape batch, a notably different wash — as a candidate reset point where a quick check on scrap is worth the small effort.

   - Most smart thermostats (Nest, Ecobee, Honeywell, etc.) keep a runtime graph per day. Pull the October and November runtime hours and the daily setpoint schedule.
   - Compare: average heat-run hours/day, and any setpoint changes. A jump from ~4 hr/day to ~9 hr/day is consistent with a ~50% electrical increase if your home uses electric resistance heat (baseboard, furnace with electric strips, heat pump with backup strips).
   - Check the "aux heat" or "emergency heat" runtime specifically -- if the heat pump locked into aux a lot in November, that single line item can double heating kWh.
   - Confirm the schedule wasn't accidentally changed (a common culprit: someone turned the hold/override on and left it at a higher temp, or the schedule got wiped).

3. Water-heater behavior
   - Electric water heaters are the second-biggest load and the easiest one to miss. Look for:
     - Any error code, "dry fire," or blinking light on the unit (a failed lower element makes the upper element run constantly -- classic phantom-load story).
     - Tank temperature setting: if it was bumped up (60 -> 70 C / 140 -> 160 F) it can add 10-15% to water-heating kWh.
     - Hot-water usage pattern: extra showers, laundry loads, dishwasher runs, a slow leak at a hot-side faucet or a running toilet mixing valve that forces the tank to keep reheating.
   - Quick at-home test: note the meter kWh reading, wait 1 hour with no one using hot water and no major appliances running, then re-read. A healthy electric water heater uses ~0.5 kWh/hr cycling; a stuck-heating or short-cycling unit can show 1.5-2.5 kWh/hr at idle. Compare against an hour when you fully shut the breaker to the water heater (only do this if you can safely identify the breaker).

Decision rule before escalating:
  - If the thermostat history shows a clear heating-hours increase AND/OR the water heater shows abnormal idle draw, you've found the cause -- no utility call needed, just adjust behavior or call maintenance.
  - If the thermostat and water heater both look normal but the meter reading agrees with the bill, then the 494 kWh came from something you haven't identified yet. At that point: scan for one-time line items on the bill (rider adjustments, demand charges, prior-period corrections, credits/deposits), glance at the past 6-12 bills to see where this November falls relative to normal, and then call the utility to ask them to walk through the line items and confirm the meter read.
