EIGHT-HOUR NO-USE METER TEST — PLAN

PURPOSE
Confirm and quantify whether the home is losing water through a fixture leak (most likely the guest-bath toilet flapper or fill valve, given the prior overnight 16 gph observation). The test compares two meter readings taken 8 hours apart with zero intentional water use anywhere in the home. Any flow registered during that window is leak flow, not use flow.

BEST TIME TO RUN (KEEPS IT OUT OF OVERNIGHT)
Run it during waking hours so Kibo's water needs can be met from pre-filled containers that do not pass through the meter. Recommended window: 9:00 AM to 5:00 PM on a day Riley is home. A weekend or work-from-home day is ideal. Avoid running the test when:
- Anyone in the home has a medical need that requires bathroom breaks during the window
- The forecast includes freezing temps (risk of pipe issues that complicate the reading)
- A sprinkler timer is set to run during the window (disable the timer for the day)
- The city has scheduled hydrant flushing or water main work in the area

PRE-TEST PREPARATION (T-24 HOURS)
- Confirm everyone in the home agrees to the protocol
- Identify the meter location: usually basement, utility closet, or curb box outside
- Determine meter type: analog (with sweep hand and small leak indicator — small triangle, sail, or disc on the dial face) versus digital (LCD register, often with a leak flag or flow-rate display)
- Locate the main shutoff valve and verify it works (do not turn it off for the test — just know where it is)
- Charge your phone; clean the meter face with a dry cloth so photos are legible
- Check the weather forecast for the test window

PRE-TEST HOUSEHOLD RESET (T-1 HOUR, BEFORE PHOTOS)
Run every fixture once and then leave them alone. Specifically:
- Showers: shower, drain, leave wet towels in dryer
- Bathroom sinks: use, drain, dry hands with towel
- Kitchen sink: use, drain, leave dish rack empty
- Dishwasher: run a cycle to completion (or skip if recently run); leave it latched and idle
- Washing machine: run a cycle to completion (or skip if recently run)
- All toilets: flush, leave handle down, do not flush again until test ends
- Refrigerator: dispense and fill a pitcher of drinking water from the door, then turn the dispenser OFF (or lock it via child lock). For ice makers: empty the bin and switch the ice maker OFF at the unit, or place a towel over the bin to catch any unexpected fill cycle and prevent the bin from triggering a refill
- Humidifier: empty, unplug, remove from service
- Water heater: leave on; do not run any hot taps during the window
- Steam oven, instant-hot water dispenser, pot filler: do not use
- Outdoor spigots and hose: do not use; check that nothing is dripping outside
- Boiler or furnace water-supply line: do not touch
- Recirculation pump: if it runs on a timer, note the schedule — each activation pulls a small amount of water and would invalidate the test. If it would run during the window, skip that cycle or postpone the test
- Water softener: check the regeneration timer; if it would run during the window, manually skip that cycle or postpone the test

PRE-FILL DRINKING WATER (THIS IS HOW KIBO STAYS HYDRATED WITHOUT OVERNIGHT)
All drinking water during the test must come from containers filled BEFORE the test starts. None of that water passes through the meter — the meter only sees water moving through the supply pipes. So you can pour freely from pre-filled containers without affecting the test.

For Kibo:
- Fill his normal water bowl to its usual level from the tap, then set it aside
- Fill a clean 1-gallon pitcher or large jug with tap water and place it next to the bowl
- During the test, refill the bowl by pouring from the jug — the water is already past the meter, so the meter does not move
- Offer Kibo water on his normal schedule (or per any current vet plan — small frequent sips, normal bowl access, whatever the current plan is) using only the pre-filled jug
- If Kibo is on a monitored-intake plan, pour the measured amount from the jug instead of from the tap
- Tracking: write down the time and amount of every refill from the jug so you can prove no tap water was used

For humans:
- Fill a pitcher for drinking and place it on the counter
- Fill water bottles for anyone leaving the house
- Pre-fill a kettle if anyone wants hot drinks; use it during the window without refilling from the tap
- Pre-fill the coffee maker reservoir if you plan to brew; do not add water to the machine during the test
- Tracking: same — log every pour from a pre-filled container with time and amount

For toilet emergencies (low priority — try to avoid):
- Pre-fill a clean 5-gallon bucket with tap water and store it in the bathroom
- If a flush is unavoidable, dump the bucket water directly into the toilet BOWL (not the tank). This clears the bowl without triggering the fill valve and without moving the meter. Record the time and amount — and treat the test as compromised unless the recorded pour lines up with what the meter shows precisely
- Preferred: just hold it for 8 hours. Plan meals and fluids to minimize the need

BEFORE-TEST PHOTO EVIDENCE
Take four photos of the meter in this order:

Photo 1 — Context shot. Stand back 2 to 3 feet so the photo shows where the meter is, the surrounding pipes, and any identifying features (curb box lid, basement wall label, meter serial plate). This anchors the location.

Photo 2 — Register close-up. Fill the frame with the meter's register face. Make sure the digits, sweep hand, and any leak indicator (small triangle, sail, or disc on analog meters; leak flag on digital meters) are all visible and in focus. Use flash if lighting is dim, but watch for glare on the glass cover — reposition if needed.

Photo 3 — Reading close-up with timestamp visible. In the same frame as the meter, hold a piece of paper that shows the date, the time (to the minute), and the word BEFORE in large letters. The paper must be readable in the photo.

Photo 4 — Leak indicator detail. Zoom in on the small triangle, sail, or disc (or digital leak flag) so its current position is unambiguous. This is the most important photo because even a tiny leak will move this indicator when the sweep hand barely budges.

While at the meter, record in your notes:
- Meter serial number (printed on the register face)
- Meter model and brand if visible
- Unit of measurement printed on the dial (gallons versus cubic feet)
- Full register reading — every digit, including the small sweep hand position
- Start time, exact to the minute, with timezone
- Outside temperature

PROHIBITED WATER USE LIST (ANY OF THESE INVALIDATES THE TEST)
Each item below either moves water through the meter directly or triggers a refill cycle that does. If any happens, the test is invalidated and you must start over.

- Flushing ANY toilet, including the suspect guest-bath toilet
- Running any faucet — kitchen, bathroom, utility sink, outdoor spigot
- Running the dishwasher, even for a rinse cycle
- Running the washing machine
- Using the refrigerator water dispenser or ice maker
- Using a humidifier (even if filled from the pre-filled jug — some auto-drain)
- Filling a kettle, coffee maker, or pot from the tap
- Triggering an instant-hot water dispenser
- Running a pot filler
- Opening a hose bib or running a sprinkler
- Using a steam mop or anything plumbed in
- Triggering a water softener regeneration cycle
- Letting a water heater or boiler automatic fill valve activate

DURING THE TEST (THE 8 HOURS)
You do not need to hover over the meter. Check it twice — once around the 4-hour mark and once at the end — but do not touch the meter or disturb the sweep hand. Going near it should be limited to visual checks.

Optional checks you can do without invalidating the test:
- Peek at the guest-bath toilet bowl to see if the water level has dropped or if there is a faint refill trickle sound
- Listen near the suspect toilet for occasional hiss or refill cycling
- Note any sounds of running water anywhere in the home

DO NOT DO THESE DURING THE TEST (even if tempting):
- Do not run a faucet "just to rinse a fork"
- Do not flush "just because"
- Do not check the meter more than a few times — physical contact can disturb the sweep hand
- Do not run any appliance that draws water, even briefly

If the small leak indicator is moving continuously during the test (visible spin), you have a confirmed leak. You can stop the test early if you want — but let it run the full 8 hours so you have a clean rate number to bring to a plumber or to management.

END-OF-TEST PHOTO EVIDENCE
Take the same four photos at the same angles and in the same order as the before photos. The AFTER paper in Photo 3 should show the new date and time. If you moved the camera position at all between before and after, redo the before shot from the new angle — consistency is what makes the photos comparable.

Record in your notes:
- End time, exact to the minute, with timezone
- Full register reading — every digit, including the small sweep hand position
- Sweep hand revolutions: count the number of full revolutions plus the fraction of the next revolution. This is your leak volume in the meter's smallest unit
- Outside temperature at end

STOP OR INVALIDATE THE TEST IF ANY OF THESE HAPPEN
- Anyone uses any water through the home's plumbing for any reason (including a single toilet flush)
- The refrigerator ice maker or water dispenser activates
- A sprinkler, hose, or outdoor fixture runs
- The water softener enters a regeneration cycle
- A burst pipe, leak, or any plumbing emergency occurs
- The meter is disturbed, jarred, or read inconsistently between before and after photos
- Severe weather (frozen pipes, flooding) that could affect the supply or the meter
- City-side work on the water main or hydrant flushing during the window
- Power outage lasting long enough that you cannot verify the meter is behaving normally
- A building-wide event (for example, neighbor-side shutoff) that could cause the meter to behave unexpectedly
- You forgot a step (left a humidifier on, did not lock the ice maker, did not skip the softener cycle) — better to abort and restart than to record a compromised number

If any of these happen, abort cleanly: take the after photos, note what happened and when, then reschedule the test for another day. Do not try to "correct" a partially invalid run by subtracting estimated water.

CALCULATIONS AND INTERPRETATION
Two ways to read the result.

Method A — Total flow. Subtract the before register reading from the after register reading. If the meter reads in gallons, the difference is the gallons lost during the 8 hours. If it reads in cubic feet, multiply by 7.48 to convert. Divide the result by 8 to get the average gallons-per-hour leak rate.

Method B — Sweep hand. Each full revolution of the small sweep hand is a known volume (printed on the meter dial, often 1 gallon or 7.48 gallons depending on the meter). Count revolutions during the test and multiply. This is the more sensitive method for small leaks. For digital meters, use the meter's flow log or leak flag if available; otherwise rely on the register difference in Method A.

What the numbers mean:
- 0.0 gallons, no sweep-hand motion: no leak detected in the tested fixtures. The original overnight reading may have been a one-time event, a city-side event, or a leak that has since stopped
- 0.1 to 1.0 gallons over 8 hours: very slow leak, possibly a flapper beginning to fail; still worth addressing
- 1 to 10 gallons over 8 hours: a definite fixture leak, consistent with a flapper that does not seal or a slow fill-valve issue
- 10 to 100 gallons over 8 hours: serious leak, consistent with a fill valve running intermittently or a flapper fully open
- Anything close to the original 16 gph overnight observation (about 128 gallons over 8 hours) confirms the original problem is still active

If the result is non-zero, the next diagnostic step is to shut off the supply stop valves to each fixture one at a time and re-run a shorter (1 to 2 hour) test to isolate which fixture is leaking. The guest-bath toilet is the prime suspect from the prior overnight reading.

RECORDS TO KEEP
Make a single document (paper or digital) and fill it in during the test, not from memory afterward. Include:

- Date and exact start time (with timezone)
- Exact end time (with timezone)
- Total elapsed minutes
- Before register reading, all digits
- After register reading, all digits
- Difference in the meter's native units
- Difference in gallons (with the conversion factor used)
- Average gallons per hour
- Sweep hand: revolutions counted, fraction of last revolution, volume per revolution, total volume
- Outside temperature at start and end
- Weather conditions (clear, rain, freeze risk)
- Meter serial number
- Meter model, brand, and unit of measurement
- Photo file names or timestamps for all four before and four after photos
- List of every fixture confirmed off (each item from the prohibited-use list, checked)
- Kibo water management: time and amount of each refill from the pre-filled jug
- Human water management: time and amount of each pitcher or bottle refill
- Any anomaly, sound, or observation during the 8 hours
- Any stop or invalidate event (with time and reason)
- Final interpretation: leak rate, likely source, next step

QUICK CHECKLIST
T-24h: confirm household, locate meter, identify meter type, charge phone
T-1h: run every fixture once, then leave alone; turn off ice maker, dispenser, humidifier; skip softener cycle; pre-fill drinking water for humans and Kibo; pre-fill toilet emergency bucket
T-0: take 4 before photos, record meter reading and serial
0 to 8h: no plumbing use; pour from pre-filled containers only; check meter at about 4h and again at end; note any sounds
T+8h: take 4 after photos from the same angles, record final reading
T+15min: compute total gallons and gallons per hour; file all photos and notes in one place
T+next day: if leak confirmed, book plumber or notify management with the photo set and the gallons-per-hour number

The held-state invariant from the previous rollback work ("paused, unreleased, held rows still held") depends on the consumers being coherent during the revert window; if they're not, a held row could become "eligible" via one consumer's stale read while another consumer is still HOLD-ing it, which is the disagreement the contract was designed to prevent in the first place.

Each consumer has its own revert mechanism (Helio Start reporting via the reporting deploy, Expansion Assist via the monthly-selection job, lifecycle preflight via Customer.io configuration), and the kill switch stopping the transport is a separate step. Three independent reverts plus one transport stop, with no assertion that all four converge before anyone declares rollback done.

Proposed addition for the runbook, before any production release approval:

1. Define "rollback complete" explicitly: the moment at which all three consumers (Helio Start reporting selector, Expansion Assist selection job, lifecycle preflight configuration) are observed reading from the prior authority, and the new shared-state transport is no longer being read by any consumer. Until that moment, rollback is in progress, not complete.

2. Add a cross-consumer authority assertion — automated, not a manual check. Each consumer exposes a signal of which authority it's currently reading. The assertion polls all three and only passes when all three signals show prior authority within a bounded window (minutes, not hours). The window itself needs a number, and that number needs to be measured in the next nonproduction dry-run against the post-release candidate state.

3. Make the assertion blocking: rollback is not declared complete, held rows are not released, and no re-enablement work begins until the assertion passes. If the assertion cannot be evaluated (consumer signal unavailable, or any consumer hasn't reached prior authority within the window), rollback is incomplete — held rows stay held, Daniela/Owen/Ines are paged, and the runbook stops at the assertion step.

4. Sequence the four steps explicitly so the order is unambiguous and the assertion is the final step: (a) revert consumer 1, (b) revert consumer 2, (c) revert consumer 3, (d) confirm transport is stopped, (e) run cross-consumer authority assertion, (f) only then declare rollback complete. The ordering between (a)-(c) can be parallel as long as (e) is the gate.

5. Carry forward the existing rollback constraints verbatim: target state remains "paused, unreleased, held rows still held"; no catch-up release of held rows during rollback; held rows stay held until their consumers perform fresh checks against the prior authority after the assertion passes.

This converts Daniela's gap into two concrete runbook items: the assertion itself and the precondition that rollback cannot be declared complete until it passes. ASSESSMENT — IS THE NON-ATOMIC ROLLBACK A RELEASE BLOCKER?

Yes. The non-atomic rollback is itself a release blocker under the
current governance, unless the next rehearsal proves three specific
properties.

Reasoning: the rollback is composed of two independent one-step reverts
(transport-schema addition; lifecycle-preflight UTC-preserving
transformation). Each step has its own atomic unit, but the COMBINED
rollback is non-atomic — there is a window between step 1 and step 2
where the system is in a mixed state. Under the rules already in force

customer contact, no catch-up release of held rows), a mixed state is
operationally indistinguishable from a corruption incident. So if the
rollback is interrupted — by a process crash, an Ines freeze, or a
reviewer pause — the corrective action itself can land the system in
the same shape it was supposed to leave.

The blocker is not the rollback existing. The blocker is the absence of:

      paused in,
  (b) a verifier that proves the system is actually in that state, and
  (c) a fail-stop that prevents continuation into a worse state.

When (a), (b), (c) all hold, non-atomic is acceptable because each
step is gated and observable. Without them, non-atomic = blocker.

Yes — this is essentially the same shape as your 2023-12-16 event, and the answer is the same: keep and refreeze everything. Here's the reasoning and a short recovery plan.

**Why everything is safe to keep**

The safety question for frozen food isn't "did it thaw a bit" — it's "did it spend time in the danger zone (40–140°F) long enough for pathogens to grow." Your freezer air is at 24°F after three hours with the door slightly ajar, which is well below 40°F. Food that is still hard, still cold, or still shows visible ice crystals has stayed at or below freezing internally — no danger-zone time, just some quality loss on the thawing/refreezing cycle.

- Sealed chicken portions: hard with visible ice crystals → safe to refreeze. Cook from frozen or refreeze; quality is fine.
- Frozen vegetables: hard with ice crystals → safe to refreeze. Texture may soften slightly after a refreeze cycle; cook normally.
- Bread: still frozen → safe to refreeze. No expected quality change.
- Ice cream: soft around the edges, still cold and partly frozen → safe to keep. Expect icy/grainy texture after refreezing — eat soon, or use in a milkshake/sauce where texture doesn't matter.

No leaks, no cross-contact, no reason to discard anything.

**Recovery plan for the freezer itself**

1. Confirm the door is fully latched now.
2. Resist opening it for the next several hours so the cold mass recovers.
3. Check the thermometer hourly:
   - Should start dropping within the first hour.
   - Should be back in the teens by hour 6.
   - Should approach 0°F within 24 hours.
4. Flag a problem if: the temp does not drop, or the compressor runs constantly without the temp falling. That's a sealed-system or door-gasket failure, not a "wait it out" situation.
5. Once the freezer is back near 0°F, do the dollar-bill gasket test: close the bill half-in / half-out of the door and tug. If it slides out easily anywhere, that spot isn't sealing — clean the gasket with mild soapy water, dry it, and retest. If it still fails to hold, order a replacement gasket for the model.

The 24°F after three hours of being slightly ajar actually means the freezer held its cold well — door was probably open just a crack, not wide. Good outcome given the scare.

Without smell or taste, the only signals you can trust are: probe-thermometer temperature of each item, time/temp history, food category (risk profile), and texture (firmness, ice crystals, pooled liquid). Three hours is one hour shy of the cumulative 4-hours-above-40°F discard threshold, so until you prove otherwise, treat the worst items as if they have burned most of their budget.

WHAT I STILL NEED FOR PER-ITEM VERDICTS

  1. Current freezer thermometer reading (appliance dials are often off by several degrees — use a separate plug-in thermometer if you have one)
  2. The actual food list and approximate quantity
  3. Freezer fullness (full freezer = much more thermal mass = contents may have stayed at or below 0°F the entire 3 hours)
  4. Instant-read probe readings on a few representative items (the single fastest path to collapsing the decisions below)

Send me those and I'll do item-by-item. In the meantime, here is the framework you can apply yourself.

CONSERVATIVE KEEP / DISCARD BY CATEGORY
(no smell, no taste — temperature, texture, category only)

These rules assume you CANNOT prove the item stayed at or below 0°F for the full 3 hours. If you CAN prove that (probe still reads 0°F or below internally), you can refreeze freely.

HIGH-RISK — raw or cooked protein, dairy, eggs, cooked starches, custards

  - Raw poultry, raw ground meat, raw fish, raw shellfish: probe ≤0°F = KEEP, refreeze. Probe 1–34°F = cook today to 165°F (poultry) / 145°F (meat, fish with 3-min rest), eat hot, do not refreeze raw. Probe ≥40°F after ~3 hours = DISCARD, no exceptions. Cooking does not reliably neutralize the toxins some bacteria produce in this window.
  - Cooked meats, casseroles, soups, stews, gravies: same rule. Reheat to 165°F and eat immediately, or discard.
  - Cooked rice, cooked pasta, custards, puddings, cream sauces: DISCARD if any uncertainty. Bacillus cereus and Staphylococcus aureus toxins are heat-stable — reheat does not fix it.
  - Milk, cream, soft cheeses, yogurt: DISCARD if internal temp reached ≥40°F. Hard cheese (cheddar, parmesan, romano): borderline KEEP if still firm and temp in the 30s — shred, use within 1–2 days.
  - Eggs in shell: KEEP if shell intact and internal ≤40°F. Cooked egg dishes: discard if unsure.

MEDIUM-RISK — vegetables, fruit, vegetable-based sauces

  - Plain frozen vegetables: probe ≤0°F = KEEP, refreeze. Probe 1–34°F = cook thoroughly today (boil / steam / sauté until hot throughout), eat, do not refreeze raw. Probe ≥40°F = cook as above or discard.
  - Vegetable sauces, veg soups: same as cooked foods — bring to a rolling boil ≥1 minute, or discard.
  - Fruit (whole, sliced, in syrup): KEEP and refreeze if still icy. If soft and weeping, bake into something or discard.

LOW-RISK — starches, baked goods, fats, sugars

  - Bread, rolls, bagels, muffins, cookies, cake: KEEP and refreeze. Quality suffers; safety is essentially fine.
  - Tortillas, pita: KEEP and refreeze.
  - Butter, hard margarine, ghee: KEEP and refreeze.
  - Chocolate, chocolate chips: KEEP. Quality issue only (sugar/fat bloom may show).
  - Nuts, seeds, dried fruit: KEEP.
  - Ice cream, gelato, frozen yogurt: DISCARD if soft or partially melted, even if you plan to refreeze. Texture is ruined and dairy-based frozen desserts that spent real time in the danger zone carry a Listeria / Staph risk. Rock-hard the whole time = refreeze OK.

PHYSICAL CHECKS YOU CAN USE (smell and taste are off the table)

  - Instant-read probe thermometer (ThermoPro, Thermapen, or any food-grade probe). Probe the THICKEST part of the item, not the surface.
  - Texture of the item itself: rock-hard with visible ice crystals = strong refreeze signal. Soft with no crystals and the item is above 40°F = discard signal.
  - Pooled liquid under raw meat / poultry / fish: that item is DISCARD regardless of probe, and anything it touched inherits the same risk.
  - Cross-contamination: any package that leaked onto another food = treat the receiving food as if it were in the danger zone too.

RESTORATION PLAN (in order)

  1. Close the door firmly. Listen for the latch.
  2. Note the current freezer thermometer reading before you open again. This is your baseline.
  3. Verify the compressor is running — you should hear a low hum from the back/bottom within 5 minutes. Silence after 5 minutes is an emergency; transfer food to a cooler with ice and call service.
  4. If there is no separate thermometer inside, slide one in now (one quick door open), close the door, and do not open again for 6 hours. This is your only opening.
  5. Inspect the door gasket: look for an uneven frost pattern on the seal (suggests a leak). Run the dollar-bill test — close the door on a bill and pull; if it slides out easily the seal is bad. Find and fix the cause (misaligned door, gunk on the gasket, weak latch, items leaning against the door) before you trust the recovery.
  6. Do not open the freezer for at least 6 hours. Every opening dumps the cold you are trying to rebuild.
  7. Do not add new food until the freezer is back to ≤0°F.

MONITORING PLAN (thermometer and time, not feel)

  - Hour 0 (now, after closing): record the thermometer reading. Baseline.
  - Hour 1: should be dropping or already low. If unchanged from baseline, the door is not sealing.
  - Hour 2: a full freezer is visibly dropping by now; a partially empty one may still be flat.
  - Hour 4: should be ≤10°F if sealed and the compressor is functional.
  - Hour 6: should be ≤0°F or very close.
  - Hour 24: should be 0°F or below and stable across a few hours.

Escalate (transfer food to a cooler with ice, call appliance service) if:

  - Temp does not start dropping within 1 hour of closing.
  - Temp stops dropping and rises again.
  - Compressor runs constantly without the temp moving.
  - Frost or ice builds on the back wall (low-refrigerant symptom).
  - New condensation or frost on the OUTSIDE of the door or around the gasket (ongoing seal failure).

Send me the food list, the current thermometer reading, and a probe reading on one or two representative items and I'll do the per-item verdicts.

  EOB language:    "behavioral services excluded"  (on the $78 consultation line)

They're using "behavioral services" as the exclusion category while the coverable benefit is also called "behavioral treatment." That's an internal mismatch — either the policy excludes behavioral services or it covers behavioral treatment; it shouldn't do both at once.

Three things to request from the insurer, in writing:

  1. The diagnosis code (ICD-10) the clinic submitted. If it points to anxiety or another behavioral condition, a behavioral consultation is the first clinical step of behavioral treatment — the exclusion doesn't hold.

  2. The exact policy section and page that defines "consultation" as a separate, non-covered service from "behavioral treatment." Neither term is defined in what they sent you.

Want me to draft the reply to the insurer along those lines, or a separate ask to the clinic to confirm the diagnosis code on the claim?

Reconciliation between disposition and policy wording

An insurer's $78 exclusion can line up with policy text in several mechanically distinct ways, and the reconciliation you need is identifying which one applies before you decide to accept or appeal. The most common reconciliations:

  - Covered service, excluded setting or cause. The CPT/HCPCS code is listed as a benefit, but the circumstance of the service falls under a named exclusion clause — "not medically necessary," "experimental or investigational," "cosmetic," "out-of-network without approved referral," "rendered outside the U.S.," "pre-existing waiting period," "no prior authorization when required," "not part of the approved treatment plan."
  - Covered service, frequency or sub-limit hit. The code is paid under the benefit, but a per-year visit cap, per-lifetime maximum, dollar sub-limit, or "one per 24 months" frequency rule ate $78 of the line.
  - Network or contracting gap. The rendering or prescribing provider is out of network, or an ancillary (anesthesiologist, assistant surgeon, DME supplier, reading radiologist) is OON even though the primary provider is in-network.
  - Coding-edit gap. The billed code was downcoded, bundled, or split — for example, a 99215 paid at 99213, two procedure codes bundled into one, or a -25/-59/-KX modifier not recognized.
  - Cost-share reframed as exclusion. The $78 is actually deductible, coinsurance, or copay under the schedule of benefits; the EOB may call this an exclusion when the policy treats it as patient liability. These are legally different — cost-share usually has no appeal route other than a coordination-of-benefits or cost-share-error challenge.
  - Coordination-of-benefits or timely-filing exclusion. Another carrier should have paid first (Medicare, spouse's plan, COBRA), or the filing window lapsed.

The reconciliation question is whether the reason code(s) on the EOB line map cleanly to a clause in the Evidence of Coverage you can quote verbatim, or whether the disposition is doing something the policy text does not actually authorize.

Policy questions to ask the insurer (verbatim, in writing where possible)

  1. What is the exact benefit category under which this line was processed, and the exact section and page of the EOC or Certificate that governs it?
  2. What is the verbatim exclusion language from the EOC that you are applying, and are you citing a hard exclusion, a frequency/sub-limit, or a medical-necessity clinical edit?
  3. Is the $78 being treated as a contractual exclusion (no payment, no patient liability beyond in-network write-off) or as patient cost-share (deductible, coinsurance, copay)? Which appeal pathway applies to each?
  4. If this is a medical-necessity edit, what clinical criteria source are you applying — MCG, InterQual, or your own internal medical policy — and what is that policy number?
  5. Is there a rider, endorsement, or amendment that could either expand or further restrict this benefit for the date of service in question?
  6. Was the provider's network status applied correctly — specifically, the rendering provider's network status at the date of service, not today?
  7. Does the federal No Surprises Act or the state surprise-billing statute apply to this line, and does it cap the patient's exposure?
  8. What is the internal appeal deadline, and what is the escalation path from internal review to external / independent review organization (IRO)?
  9. Does the policy allow a peer-to-peer review between my provider and your medical director before a formal written appeal?
  10. Will a successful appeal reopen the claim for reprocessing, or only refund what was already paid?

Coding questions to ask the provider's billing office and the insurer

  1. What CPT/HCPCS code(s) were billed, and what code(s) did the insurer accept or substitute on the adjudication?
  2. What ICD-10 diagnosis code(s) were on the claim, and which diagnosis code(s) did the insurer accept as supporting medical necessity?
  3. Were any modifiers applied (-25, -59, -LT/-RT, -KX, -GA, -GZ), and did the insurer recognize each one?
  4. Was the line downcoded (e.g., 99215 → 99213), bundled, or split into multiple lines? If bundled, what edits were applied (NCCI, internal)?
  5. Were there alternate codes available that would have mapped to a higher allowed amount, and did the billing office consider them?
  6. Was the place-of-service on the claim (office, outpatient hospital, ASC) different from where the service was rendered, and did that drive the gap?
  7. If DME, was the HCPCS billed at the rental or purchase price, and did the insurer apply the capped rental or purchase option?

Claim-specific questions to confirm before accepting or appealing

  1. What is the claim number, date of service, and date the insurer received the claim?
  2. What were the original billed amount, the allowed amount, the insurer payment, the contractual provider write-off, and the patient responsibility — broken out line by line on the EOB?
  3. What are the exact CARC/RARC reason and remark codes on the $78 line (e.g., CO-50, CO-97, CO-16, CO-29, PR-1, PR-2, PR-3, N130, N290)?
  4. Was a prior authorization obtained? If yes, what was the auth number, the authorized codes, and the dates of authorization? If no, was a retro-auth possible and was it attempted?
  5. Was the claim filed within the contractually required timely-filing window from date of service, and from the date of the primary payer's EOB if COB applies?
  6. Is there another carrier that should have been primary — Medicare, a spouse's plan, COBRA, workers' comp, auto MedPay — and was coordination of benefits confirmed in writing?
  7. Did the provider already submit records or a letter of medical necessity with the original claim or on first contact, and what was the insurer's specific clinical objection in response?
  8. Has the provider filed an appeal on your behalf, or is the appeal right only yours to exercise?
  9. If the provider is in-network, are they contractually required to write off the $78 and forbidden from billing you, or may they balance-bill you for it?
  10. Is the $78 in dispute the same dollar amount the provider is currently billing you, or has the provider billed you a different amount pending the appeal?

Once you have the answer to questions 3 (policy), 3 (coding), and 3 (claim) side by side, you can usually tell in one read whether the disposition fits the policy or whether the appeal route is open — and I'll stay in evidence-only mode until you've decided.

Q2 — How did you keep the cool window light from flattening the warmer counter edge?
The cool wash goes down first across the window side, and I let it dry just enough that it doesn't run. Then I bring the warmer counter edge in while the paper is still slightly receptive — damp enough to take the warmth close to the surface, not so wet that it floods back into the cool and turns the whole room one temperature. RETAIN (keep the form intact)
  Keep the original 1099-INT in her 2024 tax file — do not discard, redact, or staple over the print. The IRS treats the payer-issued form as the official record even when Mom also has bank statements.

RECONCILE (compare to bank records)
  Pull her December 2024 bank statement(s) and the bank's year-end interest summary for the account(s) named on the 1099-INT.

    - The reporting period is calendar year 2024 (Jan 1 – Dec 31).
    - The total interest posted to that account for 2024 equals the 1099-INT amount, allowing for normal posting-cutoff differences.
  Common, benign sources of a small gap like 17 cents on a $12.01 figure:
    - Year-end cutoff: interest that accrued Dec 31 but posted Jan 1–3 is typically reported on the next year's 1099-INT, not this one. A few days' interest at her rate on the closing balance is the right order of magnitude for 17 cents.
    - Fees, service charges, or a small reversal that the bank netted against interest before reporting.
    - Rounding when the bank summarizes daily accruals.
    - Interest posted in a different account (e.g., a money-market sweep) that the 1099-INT is combining but her statement separates.

  - She should NOT contact the IRS about a 17-cent difference. The IRS will not act on a discrepancy this small, and the IRS already has a copy of the form the bank filed.

WHEN REFILING OR AMENDING IS WARRANTED
  - The bank issues a corrected 1099-INT showing a different amount.
  - The original 1099-INT was for an account she never owned or for someone else's SSN (possible identity-theft signal — same category as the AGI mismatch she was warned about earlier; in that case the IRS number she has is 800-829-1040).

WHEN NO FOLLOW-UP IS NEEDED
  - The 17-cent difference is explained by posting cutoff, fees, or rounding in her December statement.
  - The name, TIN, payer, and account all match her records.
  - Her 1040 reports $12.01 of taxable interest, consistent with the form she received.
  - No corrected 1099-INT arrives from the bank.

Date drafted: 2025-03-04

   The kitchen-only repeat on Saturday 2025-03-01 satisfied the three

   hold stability) without guest exposure. That result is production-execution
   evidence, not guest-demand evidence. This proposal defines a single,
   bounded guest-facing test whose sole purpose is to produce guest-demand
   evidence under service pressure. It does not approve the dish, does not
   authorize recurrence, and does not validate price.

2. WHAT THIS TEST IS, AND IS NOT
   Is:    one service, one date, fixed portion count, off-menu special.
   Is not: a menu placement, a soft launch, a recurring special, a price
           test, or a substitute for the chef-owner's review of the
           kitchen-only repeat's result.

3. PRODUCTION CONSTRAINTS CARRIED FORWARD (unchanged from the kitchen-only repeat)
   - Portion count: 20.
   - Offering price: $26 (unchanged from prior tests).
   - Direct cost ceiling: ingredients + direct labor ≤ $218.40
     (ingredients target $143.40; direct labor ≤ 2.65 hr at $28/hr = $74.20).
   - Station timing: finish within the documented station target. No overrun.
   - Hold stability: 4 portions must hold 20 minutes without sauce separation,
     now measured under live service pressure, not prep-room holding.
   These four items are the same constraints the chef-owner set for the
   kitchen-only repeat. Meeting them again under service is a precondition
   for the guest-demand reading to be meaningful; failing any of them
   invalidates the demand reading and returns the dish to kitchen work.

4. TEST DESIGN
   a) Service window: one dinner service on a date agreed with the chef-owner.
      No second service is pre-authorized.
   b) Offering mechanics:
      - Off-menu special, server-scripted description, printed chit only.
      - Not listed on the printed menu. Not announced table-side as a new menu
        item. Phrased as "tonight's kitchen test" so guests are not led to
        expect recurrence.
      - First-come within the 20-portion cap; once 20 are ordered, servers
        stop offering. No rainchecks, no promise of "tomorrow."
   c) Pricing: $26 as in prior tests. No discount, no comp marketing. The
      price point itself is not under test here; only whether guests order
      it at the stated price when offered.
   d) Recording (per service):
      - Covers offered the special, tables ordering, portions sold.
      - Portions held unsold at service end (must reconcile to 20).
      - Any comp, void, or send-back, with reason.
      - Service-timing observations: station finish time vs. target, any
        table-side delay attributable to the dish.
      - Hold observation: whether any portion showed sauce separation under
        live-service holding conditions.
      - Brief guest-reaction capture per server (positive / neutral /
        negative, one line per table, no solicited commentary).

5. WHAT THIS TEST MEASURES
   - Whether guests order the dish when offered at $26, in this room, at
     this service volume.
   - Whether the kitchen can hold the three production constraints under
     live service pressure (the kitchen-only repeat removed that pressure;
     this test restores it).
   - Qualitative guest reaction at the offered price.

6. WHAT THIS TEST DOES NOT MEASURE OR DECIDE
   - It does not test whether $26 is the right price.
   - It does not test cross-cook or cross-day execution variance.
   - It does not establish a sell-through benchmark for recurring placement.
   - It does not constitute menu approval.
   - It does not authorize a second service, a second date, or any form of
     recurring placement, including informal "when available" practice.

7. STOP CONDITIONS
   - If any of the four carried-forward production constraints fails under
     service: the dish is held in the kitchen, the demand reading is
     discarded, and the next step is a further kitchen-only repeat — not
     another guest-facing test.
   - At service end, regardless of sell-through, the test closes. No
     extension, no "run it again tomorrow."

8. AFTER THE TEST
   Sam records actuals (cost, labor, station timing, hold behavior, covers

   reviews. Any further step — kitchen-only repeat, second guest-facing
   test, menu consideration, or closure of the project — is a separate

---

**1. Portion count — does not preserve the fixed count of 18 portions.**

The draft specifies 20 portions throughout. You asked for 18. Every "20" in the proposal is a hard edit:

- Section 3, "Portion count: 20." → "Portion count: 18."
- Section 4b, "First-come within the 20-portion cap; once 20 are ordered, servers stop offering." → "First-come within the 18-portion cap; once 18 are ordered, servers stop offering."
- Section 4d, "Portions held unsold at service end (must reconcile to 20)." → "(must reconcile to 18)."

- The trailing note that justifies 20 by appeal to "the prior 20-portion kitchen frames" must be rewritten or cut. A justification built on 20-portion comparability is not a justification for 18; if anything, it argues against the change. Either remove the note or replace it with the actual reason for 18 (smaller batch tests single-batch execution with one fewer portion of headroom against the hold requirement — that is a real argument and should be stated if it is the reason).

One sentence in section 3 also needs attention: "Meeting them again under service is a precondition for the guest-demand reading to be meaningful; failing any of them invalidates the demand reading and returns the dish to kitchen work." Section 4c specifies $26 correctly. Section 5 phrases the test as "Whether guests order the dish when offered at $26, in this room, at this service volume." That is correct. No numerical edit needed, but one tightening: section 6 says "It does not test whether $26 is the right price." Good, keep it. The risk in this proposal is not the number — it is that section 4c's "No discount, no comp marketing" implies a comparison frame ("could have been discounted, isn't"). For a test whose explicit purpose is not to test price, cut "No discount, no comp marketing" and replace with a single line: "Sold at $26 only. No price variation within this test." That removes the implicit pricing experiment without changing the number.

---

**3. Tested production sequence — not pinned down in the draft.**

This is the most important preservation gap. The proposal lists four "carried-forward" production constraints (cost, station timing, hold stability, portion count) but does not name the production sequence being tested. The chef-owner accepted the kitchen-only repeat because Sam executed the redesigned preparation at the documented cost ceiling, on time, with hold stability. **4. Cost ceiling — wrong number, wrong arithmetic.**

If the original 1099-INT carried a TIN that did not match Mom's SSN, the IRS may have silently dropped it from its matching file. The corrected form is what enables IRS matching, which is also what triggers a CP2000 if the income was not reported.

Records Mom should retain

My accepted return omitted this form because it was not yet available when I filed. CAUTIOUS SPOT-CLEANING SEQUENCE — sealed wood, watercolor pigment

PRECONDITION CHECK
- Finish intact + non-tacky = the seal held. Pigment is on top of, or at worst barely into, the seal. Good starting point.
- Stop everything immediately if the finish at any point dulls, hazes, whitens, softens, or becomes tacky. Those are signs the seal is being breached.

SUPPLIES
- Two soft microfiber cloths (clean / dry)
- Cotton swabs
- pH-neutral dish soap (no lotion or antibacterial additives)
- Small dish of clean water
- Only if needed later: 70% isopropyl alcohol

STEP 1 — DRY LIFT
- Pass a dry microfiber lightly over the spot with no pressure.
- Dry residue sitting on the seal often wipes off with zero risk. Stop when the cloth stops picking up blue.

STEP 2 — DAMP PLAIN WATER
- Dampen (don't soak) a corner of cloth with water. Press to the spot for 5–10 seconds, then lift straight up. No scrubbing, no circles.
- Up to 3 passes with a clean section each time. Stop sooner if the finish changes.

STEP 3 — DILUTED SOAP
- One drop dish soap in ~2 tbsp water. Same damp-cloth technique: 5–10 second dwell, single lift-and-blot. One pass only.
- Soap is a mild surfactant; it's the gentlest chemical step available to you.

STEP 4 — RINSE + DRY
- Plain-water damp cloth, single pass to lift soap residue.
- Immediately follow with the dry cloth. Don't leave moisture sitting on the surface.

ASSESS
- Shadow gone: done.
- Faint cool tint remains and finish is unchanged: sensible stop. The pigment has likely locked into the seal at a level gentle cleaning can't reach without finish damage. Stop here, not later.

ONLY IF A NOTICEABLE SHADOW REMAINS
STEP 5 — IPA, WITH A HIDDEN TEST FIRST
- 70% IPA can dissolve shellac and some lacquers. Test on a hidden spot (under furniture, inside a cabinet edge): dampen a cotton swab, hold 10 seconds, wait 2 minutes, check for softening, dulling, or whitening.
  - Test spot unchanged: IPA is likely safe on your finish, proceed.
  - Test spot changed: do NOT use IPA on the visible area.

STEP 6 — IPA ON THE SPOT
- Cotton swab, 5–10 second dwell, single lift-and-blot. No scrubbing.
- Max 2 passes. Stop the moment the swab stops showing color transfer.

WHEN TO STOP (the only rule that matters)
- Stop as soon as your cloth or swab stops picking up visible pigment. Diminishing returns means you're now trading finish for a fainter shadow — bad trade.
- If a pale blue tint is still there after a finish-safe clean, the honest options are:
  (a) live with it; sealed-surface stain-class pigment often fades with time and light
  (b) hide it under a small object
  (c) call a furniture refinisher for a localized re-seal or wax-stick blend

DO NOT USE
- Acetone, nail polish remover, lacquer thinner, bleach, vinegar, "all-purpose" solvent cleaners, or any abrasive pad. All will attack a sealed finish far faster than they will lift a stain pigment.

A NOTE
- Stubborn blue is on-brand for you. Staining pigments (phthalo, ultramarine) bind aggressively to anything microscopically textured — once water dried, the pigment essentially locked in. Your blotting was the right first move; it kept the spot from spreading. A faint shadow after a finish-safe clean is normal for this pigment family and isn't a sign you missed a step.

If after Step 4 the spot is barely visible in normal room light, you're done. Don't escalate.

CORE PRINCIPLE

  A reconstructed sidecar is not an original. It carries two
  classes of fact and is honest about which is which:

    paper_log           copied verbatim from the paper log;
                        provenance = the paper log itself
    verified_file_property
                        computed from the surviving scan;
                        provenance = this reconstruction pass

  Any field that cannot be sourced from one of those two
  classes is left blank and flagged. Do not infer. Do not
  fill a guess into a field and label it "tentative" — that
  is how provenance gets laundered. Tentative is a property
  of date codes, not a label that licenses invention.

PART 3.  STEP-BY-STEP PROCEDURE
----------------------------------------------------------------------

  Step 0.  Halt before touching anything.

    - Confirm the catalog export that lost the sidecars is
      identified (tool, version, export date).
    - Confirm the backup directory that holds the surviving
      scans but not the sidecars.
    - Confirm the prior-export checksum file exists. If it
      does not, set hash_matches_prior_export = false on every
      sidecar and note "no_prior_checksum_available" in the
      reconstruction_event block. Do not skip the field.
    - Assign initials: transcriber (T) and verifier (V).
      Distinct people. Record both in the sidecar and the
      manifest. If you cannot staff two people, STOP and ask.

  Step 1.  Two-person file check (do this once per image).

    V reads aloud from the paper log: photo ID, source_box,
    scan_date, mom_id_notes. T opens the surviving scan and
    confirms the file is the one the paper-log entry refers
    to. Both initial the check on the manifest row.

    If the file cannot be matched to the paper-log entry,
    STOP. Do not reconstruct a sidecar for an unmatched file.
    Escalate; do not guess.

  Step 2.  Compute verified_file_properties.

    For each surviving scan:

      sha256                  sha256sum <file>
      file_size_bytes         stat --printf='%s\n' <file>
                              (or equivalent; record the value, not the
                              command)
      pixel_dimensions        exiftool -ImageSize -s -s -s <file>
                              or identify -format '%wx%h' <file>
      hash_matches_prior_export
                              compare sha256 against the prior-export
                              checksum file. Record true/false. If no
                              prior checksum exists, false and note it.

    Write these into the verified_file_property provenance
    block of the sidecar. Do not write them into the paper_log
    block. Do not write paper_log strings into the
    verified_file_property block.

  Step 3.  Transcribe paper_log fields verbatim.

    Open the paper log. For each field below, copy the string
    exactly, including question marks, spelling, and casing:

      photo_id
      source_box
      scan_date_paper_log
      mom_id_notes

    If a field is unreadable, write "[unreadable]" and add a
    note. Do not paraphrase. Do not "clean up" a spelling.
    Do not convert Mom's "?" into a definite name.

  Step 4.  Set date_code and date_value.

    Pick from the existing vocabulary. If the paper log says
    "maybe 1962", the answer is "?1962" with date_value "1962".
    If the paper log is silent on date, leave both blank — do
    not write UNK as a default. UNK is a statement that the
    paper log was consulted and found silent.

  Step 5.  Set identity fields.

    Copy verbatim. If Mom wrote "Aunt Mari?" the sidecar
    carries "Aunt Mari?" — not "Aunt Mari" and not "unidentified".

  Step 6.  Build the reconstruction_event block.

    Required keys listed in Part 1. The loss_description must
    reference the catalog tool and export date. The
    reconstruction_method string is fixed.

  Step 7.  Save the sidecar.

    Place <image>.xmp next to <image>.jpg in the working
    directory. Do not delete, rename, or move the scan.

  Step 8.  Append a manifest row.

    One row per sidecar, per the schema in Part 2. The
    two_person_file_check cell is the single place the
    two-person rule is enforced visibly.

  Step 9.  Append an audit-log entry.

    See Part 4. The audit log is the system of record for
    "what happened in this pass"; the sidecar is the system
    of record for "what does this file claim to be".

  Step 10. Backup.

    Copy the working directory (images + sidecars + manifest)
    to the backup target. Verify the copy: row count of scans
    matches, row count of sidecars matches, manifest row
    count matches.

  Step 11. Do not re-import into the catalog tool until the
           backup is confirmed. Re-importing before backup
           turns a recoverable reconstruction into a single-
           point-of-failure situation.

PART 4.  AUDIT-LOG ENTRIES
----------------------------------------------------------------------

  Append-only. New entries go at the bottom. Earlier entries
  are never edited. If something needs correcting, append a

    verified_properties=sha256=<hex>;size=<bytes>;dims=<WxH>;

    date_code=?YYYY | YYYY-YYYY | UNK | ...
    date_value=<verbatim or blank>
    identity=<verbatim or blank>
    two_person_check=<T> / <V>

Three things are tangled here: the value comparison at the new $150 fee, the timing of the downgrade, and the refundability gap on the April 15 charge. Untangle them in that order.

1. VALUE AT $150 VS NO-FEE

You're comparing $150/yr against the bundle you actually used:
  - $75 travel credit (used in full)
  - 2 lounge visits (Priority Pass retail ~ $30-50/visit, so $60-100 in value)
  - Higher earn on travel/dining (premium tier minus 1.5x on the downgrade)

The benefits you named sum to ~$135-175 before counting the earn-rate premium at all. The earn-rate delta is where the rest of the answer lives — it depends on your travel+dining spend on this card.

Quick test: pull last year's travel+dining charges on this card (X). At premium tier (commonly 3x) vs 1.5x on the downgrade, the extra earn is (premium - 1.5) * X points. At ~1.5-2 cents/point that's the dollar value of the premium you'd be giving up.

If (earn-rate delta + $75 credit + $60-100 lounge value) > $150, the card is still a positive-return subscription. If it's marginal or below, downgrade.

2. TIMING — BEFORE OR AFTER APRIL 15

Two windows:
  (a) Downgrade BEFORE April 15. No fee charged. Points preserved per the offer terms. You give up the $75 credit, the lounges, and the higher earn rate, but you never pay the $150.
  (b) Pay April 15, then downgrade. You get one more cycle of $75 credit + lounge visits + premium earn. Then you request a downgrade. Whether you recover the $150 depends on refund policy.

The right window is (a) unless you specifically want to extract one more cycle of benefits AND you have a confirmed refund path. Without that, paying and then downgrading is paying $150 for benefits you'll surrender.

3. REFUNDABILITY OF THE APRIL 15 FEE

This is the part the notice leaves silent. Industry norm:
  - Most issuers treat the annual fee as non-refundable once posted.
  - Some (Chase historically, certain Capital One products) refund pro-rata or in full if you downgrade within a short window — often 30 days from fee posting — but this is policy-dependent and not guaranteed.
  - The cardmember agreement, not the marketing notice, governs.

Default assumption: non-refundable. Treat it as a sunk cost the moment it posts.

4. RECOMMENDED SEQUENCE

  i.  Pull last year's travel+dining spend on the card. Compute the earn-rate delta in dollars.
  ii. If (delta + $75 + lounge value) > $150, keep the card. Pay April 15.
  iii. If not, downgrade NOW, before April 15. Don't wait to see if you can get a refund — the default answer is no.
  iv. If you want belt-and-suspenders certainty on the refund path before committing to the $150: call the issuer and ask, "If I downgrade within X days of the April 15 fee posting, is the fee refunded in full, prorated, or not at all?" Get the rep's name and a reference number. Asking does not bind you.

The single piece of bad reasoning to avoid: paying the $150 fee on April 15 hoping to downgrade-and-refund later. That works only with a confirmed refund window; without one it's $150 for nothing.

# Travel Card Fee Decision: $150 Value Check

## Known Annual Value (pre-increase baseline)
Your last 12 months of usage on the card:
- **Points redeemed:** $218 in value
- **Travel credit:** $75 (used in full)
- **Lounge visits:** 2 included passes used
- **Earn-rate edge:** incremental return from the higher multiplier on travel and dining (the exact dollar figure is the part you still need to pull)

## The New Fee
Annual fee moves from **$95 → $150** on April 15, 2025 — a **$55 increase**.

## Break-Even Math
Previous logic: keep the card if (earn-rate delta + $75 travel credit + lounge value) > old $95 fee.

New threshold, the same logic against $150:
- **Keep** if (earn-rate delta + $75 credit + lounge value) > $150
- **Downgrade** if that total ≤ $150

The previous test was already tight at $95; at $150 the downgrade side becomes much more likely unless your travel/dining spend on the card is heavy. The points you redeemed ($218) are not a benefit you "earn" annually — they are points you accumulated from spend — so they should not be counted as annual value when deciding whether to keep paying.

## No-Fee Downgrade Path (issuer's advertised option)
- **Annual fee:** $0
- **Points:** preserved
- **Travel/dining earn rate:** drops to 1.5×
- **Travel credit:** removed
- **Lounge passes:** removed

That path is attractive only if you would have downgraded anyway — you keep the points balance but lose the perks that justified the fee.

## What You Must Verify With the Issuer Before Choosing

1. **Refundability of the April 15 charge.** Industry default is non-refundable once posted. Confirm in writing whether a downgrade within X days of the April 15 posting yields a full refund, prorated refund, or nothing.
2. **Downgrade timing / annual-fee clock.** Does a downgrade stop the next $150 charge, or does the fee already paid cover a fixed membership year that runs regardless?
3. **Points treatment on downgrade.** Confirm the "preserves existing points" claim applies to your specific balance, including any bonus categories or promo points.
4. **Earn-rate comparison in writing.** Get the exact multiplier on the no-fee product for travel, dining, and other categories — verbal "1.5×" is not enough.
5. **Credit line and account continuity.** Confirm the account number stays the same, the credit history is preserved, and the card does not reappear as a new account on your credit report.
6. **Authorized users / additional cards.** Whether any AUs on the current card carry over, and whether they have their own fee on the new product.
7. **Card artwork / network tier.** Whether the no-fee product is the same Visa/Mastercard tier (affects acceptance and travel insurance).
8. **Travel insurance, purchase protection, and other ancillary benefits** tied to the higher-tier card — these often disappear on a downgrade and are easy to miss.
9. **Product-change fee.** Confirm the downgrade itself is not a "new account" that triggers a hard inquiry or a separate processing fee.
10. **Re-upgrade path.** If you downgrade now, can you move back to the premium version later, and would you be charged a new $150 fee on that re-upgrade?
11. **Statement credit timing.** Whether any unused portion of the current $75 travel credit carries into the new product year or is forfeited on downgrade.
12. **Notice / effective date in writing.** Get the April 15 effective date confirmed in writing along with the rep's name and reference number.

## Recommendation
Given that the previous break-even was already tight at $95 and the fee is jumping to $150, the bias has clearly shifted toward downgrade — unless your travel/dining spend on the card produces a meaningful earn-rate delta. **Do not let the April 15 fee post and then try to undo it.** Resolve items 1–3 with the issuer before April 15, 2025, so you either keep the card on purpose or downgrade on purpose.

CONSERVATIVE HOME-MONITORING PLAN — KIBO
Single loose stool, ~7 days post-recall exposure, otherwise bright.

KEY ASSUMPTION (state to confirm)
- All recalled Harvest Table Turkey & Rice lot L25-0317A has been discarded and is not being fed to Kibo or any other pet in the home.
- Nothing else new in his diet, treats, table scraps, chews, yard chemicals, medications, or human food since the recall.

WHAT'S REASSURING RIGHT NOW
- Alert, drinking, interested in food, single stool (not repeated), no vomiting, no blood, no fever you can detect, belly soft, no weakness, no distension.
- Chewing grass is a common, benign cause of a single soft/loose stool (mechanical irritation, possible lawn treatment residue).
- 7 days post-recall is past the typical Salmonella incubation window in dogs (usually 6–72 hr, occasionally up to several days), but shedding can occur without symptoms, so hygiene still matters.

HYDRATION (next 2–4 hours)
- Offer 1–2 tbsp water every 15–20 min for the first ~2 hours; do NOT let him gulp a full bowl.
- If sips are kept down, normal water access by evening.
- Stop/pause and reassess if he vomits water or refuses sips.

FEEDING
- Hold food for ~2 hours after the loose stool (gut just moved faster than normal).
- Bland bridge meal tonight: plain boiled skinless chicken + white rice, 1:2–3 ratio, no salt/oil/butter.
- Offer 1–2 tbsp at a time; if held ~30–60 min, give a second small portion. Total tonight should be about 1/3–1/2 of his normal dinner.
- If bland meal is held, resume his normal non-recalled food at breakfast tomorrow.
- No treats, table scraps, dairy, fatty foods, or new chews until normal stool returns.

HYGIENE (this matters because of the recall context)
- Pick up stool immediately; bag and trash it (do NOT compost).
- Wash your hands thoroughly after handling Kibo or cleanup.
- If stool got on his hindquarters, gently clean with warm water + mild dog shampoo, rinse, dry.
- Wash any soiled bedding/towels in hot water.
- Hard-floor disinfection where stool landed: dilute household bleach (~1:32) or an accelerated hydrogen peroxide product; rinse after.
- Keep him away from other pets' food/water bowls for now; wash bowls in hot soapy water.
- Keep small children from handling stool or face-licking.

MONITORING (next 24–48 hours)
- Stool: frequency, consistency, color, mucus, blood. Photo + log time of each.
- Appetite: still eating? How much of the bland meal?
- Energy: alert vs quiet; willing to play/interact.
- Vomiting: any new vomit, frequency, content, blood.
- Gums: pink and moist (press; color returns in <2 sec).
- Belly: soft, not distended, no pain when gently palpated.
- Hydration: skin pinch at shoulder returns flat in <2 sec; eyes not sunken.
- Temperature if you have a rectal thermometer: normal 101.0–102.5°F.
- Behavior: willing to walk, normal posture, no "praying" position (front down, rear up) which signals abdominal pain.

CALL REGULAR VET (non-urgent, within 24 hours) IF
- A second loose stool or soft stool beyond 24 hours.
- Any mucus, melena (black/tarry), or streak of blood in stool.
- Mild drop in appetite but still eating some.
- Low-grade lethargy that's not improving by morning.
- Mild belly tenderness on gentle palpation.
- You want a fecal panel (reasonable ask given recall exposure even if currently mild).

GO TO URGENT/EMERGENCY VET IMMEDIATELY IF
- Repeated diarrhea (3+ episodes in 12 hr) or any frank bloody diarrhea.
- Any vomiting — especially repeated, productive, or with blood.
- Refusing water >12 hours, or signs of dehydration (tacky gums, skin pinch >2 sec, sunken eyes).
- Temperature >103°F or <99°F.
- Pale, white, blue, or brick-red gums.
- Abdominal distension, swelling, or obvious pain (whimper, growl, snap, praying posture, refusal to be touched).
- Collapse, weakness, staggering, or non-responsiveness.
- Any new or rapidly worsening symptom you weren't expecting.

DECISION ANCHOR
- One soft stool + grass chew + otherwise bright = almost always benign incidental colitis.
- Salmonella enteritis in dogs typically presents with fever + bloody/mucoid diarrhea + vomiting + lethargy, often within 6–72 hours of exposure. The pattern you're describing does not currently match it. The plan above is designed to catch a pivot early without over-escalating.

GOAL: vary the spatial reserve between the cool window wash and the warm counter edge while holding brush load, paper, and wash timing constant. The post-dry legibility of the warm edge is the readout.

Sheet and layout
One 9x12" or 8x10" 140 lb cold press sheet, undivided. Pencil a 2x3 grid: six panels, each ~3x4". Light pencil lines only. Label panels A-F in a margin.

Composition per panel (identical across all six)
Cool wash on the left ~40%, warm edge on the right ~50%, vertical boundary roughly mid-panel.

Pigment prep — done ONCE before paint touches paper, so the mix doesn't drift between panels
Cool mix: blue-violet (e.g., ultramarine + a touch of rose), single dilution, batch ~30 ml.
Warm mix: e.g., raw sienna or yellow ochre + a touch of burnt sienna, single dilution, batch ~30 ml.
Same two mixes used in all six panels.

Brush and load
One round brush, re-loaded to the same wetness before each panel.

Wash timing — held constant across panels
Paint the cool wash across all six panels in one sweep (~45-60 s total). Then loop back and apply the warm edge panel-by-panel, each within ~18-22 s of that panel's cool wash. Wet-into-wet, same timer per panel. This sits inside your backrun window and avoids the seam-or-bloom choice, so timing is not the variable.

The variable — reserve width between cool wash and warm edge:
  A: 0 mm (touch)
  B: ~1.5 mm
  C: ~3 mm
  D: ~5 mm
  E: ~8 mm
  F: ~12 mm

Read after full dry. Photograph before any later pass, because post-dry convergence is exactly what you are testing.

Prediction from your earlier articulation: A converges on drying; B-C keep the warm edge legible without a hard seam; D-F harden into a seam and lose the quiet. If B-C land where you expect, the study confirms the narrow reserve is doing the work, not the pigment load.

A few real problems with both lines — the CS proposal collapses signals that the gate model keeps deliberately separate, and the second clause overstates what actually happens. Here's where it breaks:

1. "Authority" without a qualifier is ambiguous in HS. There are at least three distinct verifications in flight: Helio admin proof (the workspace owner's attestation), connector authentication (the supported-tool auth), and external authority (the third-party system admin or agency owner who actually controls the connector's admin scope). Memory is explicit that these are tracked as separate readiness inputs — the 2023-10-10 case is the prototype where the workspace owner attested but the real admin was at an agency, and the 2025-01-16 followup is the prototype where admitting the applicant explicitly required a separate external-authority confirmation while the earlier Helio admin proof and connector authentication "remained current" and were "not relabeled as failed." "Authority verified" with no qualifier reads as if all three collapsed into one, which is exactly the failure mode those cases were designed to prevent.

2. "This account has granted the permissions" puts the grant in the wrong place. The relevant permissions in the assisted cases live with the third-party admin or the agency, not with the workspace/account. The 2023-10-10 case is literally an instance where the workspace owner could not grant what was needed because the admin lived elsewhere. Phrasing it as the account granting the permissions will mislead operators into reading a self-serve confirmation where the model requires an external one.

3. "Automated outreach allowed" overstates the routing. What actually happens when external authority is confirmed is that Helio admits the workspace and releases the setup prompts it had been holding (2025-01-16 case). It's not a separate "Helio contacts the admin" action that turns on; it's the end of a hold. And the 2025-03-07 PMM draft already burned us once on a "companywide automation" claim that didn't match the gate model — this label has the same shape.

4. Quietly conflicts with "assisted = routing, not penalty." If a CS operator reads "automated outreach allowed" on an assisted-route account, the natural reading is that the assisted path has cleared and self-serve is now in force. But the assisted path is a route, not a status to be cleared — the workspace's HS routing is what it is, and external-authority confirmation doesn't re-grade the account.

Suggested revision (keeps the operator read fast, doesn't collapse signals, doesn't overstate):

  Label:  "External authority confirmed"
  Help:   "The third-party admin who controls the connector (e.g., the
          Okta / Salesforce / agency owner) has confirmed they can
          authorize this setup. Helio admin proof and connector
          authentication are tracked separately and were not changed by
          this confirmation."

If CS wants a one-second read on what the operator should do next, add a second line below the help text — outside the tooltip — like "Action: release held setup prompts." That keeps the tooltip honest and puts the action cue where operators will actually look.

Yes — the bottom-up clearing in ~30 seconds, with no sediment, color, or odor, fits trapped air in the lines (entrained microbubbles that scatter light, then float up and dissipate). The glass test is the classic confirmation. Conservative cold-water flushing sequence below, with the signs that mean it isn't air.

Conservative cold-water flushing sequence (after a planned common-line shutoff)

Prep
  - Place a dry paper towel under the kitchen cold shutoff (documented history — confirm it stays dry through and after the flush) and one under the guest-bath shutoff.
  - Unscrew the aerators on the kitchen cold tap and the bathroom cold taps; set them and their rubber washers in a cup so they aren't lost. Aerators trap air bubbles and debris, so removing them gives a true read on the supply.
  - Open under-sink stop valves fully. Have a towel and bucket ready.

Cold-side purge (farthest from entry → toward kitchen)
  1. Toilets: flush each one twice to refill tanks and clear air from the closet supplies.
  2. Bathroom cold tap (farthest from kitchen): moderate flow, pencil-width, 3–5 min.
  3. Guest-bath cold tap: same, 3–5 min.
  4. Kitchen cold tap: moderate flow, 5–10 min. Use a clear glass to confirm clarity.
  5. Tub cold spout: 2–3 min (long air column in the horizontal run).
  6. Shower cold, if reachable: 1–2 min; showerhead can be removed if it has a tiny flow path that hides air.

Verification
  - Fill a clear glass from each fixture after step 4. Water should be fully clear with no rising bubble layer within ~30 seconds. If any fixture stays milky beyond that, give it another 2–3 minutes at the same moderate flow.

Reassemble
  - Reinstall aerators with their washers. Run each cold tap 30 seconds after reinstalling to flush any debris that was sitting in the aerator threads.

Appliances (staged, only after fixtures run clear)
  - Fridge: run the water dispenser 1–2 min, discard the first 2–3 batches of ice (the reservoir and ice line trap air). Replace the inline filter if it's old.
  - Dishwasher: empty rinse cycle, no detergent, before any real load.
  - Washer: empty rinse/drain on cold before the next real load.

Brief hot-side note: do a short hot flush at each fixture when you're ready — hot lines hold their own air pocket and you don't want to push it into the dishwasher inlet later.

Kibo: the pre-shutoff water is the safe choice until cold fixtures clear, the first fridge ice batches are discarded, and any inline filter is refreshed.

Signs it isn't air — stop using the water and contact Cherrywood management
  - Cloudiness that persists more than 15–20 minutes at any one fixture, or any cloudiness left in a glass after standing for a minute.
  - Color: yellow, brown, orange/rust, or any tint that doesn't fully clear.
  - Visible particles: sand, grit, flakes, black specks, or anything that settles to the bottom of a glass.
  - Odor: rotten egg / sulfur (anaerobic bacteria in the lines), fuel, oil, or solvent smell (cross-contamination). A faint chlorine smell is usually a utility-side flush residual and clears quickly — but if it's strong or persistent, report it.
  - Pressure changes: sudden drop, surge, or sputtering that doesn't resolve as you run the tap.
  - Leaks: anywhere on the supply side — under the kitchen sink (especially that cold shutoff), the wall valve, under any sink, behind or under the washer/dishwasher/fridge, on the riser, or a wet paper towel anywhere you placed one.
  - Boil-water or do-not-drink advisory from the utility or Cherrywood.

If any of those show up, stop using the cold water for drinking, cooking, ice, and the dishwasher/washer, keep the pre-shutoff water out for Kibo, and email Cherrywood property management describing the symptom, the fixture(s) affected, and the timing relative to today's shutoff.

Yes — this is almost certainly a smishing text, not a real notice. The pattern fits the "small-fee, shortened-link" package scam that has been running for years: the amount is small so you let your guard down, the URL is shortened so you can't see where it goes, and no specific carrier or retailer is named so you're steered toward guessing and tapping.

Why it reads as a scam:
- USPS, UPS, FedEx, Amazon, and other real carriers do not collect address-correction or redelivery fees by SMS, and they never route payment through a shortened link.
- The generic "a package" framing with no carrier or order number is the giveaway — real notices name the carrier and the order or tracking ID.
- A sub-$1 fee is a known bait pattern: low enough to feel safe to pay.

What NOT to do (the short version for Mom):
- Do not tap the link.
- Do not reply to the text — not even "STOP" — replying confirms your number is live.
- Do not call any phone number that appears inside the message.
- Do not forward the text to anyone to ask; taps happen by accident.

How to check whether there's a real problem, using contacts she already trusts — no link involved:
1. Don't open the link. Open the app or website she normally uses for that store or carrier (Amazon, UPS, FedEx, USPS, Target, etc.). If she's not sure which, pull up the order-confirmation email from when she placed the order — that email has the real tracking link and the real contact info.
2. On that app or site, look at the order status. If it shows in transit, out for delivery, or delivered, there's nothing to pay and nothing to fix.
3. If she wants a human, call the number printed on her paper statement, on the back of her card, or in the order-confirmation email. Never a number from the text.
4. If she has no order she expects, the answer is the same: ignore the text. There is no fee because there is no package.

How to report, block, and delete:
1. Screenshot the message first — captures the sender's number, the body, and the timestamp.
2. Forward the screenshot to 7726 (SPAM). Free, works on all major US carriers, routes the report onward.
3. If the text claimed to be USPS, also email the screenshot to spam@uspis.gov.
4. File a short report at reportfraud.ftc.gov — about five minutes, no account needed.
5. On her phone: open the message → tap the sender's number → Info → Block this Caller. On Android the wording is slightly different but it's under the conversation details.
6. Delete the message, then clear or delete the conversation thread so the link isn't a tap-away later.

Walking the last half mile was the right call. The two skips under load on a climb match the pattern from 2024 (load-dependent skip, silent under light pedaling), and this is now a recurrence that has outlived at least one chain-and-cassette replacement cycle. Treat the bike as out of service for commuting until a shop has looked at it.

Keep the bike out of commute use: yes

Do not ride this bike to work, to the coffee shop, or anywhere that involves intersections, traffic, or a climb under power. The failure mode is a sudden loss of drive at exactly the moments when you need predictable power delivery — pulling away from a stop, accelerating across a lane, climbing a short grade, or pedaling out of the saddle in traffic. On a climb you can coast to a stop; in front of a car you cannot. You have the bus as a fallback (used it in 2024) and walking is also fine for short hops. The bike is fine for pushing by hand and for the stationary checks below.

Stationary inspection sequence (no-load, no pedaling-under-power, no pushing the bike while you pedal)

Do these in order. If anything looks off, stop and book the shop — do not "test" by riding.

  1. Tire and wheel baseline (rear first, since that side failed last August and the sidewall cut is on file)
     - Squeeze both tires. Note pressure roughly. Look at the rear sidewall — any new cuts, bulges, or visible casing? Spin each wheel in the stand and watch for lateral hop or rub against the brake pads.
     - Confirm the wheel is fully seated in the dropouts and the quick release or thru-axle is closed and tight.
  2. Chain wear with a gauge
     - Drop the chain on the largest rear cog (the gauge reads most accurately there). A reading at or past 0.75 percent means the chain is stretched and almost certainly contributed to today's skip.
     - The Oct 15 2024 shop reading was 0.75 percent, and the chain has been ridden six more months plus whatever commute use since.
  3. Cassette teeth, one cog at a time
     - With the chain off the cog you're inspecting, look straight down at the tooth profile. Symmetric trapezoid teeth are healthy. Asymmetric, hooked, or "shark fin" teeth are worn and will skip under load even on a new chain.
     - Pay extra attention to the cog you were in during each of today's two skips. If you don't remember which cog it was, inspect all of them — the climb profile (steepest grade on your commute) will tell you roughly where to look.
  4. Stiff chain link
     - Shift to the smallest chainring and a middle cog. Lift the chain off the cog and flex it sideways by hand, link by link, through a full revolution. A stiff link resists flex and feels rigid. The chain should flop freely. A single stiff link will mimic cassette wear symptoms.
  5. Front chainring teeth
     - Same inspection as the cassette. Look down each tooth for hooking or asymmetry. Front chainring wear is a common cause of "skip that came back after a new chain and cassette."
  6. Cable housing and ferrules
     - Look at the rear derailleur cable housing where it enters the rear derailleur — is the ferrule fully seated in the housing stop? This was the exact failure mode in Sept 2024 and was easy to miss. Check the housing stops on the frame as well.
     - Look for a frayed cable strand poking out anywhere. Pull the cable gently at the derailleur and feel for any "gritty" spots as it moves through the housing.
  7. Derailleur hanger alignment
     - Crouch behind the bike and sight down the cassette. The hanger should look parallel to the cassette cogs, no twist. A bent hanger causes ghost shifting and load-dependent skip even with a new chain and cassette. Do not try to straighten it yourself — measurement with a hanger gauge is a shop job.
  8. B-tension screw
     - The upper jockey wheel should sit roughly five to six millimeters below the largest cog teeth when shifted into the biggest cog. If it's way off, indexing will be wrong on the gears you actually use for climbing.
  9. Brakes, just to rule them out as a contributor to your "felt normal" check
     - Squeeze each lever. Firm lever, pads contact, no sponginess, no lever travel to the bar. Spin each wheel — no rub, no pulse.
  10. Cranks, pedals, bottom bracket
      - Hold a crank arm and try to rock it in and out toward the bike. Play here is unrelated to the skip but worth noting while the bike is in the stand.

What NOT to do at home

  - Do not stand on the pedals and push. That is a loaded test.
  - Do not push the bike along the sidewalk while pedaling. Also a loaded test.
  - Do not shift under load. Shift only while pedaling very lightly with the bike held still in the stand.
  - Do not try to "feel out" the skip by spinning the cranks hard with the rear wheel off the ground. A freewheel unloaded is exactly the condition that hides the problem you actually have.
