CONSERVATIVE IPHONE CLEANUP — baseline 4.1 GB free, ~2 wks before PDX 5/9–5/11

The verification step you asked for is Phase 0 below. Nothing in Phases 1–3 deletes until that gate is green.

PROTECTED (do not touch at any phase):
  - Family photos (Camera Roll, any album)
  - Travel confirmations (Wallet boarding passes; airline/hotel/rental emails + apps)
  - Authentication apps (Authy, Google Authenticator, banking, work MFA)
  - Message history (Messages, WhatsApp, Signal, email — including attachments)

------------------------------------------------------------
PHASE 0 — PRE-DELETION VERIFICATION (the gate)
------------------------------------------------------------
0.1  Confirm iCloud Photos is healthy:
     Settings → [your name] → iCloud → Photos → "Sync This [iPhone]" ON.
     If a "X items pending" sits for >10 min, wait it out before deleting local copies.

0.2  Screenshot the current state:
     Settings → General → iPhone Storage. Record free space (4.1 GB) and the top categories.

0.3  Force a fresh iCloud backup:
     Settings → [your name] → iCloud → iCloud Backup → Back Up Now.
     This is cheap insurance against anything you delete in Phases 1–3.

0.4  Open each auth app (Authy, Google Authenticator, banking, work MFA) and confirm tokens are present. Do not delete, reinstall, or offload any auth app.

Gate: only proceed when 0.1–0.4 are green.

------------------------------------------------------------
PHASE 1 — REVERSIBLE DOWNLOADS (safest, re-downloadable)
------------------------------------------------------------
1.1  Podcasts:
     a) Settings → Podcasts → "Automatically Delete After Played" → "After 1 day" (prevents re-accumulation).
     b) Podcasts → Library → Downloaded → sort Oldest First. Delete episodes you've already finished.

1.2  Streaming video downloads — delete all offline downloads from:
     Netflix, YouTube/YT Premium, Disney+, Prime Video, Max, Peacock.
     These re-download from your subscriptions at any time.

Expected from Phase 1: 4–10 GB.

------------------------------------------------------------
PHASE 2 — DUPLICATE MEDIA (reversible: trash stays 30 days)
------------------------------------------------------------
2.1  Photos → Albums → Utilities → Duplicates. Tap "Merge" only when one of the pair is clearly the larger / better-quality original. Skip pairs you're unsure about.

2.2  Do NOT empty Recently Deleted yet — keep the 30-day safety window.

2.3  Camera smoke test (proves the camera pipeline still works):
     - Take one new photo
     - Take one 5–10 sec video
     - Confirm both appear in Photos → Recents within ~30 seconds
     - Delete the test VIDEO
     - Keep the test PHOTO for now; delete it in Phase 4

If the smoke test fails, STOP cleanup and troubleshoot before continuing.

Expected from Phase 2: 1–4 GB.

------------------------------------------------------------
PHASE 3 — APP-DATA REVIEW (only after Phase 2 is verified)
------------------------------------------------------------
Settings → General → iPhone Storage → "Review Large Attachments" surfaces the targets.

3.1  Messages → Review Large Attachments:
     PROTECT — anything from your airline/hotel/rental, anyone you'll message while traveling, anything dated in the last 14 days, any photo of a document (ID, insurance card).
     DELETE — large videos/photos in clearly old, non-essential threads.
     Do not mass-delete whole conversations.

3.2  WhatsApp → Storage and Data → Manage Storage. Use "Review and delete" on clearly old, non-essential chats. Don't clear conversation history wholesale.

3.3  Signal → Settings → Storage. Same rule: only clear large media in old, non-critical threads; keep text history intact.

3.4  Mail (only if you use Apple Mail): Settings → General → iPhone Storage → Mail. Don't delete messages you may need while traveling.

3.5  Safari cache (NOT history):
     Settings → Safari → Advanced → Website Data → Remove All Website Data.
     Frees cache without clearing history, bookmarks, or saved logins. You'll be re-prompted for logins on sites.

3.6  Offload unused apps (low-risk, reversible):
     Settings → General → iPhone Storage → tap an unused app → "Offload App".
     Offloading removes the binary but keeps app data; tap the icon to reinstall. Do NOT offload any auth app or any app you'll need on the trip.

Expected from Phase 3: 2–6 GB.

------------------------------------------------------------
PHASE 4 — POST-CLEANUP CHECK + RECENTLY DELETED
------------------------------------------------------------
4.1  Settings → General → iPhone Storage — confirm free space.
     Target: ≥8–10 GB free before departure (room for trip photos/video + offline maps).

4.2  Photos → Recently Deleted → Select All → Delete. Do this only after you've confirmed the merged/removed items are duplicates you intended to remove.

4.3  Delete the Phase 2 smoke-test photo.

4.4  Final protected-item spot check:
     - Open one auth app → token still present
     - Wallet → boarding passes still present
     - Messages → search airline name → thread intact
     - Photos → Recents → family photos still present

------------------------------------------------------------
EXPECTED RECOVERY
------------------------------------------------------------
Phase 1: 4–10 GB · Phase 2: 1–4 GB · Phase 3: 2–6 GB
Realistic total: 7–20 GB. Mom's Dec '23 cleanup moved 126.7 → 108.9 GB (~17.8 GB freed) with the same podcast + duplicate-video pattern, so this magnitude is plausible for you.

------------------------------------------------------------
HARD DO-NOTS (during cleanup)
------------------------------------------------------------
  - Do not run an iOS update (storage pressure can corrupt it).
  - Do not sign out of iCloud.
  - Do not "Erase All Content and Settings."
  - Do not mass-delete from Camera Roll.
  - Do not clear Safari history or bookmarks (Website Data only).
  - Do not delete or reinstall any authentication app.
  - Do not delete travel confirmation emails or Wallet passes.

------------------------------------------------------------
TRIP-PREP NOTES (after cleanup, when free space is healthy)
------------------------------------------------------------
  - Apple Maps → Settings → Maps → Offline Maps → Download Portland region.
  - Confirm you can reach at least one auth app offline or via cloud restore.
  - Take one final iCloud backup right before you leave.

SITUATION SNAPSHOT

Good news first: no staining, buckling, odor, or visible transfer means the contact has been brief enough or the cardboard is mild enough that no acid migration has registered on the sheet. You are in the preventive window, not the remedial one. The 1.5-inch fiber lift from January is reported flat as of 02/02 and not visibly progressing, so the immediate concern is the backing system, not the paper's structure.

Why ordinary cardboard is a long-term problem even when it looks fine today:
- Most framing-grade cardboard is wood-pulp (lignin-rich) and either acidic or only mildly buffered. Lignin breaks down into acids; acids migrate to whatever the board touches.
- Over years this produces mat burn (a brown rectangle outlining the board), foxing (small reddish-brown freckles), overall yellowing, and embrittlement of the paper edge that touches it.
- "Acid-free" claims on craft-store backings are unreliable — true archival board is alpha-cellulose or 100% cotton rag with a calcium-carbonate buffer (pH ~8.5–9.0). The label alone doesn't prove it.

CONSERVATIVE OPTIONS

A. Interleave without disturbing the current housing
- Slip a sheet of 100% cotton rag or alpha-cellulose board between the watercolor and the cardboard back, cut slightly smaller than the frame's interior so it seats flat.
- This works only if the sheet is genuinely loose in the frame (not taped or glued to the cardboard). If anything adheres it to the cardboard, this option is off the table without further work.
- Limited benefit because the cardboard remains in the sealed back, still off-gassing onto the new sheet. A stopgap, not a fix.

B. Re-house on archival backing (recommended)
- Remove the sheet, document condition (photographs, notes), and re-mount on proper board. This is the standard archival reframing approach and what a trained framer would do for a piece going back into regular display.
- Composition: archival mat board window (or full archival back board) → sheet hinged at top edge with Japanese tissue + wheat-starch paste → spacer/offset to keep art away from glazing → glazing → sealed back panel.
- For the prior fiber lift, a window mat with the planned ~1/8 in overlap continues to hide it; you do not need to repair it further.

C. Bring it to an archival framer for a full re-frame
- Same materials as B, done by someone trained to handle paper safely. Typical cost for a small piece is modest and worth it if you want this back on a community rotation soon.

SAFE MATERIALS (the short list to source)

Backing and mat board:
- 100% cotton rag, calcium-carbonate buffered, pH 8.5–9. Bainbridge Alpharag, Crescent RagMat (Conservation line), or Rising Museum Board are the usual archival choices. Look for the "conservation" or "museum" designation, not "acid-free" alone.

Sheet support (optional, for the past edge):
- A thin alpha-cellulose conservation sheet or light-weight cotton tissue behind the watercolor can give the lifted edge a soft backing without making the repair permanent.

Hinging (you already have these):
- Long-fiber Japanese kozo tissue and your wheat-starch paste. Two small hinges on the top edge only, well above the image area.

Glazing:
- UV-filtering glass or museum glass (e.g., Tru Vue Museum Glass). Optium Museum Acrylic is the archival acrylic equivalent if weight or breakage is a concern.

Spacer:
- Self-adhesive archival foam spacer strips, or thin strips cut from acid-free foam board, set around the inside perimeter so the sheet cannot migrate forward to touch the glazing.

Back seal:
- Archival paper dust sheet behind the back panel, or foil tape (not duct tape, not regular masking tape) sealing the back.

HANDLING PRECAUTIONS

Workspace and self:
- Clean, dry, flat surface with a blotter or glassine down. Wash hands and skip lotion that day. Nitrile gloves are fine if you're used to them; otherwise clean dry hands are equally acceptable for paper.
- No food, drink, or pens near the sheet. Use a soft pencil only, and only on backing material — never near the image.
- Camera or phone ready before you start, to photograph the sheet as found and at each step.

Handling the sheet:
- Two-handed lift from opposite corners of the backing it sits on. Never touch the painted surface.
- Keep horizontal. Do not flex, bow, or roll.
- No tape of any kind — including low-tack — given the prior fiber lift history. If you ever need to lift a hinge later, the wheat-starch paste releases with water.
- Avoid direct sunlight, heating/cooling vents, kitchens, bathrooms, basements, and exterior walls while it is out of the frame.

Environment:
- Stable relative humidity in the 40–55% range. A finished basement or attic is the wrong storage location long-term.

SIGNS THAT JUSTIFY A PROFESSIONAL

Bring it to an archival framer (custom framer with archival training, e.g., PPFA or AAA accredited) when:
- You want a proper re-mount but no conservation treatment is needed.
- The 1.5-inch edge lift needs to remain hidden under a mat without re-lifting.
- The piece is going back into any kind of rotation or loan and you want a documented archival housing.

Bring it to a paper conservator (American Institute for Conservation "Find a Conservator" directory, mail-in evaluation is standard) if any of these appear:
- New staining, tide lines, or a brown rectangle outlining where the cardboard sat.
- Foxing (small reddish-brown freckles, often clustered).
- Musty or moldy odor, or any fuzzy growth.
- Pigment cracking, flaking, lifting, or chalking.
- New tears, losses, punctures, or brittleness at the edge that contacts cardboard.
- Cockling or buckling that does not relax under flat blotting.
- Any sign of prior water damage.
- Visible adhesive residue or previous repair attempts.
- You are uncertain whether the old edge lift is stable when you re-mount it.

DECISION

For this piece as described — no current damage, healed edge, sheet loose in the frame, cardboard now confirmed as ordinary — an archival framer is the right first call, not a conservator. A conservator is reserved for if anything in the red-flag list above shows up. If you want to do it yourself and are comfortable with wheat-starch paste hinging, sourcing the four key materials (rag mat board, Japanese tissue, spacer, UV-filtering glazing) gets you most of the way; everything else you already have.

PRACTICAL REPLACEMENT FRAMEWORK

Triggers (replace when any one is present):
- Mileage: 300–500 mi for trail shoes (lake-trail terrain is at the abrasive end)
- Lateral heel tread nearly smooth — grip on cambered trail sections is reduced, which can subtly alter foot placement
- Pronounced midsole creasing — foam has compressed and lost rebound; cushioning is usually gone before the tread is
- New or returning aches that don't appear in older, similar-effort runs

Why timing matters for you specifically:
A worn midsole changes how the foot loads, which can shift stress proximally. Given your ankle history, you want cushioning and lateral stability intact rather than running on a "treaded but dead" pair. 480 mi + smooth lateral tread + visible creasing means the shoes are due, not early.

Selection match-points (so the new shoe isn't a second new variable):
- Same heel-to-toe drop as the current pair (keeps ankle loading pattern identical)
- Similar stack height (don't go from a low trail shoe to a max-cushion one in the same week)
- Same category: trail, neutral, similar width in the toe box
- Secure heel counter — this is non-negotiable for you given the prior left-heel hot spot
- Avoid changing drop, stack, and brand simultaneously

CONSERVATIVE TRANSITION PLAN

Phase 1 — Walk-only (2–3 days, no running):
- Wear the new shoes around the house for an hour or two, then a 20–30 min easy outdoor walk on flat ground
- Left-heel-specific checks: any lift at the collar? rub at the Achilles notch? pressure on the medial side?
- If anything rubs or slips, return or swap the lacing before phase 2 — do not "run through it"

Phase 2 — First run in new shoes:
- Same week as a normal nonconsecutive 30-min run, but shorten to ~20 min, same easy effort, same lake-trail loop
- This is the conservative move: you're isolating the shoe as the only new variable
- Symptoms to watch during: focal ankle sensation (any location), left heel rub, gait change, knee/hip shift
- Symptoms to watch the following morning: same list, plus delayed-onset anything at the left heel

Phase 3 — Second run that week:
- If phase 2 was clean during the run and the next morning, do the second nonconsecutive run at the normal 30 min, same easy effort
- If anything was off, repeat phase 2 the following week before going to 30 min

Phase 4 — Hold steady:
- Keep two nonconsecutive 30-min runs for at least 2 weeks after the swap before considering any duration or frequency change
- Don't stack a third run, a longer run, or new terrain onto the same week as the shoe swap
- Keep the old shoes unworn-in-a-closet for 2 weeks, in case the new pair develops a fit issue worth returning

LEFT-HEEL PRECAUTIONS (prior hot-spot history)

- Use the extra top eyelet for a heel-lock lace on the left shoe only if needed; keep laces even across the midfoot so you don't create a new pressure point
- If a hot spot appears: stop the session, clean and dry the area, no further friction that day, cover with a hydrocolloid or simple dressing before the next session, and if skin is broken or the spot returns at the same place in the next run, return the shoes rather than continuing to break them in

PRESERVED RULES (unchanged)

- Session + following-morning symptom-free is the gate for any advance
- Any focal ankle pain → hold running and contact the therapist; this applies whether it happens during the run, that evening, or the next morning
- New shoes never share a week with a duration or frequency increase
- Easy cycling and ankle-and-calf strengthening continue as adjuncts, not as progression tracks

     Frequency baseline for most drivers: ~1 comp/coll claim every 7-10 years.

2. Lost rental coverage (per repair incident)
     If the cheaper option drops rental entirely: every at-fault, hit-and-run, or
     animal-strike repair where you need a loaner costs you out of pocket at
     market rental rates (~$45-60/day right now from Enterprise/Hertz).
     Typical at-fault body-shop repair: 10-21 days.
     If the cheaper option just lowers the daily cap: exposure =
     (OldDailyCap - NewDailyCap) x DaysNeeded.

DECISION AXES

Axis 1 — Liquidity
     Can you cover the deductible delta from cash savings today without
     disrupting anything (emergency fund, SBT growth work, etc.)?
     - Yes: higher deductible is fine. You self-insure the gap.
     - No: pay the $72 and keep the lower deductible.
     Rule of thumb I use: if deductible delta > 25% of your liquid emergency
     fund, keep the lower deductible.

Axis 2 — Rental coverage value (the axis you flagged)
     Rank your realistic fallback if your car is in the shop for 2 weeks:
       a) You have a partner/household car you can borrow
       b) You're fine on rideshare + transit + walking for 2 weeks
       c) No realistic substitute
     - If (a) or (b): rental coverage is low-value to you. Drop it freely;
       the $72 is a clean win.
     - If (c): rental coverage is load-bearing. Calculate what 14 days at
       market ($50/day = $700) costs out of pocket. The $72/year premium
       difference becomes a $700-per-incident exposure swing.

THREE-BUCKET OUTPUT

  1. Take cheaper option: liquid on the deductible AND substitute transport
     available. Save the $72, accept the higher comp/coll deductible.
  2. Take pricier option: illiquid on the deductible delta OR no substitute
     transport. Pay the $72, keep the lower deductible + full rental.
  3. Hybrid (often the best): ask the carrier if you can raise comp/coll
     deductibles while keeping rental coverage intact. Many will let you.
     That usually captures most of the savings without the rental exposure.

WHAT I'LL COMPUTE ONCE YOU GIVE ME THE NUMBERS

  - Break-even years on the deductible alone: (Deductible Delta) / $72.
    E.g., a $500 deductible bump needs ~7 claim-free years to pay off vs.
    the premium saved.
  - Per-incident exposure if you skip rental: Days x DailyMarketRate, for
    both 14-day and 21-day scenarios.
  - Combined expected annual cost: Premium + (ClaimProbability x
    Deductible) + (RentalClaimProbability x RentalCost).
  - A one-line recommendation tied to your liquidity position and rental
    fallback — not a generic "cheaper is fine."

Comparison and recommendation

The two options differ on three variables that matter for an ankle with your history: drop, cushioning firmness, and mass. Only one of them changes more than one of those at a time.

Option A (8 mm drop, firmer, 9.2 oz)
- Keeps drop identical to your current shoes, so ankle dorsiflexion demand at toe-off is unchanged.
- Slightly firmer midsole gives clearer proprioceptive feedback, which tends to be friendly to a recovering ankle.
- Lighter by 1.2 oz, so per-step calf and peroneal load is a touch lower.
- Net new variables: firmness and a small mass drop. Drop is held constant.

Option B (10 mm drop, softer, 10.4 oz)
- Raises drop by 2 mm, which shortens the ankle's working range slightly and changes calf and Achilles loading in a way your ankle has not been conditioned to in the last 480 miles.
- Softer midsole absorbs more impact but gives less positional feedback, so the stabilizers fire a bit later in the gait cycle.
- 1.2 oz heavier than A, and 1.2 oz heavier than what you are used to.
- Net new variables: drop, firmness, and mass all moving at once.

Recommendation: Option A

The reason is variable count, not which shoe is "better." Drop is the single change most likely to shift ankle biomechanics, and Option B moves drop, cushioning, and weight together. Option A moves only cushioning and weight, in the favorable direction on both. A firmer, lighter, same-drop shoe is the closest mechanical continuation of what your ankle has already tolerated through 480 symptom-free miles and two consecutive weeks of 30-minute easy runs. That is the conservative pick.

If for any reason Option B is the only one available, the transition below still works but you should add an extra walk-only day at the front and treat the first run as a true test of the new drop rather than a normal session.

Transition plan for Option A (this is the same four-phase structure we have used before, applied to the new shoes)

Phase 1, walk-only, days 1 to 3
- Wear the new shoes for normal daily walking only: the morning loop, any errands, stairs.
- Do not run in them yet.
- End of each day: heel-check inside the right ankle against your usual baseline. Any awareness beyond the normal "I walked a lot" feeling means the new shoes do not get a run yet, and you contact the therapist.

Phase 2, first run, day 4 or 5 (still in the same week)
- One of the two weekly sessions, shortened to about 20 minutes, easy effort, same easy pace and lake-trail surface you have been using.
- Walk 3 to 5 minutes warm-up before the clock starts, walk 3 to 5 minutes cool-down after. Do not count those in the 20.
- Stop at 20:00 regardless of how it feels.
- This week is the shoe-change week. Duration and frequency are both held flat. Do not add a third session, do not extend to 35 minutes, do not move the second run closer to the first.

Phase 3, second run, the other nonconsecutive day of that same week
- Only proceed if both the Phase 2 run and the morning after Phase 2 were symptom-free.
- Return to the normal 30-minute easy effort, same warm-up and cool-down.
- If anything focal shows up in the ankle during the run or the next morning, this run becomes the last one in the new shoes for that week, and you go back to the old pair until you can talk to the therapist.

Phase 4, hold steady, full two weeks
- Two nonconsecutive 30-minute easy runs per week for at least two full weeks before any change in duration or frequency.
- Keep the old shoes unworn for those two weeks so they are a clean fallback if anything regresses. After that, retire them, since the tread is already nearly smooth and the midsole is creased, and a fallback that has lost its own structure is not really a fallback.

Hard rules for this transition (unchanged)

- No duration increase and no frequency increase in the same week the new shoes arrive. Pick the week, do the swap, hold all other variables flat.
- Session-plus-following-morning symptom rule applies on every run. A focal inside-right-ankle ache during the run or the next morning stops the progression and triggers a therapist contact before the next run.
- Strengthening routine continues unchanged. The shoes change, the routine does not.
- Easy effort only. The new shoes are not an excuse to test pace.

What I would flag for you to watch specifically with Option A
- The slightly firmer midsole can feel "flat" or jarring on the first one or two runs, especially under the heel. That is a feel change, not a symptom. If it is purely a firmness perception and there is no focal ankle ache during the run or the next morning, proceed.
- The 1.2 oz drop in mass is small enough that you should not feel it as a change. If the shoes feel noticeably lighter in a way that tempts you to push pace, do not. Easy effort is the point.

If at any point in Phase 1 to 3 you get focal inside-right-ankle pain, or the run feels meaningfully different in gait or stability, hold the next run in the new shoes, switch back to the old pair for that session, and contact the therapist before the next attempt.

Here's a compact packing method for the six loose photographs in Mom's carry-on. It protects image surfaces and any verso writing, keeps the photographs in the order she took them out of the box, and stays neutral on P027 and on a specific date.

Materials (small, carry-on-friendly):
- Six acid-free paper sleeves, each slightly larger than the print (or clean glassine envelopes if you already have them).
- One piece of buffered archival board or a small rigid folder, sized to hold the six sleeved prints flat without bending.
- One soft pencil (HB) and one small slip of paper for a travel-order note.
- One clean, soft cloth or lint-free wipes.
- Optional: a soft cotton face mask or clean scarf to act as a light overlay if the tote gets jostled.

Step-by-step:
1. Clean hands and a clean surface. Skip hand lotion that day. Keep prints away from food, drinks, and pens.
2. Do not write on or attach anything to the photographs themselves.
3. For each photograph, visually note which side is the image and which side has the handwriting. Do not guess at the content; the note is just about handling, not identification.
4. Slip each photograph into its own paper sleeve so the image side is protected and the written side faces the back of the sleeve where it cannot be smudged. If the writing is soft pencil, sleeve it image-side out and writing-side facing a clean sheet of paper so nothing rubs it.
5. Preserve the order in which the photographs came out of the box. Number the sleeves 1 through 6 on the outside corner in soft pencil, matching the order Mom removed them.
6. On a small slip of paper (kept with the sleeves, not on them), record only: "From stored box — Mom's carry-on, travel Aug visit — six prints, order 1–6 preserved." This gives provenance without claiming dates or subjects.
7. Lay the six sleeved prints flat on the archival board or in the rigid folder, in the same 1–6 order, with a clean sheet on top.
8. Place the flat bundle inside a soft pouch or the center of the carry-on, between layers of clothing for cushioning. Keep it away from liquids, headphones, chargers, and zippers.
9. During travel, keep the carry-on in the cabin (not a checked bag) so temperature and pressure stay stable.
10. On arrival, take the bundle out before unpacking clothes so the prints do not sit compressed. Let them rest flat, still sleeved, until Mom is ready to look at them together.

Reading the 7/12 swatches against your prior work, here's what each mix is actually telling you, then a tight setup that locks in the working method.

WHAT EACH MIX DID

1) Blue + brown neutral — clearest value separation at the warm doorway edge after drying.
This is the keeper and it confirms the principle from 4/6 at Cherrywood: the doorway reads warm because the window wash is cool, not because the door is saturated. The brown neutral sits low-chroma on the value scale, so when the cool wash lands beside it there's a real step, not a hue fight. The warm edge survives drying because nothing has to compensate chromatically.

2) Blue + red — lively, but pulled the eye into the street wash.
The red carries too much chroma for the doorway role: it competes with the warm edge instead of letting the cool wash define it. The pair isn't broken, it's miscast — it'd be the right tool for a street-wash-forward study where the doorway is secondary. For doorway-as-subject work, it makes the wrong thing loud.

3) Three-pigment mix — darkest rain interruption, but muddied when rewetted.
The pigment load gave you the value you wanted in one pass, but the moment you touched damp paper to adjust, the third pigment turned to mud. This is a single-pass-only tool: it works only if you commit on the first lay and don't go back. That's a constraint you don't need to accept on the doorway edge.

RECOMMENDED NEXT SETUP

Run a narrow three-panel value-separation grid using the Blue + brown pair only. The 7/12 swatches settled the mix question; this study settles the practical minimum separation. Don't re-test the full mix range — that's already answered.

The arithmetic by hand:

**Scenario 1: Same cup volume, lower calories per cup**

Old bag: 380 kcal/cup
New bag: 365 kcal/cup

If Kibo gets the same 1-cup portion:
- Old: 380 kcal
- New: 365 kcal
- Difference: 15 kcal less (3.9% reduction)

For a typical ~30 lb dog's maintenance of ~400–500 kcal/day, 15 kcal is about 3–4% of daily intake — negligible.

**Scenario 2: Scaling to keep calories constant**

To deliver the same 380 kcal from the new food at 365 kcal/cup:
- Required cups = 380 ÷ 365 = 1.0411 cups
- That's about 1 cup + ~⅓ tablespoon extra (1 cup = 48 tsp; 0.0411 cup ≈ 2 tsp)

**Scenario 3: Following the new bag's feeding table blindly**

This is the trap. The new table is calibrated to 365 kcal/cup. If you keep feeding 1 cup because "that's what the old bag said," Kibo loses 15 kcal per cup. If the new table says 1 cup and you assume it equals the old 380 kcal — you'd underfeed by 15 kcal per cup. Over a day at 2 cups, that's 30 kcal — still small, but over weeks it adds up if you're scaling portions.

---

**Recommendation:**

Kibo has no symptoms, the new food is the same product/recipe lineage (just updated), and you have leftover old food. The cleanest approach:

1. **Finish the old bag first** — it's already open and you're mid-bag. Switching mid-bag creates the real digestive risk (any formula change, even minor, can briefly soften stool).
2. **When you open the new bag, transition over 3–4 days** like any diet change — roughly 25% new / 75% old on day 1, 50/50 day 2, 75/25 day 3, then 100% new.
3. **Use the new bag's feeding table as the starting point**, but verify against calories: if Kibo's weight has been steady on the old food at portion X, set the new portion to roughly X × (380/365) ≈ X × 1.041. In practice, round to the nearest ¼ cup and then monitor weight and body condition over 2–3 weeks before adjusting further.
4. **Watch stool** for the transition week — any recipe tweak can shift fiber or fat slightly. If stool softens but stays formed and Kibo is comfortable, it's expected. If you see persistent loose stool, appetite drop, or vomiting, pause and call the vet.

The 15-kcal-per-cup difference is small enough that weight drift is unlikely to be meaningful if you hold caloric intake roughly constant. The bigger variable is the recipe itself — ingredients and fiber ratios can change more than the calorie number suggests, which is why the gradual blend matters more than the math.

One thing worth doing: check whether the new bag lists an "old formula" or "new formula" feeding guide on the manufacturer's site or your last vet receipt, so you're not anchoring to a stale table. And if Kibo's been on the same lot for a while without issue, this is the kind of low-stakes switch that doesn't warrant a vet call unless something changes once you start the new bag.

Farro-egg skillet with burst tomatoes and corn.

Cooked farro holds the base, eggs bind, tomatoes and corn carry the sweetness, scallions and herbs finish. One pan, one bowl, one board.

Timed sequence (start at 0:00):

  0:00  prep — halve tomatoes, slice scallions (whites and greens separate), cut corn off the cob, chop herbs, beat 6–8 eggs in a bowl with salt, pepper, and most of the herbs
  0:05  heat a generous slick of olive oil in the skillet over medium-low; soften scallion whites with a pinch of salt, ~3 min
  0:08  add tomatoes; press a few with the spatula to burst, cook ~5 min until the juices thicken a bit
  0:13  add corn; stir 2 min to warm through
  0:15  add farro; toss to coat, then press into an even layer; adjust salt
  0:18  pour beaten eggs over; tilt to distribute, press gently with the spatula so the farro embeds in the eggs
  0:20  cover; drop heat to the lowest setting; cook 10–12 min — peek at 10; the top should look matte, not glossy, when set
  0:32  off heat, keep covered; rest 5 min so the center finishes gently without overcooking the bottom
  0:37  scatter reserved scallion greens and herbs; cut into wedges; serve from the pan

Total active ~20 min, hands-off ~12 min, ~10 min of slack inside the 45. Plenty of room to pour wine while it rests.

Q1 — "If authority is verified, does that also mean outreach is allowed?"
Answer: No.
Authority verified only means the external system (e.g., Helio) is permitted to perform the connector's required owner-level action or is network-allowlisted to do so. It is connector-readiness, not contact permission. Outreach still requires every other required state for the specific decision being evaluated to be current and supported — including active-admin, current entitlement, and the absence of active Customer Success adoption or renewal work. Per the guide: "Proceed: All required state for this evaluated decision is current and supported. This does not create blanket permission for other contact." Authority verified is at most one precondition among several; it never stands alone as outreach permission.

Q2 — "Can a proceed result clear a hold in another workspace for the same person?"
Answer: No.
A proceed is decision-specific — it confirms all required state is current for the evaluated decision. A hold is field-specific — it persists on the affected field until a fresh source check and system reevaluation. A proceed in workspace A does not refresh a stale field in workspace B, and Operations does not manually release holds. The cross-surface dependency rule reinforces this: a held field also constrains adjacent lifecycle messages that depend on that field, so stale state in one surface can keep holding related messages elsewhere until the source is re-checked and the system re-evaluates.

Q3 — "If entitlement is stale but Customer Success work is current, which reason should the operator show?"
Answer: Held.
Stale entitlement is a missing/stale/conflicting required state, which is the held condition. CS-work being current — i.e., no active Customer Success adoption or renewal work — only means suppression does not apply. Suppression and field-specific hold are evaluated independently; the stale entitlement blocks the decision regardless of CS-work status. The operator-facing reason is therefore Held, until a fresh source check on entitlement and system reevaluation refreshes the field.

PHASE 1 — RIGHT NOW (do not open)
 1. Keep both doors closed. Every opening costs cold mass.
 2. Confirm thermometer is on the middle shelf, not against a wall or in the door.
 3. Note positives: no electrical odor, no equipment fault, frozen items still solid, no leaks. The fridge will recover now that power is back.
 4. Set a 1-hour timer and recheck the fridge thermometer.

PHASE 2 — DECISION POINT AT 1 HOUR
 - ≤40°F: move to Phase 3 inventory.
 - 41–44°F: wait another hour; if still over 40°F, transfer high-risk items to a cooler with ice while you decide.
 - Still 45°F+ at 2 hours: an equipment fault beyond the outage. Treat the whole fridge as compromised and call an appliance tech.

PHASE 3 — DISCARD (high-risk, do not try to save)
 Raw poultry, raw ground meat, raw fish, raw shellfish
 Cooked meats, casseroles, soups, gravies, stews
 Cooked rice, cooked pasta
 Milk, cream, yogurt, soft cheeses (brie, ricotta, cream cheese), cottage cheese, custards, opened baby food
 Cooked eggs, egg salad, quiche
 Cut melon, cut tomato, leafy greens, sprouts, cut fruit
 Anything that felt room-temperature, had off smell, slime, or pooled liquid
 Anything in the DOOR of the fridge (warmest spot) — discard if it's on this list

Bag them, tie off, take to an outdoor bin. Do not leave them accessible to Kibo (see below).

PHASE 3b — KEEP OR REFREEZE
 Frozen items still hard with visible ice crystals: refreeze, or cook today from frozen
 Hard cheese blocks (parmesan, cheddar, swiss) — keep
 Butter, ghee — keep
 Whole uncut fruit and whole vegetables — keep
 Bread, rolls, muffins, tortillas, cookies, cake — keep and refreeze
 Condiments (ketchup, mustard, soy sauce, hot sauce, jam, honey) — keep
 Whole eggs in shell, unbroken, in carton — keep
 Nuts, dried fruit — keep
 Ice cream: discard if soft or melted at the edges; keep only if it remained rock-hard

PHASE 4 — COOL PROMPTLY / RESCUE
 For items you want to try to keep:
 - Move them to the back / middle shelf of the fridge (coldest spot).
 - Probe each questionable item with a quick-read thermometer. ≤40°F = keep. 41°F+ = cook it today to a safe internal temp and eat, do not refreeze: 165°F for poultry, stuffings, leftovers, casseroles; 160°F for ground meat; 145°F for whole cuts, fish, eggs.
 - For frozen items that are firm but no longer have crystals: cook now, don't refreeze.

PHASE 5 — SANITIZE AFTER EMPTYING
 - Wipe shelves, walls, drawers, door gaskets, and handles with hot soapy water OR dilute bleach (1 tbsp unscented liquid bleach per gallon of water). Rinse, dry.
 - Wash hands thoroughly after handling discard bags.
 - If you used a cooler with ice for any items, empty, wash, and sanitize that too.

UNCERTAINTY — TREAT AS DISCARD
 Peak temp during the outage is unknown. 44°F is the reading NOW, with the door closed and power restored — it likely went higher between noon and 4 pm. Don't anchor on 44°F as the worst case.
 Cumulative time above 40°F has almost certainly exceeded 4 hours for the fridge compartment. That is the hard threshold for high-risk items.
 Anything you can't probe or visually verify should default to discard if it's on the high-risk list.
 Anything that crossed contamination lines (raw meat juices near other food) should be discarded regardless of category.
 If you genuinely can't tell, throw it out. The cost of replacing food is lower than the cost of foodborne illness.

FOR KIBO
 Before you bag the discard pile, make sure none of it is reachable:
 - Toxic to dogs: chocolate, grapes, raisins, currants, onions, garlic, leeks, chives, xylitol (gum, candy, peanut butter), macadamia nuts, raw bread dough, spoiled food

 - Cool interior room with water is fine for him; keep him out of the kitchen while you clean

POST-EVENT CHECK
 New thermometer stays on the middle shelf. Confirm it holds ≤40°F for 4 consecutive hours before you consider the fridge trustworthy.
 If it climbs back above 40°F after recovery, there's a separate issue — call an appliance tech, do not reload food.

Hold off until the sheet is bone-dry. The flattening you're seeing is mid-dry settling — pigment dries lighter on average, and edges optically merge as water leaves the paper. Mid-dry is the worst read; bone-dry is the real one. (The 7/12 blue+brown swatch held its doorway separation at dry specifically because that test waited for bone-dry, not because the mix is intrinsically warmer.)

When you read it dry, the convergence will land in one of two places, and that decides the move:

1.  Edge collapse — the doorway boundary itself went soft or now shares a value with the street wash. Restore separation with a thin, low-chroma glaze right along the edge: your doorway mix (blue+brown), watered down further than the first pass, applied as a narrow band at the boundary with a small brush. This re-opens the value gap by dilution, not by pigment. Single pass; do not rewet the street side.

2.  Body convergence — both washes dried to similar middle values across their areas, not just at the boundary. Don't fight it on this sheet. This is exactly what the 3mm / 5mm / 8mm reserve panel study is designed to isolate. Treat the current sheet as a reference (note which reserve you used and what you saw), and start Panel A at 3mm on the next sheet.

For the next panel, hold your established constants:
    - Same brush, load, and water-to-pigment ratio as today's first pass
    - Soft-edge timing at T+20s ±2s
    - Single pass during the lay-in — no rewetting, no glazing, no second touch on the doorway edge
    - Bone-dry before any read or intervention

Both flags are real — each one shifts the internal triage default in a way that contradicts the fail-closed design. Worth fixing before the FAQ gets used as the reference for the next batch of held applicants.

**"Pending assistance sounds like the workspace may already be admitted."**
The risk: a reader scans "pending assistance" and assumes the workspace has cleared admission and is just waiting on CS follow-up. That inverts the actual state. Pending assistance is a *pre-admission hold*. The applicant hasn't been admitted; routing is queued. The fix is to name the state as pre-admission explicitly and pair it with the routing fact (held, not admitted). Something like: "Pre-admission hold / pending assistance — workspace has not been admitted; routed to CS for follow-up before admission." Avoid any standalone use of "pending" where it could attach to "admitted" in the reader's mind.

**"Supported admission could be read as automatic after one successful check rather than after all required checks."**
The risk: "supported admission" sounds like a state the system moves into as soon as one check passes. The actual rule is that admission is a single gate — it opens only when every required check (Helio admin proof, connector auth, external-system authority) is verified. No partial pass opens the gate, and no setup prompt fires until it does. The FAQ should make that ordering explicit. Replace "supported admission" with phrasing that names it as the *outcome after all required checks*, e.g., "all-checks-verified admission" or "admission after all required checks (supported admission)."

**Concrete edits I'd propose:**
  1. Replace any standalone "pending assistance" with "pre-admission hold — pending assistance."
  2. Replace "supported admission" with "all-checks-verified admission" everywhere it appears in the outcomes section.
  3. Add a single sentence at the top of the outcomes section: "Admission is a single gate. It opens only after every required check completes. No partial state opens the gate or fires a setup prompt."
  4. Keep the existing "verified external authority = connector-readiness, not outreach permission" note — that part is already correct and shouldn't move.
  5. Where the FAQ currently lists routing outside self-serve, mirror the same fail-closed phrasing so the three outcomes (pre-admission hold, all-checks-verified admission, assisted routing) all read as gate states, not progress states.

SINGLE CONTROLLED SEQUENCE — RAINY DOORWAY, DARK RAIN AT INTERMEDIATE TIMING

PURPOSE
  Test one intermediate timing for the three-pigment dark rain
  interruption while keeping pigment mix, paper, and brush load
  constant, and preserving the continuous cool wash and warm edge.

WHAT IS HELD CONSTANT
  Pigment mix: pre-mixed three-pigment dark rain pool (per the
    new rule); pre-mixed blue+brown pool for cool wash and warm
    counter.
  Paper: 140 lb cold-press, 9×12 or 8×10, taped flat.
  Brush: same round brush as the 7/20 session, same load,
    same water-to-pigment ratio.
  Warm-edge reserve: ~5 mm (working minimum from the 4/6
    Cherrywood study — value separation, not added orange).
  One pass per panel, no rework, no glaze, no rewet.
  ~40 min time budget, no title, no framing.

WHAT VARIES (THE TEST)
  Dark rain application timing on three fresh scrap panels,
  bracketing the new rule's T+20 s soft-edge window:
    D1 — T+15 s   (intermediate, wetter side)
    D2 — T+20 s   (the new rule's soft-edge window, central
                   reference)
    D3 — T+25 s   (intermediate, crisper side)

WHAT IS PRESERVED
  Continuous cool wash: laid uninterrupted in one pass on
    Sheet A; no dark rain applied on top.
  Warm edge: let dry untouched on Sheet A before any dark
    rain is read beside it.

SHEET A — continuous cool wash + warm edge (preserved)
  Pencil a 1×3 grid, three panels roughly 3×4 in, labeled
    C1, C2, C3.
  For each panel, in one continuous motion:
    lay the blue+brown pool as the cool window wash, then
    apply the warm counter edge with ~5 mm reserve from the
    cool wash, using the same brush and same load.
  Do not lift, glaze, rewet, or second-touch the warm edge.
  Let the sheet bone-dry.

SHEET B — dark rain timing test
  Use a 5×7 in scrap or quarter-sheet of the same 140 lb
    cold-press.
  Pencil three small panels labeled D1, D2, D3.
  For each panel: pre-load the same round brush with the
    pre-mixed three-pigment pool; start a stopwatch the
    moment the pool touches paper; apply the interruption
    and read at the corresponding timing.
  Each D panel is a fresh application — no glaze over a
    prior D panel, no rewetting of a dried panel.

EXECUTION ORDER
  1. Pre-mix both pools before touching paper.
  2. Lay Sheet A panels C1–C3 in one continuous pass; do
     not interrupt to set a timer.
  3. Let Sheet A bone-dry, untouched.
  4. On Sheet B, run D1, D2, D3 with a few minutes between
     so each application starts on a dry, fresh scrap area
     with no carry-over wetness.
  5. Place Sheet B scrap beside Sheet A Row 1 for the

Reality check on rates (the part you asked me not to assume away)
The 13.4¢ "all-in based on 1,000 kWh" line almost always contains tiered or pass-through components: an energy charge, possibly a transmission/distribution rider, and sometimes a capacity or demand component that scales with usage. Three common patterns to check on the Electricity Facts Label before signing:
1. Declining-block energy charge (e.g. first 500 kWh at X¢, next 500 at a slightly lower Y¢). At 820 kWh you'd pay a blended rate modestly above 13.4¢; at 1,050 kWh modestly below. The 13.4¢ headline is the 1,000-kWh blend.
2. Flat energy charge + separate monthly customer charge (e.g. $5–$10/mo). Doesn't change the spread, but raises both columns.
3. Variable-rate riders that track wholesale price (more common on the M-to-M side). If M-to-M has a fuel-adjustment clause, its 14.8¢ is a snapshot, not a guarantee, and the spread can widen in summer peak months.

Bottom line on rate realism: at your band, the all-in cost per kWh on the fixed plan is probably within ±0.3¢ of 13.4¢ — so the spread above is reliable to within roughly ±$2–$4/month. Treat the $11–$15/month saving as the central estimate, not a precise one.

- At 820 kWh: $150 ÷ $11.48/mo ≈ 13.1 months of use
- At 935 kWh: $150 ÷ $13.09/mo ≈ 11.5 months
- At 1,000 kWh: $150 ÷ $14.00/mo ≈ 10.7 months
- At 1,050 kWh: $150 ÷ $14.70/mo ≈ 10.2 months

If you exit on day 1 of the fixed term, the worst-case cost is roughly the M-to-M bill you would have paid plus the $150 ETF — so the fixed plan is only worse than M-to-M if (a) you exit inside ~11 months AND (b) M-to-M's rate doesn't spike above 14.8¢ during that window. For atmospheric pieces where the bloom reads as rain-soaked paper, 5 min is workable. For a clean doorway edge in finished reading, it is not yet a replacement for 7 min.

Next study, single-variable change to interruption timing: 5 → 6 minutes. Hold paper, blue+brown mix, brush load, large cool wash, and warm-edge goal constant. One pass, no rewetting, no glazing, no softening pass on the rain interruption.

Why 6 and not 4: 4 min sits closer to the known-broken 3 min result and likely produces a softer version of breakage rather than a cleaner dark. 6 min sits closer to the known-clean 7 min, so any improvement at 6 is incremental toward a faster working window. If 6 min gives you continuity + warm edge + no bloom, you have located a working band between roughly 5.5 and 7 min — meaningful turnaround for real sessions. If 6 min still shows a bloom, the bloom zone runs from roughly 3.5 to 6 min and 7 min is your floor for clean reading.

Read at bone-dry: cool-wash continuity, warm doorway edge clarity, presence or absence of the entry bloom. The bloom is the only variable you expect to move between 5 and 6 min.

Optional paired panel: if you want to bracket the threshold in one sitting, run a second panel at 6 min 30 sec alongside the 6 min panel. That gives you 5 / 6 / 6:30 to read against the established 7 min.

Here's how the plan and the bill should reconcile, what the partial-period split is doing, and what the quoted all-in rates actually mean.

1. Plan dates vs. written confirmation
- Confirmed plan: 12-month fixed, active 2025-08-13 through 2026-08-12. The August 19 written confirmation is the supplier's matching confirmation, so the dates are consistent on the enrollment side.
- What you're checking on the bill: the service/billing period header. The first bill under this plan should start on 2025-08-13. If the period header shows a different start (for example, the previous bill's end date, or 2025-08-14, or 2025-08-12), the supplier has used a wrong service-start date and the pro-rata days and any prorated base charges will be off. The day count on the bill should also make sense for a partial first period — typically 19 days from 2025-08-13 through the end of August, not a full ~30-day month.

2. Fee treatment vs. what the confirmation says
- The plan itself carries no recurring monthly fee and a $150 early-termination charge. Neither of those is a per-bill recurring line item.
- On a first bill you should therefore expect to see: a prorated energy charge for the partial period, any taxes/regulatory pass-throughs, and nothing labeled "plan fee" or "ETF." If a recurring plan fee appears on the bill, the supplier is mis-billing the product. A one-time setup/account charge, by contrast, is not the same thing as the recurring plan fee and can legitimately appear on the first bill if the supplier's terms allow it — but it should be a discrete one-time line, not a monthly fee.
- Per your stated preference, the first statement should be broken down so that any one-time setup charge is on its own line, separate from the recurring partial-period energy and pass-through charges.

3. Why there's a partial-period split at all
- The plan term is 12 months, but the first bill almost never covers a full month because enrollment landed mid-month on 2025-08-13. The supplier pro-rates: they take the daily energy charge (effectively the rate × kWh used over the partial period) and apply it for only the days you were actually on the plan. That's why the first statement is "partial" — it's not a separate product, just the standard proration of a fixed-rate plan across the days remaining in the first month. From the second bill onward, you're back to full monthly periods through 2026-08-12.
- A line labeled "partial period," "prorated," or "service from 08/13 to 08/31" is the supplier's way of showing that proration explicitly. If the bill shows a full-month energy charge without any proration note, the supplier probably used the wrong start date.

4. What the supplier's 14.1¢ / 13.5¢ / 13.3¢ rate points do and don't guarantee
- What they are: "all-in" means the quoted rate is meant to include the energy charge and all pass-throughs (transmission, distribution, and regulatory charges that vary by supplier). The three numbers are bracket points — typical-usage scenarios — not a schedule. They are designed to let you compare the fixed plan against the variable plan (15.2¢) at a glance.
- What they guarantee: they guarantee the rate per kWh inside each usage band will not change during the 12-month term. They are not an estimate of your specific bill — they don't know your usage.
- What they don't guarantee:
  - They don't pin a single rate to your exact usage. If you use 900 kWh, you don't get 13.5¢ for all 900; the supplier's pricing design is built around the 500/1,000/2,000 kWh reference points, and your actual blended rate depends on how the supplier weights tiers and pass-throughs inside the band. At your 820–1,050 kWh usage, 13.5¢ is the relevant reference point for comparison with the variable plan, but your bill won't necessarily equal usage × 13.5¢ to the cent.
  - They don't fix your total bill. Only the per-kWh rate is fixed; your total is still rate × kWh used. A high-usage month (A/C in August, heaters in winter) still costs more; a low-usage month costs less.
  - They don't include the $150 early-termination charge if you exit early.
  - They don't include any one-time setup/admin charge the supplier may apply on the first bill, if their terms allow one.
  - They don't include local sales tax or any municipal franchise fee if your municipality charges one on top of supplier charges.
- How to use them when comparing to this bill: the bill's "rate × kWh" line, plus all pass-through lines, should reconcile to an effective per-kWh figure close to one of the three points — most likely near 13.5¢ for your usage band. If the bill's effective per-kWh lands noticeably above 13.5¢, the most common reasons are (a) the supplier added a recurring fee the Facts Label said was zero, (b) a one-time setup charge is being amortized into the energy line rather than shown separately, or (c) the supplier is using a different rate class than the one the Facts Label assumes. Those are the things worth confirming on the bill itself.

The two panels are bracketing the integration threshold cleanly:

- 5 min — the wash is still damp enough that the dark mark blooms outward; you're on the wet side, where the rain pulls pigment with it and you lose the mark shape
- 6 min — the wash has set enough to hold the mark, the cool field stays continuous, the warm doorway edge survives; the trade-off is that the surface has lost just enough receptivity that the dark sits a hair on top rather than melting in

So 5 min = too wet, 6 min = essentially right with a slight crispness tax. 6 min is already a usable answer for the rain interruption — the crispness is a quality issue, not a structural break in the wash or edge.

On 5:30 as the next test:

Yes, it's the most useful controlled move. It bisects the 5-vs-6 result cleanly, and holding everything else constant means any difference is timing alone.

What the 5:30 panel will tell you:

- If it blooms even slightly, the threshold is narrow and 6 min is at the dry edge of acceptable
- If it reads clean like 6, the threshold sits between 5 and 5:30 and 6 min is comfortably safe

One alternative worth knowing about: the 6-min crispness may not be a timing problem at all — it might be a load problem. If the rain brush is carrying more pigment than the wash can quietly absorb at 6 min, a lighter-loaded brush at the same 6 min could integrate the mark without losing the wash or edge benefit. So after 5:30 confirms the timing threshold, a useful second experiment is 6 min, same setup, but rain brush one notch lighter.

If you have time for one panel: do the 5:30. If two: 5:30 plus 6 min with the lighter rain load.

CHICKEN RICE SKILLET WITH LIME
25 min, one skillet, one portion set aside for Sam

Why this shape
Day-old rice + already-cooked chicken + a couple of eggs is a fast fried-rice pattern. The eggs scramble INTO the rice (not on top) so Sam's reheat holds up — a fried egg goes rubbery in the microwave. Spinach wilts in at the end, and scallion greens + lime go on AFTER heat so the reheated bowl still tastes fresh.

PAN SPLIT
- Cooked rice: about 2.5 cups (cold is best; clumps break easier, less mushy)
- Roasted chicken: 6–8 oz, shredded or cut into small bites
- Corn: about 3/4 cup (drained if canned, thawed if frozen)
- Eggs: 2, beaten with a pinch of salt
- Spinach: 2 generous handfuls, rough-chopped if leaves are large
- Scallions: 3–4 — whites and greens sliced thin, kept in separate piles
- Lime: 1 half juiced now, 1 half cut into 2 wedges
- Oil or butter: 1 Tbsp
- Salt, pepper

TIMED SEQUENCE (active ~15 min, hands-off ~5 min)

  0:00  PREP while the skillet heats
        Slice scallions (whites/greens separate), shred chicken, chop
        spinach, beat eggs with a pinch of salt in a small bowl, juice
        half the lime and cut the other half into wedges. Heat a 12-inch
        skillet over medium-high with 1 Tbsp oil/butter.

  0:05  AROMATICS
        Add scallion whites. Stir 60–90 seconds until softened and
        fragrant. (If your corn is frozen, add it now with the whites so
        it dries a bit.)

  0:08  CHICKEN + CORN
        Add chicken and corn. Spread in an even layer, leave 90 seconds
        undisturbed for some color, then toss. About 3 min total — chicken
        hot through, corn with a few brown spots.

  0:13  RICE
        Add rice. Break up clumps, press flat across the pan, leave 60
        seconds for crispy bits, toss, repeat once. About 3–4 min.
        Season with salt and pepper.

  0:18  SPINACH + EGGS
        Add spinach, toss until just wilted (~60 sec).
        Push rice to one side. Pour beaten eggs into the empty side. Let
        them set 30 sec, then scramble gently and fold through the rice.
        Kill the heat.

  0:22  FINISH
        Squeeze the juiced lime half over the pan. Toss once. Taste for
        salt; add a grind of pepper.

PLATING
- Riley's bowl: about half the skillet, finish with a pinch of raw
  scallion greens and a lime wedge. Eat now.
- Sam's container: the slightly larger share (he's post-service hungry).
  Top with a small pinch of the raw scallion greens you saved at prep,
  and tuck a lime wedge alongside. Do NOT squeeze it yet.

COOL + STORE
- Let Sam's container sit on the counter 5 min with the lid slightly
  ajar, then fridge. (Don't seal hot rice airtight.)

SAM'S REHEAT (when he's home)
- Splash of water, loose lid, microwave 90 sec at 70% power, stir,
  another 30–60 sec until hot through.
- Squeeze his saved lime wedge and scatter the saved scallion greens.
  That fresh finish is what keeps it from tasting like leftover rice.

CLEANUP (5 items, that's it)
- Skillet, spatula, cutting board, knife, small egg bowl
- Plus Riley's plate and Sam's container

NOTES
- Two eggs split across both portions is the right amount — more and the
  rice goes eggy, less and the reheat feels dry.
- If the rice is fresh and warm (not cold), spread it on a plate for 5
  min while you prep; cold rice fries up much better.
- Chili crisp or hot sauce on the table is a one-bottle upgrade if you
  have it. Nothing else needed.

A.  Filter — the user-serviceable part
    - Twist out the cylindrical filter assembly at the bottom of the tub per your manual.

-   Burning or electrical smell.
-   Sparks or visible arcing.
-   Water actively leaking onto the floor and the level rising.

PROMPT 1 — How advance counts preserve seasonal menu quality

  Core: a confirmed headcount 48–72 hours out lets the menu stay seasonal instead of generic. Once you know how many covers, you can buy at peak that morning, not pre-order Tuesday and hope it holds.

  Flex into:
    - Peak produce is short-window. Same-day tomato vs 5-day-old tomato is a different dish.
    - Headcount sizes every part of the plan: protein portions, sides per tray, bread counts, pacing.
    - Without an advance count, the kitchen defaults to "safe" — over-portioned, generic, built to absorb uncertainty. That's where menu quality erodes.
    - "Seasonal" is a real promise only when the kitchen knows what's coming and how many.

PROMPT 2 — How menu + production authority can remain separate from service attendance

  Core: authority lives in the document, not in the chef's body on the floor. The menu and production plan is what gets approved — the assigned service lead executes it.

  Flex into:
    - Head chef owns: what the menu is, what the recipes are, how the kitchen produces them (sourcing, timing, plating spec).

    - The plan has to be specific enough that an experienced lead can execute it without phoning the chef mid-event.

PROMPT 3 — When a private-dining team should decline customization

  Core: customization has a real ceiling, and naming the ceiling is what protects the kitchen's quality reputation. Decline isn't "no" — it's "let me build the right version of this for you."

The dry, flaking black album-paper residue at the corners is almost certainly the remains of a corner-mount adhesive or backing sheet from the album the print was originally in. The print is not stuck to anything else, the image layer looks intact, and the handwriting on the back is still the primary provenance carrier — so the goal is to stabilize, not intervene. Below is a sequence that does no mechanical work on the print itself.

1.  Prepare a clean work area.
    -   Flat, dry, ventilated surface. Lay down a single sheet of plain copy paper as your work surface (not newspaper, not fabric).
    -   Wash and dry your hands. Put on nitrile gloves. Have an N95 or dust mask within reach in case any flakes lift during handling.
    -   Have ready: a phone or camera, a soft 2H or HB pencil, and four-flap paper enclosures or glassine sleeves (one for this print, spares).

2.  Document the print AS FOUND before moving it.
    -   Photograph: the front full-frame, the back full-frame with the handwriting in focus, a close-up of each of the two residue corners, and a context shot showing it lying on the work surface in its position in the six-print sequence.
    -   Put a small ruler or coin in the close-ups for scale.
    -   On a separate slip of paper (not on the print), note in pencil: "Pair 05 — dry flaking black album-paper residue at two corners; image layer intact; handwriting legible; [date observed]; [ambient temp/RH if you have a hygrometer]."

3.  Lift and house the print.
    -   Slide a clean sheet of paper under the print, lift the paper-and-print together, and transfer it into the enclosure. Do not pinch, slide, or flex the print directly. Do not touch the residue corners.
    -   Four-flap paper enclosure: open all four flaps, set the print print-side up, fold the flaps over each other without folding them across the residue. The print sits inside; the flaps hold it.
    -   Glassine sleeve: slip the print in so the back faces the back of the sleeve (glassine is translucent, so the handwriting will read through). Glassine is the better choice here because any flake that does detach will stay contained inside the sleeve.
    -   For older black-and-white or color prints, prefer unbuffered paper or glassine — buffered materials can interact with some image layers over time.

4.  Label and isolate.
    -   Mark the OUTSIDE of the enclosure only: "Pair 05 — DO NOT HANDLE — RESIDUE — DO NOT CLEAN." Use pencil. Nothing on the print itself.
    -   Keep this enclosure between pair-04 and pair-06 in the six-print stack — do not re-sort the sequence today. The physical order is part of provenance, and Marcus has asked for order preserved.

5.  Store flat and stable.
    -   Flat in an archival folder or box, in a stable environment: roughly 65–70°F and 30–50% RH. No attic, basement, bathroom, kitchen, or car.
    -   Dark or inside a closed archival box. Avoid direct light, especially sunlight and UV.
    -   Do not stand the prints on edge, do not stack under weight, do not lean anything against them.

6.  Note the provenance the residue carries.
    -   The residue is itself a small piece of evidence that this print was once corner-mounted in an album. You do not need to write that on the print; the residue is the record. A separate slip reading "Pair 05 was corner-mounted in an album; residue remains at two corners" is enough.

Materials and actions to AVOID:

  -   Bare hands or cotton gloves. Cotton can snag on dry flakes and lift them; nitrile is smoother.
  -   Water, saliva, steam, humidification, or any solvent on the residue or the print.
  -   Tape, adhesive strips, photo corners, glue, mounting squares — on the print, near it, or touching it.
  -   Plastic bags for storage (polyethylene zip bags are fine for short transport, not for storage; PVC is bad).
  -   Mechanical removal: pick, tweezers, brush (except to recover a flake that has fallen onto the work surface and must be re-housed), eraser, kneaded eraser, microfiber cloth.
  -   Heat: hair dryer, warm breath, sunlight on the print to "dry it out."
  -   Pressure: stacking, leaning, folding, rolling, bending, weighing down.
  -   Any writing on the print or on the residue. Pencil, pen, marker, adhesive label — all go on the enclosure.
  -   Re-arranging the six prints by visual guesswork. The physical order is provenance.

Signs that justify involving a photograph conservator soon (do not wait for the next family-photo session):

  -   Any flake detaches from the print and ends up loose in the enclosure — the residue is losing cohesion.
  -   The residue looks tacky, shiny, or smears when a gloved finger brushes near it — could be active adhesive failure or mold.
  -   Visible mold anywhere on the print or residue — fuzzy growth, white, green, or black.
  -   The image layer lifts, cracks, or flakes.
  -   The print warps, cockles, or curls on its own — possible moisture event.
  -   A faint musty or sweet smell from the print.
  -   One corner is in noticeably worse condition than the other — asymmetric deterioration.
  -   You cannot read the handwriting on the back without moving or touching the print in a way that risks the residue.

When you do contact a conservator, the photos from step 2 and the slip from step 2 are exactly what they want to see. Send those plus a short note: "Pair 05, two corners, dry flaking black album-paper residue, image layer intact, handwriting on back needs to remain readable, no intervention attempted, currently housed flat in [enclosure type] at [temp/RH]."

If you'd like, I can draft the conservator inquiry email in the same shape as the earlier one, or update the temp family-photo index so pair 05's row carries today's residue observation.

The interesting move in this one is that it's not about *whether* a record exists or *whether* it's accurate; it's about the institution's posture toward the record. Visibility is being offered as a substitute for remedy — "we documented it" standing in for "we responded to it." That puts it next to, but distinct from, the earlier ledger/observation-as-harm and flooded-rooms/erasure-as-harm passages: this one is about the third move, where the record itself becomes a way of declining to act.

What do you want from me on it? A single discussion question, an interpretive angle, a way to bridge it back to the August 26 reading, or a framing for the session as a whole?

Recording a problem keeps it available. It says: this happened, this is here, this can be revisited. It does not promise anything else. Responding commits you — it costs attention, time, a posture, sometimes a relationship. The same problem can sit in a notebook for years and never be met, or be answered once and closed without ever being written down. Both moves can be honest. The trouble comes from confusing them: treating a clean record as a substitute for a response, or acting without ever giving the problem a shape it can return to later.

Two readings worth keeping open without choosing:
(a) Recording is the precondition for any response. Until something is named and held, there's nothing to meet.
(b) Recording is the dressed-up form of avoidance. It gives the comfort of engagement without the cost.

Question for the room: At what point does the act of recording start to do the work that responding should be doing — and how would you tell the difference in your own life?

WHAT THIS NOTICE ACTUALLY IS

The Annual Notice of Change (ANOC) is a document the current plan (Hill Country, based on your earlier notes) is required by Medicare to send each fall. It describes what the plan itself is changing for next year — premium, copays, drug coverage tiers, network, etc. — and what is staying the same. It is a description of changes, not a recommendation. It does not compare the plan to other plans, and it does not tell you whether the changes are good or bad for your mother.

WHAT THE NOTICE CONFIRMS

  - That the plan will continue in some form next year, with the listed terms effective January 1.
  - The premium, deductible, copay/coinsurance, and out-of-pocket maximum the plan is committing to.
  - The drug tiers and pharmacy network scope the plan is committing to.
  - Items not listed as changing are presumed unchanged, but "not mentioned" is not the same as "verified unchanged" — the Evidence of Coverage is the full legal source.

WHAT THE NOTICE DOES NOT CONFIRM

  - Whether switching is better for your mother.
  - Whether her doctors or neighborhood pharmacy will still accept the plan — that needs the provider and pharmacy directories.
  - Whether the as-needed medication will cost the same — that needs the new formulary plus her actual dosing pattern.
  - Whether the $0 vaccine cost applies at her specific pharmacy.
  - Whether Hill Country's mail-order is workable for an as-needed medication given its fill limits.
  - Whether any other available plan would be cheaper or cover her better.

CHECKLIST FOR THE REVIEW WITH MOM

Bring these documents first:
  [ ] The ANOC itself, with changes highlighted.
  [ ] Evidence of Coverage (EOC) for next year — the full legal plan document.
  [ ] Summary of Benefits — the shorter comparison version.
  [ ] Formulary (drug list) for next year.
  [ ] Pharmacy Directory for next year.
  [ ] Provider Directory for next year.
  [ ] Mom's medication list with doses and how often she actually fills each one.
  [ ] Mom's list of doctors and her preferred pharmacy.
  [ ] Last 12 months of pharmacy claims or receipts, to estimate real use.

Then walk through these in order:

  Medications
  [ ] Is each drug still on next year's formulary?
  [ ] What tier is it, and did the tier change?
  [ ] Does the deductible apply to that drug?
  [ ] Are there new quantity limits or step-therapy rules?
  [ ] For the as-needed medication specifically: is the four-fills-per-year estimate realistic for how she actually uses it, and what happens if she exceeds it?
  [ ] Is mail-order a workable option for this drug under the new rules, or does it create friction?

  Pharmacy
  [ ] Is her neighborhood pharmacy still in-network for next year?
  [ ] Does the $0 vaccine cost apply at her specific pharmacy, or only at preferred pharmacies?
  [ ] If mail-order is being pushed, is that actually a better fit for how she uses the as-needed medication?

  Doctors
  [ ] Are all of Mom's doctors still in-network for next year?
  [ ] If any doctor is leaving the network, is she willing to switch, or does she need a continuity-of-care request?

  Plan totals
  [ ] Premium change.
  [ ] Deductible change.
  [ ] Out-of-pocket maximum change.
  [ ] Copay changes for the services she actually uses.
  [ ] Total estimated annual cost: premium + expected copays + expected medication costs.

  Comparison to other plans (only after the above is done)
  [ ] Pull at least one alternative Medicare Advantage plan and/or an Original Medicare + Part D + Medigap option available in her zip code.
  [ ] Run Mom's actual medication list through each alternative's formulary tool.
  [ ] Check each alternative's provider directory for her doctors.
  [ ] Add up realistic annual cost for each option using her real usage, not worst case.

  Questions to write down and ask the plan or a SHIP counselor
  [ ] Is the as-needed medication on next year's formulary and at what tier?
  [ ] Does the deductible apply to that medication?
  [ ] Is Mom's pharmacy in-network for next year?
  [ ] Are Mom's doctors in-network for next year?
  [ ] Has the mail-order policy changed for as-needed medications?
  [ ] What is the appeals or exception process if a medication is dropped or moved to a higher tier?

GUARDRAILS BEFORE ANY DECISION

  - The ANOC alone does not prove switching is better. It only proves the current plan is changing in specific ways.
  - A plan can lower its premium and raise drug tiers, or the reverse. The headline number is not the answer.
  - If Mom's usage is stable, her last 12 months of claims are the best predictor of next year's cost.
  - Medicare Advantage switches lock in for the full calendar year, so the decision is not reversible until the next open enrollment.
  - A State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) counselor can review this with Mom for free, with no sales angle. That call is worth making before any switch.

- The label rate is advertised as "all-in," so it should already include delivery and taxes.
