Three options for the December 4 monthly hands-on audit, assessed against your four dimensions, then a recommendation.

OPTION 1 — Rotating deep recheck of one evidence lane after closure
  Direct system contact: high. You fully walk one lane's evidence pipeline, source through claim-prep.
  Duplicates Owen: high. Owen already closed source completeness across all four lanes under the September 24 boundary. A deep recheck of the same lane, after his closure, is structurally a second-pass source review even if you call it something else.
  Owner ambiguity: high. Reads as parallel source authority, especially for the lane currently in rotation.
  Queue risk: high. Anything labeled "recheck after closure" is one rename away from "approved for use."
  Net: strongest audit in absolute terms, worst fit for the current owner map.

OPTION 2 — Targeted sample drawn from that month's exceptions
  Direct system contact: medium. You touch exception records, late-arriving events, mismatched joins, exclusions, claim-prep flags — not full source pipelines.
  Duplicates Owen: low. Owen's closure is about whether the source is complete and reliable. Exceptions are what surface after his closure — the messy edges where completeness meets treatment. Different surface.
  Owner ambiguity: low. Sits cleanly in the claim-prep space none of the four lane owners currently hold.
  Queue risk: low. Sampling exceptions is investigative, not gatekeeping. Findings either escalate to you under existing triggers or sit as learning notes.
  Net: highest learning yield per minute of system contact; lowest collision with current roles.

OPTION 3 — Small cross-lane trace of governed fields and claim treatment
  Direct system contact: medium-high. Narrow slice across multiple systems, focused on field definitions and treatment consistency.
  Duplicates Owen: low. Owen works per lane; cross-lane governed-field consistency is structurally outside his closure scope.
  Owner ambiguity: medium. Governed fields abut Daniela's system-control territory for auto-nudge and the pricing-page continuity owner for path-quality fields. Needs explicit scoping to definitions and treatment, not control behavior.
  Queue risk: medium. If the trace outputs "this cross-lane claim is clean," that smells like approval. Needs framing as consistency observation, not sign-off.
  Net: valuable as a periodic check, expensive as a monthly mode.

RECOMMENDATION
  Carry Option 2 as the standing monthly hands-on mode. It preserves the investigative character of the existing four-mode design while removing the duplication and queue risk that come with full-lane rechecks. Run it as the Week 3 90-minute session, scoped to this month's exceptions across all four lanes — exceptions only, not routine rows. In practice this is the "exception" mode of the existing design elevated to standing, with the other three modes available on demand rather than on rotation.

  Add Option 3 as a quarterly mode, not monthly. Once per quarter, run the cross-lane governed-field trace. Cross-lane consistency drifts slowly, and the queue-risk surface is real enough that monthly exposure would compound it. Quarterly keeps the learning without normalizing a second approval queue.

  Drop Option 1 from the standing design. If a future rotation genuinely needs depth on a specific lane, scope it as a one-time investigation under your authority, not a recurring mode. Reserving it for triggered use also avoids creating a default expectation that lanes get re-closed every few months.

WHAT TO CARRY INTO THE PROPOSAL
  - Monthly mode: exception sampling, Week 3, 90 minutes, all four lanes, exceptions only.
  - Quarterly mode: cross-lane governed-field trace, narrow slice, framed as consistency observation.
  - On-demand: re-derive and discrepancy modes retained as one-time investigation tools, invoked under your authority when an exception sample surfaces something that warrants depth.
  - Explicit non-goals for the audit: no source re-closure, no revenue or forecast decisions, no narrative edits, no system-control changes, no claim approval.
  - Output framing: investigative findings plus surfaced escalation triggers, delivered to you. Never "approved for use." Never a status that downstream claim work can rely on without your separate decision.
  - Owner map restated inside the proposal: Owen (source completeness, September 24 boundary), Marcus (forecast), Tomás (narrative), Ines (Expansion Assist source), Daniela (CS auto-nudge control), you (claim treatment, board readiness, escalation review, executive language).

AUTHORITY PRESERVATION
  Existing escalation triggers remain unchanged. Your authority over causal claims, revenue treatment, forecast credit, board-readiness, and final-claim language remains unchanged. Owen's source-completeness closure boundary remains unchanged. The audit produces findings and surfaces triggers; it does not decide. Any finding that would reopen a closed source packet still routes to you under the existing triggers, not to the audit itself.

PROPOSAL FRAMING
  This remains a proposal for review on December 4, not an approved or early role change. The language should describe a proposed monthly-and-quarterly cadence with explicit non-goals and preserved authorities, and should describe the audit as preparation for the January 1 handoff rather than as a new recurring role for you. Per Priya's November 9 instruction, do not imply that Owen's source-completeness closure transfers claim authority, and do not imply that you have already stepped out of the routine monthly reviews. The audit is a designed surface; the handoff is a separate decision.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

The second edge isn't in the still life — it's the foam board acting like a near-mirror fill source. When the reflector sits too close and roughly parallel to the cup's belly, the cup "sees" a second soft terminator where the bounce falls off. Your eye reads it as a shadow edge because it's adjacent to a real value jump.

ADJUSTMENT SEQUENCE

1. Lamp first. Raise it 2–4 inches above where it is now and re-aim a bit more downward (toward the paper, not across it). Higher lamp = longer, softer primary shadow with a gentler falloff, which dilutes any competing edge before you touch the reflector.

2. Reflector second. Pull it back 6–10 inches from the cup and tilt the TOP edge away from you. You want the bounce to arrive from above-and-across as a broad gradient, not horizontally into the cup's midline. Broad gradient fill = no visible terminator.

3. Recheck from your seated painting posture — not closer. The second edge should soften to nothing or to an imperceptible gradient. If it still reads as a line, the reflector is still too parallel to the cup; tilt it more.

NEUTRAL-VALUE CHECK (DRY ONLY)

- Don't lay water. Use a small dry scrap with a single mid-value swatch held next to the cup in the painting.
- Squint, or use a value finder (a postage-stamp hole in a dark card) held at arm's length. Count value zones on the cup: lit side → primary shadow → reflected side. You want exactly two readable jumps (lit/shadow, shadow/bounce). A third jump inside the bounce = reflector still too close.
- Toggle the lamp off for ~5 seconds, then on. The second edge should disappear entirely when the lamp is off. If it does, it's setup, not paint.

STOP CONDITION

Stop when:
- The cup reads as lit side + one primary shadow + a soft gradient bounce. No second terminator line.
- The reference swatch holds the same value lamp-on vs lamp-off (within a hair).

DO NOT:
- Glaze or wash to "match" the second edge. That bakes the reflector artifact into the painting. The still life doesn't have that edge.
- Lower the lamp to sharpen the primary. Lower = harder primary AND more visible second edge.

If after one full pass the second edge still reads, the fix is to remove the reflector entirely and rely on the lamp alone — a single light source never produces a competing terminator.

OVEN-CENTERED SEQUENCE
Cook starts ~1:00pm, you eat at 2:00pm, Sam's plate goes in the fridge by ~2:30pm.

THREE VESSELS (cleanup kept tight)
  - 1 rimmed sheet pan, foil-lined (chicken + sweet potato)
  - 1 small baking dish, foil-lined or disposable foil pan (stuffing)
  - 1 large skillet (green beans, stovetop only)

PREP — 12:45 to 1:00pm
  - Halve the sweet potato lengthwise; if it's a large one, cut each half into 2 wedges so the centers cook in the same window as the chicken. Rub cut sides with butter, salt, pepper.
  - Pat the 4 thighs dry. Rub with butter, salt, pepper, and a little minced garlic.
  - Trim the green beans.
  - Mix the stuffing per the box using stock + butter. Spread in the baking dish and cover with foil.
  - Mince 2 garlic cloves; zest the lemon; reserve the lemon half for serving.

OVEN SEQUENCE
  1:00pm  Preheat oven to 375°F.
  1:10pm  Load the oven together:
            - Sheet pan: chicken skin-up on one side, sweet potato cut-side down on the other.
            - Stuffing dish, foil-covered, on the rack below.
  1:30pm  Stovetop green beans: melt 1 Tbsp butter in the skillet, garlic 30 sec, add the beans plus 2 Tbsp stock, cover, steam 5 min. Uncover, salt, pepper, lemon zest. Hold covered off-heat.
  1:35pm  Pull the stuffing, uncover to crisp the top.
  1:40pm  Check the chicken (target 175°F in the thickest part, no pink at the bone) and poke the sweet potato (fork should slide in easily). Pull the sheet pan. If either needs a few more minutes, leave the pan in 3-5 min uncovered.
  1:45pm  Rest the chicken 5 min, loosely tented with foil.

PLATING
  1:50pm  Your plate (eat at 2:00pm):
            - 1 thigh
            - half the sweet potato (split open, add a pat of butter + salt)
            - roughly a third of the beans
            - roughly a third of the stuffing
            - squeeze the lemon over the beans at the table.
  Split however you like, but a 1-and-3 thigh split leaves Sam a generous late plate.

SAM'S LATE PLATE — COOL + REFRIGERATE
Do this while you eat or right after — don't let the food sit on the counter for hours.
  - Portion Sam's food into 2 shallow containers (no more than ~2 inches deep): one for the chicken + sweet potato, one for stuffing + beans.
  - For 2 of the 3 thighs, pull the meat off the bone in large pieces. (Bones hold heat; deboned meat drops out of the danger zone faster and reheats more evenly.) Leave the third thigh whole if he prefers.
  - Spread loosely in the containers. Do NOT snap lids shut yet.
  - Optional but worth it: 8-10 min ice bath in the sink — set the containers in ice water and stir once. Drops food to ~70°F fast.
  - Cool on the counter no more than 30 min total from when the food came out of the oven.
  - 2:30pm  Loosely cover (lid slightly ajar or vented wrap) and put in the fridge.
  - ~4:00pm Food should be fully cold; tighten the covers.

SAM'S REHEATING (he gets home ~10:30pm, plate has been in the fridge ~8 hours)
Heat to 165°F in the thickest piece of chicken.

Microwave — fastest, ~4 min
  1. Pull the plate; sprinkle 1 Tbsp water over the stuffing so it doesn't dry out.
  2. Loosely cover with a damp paper towel.
  3. Microwave at 70% power for 2 min. Flip/stir, then 60-90 sec bursts until 165°F.
  4. Rest 1 min before eating.

Oven — hands-off, ~20 min
  1. Preheat to 325°F.
  2. Splash 1 Tbsp water or stock over the stuffing.
  3. Cover the plate loosely with foil.
  4. Heat 15-20 min until 165°F in the chicken (check with a thermometer).

ONE-PAN THANKSGIVING HASH — serves 2, ~18 min active, eats at 2:00pm

Start at 1:42pm so you're plating around 2:00.

PREP (0:00, ~3 min):
- Cube sweet potato ~1/2"
- Cut green beans into 1" pieces
- Slice chicken thigh into ~3/4" chunks (bigger than you think — small pieces dry out)
- Crumble stuffing into rough pebble-sized crumbs
- Pull all four out of the fridge NOW (5-10 min off-chill = more even reheating and shorter pan time)

PAN — 12" skillet, 1 Tbsp oil, medium-high:

- 0:03  sweet potato in, salt + pepper, leave it alone 3-4 min to actually sear (not steam)
- 0:07  toss, push potatoes to one side, drop stuffing crumbs onto the bare half to toast
- 0:10  add green beans, toss with potatoes, season
- 0:13  add chicken + 2 Tbsp water + 1/2 Tbsp butter, toss gently, COVER (lid or foil) 90 sec — the steam is what heats chicken through without drying the outside
- 0:15  uncover, toss everything together, fold stuffing back in
- 0:17  cut a chicken chunk — should be steaming hot through, no cool center; season to taste, optional pinch of garlic powder or smoked paprika
- 0:18  plate

WHY THE CHICKEN STAYS MOIST: you slice it thicker, add it last, and reheat with trapped steam instead of dry contact. Searing the sweet potato first also means the pan stays hot enough that the steam step is brief.

FOOD-SAFE NOTES:
- Target is visibly steaming, 165°F at the center of a chicken chunk
- Plate and eat immediately — don't hold on the warm burner; poultry leftovers shouldn't sit in the "danger zone" a second time
- If the stuffing or sweet potato has been in the fridge >4 days, skip it; cooked stuffing is the highest-risk item here
- If the chicken smells off or the surface looks slimy when you cut into it, stop

Three-cadence comparison for the monthly hands-on audit
Added 2026-11-30 in response to Priya's note on the Nov 25 draft
============================================================

Frame: the audit is a 90-minute Week 3 session that runs in four modes (re-derive, trace, discrepancy, exception). The cadence question is *how often* a lane gets the deep treatment — not *what* the modes are. Existing escalation triggers are preserved in all three, and the four authority surfaces stay split: Owen = source closure, Ines = owner certification, audit = direct evidence inspection only (no release/suppress/restore/rollback; no routine approval of Ines's certification), Riley = final claim.

OPTION A — Monthly rotating one-lane
Each month, one of the four lanes (source completeness / owner certification / reliability / messaging-state) gets the deep recheck. Over four months, every lane has been touched once; on month five the cycle repeats.

- Direct system contact: HIGH. One lane every month gets a fresh re-derive or trace against the live evidence system. Over a quarter, all four lanes see direct contact.
- Duplicate work: HIGH. The recheck re-walks source-completeness closure work Owen already did, and traces messaging-state alignment that Ines already certified. For the month the lane is "live," the audit is essentially repeating the owner's preparation under a different lens.
- Owner-role ambiguity: HIGH. Owen and Ines both have to wonder whether this month's "audit" is them re-doing their own work or someone reviewing them. Especially in source-completeness months, it reads like a parallel closure.
- Second-approval-queue risk: HIGH. A deep monthly recheck on a closed lane reads like a second sign-off. Both Ines's constraint (no routine approval of her certification) and Daniela's constraint (no release/suppress/rollback by the audit) are in tension with this shape — the audit will be tempted to act on what it finds.

OPTION B — Quarterly rotating one-lane
Same shape as A, but one lane every three months instead of every month. Two intervening months have no scheduled deep lane recheck.

- Direct system contact: MEDIUM-LOW. Once per quarter each lane sees a deep recheck; the other two months, contact depends on exception triggers (see Option C) and ad-hoc calls.
- Duplicate work: HIGH in the active month, ZERO the other two. Net quarterly load is lower than A, but the active month still has the same duplication problem — Owen's source-completeness work is still being re-walked.
- Owner-role ambiguity: HIGH in the active month, LOW the other two. Same shape as A but episodic; owners can predict "this is an audit quarter for my lane" and brace, but it still reads as a parallel pass.
- Second-approval-queue risk: MEDIUM. Lower frequency lowers the queue feel, but in the active month the audit still has to be careful not to act on what it finds. Quarterly cadence also means a long gap between deep contacts on any one lane — issues that surface in month two may not be caught until month four's rotation.

OPTION C — Exception-triggered only
No scheduled deep lane recheck. The 90-minute Week 3 session runs every month, but it samples from this month's exception set (messaging-state treatments, failed certifications, reliability signals, owner-completeness gaps). The four modes are available on-demand when an exception warrants deeper review.

- Direct system contact: MEDIUM. The session still opens the live evidence system every month, but contact is scoped to exceptions rather than a full lane walk. Re-derive and discrepancy modes stay available on-demand when an exception sample surfaces a matter warranting deeper review.
- Duplicate work: LOW. The audit inspects the exception set, not a closed-and-certified lane. It does not re-derive what Owen already produced, nor re-trace what Ines already certified — it inspects whether the *agreement* between evidence and messaging-state held across this month's edge cases.
- Owner-role ambiguity: LOW. The audit is reading the exception summary, not re-running an owner's preparation. Owen and Ines keep their lanes; the audit is a designed inspection surface.
- Second-approval-queue risk: LOW. Findings do not reopen a closed packet unless they meet an escalation trigger, and the audit has no release/suppress/restore/rollback authority. This shape is the cleanest fit for Ines's "no routine approval of my certification" constraint and Daniela's "no engineering control transfer" constraint.

60-minute sequence — crumpled silver ribbon on brown kraft (Cherrywood corner, 140-lb cold-press, 9×12)

Palette: burnt sienna, yellow ochre, ultramarine. No black, no white.

PRE-MIX (before brush touches paper)
- Kraft mix: 2 parts burnt sienna + 1 yellow ochre + water to a mid-value wash. Test on scrap — should read muted warm brown, not orange.
- Silver-shadow mix: 3 parts ultramarine + 1 burnt sienna (tiny). Cool blue-violet, neutralized away from green. Set a slightly concentrated well for the deepest creases later.
- Water pot: clean, two rinses — mud is the failure mode here.

VALUE MAP (30 sec of light pencil, then hands off)
- Kraft: mid-warm, value 2–3, soft uneven texture
- Ribbon shadow faces: cool, value 4
- Ribbon highlight faces: paper white, value 1 (RESERVED, not painted)
- Bounce light under ribbon: cool, value 2 — separate value band from kraft
- Specular pinpoints: tiny, sharp, paper white

0:00–0:08 — Kraft wash
Single even pass. Mild unevenness is fine; the paper itself does the texture. Leave a *slightly* damp margin where ribbon meets kraft — that damp zone is a built-in lost-edge opportunity for later. Let dry fully before touching the ribbon. Do not start early.

0:08–0:22 — Ribbon first wash (the cool-neutral pass)
Paper dry or barely damp — not wet. Paint only the shadow faces. Where two folds meet in shadow, let one shape melt into the next (lost edge, free). Where the ribbon turns toward the light, stop short of the highlight and leave paper. The bounce light under the ribbon gets the same mix, lighter, kept as a distinct value band from the kraft behind it — do not let it converge.

0:22–0:38 — Selective edges
- Hard edges: the ribbon's silhouette against kraft, plus any tiny specular pinpoint sitting at a fold crease. A dry-brush pull along these keeps them crisp.
- Lost edges: pick ONE or TWO spots where a shadow face should bleed into the kraft — clean damp brush, light drag, while the ribbon wash is just damp. Don't chase every fold.
- Reserve check: any impulse to "add one more crease" = stop. Put the brush down for 60 seconds.

0:38–0:50 — Deepest accents only
Concentrated silver-shadow mix. Two, maybe three dabs at the deepest creases. If a dab wants to become a stroke, it's already too much — silver's depth comes from the highlights you reserved, not from dark pigment layered on top. This is the overwork zone; move through it quickly.

0:50–1:00 — Review and stop
Hold the study at arm's length. Four checks:
- Does the silver read cool against the warm kraft? (yes if value separation held)
- Are the reserved highlights still paper white? (if not, lift now with a clean damp brush and blot — do not paint over)
- Any area reading as flat gray rather than silver-cool? (stop; lifting into it makes mud)
- More than three "I should add one more…" impulses? → stop.

BINDING STOP CONDITION
At 0:50 the brush goes down regardless of progress. The moment you start chasing a fourth reflection or re-touching a fold you've already painted, the ribbon turns to gray putty. Silver foil earns its life from the highlights you did NOT paint.

Black-Eyed Peas & Collards over Rice
serves 2  /  ~25 minutes  /  one large skillet + something to warm the rice

WHAT TO HAVE READY
  2 cans (15 oz each) black-eyed peas, drained and rinsed
  1 bunch collard greens, stems removed, leaves sliced into ribbons
  3 cups cooked rice
  4-5 garlic cloves, minced
  1 cup vegetable broth (plus a splash more if needed)
  2-3 tbsp olive oil
  1 tsp smoked paprika, plus more to taste
  Salt and black pepper
  1 lemon, halved

DO IT
  1.  Warm 2-3 tbsp olive oil in a large skillet over medium heat.
      Add the garlic and stir 30-60 seconds until fragrant — don't
      let it brown.
  2.  Add the collards and a small splash of broth. Toss to coat,
      cover, and cook 3-4 minutes until wilted and tender.
  3.  Add the black-eyed peas, about 3/4 cup broth, and 1 tsp
      smoked paprika. Stir gently, bring to a low simmer, and cook
      5-7 minutes to let the flavors come together. Season with
      salt and pepper.
  4.  Squeeze in lemon juice — start with half the lemon, taste,
      add more if you want it brighter. Adjust salt and pepper.
  5.  Warm the rice: microwave covered with a splash of water and
      a pinch of salt, OR toss in a small pot with a little broth
      and olive oil over low heat until just heated through.
  6.  Spoon rice into bowls, top with the pea-and-collard mixture,
      finish with a drizzle of olive oil and a crack of pepper.
      A little extra smoked paprika on top is nice.

A FEW NOTES
  This is the classic Hoppin' John / New Year combo — peas for
  luck, greens for prosperity, rice as the foundation. A good
  tradition for a Jan 1 lunch.

  If the collard stems are tender, slice them thin and start
  them a minute or two before the leaves so they soften.

  Reheats well: if you make more than you eat, Sam can have it
  later in the week with a small splash of broth to loosen it.

  Pair with a glass of cold water with lemon, or whatever Sam
  wants — a quiet, easy meal after a late NYE.

One-pot tomato-chickpea orzo with kale (lunch, ~30 min, 2 + 1 leftover)

Ingredients (pantry + a few fresh bits)
- 1.5 cups dry orzo
- 1 can (15 oz) chickpeas, drained
- 1 can (14.5 oz) crushed tomatoes
- 3.5 cups chicken or vegetable broth
- 3-4 cups chopped kale (stems removed)
- 3 garlic cloves, minced
- 1/3 cup grated Parmesan (plus the rind if you have it)
- 2 tbsp olive oil
- Salt, pepper, optional red pepper flakes

Timing
0:00 - prep: chop kale, mince garlic, drain chickpeas, open cans.
0:05 - pot over medium heat, olive oil, garlic 30 sec until fragrant.
0:06 - add orzo, stir 1 min to toast slightly.
0:07 - add crushed tomatoes, chickpeas, broth, Parmesan rind, 1/2 tsp salt, pepper. Stir, bring to a simmer.
0:12 - simmer gently, stirring occasionally so orzo doesn't stick, ~8-10 min until orzo is just tender and liquid is mostly absorbed.
0:22 - stir in kale and another pinch of salt; cook 2-3 min until wilted.
0:25 - kill heat, stir in grated Parmesan. Rest 2 min (it thickens as it sits).
0:27 - plate two bowls; portion the rest into one container for the leftover lunch.

Cooling the leftover safely
- Don't leave the pot on the counter more than ~90 min total (USDA guideline is 2 hr, but tighter is safer with starch + dairy).
- Within 30 min of cooking, transfer the leftover to a shallow container (no more than ~2 inches deep) so it cools fast. Stainless or glass works well.
- To speed it up: set the container in an ice bath in the sink for 5-10 min, stirring once, until it's no longer warm to the touch.
- Then lid on, into the fridge. Use within 3-4 days.
- To reheat Sam's lunch: splash in 1-2 tbsp water or broth, microwave covered 60-90 sec, stir. Or warm gently on the stovetop.

Cleanup: one pot, one spoon, one knife, one cutting board, two bowls, one storage container.

Kibo paw plan for deicer exposure (31°F overnight, granules visible):

PRE-WALK (1 min)
- Thin smear of plain dog paw balm or petroleum jelly on all four paws — pads, between toes, around nail beds. Creates a barrier so granules don't sit on skin.

WALK
- Shortest necessary route only. Avoid visible granule piles, freshly treated patches, and grass edges where pellets collect. Stay on dry, untreated pavement where you can.

ON RETURN — IMMEDIATE, IN ORDER
1. Wipe: damp, lukewarm plain washcloth or unscented dog paw wipe. One paw per cloth section. Get between toes and around nail folds — granules hide there.
2. Rinse: shallow dish of lukewarm plain water (or sterile saline). Dip each paw 30–60 sec and gently flex the toes so water reaches pad edges. Don't pour hot water; don't use peroxide, alcohol, chlorhexidine, or essential oils.
3. Pat dry thoroughly — especially between toes. Dampness left between pads lets residual salt crystallize and crack skin overnight.
4. Inspect: pads, webbing between toes, nail beds. Look for stuck granules, redness, cracking, cuts.
5. Re-apply thin paw balm after dry.

FOR TONIGHT
- Keep water available but don't let him lick paws before you've cleaned them.

VET-CALL TRIGGERS (granule-specific, plus the usual)
- Repeated vomiting, heavy drooling, refusal of food or water — ingestion concern (calcium chloride, urea, and magnesium chloride deicers are the toxic ones; regular NaCl is milder but still irritating in quantity).

- Pad looks burned, blistered, cracked deep, or is actively bleeding after cleaning.
- Granule visibly embedded and won't rinse free — don't dig, call.

- Licking that doesn't stop within 30–60 min of clean + balm — he's reacting to something still on the skin.

Sunday watercolor — Jan 3, 2027 — 75 min, glass jar + two rosemary stems

The instinct you named is the right one to lead with: the glass wants lines and the shadow wants soft. The whole block can hang on that distinction. Treat the jar as a held absence — wall shows through it, shadow shows through it, stems refract through it — and let the two rim highlights + the shadow do the defining. The rosemary is your only place for hard work, and even there, less needle than you think.

Palette — three cool-leaning pools, all from the same tube set so the shadow and the stems stay related:

  Pool A (wall):        mostly water + 1 ultramarine + a breath of burnt sienna. Cool, neutral, pale. This is value 1 — almost the paper.
  Pool B (shadow):      ultramarine + tiny yellow ochre + a touch of burnt sienna. Reads as quiet gray-green at mid value.
  Pool C (stems):       more ultramarine + burnt sienna + a little yellow ochre. Olive-gray, value 3. Dilute for above-water, denser for in-water.

Three-value map:
  - Wall          = value 1 (lightest, paper-white to Pool A)
  - Shadow + jar interior = value 2 (Pool B, soft-edged)
  - Stems, in-water compression, jar base = value 3 (Pool C)
  - Rim highlights = value 0 (the paper itself, untouched)

Sequence

  0–5    Setup. Mix the three pools. Tiny thumbnail on scrap: pale rectangle (wall), soft pillow shape (shadow) overlapping the lower-right, two thin vertical lines (stems) with a wobble where they cross the water line, two small white dots at the upper rim.

  5–15   Wash the wall. One even, very pale pass of Pool A. Let it dry flat. Do not go back over it.

  15–32  The shadow is the heart of the painting. Wet-on-dry with Pool B, soft-edged. Drop it in where it falls, let the brush do the feathering at the cast edges — that's the quiet you came for. The densest part of the shadow is right under the jar's base; let it pool slightly darker there. Stop while it still looks like a shadow, not a shape. Bone-dry.

  32–50  Stems above the water line. Hard edges, wet-on-dry, small brush. Silhouette first — two slender verticals with a faint lean — then a few darker accents where stems overlap or turn toward you. Resist the needles. Two stems, not a botanical. Vary the dilution of Pool C; let some passages stay mid-value.

  50–62  Stems through the water. This is where the painting lives or dies. Wet-in-wet or wet-on-damp into a faintly dampened rectangle where the water sits — Pool C, slightly diluted so the in-water stems read lighter than the above-water ones (light passes through). One stroke per stem is the rule. The wobble is the truth. If you feel the urge to "correct" the distortion, stop and dry the brush.

  62–70  Rim highlights. Do not paint. Lift any pigment that crept into the upper-rim dots with a damp brush, blot, repeat. The lower-rim highlight is smaller and softer — leave it alone unless a stem ran into it.

  70–75  Quiet pass. One optional move: a single soft cool note in the lower body of the jar where the water catches a faint cast shadow. Otherwise stop.

Stop conditions — all must hold:
  - Wall is a single pale value, no streaks, no glazing
  - Shadow reads as soft gray-green, edges feathered, not outlined
  - Jar is defined by shadow + rim highlights + stem refraction, never by a drawn line
  - Rim highlights are paper-white; no pigment sits in them
  - Stems feel like two rosemary stems, not a study of one
  - You can see the wall through the jar's body

Cautions for the hour:
  - Do not outline the jar at any stage — every line you add will tighten what should breathe
  - Do not paint the highlights — lift if they get touched
  - Do not chase the reflections on the curved glass — one quiet note is the budget
  - Do not detail the needles — silhouette + value carries the read
  - Do not glaze — every pass dries before the next
  - When the timer hits 75, stop even if the stems feel unfinished. Unfinished is the discipline of this one.

The rosemary is doing you a favor by being two stems, not a bouquet. One stem can be tempted into a portrait. Two stems stay a Sunday morning.

Act now while it's still wet. The coffee itself is the easy part — black, no milk/sugar is mostly tannins and lifts cleanly from cotton when handled cold. The risk is the *dye*, since the fabric hasn't been colorfast-tested.

Order of operations:

1. Blot, don't rub. Press a clean cloth or paper towel against the spot to wick up liquid. Rubbing spreads it and can lift unset dye.

2. Cold-water flush from the back. Hold the cuff under a cold tap with the stained side face-down so water pushes the coffee *out* of the fabric rather than deeper in. Hot water sets tannin stains and could encourage dye to bleed — the label's "cold" is doing real work here.

3. Colorfastness spot test before any detergent. Pick a hidden area — inside the cuff fold or an inside seam. Touch it with a cotton swab dipped in cold water plus a drop of whatever you intend to use (mild detergent, or an oxygen-based stain remover like OxiClean; do *not* use chlorine bleach — the label forbids it). Wait 2–3 minutes. If any color transfers to the swab, stop: either hand-wash the cuff alone in cold water or take it to a dry cleaner. Do not put the jacket in a machine wash where dye could migrate to other areas.

4. If the test holds: gently work a little detergent or an oxygen-based paste into the spot. Let it sit 5–10 minutes.

5. Machine wash cold per the label, alone or with similar darks.

6. Air dry only. Do not tumble dry — heat will permanently set any tannin you missed. Inspect while still damp. If a faint shadow remains, repeat steps 4–5 *before* drying again.

If the cuff looks clean after one air-dry, you're done. A ghost of a tannin stain often lifts fully on a second cold pass — but only if you never let it hit the dryer in between.

Context is clear: this is the follow-up to the 1/3/27 black-coffee spill on the cotton jacket cuff (label: cold machine wash, no bleach, no tumble dry). Given the memory says the prior protocol was a six-step coffee-stain plan with spot-test, oxygen-based paste, cold machine wash, and air-dry, I'll build on that and tighten it around "conservative" — emphasizing no-spread, no-heat-set, colorfast-first.

Conservative coffee stain sequence — cotton jacket cuff (cold wash, no bleach, no tumble dry)

1. Stop the spread
   - Don't rub. Don't wipe outward.
   - Hold the cuff stained-side down over a folded dry towel so gravity pulls coffee into the towel, not deeper into the weave.
   - Press a clean dry microfiber straight down, lift, rotate to a clean spot, repeat. Stop the moment the cloth comes up clean — more passes just work the stain around.

2. Cold water flush from the back
   - Hold the cuff under a cold (not warm) tap with the stained side facing down.
   - Let water run through the back of the fabric so it pushes the coffee out the front, not deeper in.
   - 1–2 minutes is plenty. Do not use warm/hot water — heat sets tannin stains.

3. Colorfastness spot test (do this before any soap or remover)
   - Pick a hidden spot: inside the cuff fold or behind a button placket.
   - Dampen a cotton swab with cold water + a tiny drop of mild liquid detergent. Press on the hidden spot for 10 seconds, then blot dry with a white cloth.
   - Check: any color transfer onto the white cloth, any change in the fabric's surface, or any dye bleed = stop the test, do not proceed to step 4. Send the jacket to a dry cleaner and point out the coffee spot.
   - If clean, also test a tiny dab of an oxygen-based remover (e.g., sodium percarbonate) the same way. Skip if you don't have one.

4. Treat the stain (only if the spot test passed)
   - Option A (gentler): work a tiny drop of mild liquid detergent into the damp stain with a fingertip. Let sit 5 minutes, no longer.
   - Option B (slightly stronger): make a thin paste of oxygen-based remover + cold water, apply just to the stain, let sit 5–10 minutes. Don't let it dry on the fabric.
   - Re-flush from the back with cold water until the water runs clear.

5. Wash — per care label
   - Machine wash cold, separately or with similar darks, using your regular detergent.
   - No bleach. No fabric softener on the cuff (it can set residue).
   - Check the cuff before the jacket goes in the dryer: if any shadow remains, repeat steps 1–4 on the still-damp area and re-wash. The label forbids tumble drying, but more importantly, dryer heat will set any remaining coffee tint permanently.

6. Air-dry
   - Reshape the cuff and hang or lay flat.
   - Air-dry away from direct sun and any heat source (radiator, heater vent).
   - Only evaluate the result once fully dry. A faint shadow that looks alarming while damp often fades as it dries.

Stop conditions — call a professional cleaner instead of continuing
- The spot test bleeds or changes the fabric.
- The stain has spread or darkened after step 4.
- The cuff is lined, trimmed, or structured in a way you can't tell whether the coffee soaked through.
- You've done two full treatment cycles and a faint tan/brown ring still remains — that's tannin set into the fiber, and a dry cleaner has tools (and wet-side tannin reducers) you don't.

What's deliberately excluded because it would spread or heat-set the stain: rubbing, scrubbing with a brush, warm/hot water at any stage, bleach or "color-safe" bleach containing sodium hypochlorite, vinegar before washing, hairspray/alcohol "tricks," putting the jacket in any dryer, and ironing the cuff to "dry it faster."

Case for 90-day:

WITH COUSCOUS + LEMON-TAHINI

SETUP (one trip to the kitchen, do it all before you start):
- Oven to 425°F. Line a rimmed sheet pan with parchment (zero scrub later).
- Peel + cube sweet potato ~½". Cut broccoli into medium florets (bigger = won't overcook). Drain chickpeas, pat dry with a towel.
- Mince 1 garlic clove for the sauce.

0:00  On the sheet pan: sweet potato, broccoli, chickpeas + ~3 Tbsp olive oil, 1 tsp smoked paprika, ½ tsp salt, pepper. Toss with your hands, spread in a single layer (crowding = soggy).
0:03  Into the oven. Timer 25 min.
0:05  Sauce, one bowl + fork: 3 Tbsp tahini + juice of ½ lemon + 1 minced garlic clove + pinch salt. Whisk; loosen with 1 Tbsp water at a time until it pours (about 2-3 Tbsp total).
0:07  Couscous, one bowl: 1 cup dry couscous + 1¼ cup just-boiled water (use the kettle — no standing at the stove) + pinch salt. Stir once, cover with a plate, leave it.
0:12  Skip the halfway toss — one less trip. (Toss at 12 min if you want even browning; not required.)
0:30  Pull pan. Sweet potato should be tender; chickpeas crisp at the edges.

0:34  Portion Sam's lunch (below). Eat.

LUNCH STORAGE — SAFE COOLING:
- Veg + chickpeas: SHALLOW container (single layer depth, not piled deep). Lid OFF for ~10 min on the counter so steam escapes — deep hot piles are the slow-cooling trap. Then lid on, into the fridge.
- Couscous: separate container. Spread thin on a plate for 5 min before lidding — it cools much faster that way.
- Sauce: small jar with lid, fridge.
- Eat within 3 days. Reheat veg until steaming hot; couscous with a splash of water and a quick cover so it doesn't dry.

- One sheet pan, two bowls, one fork, knife, cutting board — total cleanup.

Short answer: paint the cool shadow first, let it dry, then glaze the warm reflection on top. Keep the mug itself as reserved paper throughout — the warm and cool are both thin glazes over white, not fills.

Why that order:
- The cool shadow is the harder edge to control cleanly and it anchors the form. If you do warm first and then cool, the second wash will either lift the warm or bleed into it and you'll get a muddy seam where they meet.
- The warm reflection is a glaze — thin burnt sienna + a touch of yellow ochre at tea-strength — and it sits more cleanly on dry paper than on top of a fresh cool wash.
- The bright white of the mug is the paper. You never "put down" the mug; you darken around it.

Practical sequence for the 75 minutes:

0–5 min   Setup. Tape if you want a clean edge. Pre-tone three puddles on the palette: (a) ultramarine + burnt sienna (2:1, lots of water) for the cool shadow, (b) burnt sienna + a touch of yellow ochre, tea-strength, for the warm reflection, (c) the same warm mix one step lighter for the softest bounce on the mug's far cheek.

5–15 min  Cast shadow on the table — blue-gray, graded from darker near the mug base to lighter at the far edge. This is your composition anchor. Let it dry.

15–30 min Cool form shadow on the mug. Wet-on-dry, single pass, graded from the deepest value at the terminator (the line where window light dies on the mug's body) to nothing at the highlight side. Don't fill the mug — paint the shadow side only. Bone-dry before you go on, or the warm glaze will mud into it.

30–45 min Dry. Don't rush this; "dry to the touch" still has too much moisture for a clean glaze next to it.

45–60 min Warm reflection. Apply the warm glaze on the orange-facing side of the mug, wet-on-dry. Single pass, broken strokes if the surface is curved. If the transition line between warm and cool wants to be soft, stop the warm glaze about a millimeter short of the cool, then re-wet that thin strip with a damp brush and drop in a very thin warm wash to bridge — one pass, no scrubbing.

60–70 min Halved orange and any refinements to the terminator or cast shadow edge.

70–75 min Final look. Stop.

Two cautions specific to this setup:

- Do not glaze the brightest specular spot on the mug or you'll kill the "white ceramic" read.
- Do not add a second cool pass over the shadow once the warm is down. If the cool isn't dark enough at 30 min, deepen it then — not after.

The value separation is doing the work here: warm ochre at tea-strength reads lighter than cool blue-gray at the same dilution, so the warm reflection will feel luminous against the cool shadow without you needing to push either one. That's the same principle from the November study — let value do the separating, not saturation.

Immediate value
A workaround solves a real problem in the moment — it lets people complete a task, reach a service, or meet a need without waiting for the institution to close the underlying gap. The benefit is concrete and felt: time saved, harm avoided, dignity preserved. To the person using it, the workaround usually reads as competence, not as evidence that something upstream is broken.

How success can conceal failure
When the workaround works, the institution never receives a clean signal that something is missing. The user sees a path forward, the system records a resolved case, and the structural deficit — understaffing, absent policy, broken handoff — stays out of view because no one has to escalate it. Over time, the workaround can become normalized, then expected, then quietly required, while the gap it papers over goes unaddressed or widens as resources flow elsewhere.

Two questions that leave both readings open
- What would have to change for the workaround to stop being necessary, and who would have to notice first — the people using it, or the institution it works around?
- Does the workaround's success belong to the person who devised it, to the institution that failed to prevent the need, or to both in ways that resist being cleanly separated?

Reserve the apple as a held shape from the very first wash and build the bag around it, and the more important move: let the folds DELIBERATELY soften and lose value contrast as they approach the apple's edge. That's what makes the bag read as fabric the apple is sitting *inside*, not as a second drawing parked behind it. Right now the folds are probably running at full strength all the way up to the boundary, which is why the bag keeps pulling focus — fabric draped over a sphere goes quiet right where it touches the sphere, and yours isn't.

Concrete sequence for the remaining hour:

- Roughly silhouette the apple in pencil, then mentally widen it by about 1/8" — that margin is bag, not apple. Paint the bag's first wash right up to that line, treating the apple as a hole.
- Two values on the bag is enough: a mid warm neutral (raw umber + a touch of burnt sienna) for the general crumple, and a darker accent only in the deepest creases. Save your strongest, crispest folds for the empty bag behind and beside the apple — never where it touches.
- Apple last, and onto a dry bag. Pale yellow ochre undertone on the shadow side, then red on the lit side, brightest highlight as paper. Pull the red's chroma *down* where it meets the bag so the bag's darkest fold can still win locally.
- One small hard cast shadow where the apple sits on the bag ties them together — but keep it small.

Red flags (any one is enough to treat it as suspicious):
- Urgency or threat — "act now," "within 24 hours," "account will be closed," "final notice"
- Generic greeting — "Dear Customer" instead of your name
- Sender address doesn't match the company (e.g., support@amaz0n-security.com, or a free webmail like @gmail.com/@yahoo.com)
- Link text says one thing but the real destination is different — long, weird, or misspelled
- Reply-to address is different from the sender

- Unexpected attachment, especially .zip, .html, or an invoice you didn't expect
- Spelling or grammar that's "off"
- You weren't expecting it

Given the context (two small holes in folded wool, one dry empty casing, cotton linens clean, Kibo has room access), the casing is almost certainly a clothes-moth pupal case — they prefer animal fiber and ignore cellulose. Here's a tight, pet-conscious sequence.

A. Isolate the room now (next 30 min)
- Close the room door. Do not shake or brush the throw — vibration drops eggs/casings.
- Bag first, move second: place the throw in a sealed plastic bag (zip-lock or tied trash bag) before carrying it out of the room. This stops anything from falling into the carpet/baseboards.
- Move the bagged throw to a hard-floor area (kitchen counter, bath floor) away from Kibo's usual spots.
- Vacuum the storage area slowly: seams, folds, shelf corners, baseboard edges, and any adjacent closet walls. Use the crevice tool.
- Empty the vacuum canister or remove and bag the bag immediately and take it to the outdoor trash. Eggs and larvae can survive and re-emerge from a vacuum left sitting.
- Wash your hands and change clothes if you handled the throw before bagging.

B. Inspection sequence (work over a white towel so anything that drops is visible)
- Examine the casing while still in the bag or over the towel: a clothes-moth pupal case is roughly 1/4–1/2 inch, silky, off-white to tan, with one open end where the adult emerged.
- Pull the throw out flat and check the holes under a flashlight — note whether edges are chewed (irregular) or cut (straight). Moth feeding leaves irregular holes, often with webbing or fine sand-like frass nearby.
- Inspect every wool item stored in the same area (sweaters, scarves, other throws, felted hats). Casings/larvae hide in folds and seams.
- Flashlight the shelf/closet corners, drawer bottoms, and any undisturbed wool item for additional casings, webbing trails, or frass.

C. Wool-appropriate cleaning options (all pet-safe as described)
Pick one — freezing is the easiest with a cat in the home.

- Freezing (recommended): seal the throw in a clean plastic bag, squeeze out air, freeze at 0°F / -18°C or below for 72 hours. Thaw 24 hours, refreeze 72 hours, thaw again. Then vacuum the throw slowly on both sides with the upholstery tool to remove dead larvae/eggs/webbing.
- Hot-tumble (only if care label permits): 30+ minutes at the highest heat setting in the dryer, alone. Effective for all life stages. Skip if the label says no tumble.
- Hand wash: cool water, wool wash (Eucalan or Soak — no essential oils, no conditioner with fragrance). Lay flat to dry on a towel. Washing alone doesn't reliably kill eggs, so combine with freezing if possible.
- Dry cleaning: appropriate and kills all stages; standard route if the throw is "dry clean only."
- Do not use around Kibo: mothballs (naphthalene/PDCB), cedar in a confined closet space, essential oils (lavender, tea tree, eucalyptus, citrus, peppermint — toxic to cats even via inhalation), vinegar or any "natural spray" on the wool, and indoor foggers/bug bombs (already off the table).

D. Monitoring (next 2–4 weeks)
- Place 1–2 clothes-moth pheromone traps (wing-style sticky traps) on the wall of the closet or storage area — these are pet-safe and catch males so you know if adults are active.
- Weekly check of all wool in storage: unfold each item, look for new holes, casings, or frass.
- Track Kibo: clothes moths don't bite or bother cats, so behavior is not a concern. The only risk is product exposure, which the cleaning options above avoid.
- Wash or freeze any wool item that sat within ~6 feet of the stored throw as a precaution, even if it looks clean.

E. Call a professional pest inspector if any of these show up
- More than one casing, or live larvae/adults found across additional items.
- New holes appearing on wool during the 2–4 week monitoring window.
- Visible frass (fine sand-like droppings) accumulating in the storage area.
- Adult moths seen flying in the room in low light (they tend to flutter rather than fly directly).

Removing a sheet from a glued block — sequence

Before you start
- Confirm the painting is bone-dry, not just touch-dry. If it has any cool feel, wait longer; trapped moisture weakens the surface fibers and makes them lift.
- Clear a flat, well-lit workspace and have a clean scrap sheet or blotter ready.

Stabilize the block
- Place the block face-up on a flat surface. The backing board already gives it rigidity, so you do not need to clamp it.
- Put a thin rubber shelf liner or a barely-damp folded towel underneath. Either keeps the block from sliding when you apply lateral pressure, and a soft towel gives a tiny bit of give if the tool tips downward.
- Keep the painted surface clearly in view the whole time so you can spot any fiber lift immediately.

Tool
- Best: a bone folder. It is blunt, slightly beveled, thin enough to enter the gap, and will not slice paper.
- Acceptable substitutes: a dull or burnished palette knife (the rounded, non-sharp edge), or an old plastic card with a smoothed corner.
- Avoid utility knives, X-Acto blades, scissors, or anything truly sharp. The goal is to push the glue apart, not cut paper.

Direction of cut
- Slide the tool parallel to the sheet edge, between the top sheet and the second sheet — not down into the stack.
- Hold the tool almost flat to the paper, around 10–20 degrees. The leading edge advances laterally through the glue line.
- Pressure goes sideways, not downward. Imagine slipping a card between two sheets of paper lying on a desk.

Sequence
1. Find the unglued gap. It is usually at one corner or along one short edge.
2. Insert the tool tip into the gap at a shallow angle. Aim between the top sheet and the sheet below, not into the glue bead itself.
3. Advance in small increments — roughly a centimeter at a time. After each increment, lift the tool slightly and check that the top sheet is separating cleanly and the sheet below is undisturbed.
4. At a corner, ease around it. Do not lever upward to pry the corner free; continue along the next edge with the same shallow, lateral motion.
5. Work all four edges. As more of the sheet releases, it will feel looser and gravity starts to help.
6. Once every edge is free, lift the sheet straight up off the block with both hands, supporting the whole sheet evenly. Do not drag it across the sheet below.

When to stop
Stop immediately and back the tool out if any of the following happens:
- The tool stops sliding smoothly and begins to catch or grab.
- You feel sudden resistance or a tug instead of a clean glide.
- Fibers lift on the painted side, or the sheet below starts to roughen.
- The top sheet buckles, wrinkles, or rises in a wave ahead of the tool instead of releasing cleanly.
- The sheet below begins to move up with the tool.

If any of these occur, do not force it. Pull the tool back, leave the partially released sheet in place under a clean blotter for an hour or two, then try again from a slightly different point in the gap with even lighter pressure. Forcing through a catch is what tears the painting or scores the next sheet.

Bike tire, rear at 38 psi against a 50+ psi operating range, no visible damage, not currently being ridden. Given the ankle rehab timeline there's no commute pressure, which lets you run a careful leak test instead of rushing the bike back into service. Here's the conservative sequence.

INFLATION SEQUENCE (stationary, bike upright and unloaded)

  1. Pre-inflation visual: run a finger around the inside of the tread (you've done this before — small glass/wire shards can hide in the tread pattern and only show up by touch). Look at both sidewalls, both beads, the valve stem and base, and the rim tape through the valve hole if you can see it.
  2. Confirm the front (54 psi) is in range so you have a reference point if anything odd shows up later.
  3. Inflate the rear to the BOTTOM of the marked range (50 psi), not higher. Reasons: (a) it gives a real leak test without over-stressing a tire that may have an unseen defect, (b) staying at or below the marked minimum keeps the sidewall from masking a bulge by inflating past it, (c) you don't want to chase the loss back up to 60–70 psi only to discover a slow leak at the higher pressure.
  4. During inflation, listen at the valve for hiss and feel the hose/valve junction for air. A valve leak will often show here before it shows on the gauge.
  5. Remove the pump, immediately re-gauge at the same spot on the rim with the valve at the 6 o'clock position so the gauge reads consistently.

SHORT-INTERVAL PRESSURE RECHECK

  - T+5 min: primary valve/seal check. Should hold within 0.5 psi if nothing is leaking at the valve or bead.
  - T+30 min: slow-leak check. Loss of more than ~1 psi here is meaningful.
  - T+2 hr: confirmation reading.
  - T+24 hr cold, before moving the bike: this is the definitive stability reading. Bike tires at room temp vs. cold can differ by 1–2 psi, so compare cold-to-cold.
  - Compare each reading against the 38 psi baseline you found today — that's the unexplained loss you still need to account for.

VISIBLE-DAMAGE SEQUENCE (do BEFORE and AGAIN AFTER inflation; pressure can reveal what flat pressure hides)

  - Bead, both sides, full circumference: no lift, no pinch, uniform seating all the way around. After inflation the bead should sit evenly; any spot that looks lower than the rest is suspect.
  - Tread: full 360, finger-sweep as well as eyes. Look and feel for glass, wire, thorn, staple. Pinholes from small debris often don't hiss audibly but will show as a tiny wet/dark spot if you listen close or run a wet finger across the tread.
  - Sidewalls: bulges, cuts, scuffs, brake-rub marks. A bulge that wasn't visible at 38 psi can become visible at 50 — recheck after inflation.
  - Valve: stem straight, no cuts or splits, base flush to the rim, lockring (if Schrader) snug, no sealant/paste residue suggesting prior leak. With your 2026-10-29 car experience, a leaking valve core is a plausible culprit on this tire too.
  - Rim tape: through the valve hole or by feel — no spoke ends poking into the tube cavity, tape not shifted.
  - Spokes and nipples: any loose nipples can contact the tube and wear a slow hole; quick check by squeezing pairs.
  - Soapy water or spit test on valve and suspected spots if you have any — bubbles will show a leak the gauge catches only slowly.

CONDITIONS FOR LEAVING IT UNRIDDEN FOR SHOP INSPECTION

  Take it to a shop (don't ride it) if ANY of the following is true, even if the tire holds pressure through the full recheck schedule:

  - Pressure drops more than ~1 psi between any two readings in the first 24 hours.
  - The pre- or post-inflation inspection finds any embedded object, sidewall bulge, bead irregularity, rim-tape damage, loose spoke/nipple, or visible valve defect.
  - The soapy-water/spit test shows bubbles at valve, bead, or any tread spot.
  - The tire holds pressure perfectly AND no damage is found AND you still want the conservative answer: take it to a shop anyway, because:
      * 12 psi below the marked minimum is too large a loss to write off to temperature or non-use alone.
      * Slow leaks frequently seal temporarily on tiny debris and re-open days or weeks later — a stable 24-hour reading is not the same as "no leak."
      * You have an ankle rehab window with no commute deadline, so the cost of a shop visit is just time, not a missed obligation.
      * The shop can confirm tube vs. tire damage and patch or replace properly before you load it back into a commuter rotation.

  Inflation holding is necessary information, not sufficient proof. The decision tree is: stable pressure + zero visible damage + shop confirmation = road-ready. Stable pressure + zero visible damage alone is "ready for the shop," not "ready to ride."

Given your patch-kit experience from 2023-12, you could self-repair a confirmed small tube puncture, but with the size of the unexplained loss and no commute pressure, a shop inspection is the cleaner path and preserves the spare tube you chose to keep for commuting.

The cleaner's caveat is the right one — a textile cleaner can remediate the throw itself (kill any remaining eggs/larvae/casings on it via wet or solvent cleaning; restore the cosmetic darning) but cannot speak to whether the home still harbors an active population. Those are two separate questions, and conflating them is how people end up "cleaning" their way into a recurring problem.

Repair vs. replace is functionally a $28 question. That gap is small enough that the decision turns on whether you want this specific throw back, not on cost. And both options are wool, so both are equally vulnerable if the home has an active infestation — replacement doesn't insulate you from that.

The bigger variable is what monitoring has shown. You're 12 days into a 2–4 week window as of today:

    - Any new casings, holes, or frass on other stored wool within ~6 ft?
    - Any webbing along shelf corners, drawer bottoms, or closet walls?
    - Any change in Kibo's behavior around the storage area (sniffing, pawing)?

If the window closes clean, repair at $100 is the obvious move and the cleaner is the right call. If new signs appear, replace at $128 is reasonable but doesn't fix the underlying issue — you'd still need to address the broader infestation (continued pheromone traps, isolate and treat the rest of the affected wool, possibly a textile-pest inspection) before bringing in any new wool.

I'd hold the decision until the monitoring window completes — Feb 8 at the earliest (2-wk mark), Feb 22 if you want the conservative end (4-wk). No urgency on the throw itself; it's sealed and isolated, and the cleaner's quote presumably holds.

How's the monitoring looking so far?

Framing this around what's actually on the throw (two small holes, one empty casing) without drawing any pesticide or infestation claim from a cleaner's quote. Cost ranges are typical US shop/retail norms; actual quotes vary by region and shop.

1. Professional cleaning only
   - Cash cost: roughly $20–$60 for a wool throw at a standard cleaner; $40–$80 if you need a pet-safer process (wet cleaning, CO2, or silicone-solvent) rather than perchloroethylene "perc" dry cleaning. Out of pocket; no insurance angle.
   - Does: removes soil, body oils, and loose organic material in the fiber; the casing comes back either cleaned away or removed during processing.
   - Doesn't: doesn't repair the two small holes; doesn't stabilize the weakened fibers around them; doesn't address any environmental factor (which lives on the monitoring track, not the cleaning track).
   - Practical outcome: lowest spend, throw returns clean but visibly damaged at the two holes.

2. Cleaning + darning
   - Cash cost: cleaning $20–$80 (pet-safer process) plus darning at a textile repair shop, typically $15–$40 per hole for a small repair, $25–$60 per hole for invisible or yarn-matched visible mending. Realistic total $50–$200 for two holes. DIY with a wool darning needle and a small skein of matching yarn is under $10 in materials.
   - Does: closes and stabilizes the two small holes; textile is functionally whole again; cleaning still removes soil and loose organic material first.
   - Doesn't: darning only reinforces the patched zone, not the whole throw; matched yarn is hard to source, so most repairs are visible (which is fine and increasingly common, but visible); still doesn't address environmental factors.
   - Practical outcome: moderate spend; holes closed and stable; the right call if the throw has specific value you want to keep.

3. Replacement
   - Cash cost: new wool throw runs $50–$150 for entry tier (basic Pendleton, wool blends at home goods), $150–$400 for mid-tier (Brahms Mount, Garnet Hill, Faribault, Brooklinen wool), $400+ for premium or heirloom. Old throw goes into the trash in a sealed bag.
   - Does: clean baseline; no holes; no carry-over history on the item; lets you reset weight, size, and color to what you actually want.
   - Doesn't: doesn't resolve any environmental factor at the storage site (the new throw is just as exposed as the old one was); highest cash outlay of the three.
   - Practical outcome: clean slate if the old throw is interchangeable in your mind; non-trivial spend if you were hoping to keep it.

Two notes specific to your situation, kept separate from the comparison itself:

- Cat-safe cleaning: perc is the cheapest professional route but perc residue is a real concern with Kibo in the house. Wet cleaning / CO2 / silicone-solvent at a green cleaner runs a bit more and is the safer pick. Either way, let the throw air out before it goes back into a closed closet.
- The casing and the holes are observable facts. This comparison doesn't read a pest-control claim out of any cleaner quote, and any monitoring question (cotton linens, closet, surrounding wool) stays on its own track with its own timeline.

Decision logic in one line: replace if the throw is interchangeable, clean + darn if it has specific value worth keeping, clean only if you want the cheapest path and don't mind the holes remaining.

What you're describing — brown tips plus slightly drooping newer growth on a rosemary that was just brought in — is most often a normal acclimation response to indoor air being drier and dimmer than outdoor conditions, plus an adjustment in the watering rhythm. Nothing in your observations points to an emergency, so the goal here is steady conditions and patient observation, not intervention.

Watering (conservative)

  - Since the upper inch is dry now, water once thoroughly at room temperature until you just see drainage at the bottom holes, then stop.
  - Empty any saucer 15–20 minutes after watering. Never let the pot sit in standing water.
  - Plan on roughly a week to ten days between waterings indoors, but let actual dry-down guide you rather than the calendar. Lift the pot briefly after watering and again a few days later — heavy means wet, light means dry. That weight cue becomes more reliable than poking the soil.
  - Water at the soil surface, not over the foliage. Rosemary wants a cycle of moist-then-dries-out, not a continuously damp root zone.

Light

  - Bright window placement is right. Rotate the pot a quarter turn each week so growth stays even instead of leaning toward the glass.
  - Watch the new stems over the next couple of weeks. If they keep stretching and leaning noticeably toward the window, that's a sign the light is on the low side and a small grow light on a simple timer would be the next step — still not fertilizer, not repotting.
  - Keep it away from the heating vent, which you've already done — that's the right call.

Drainage

  - Free drainage plus a dry upper inch is what you want to see. Just confirm there's no decorative sleeve or cache pot holding water at the base, and that the drainage holes aren't blocked.
  - A gritty, fast-draining mix is ideal for rosemary long-term, but I wouldn't repot now while it's adjusting.

Acclimation

  - Indoor winter air is typically much drier and dimmer than outdoor air even at a sunny window. Tip burn is the most common fingerprint of that transition.
  - If daytime temperatures climb back into the 50s°F on calm, sunny days, a few hours outside in a sheltered spot during the day and back inside at night can ease the transition. That's optional, not required.
  - Pick a spot and leave it there. Rosemary dislikes being shuffled between windows.

Monitoring over the next two to three weeks

  - Week 1: water once if dry, otherwise leave it. Photograph the current state so you have a baseline.
  - Week 2: check whether new growth is firming up, whether existing brown tips are stable rather than progressing, and whether drooping is recovering.
  - Week 3: reassess. If new growth looks healthy and the brown tips aren't spreading, you've effectively found the new normal for this winter.

When a local plant professional is worth contacting — without diagnosing anything here, just describing patterns that warrant a second set of eyes

  - Browning that travels down from the tips into the stems rather than staying at the very ends.
  - New growth that wilts or collapses while the soil is appropriately moist — that's a different pattern from acclimation stress and warrants a look.
  - Soft or mushy stems near the soil line, or a sour smell from the soil.
  - Any visible spotting, unusual discoloration patterns, lesions, or growths on stems or leaves that don't match the brown-tip pattern you already see.
  - Persistent droop that doesn't respond to a corrected watering rhythm over a full two to three weeks.

Hold the line on: no fertilizer this season, no repotting. Both add stress to a plant that's still settling in, and rosemary grown indoors over winter is naturally slower-growing than it would be outside in May.

Here's a tape-free sequence for today's painting, organized around the four concerns you named.

CLEAN MARGIN - PAINT A PRE-WET MARGIN BEFORE THE WASH
This is your replacement for the tape line. With a small round brush (a #4 or #6) and clean water, paint a thin "caution zone" roughly 1/8 to 3/16 inch inside the paper edge, all the way around or only on the edges you want to keep white. Work one or two edges at a time so the strip stays damp when your wash arrives. If it dries before your wash reaches it, recharge it. The damp strip repels incoming wet wash - pigment migrates toward drier paper, not wetter, so the white edge holds.

BLOCK STABILIZATION
The glued block is already rigid from the gum binding, so it sits flat on its own. Place it on a clean surface; prop one edge on a folded card or cork trivet if you want a working tilt for gravity-assisted wash control. A thin rubber shelf liner underneath adds grip if the block slides. Skip the damp towel under the block today - damp against the gummed edges over a long session can soften the binding.

WASH CREEP CONTROL DURING PAINTING
- Mix slightly wetter than usual so the wash flows, but load the brush less.
- Work interior-to-edge, stopping the brush roughly 1/4 inch short of the damp margin.
- Drop to a smaller brush (one size down) within an inch of any edge you care about.
- Tilt the block so gravity carries the wash away from your most critical edge.
- Keep a folded paper towel pinched in your off-hand. If a bead of pigment crosses into the damp margin, touch the towel to the inside of the bead and pull it back. Do not chase it with the brush.

SAFE-STOP CONDITIONS - STOP IMMEDIATELY IF:
- The brush tip snags on the glue seam at the paper edge. You have hit the binding glue; a hard pigment ring will form there.
- A tide line develops along the inside of your damp margin. The strip is drying faster than the wash, or pigment is concentrating at the boundary.
- The damp margin dries out before the adjacent wash finishes. Either re-wet it with clean water or stop and reassess - do not let a hard edge set.
- The block edge begins to buckle or lift. Rare on a glued block, but if it does, stop and let it flatten dry before continuing.

AFTERWARDS
Let the painting dry flat and bone-dry. The white margin is preserved by the technique itself - nothing to peel, nothing to lift.

Two honest caveats:
- The pre-wet margin gives a soft white edge, not a hard tape-line rectangle. That is a watercolor convention, not a flaw. If you ever want a hard rectangular edge on a future painting, frisket/liquid mask is the alternative, but it carries its own risks on cold-press and you'd want to test on a scrap edge of this same block first.
- This sequence covers the painting phase. If you later separate today's sheet from the block, the bone-folder sequence you already have (shallow 10-20° angle, stop on catch) still applies.

For an unaltered preservation master, the goal is to capture what the sensor actually saw — no interpretive adjustments — and to keep every future tweak in a sibling derivative file, never written back to the master. Two parts follow.

1. Automatic corrections to DISABLE on the master capture

  Tone / exposure
    - Auto-exposure, auto-tone, auto-levels, auto-contrast
    - Highlight recovery / shadow recovery / D-lighting-type shadow lift
    - Backlight correction
    - Adaptive lighting / scene modes (portrait, document-auto, etc.)

  Color
    - Auto white balance, auto-color, color restoration / fade correction
    - Skin-tone correction, red-eye, face-enhancement modes
    - Out-of-gamut clipping / saturation boost

  Sharpening / texture
    - Unsharp mask, "smart sharpen," edge enhancement, micro-contrast boost
    - Noise reduction, grain reduction, luminance/chrominance NR
    - JPEG-quality smoothing if it appears as a "live" preview adjustment

  Detail removal (especially relevant for pencil backs and treated prints)
    - Digital ICE / infrared dust-and-scratch removal — erases faint pencil,
      paper texture, and graphite tooth; off for archival
    - Descreen / moire removal — alters actual pixel values
    - Spot-heal, content-aware fill, red-eye equivalent for blemishes
    - Auto background removal, auto crop, auto straighten, perspective fix

  Geometry / framing
    - Auto-crop, auto-rotate, auto-keystone — even a 0.2° "fix" rewrites pixels
    - Resolution auto-detection — set DPI explicitly (e.g., 600 ppi for prints,
      1200 ppi for pencil backs; capture once at the higher value, downsample
      in the derivative)

  Format / depth
    - Auto file-format choice (anything that picks JPEG by default)
    - Auto bit-depth (force 16-bit/channel for color masters, 16-bit gray for
      raking B&W; never 8-bit on the master)

2. Output controls so later adjustments are separate derivatives

  a. Capture the master ONCE, in lossless, maximum-fidelity form
     - TIFF (uncompressed or LZW), 16-bit/channel, explicit color space
       (embed scanner/IT8 profile; convert later in a derivative, never at
       capture). The master is the raw sensor output plus its profile —
       nothing else.

  b. Generate the access copy as a sibling at save time
     - Configure the scan app's multi-output (or "scan then save copies")
       to write:
         NN_front_color.tif            (master, unaltered)
         NN_front_color_access.jpg     (derivative, may carry light edits)
     - Anything that would normally be a "save" against the scan becomes a
       second output file. The master's filename never carries an enhancement
       tag.

  c. Naming discipline — already in your convention
     - Master:   NN_front_color.tif, NN_back_raking.tif, NN_back_raking_bw.tif
     - Derivative: NN_front_color_access.jpg (or _view.jpg)
     - Adjusted variants: NN_front_color_alt1.tif, ..._alt2.tif
       These are derived FROM the master; they are not new masters, even if
       saved as TIFF. They live in the access folder, not the master folder.

  d. Folder separation (already established)
     - .../masters/   read-only after capture, contains only unaltered TIFFs
     - .../access/    derivatives only, freely editable
     - Master filenames treated as canonical and immutable; derivative
       filenames can change without touching the master index.

  e. Permissions and integrity
     - After capture + checksum (SHA-256 in your manifest), mark the master
       file read-only / immutable at the filesystem level. This is the
       mechanical enforcement of the rule that "no adjustment writes to
       the original capture."
     - The P037 incident already showed the value of this: the altered
       file lived under P037_back_ALTERED_nonmaster_YYYYMMDD.tif while
       the verified master kept its canonical name and digest.

  f. Sidecar metadata vs. baked-in edits
     - Any descriptive or provenance metadata can live in a sidecar (XMP /
       a manifest row) without touching master pixels.
     - Any tonal/color/geometry edit is a pixel change and therefore belongs
       in a derivative file, not in the sidecar.

  g. Re-derivation, not re-capture
     - If a future access need calls for a different crop, sharpening level,
       or color conversion, produce a new _alt file from the master. Do not
       "re-save" the master with new settings, and do not re-scan the
       original unless the master itself is suspect.

Short form of the rule: disable every correction that changes pixel values from what the sensor recorded; capture once at max bit-depth into a write-protected TIFF; let every adjustment — sharpening, tone, color conversion, crop — be expressed as a sibling file in the access tree, named so it can never be confused with the master and checksummed so drift is detectable.

1. Confirm spec.

2. Get the right blade.
   - OEM from the dealer, or a quality aftermarket matched to length and attachment (Bosch, Rain-X, Trico, Anco).
   - PNW rain tends to favor a beam or hybrid blade over a traditional framed one.
3. Prepare.
   - Park level, ignition off.
   - Lay a folded towel across the windshield at the base of the wiper arm — protects the glass if the arm snaps back.
   - Lift the arm away from the windshield. Grip the arm, not the blade.
4. Remove the old blade.
   - Most modern fittings: depress the small release tab where blade meets arm hook, then slide the blade downward (away from the arm) to unhook.
   - Pin/button styles: rotate the blade perpendicular to the arm and slide off the pin, or press the side release.

5. Fit the new blade.
   - Match orientation: the rubber wiping edge should curve the same way as the old one (curves to match the windshield).
   - Slide the connector up into the arm hook until it clicks.
   - Tug gently downward to confirm lock.
   - Lower the arm back onto the glass gently.

  - Even contact across the entire sweep.
  - No exposed metal, blade not crooked or tilted in the arm.
  - Blade stays seated when the arm cycles — no lift-off.
- Drive test: low speed on a wet road (spray water if needed) — confirm clean sweep; then normal driving speed — confirm no lift, hop, or noise.

- Until the new blade is fitted and the checks above pass.
- If the new blade streaks, chatters, or leaves any unwiped arc — re-seat or replace the part.
- In freezing rain or icy conditions. Never run wipers on a dry frozen windshield: the blade can tear, the arm can be damaged, and the motor can stall/burn out. De-ice and clear ice manually first.

White bean, kale & tomato stew with toasted bread — one pot, ~25 min, 2 dinner + 1 lunch

Ingredients (approximate)
- 2 Tbsp olive oil, plus more for bread
- 1/2 medium onion, diced (~3/4 cup)
- 3-4 garlic cloves, minced (reserve 1 for bread)
- 3/4-1 tsp dried rosemary
- 1 (14 oz) can diced tomatoes, with juice
- 2 (15 oz) cans white beans — drain one, keep one with its liquid (or rinse both for cleaner flavor)
- ~2.5 cups vegetable broth
- 1 small bunch kale, stems stripped, chopped (~3-4 cups packed)
- 1 lemon — zest + 1 Tbsp juice
- 4 slices sturdy bread
- Salt, pepper

Sequence
- 0:00  Prep: dice onion, mince garlic, chop kale, open cans, zest and juice lemon.
- 0:05  Pot over medium heat: 2 Tbsp oil + onion + pinch salt. Cook 3-4 min until translucent.
- 0:09  Add garlic + rosemary, stir 30 sec.
- 0:10  Add tomatoes (with juice), both cans of beans, 2.5 cups broth, several grinds pepper. Bring to a simmer.
- 0:15  Start toast: brush or drizzle bread with oil, rub with the reserved halved garlic clove, sprinkle of salt. Into a 400°F oven or toaster oven on a small tray.
- 0:18  Stir kale into the stew. Simmer gently, uncovered, ~5 min until kale wilts and stew thickens slightly.
- 0:23  Pull toast (golden, ~5-7 min). Off heat, stir lemon zest + 1 Tbsp juice into the stew; taste for salt.
- 0:25  Plate: toast in bowls (or alongside), ladle stew over. Black pepper on top.

Lunch portion — safe cooling
- Ladle ~1/3 of the stew into a wide, shallow container (no bread — pack bread separately so it stays crisp).
- Ice-water bath: set the container in a sink or bowl of cold water with a handful of ice for 10-15 min, stirring once. This drops it from ~180°F to near room temp quickly.
- Lid, then refrigerate within 2 hours of cooking. Eat within 3-4 days. Reheat to a steady simmer (~165°F) and toast fresh bread for the lunch.

Notes
- One-pot optional: skip the oven and float the oiled, garlic-rubbed bread on top of the stew for the last 3-4 min — softer, ribollita-style, truly single vessel.
- If the stew loosens on standing, simmer a couple minutes when reheating; a splash of broth brings it back.
- Cleanup: one pot, cutting board, knife, can opener, small sheet for toast, ladle.

The first drawing mistake is that you've drawn three closed silhouettes instead of one continuous outline. The eye groups by enclosed shape — three closed shapes will always read as three objects on the paper, regardless of how careful the proportions or values are.

A key is functionally three parts but visually one silhouette. The bow has to flow into the shoulder of the shaft, and the shaft has to flow into the shoulder of the bit. If those junctions are hard corners or visible seams, the eye reads the key as three assembled pieces — handle, stick, comb — rather than one object. Two specific spots to check:

  - The bow-to-shaft junction. A real brass key has a smooth curve there, not an L. If yours reads as a circle stuck onto a rod, that junction is the culprit.
  - The teeth. If the bit looks like a rectangle with little triangular notches glued to its top edge, the teeth are reading as a separate zigzag symbol sitting on a separate bar symbol. The teeth have to be part of the bit's actual profile — the whole edge, top and bottom, drawn as one outline.

Fix before any paint goes further:

  1. Redraw the entire key as one unbroken contour. Lighten or lift the internal boundaries between bow, shaft, and bit so only the outer silhouette remains.
  2. Establish one light direction across the whole object before any value work, so the highlights agree everywhere.
  3. When you do lay in cast shadow, lay it as one continuous shape under the whole key, not three pools under each part. Three cast shadows reinforce the three-object reading as hard as three silhouettes do.

The contour is the foundation. Get one silhouette and one light source down first, and the parts will stop reading as separate symbols.
