Compact sequence, dry first wash → transparent cool glaze:

TEST SWATCH (60 sec)
  Two puddles on the palette: cool glaze at working strength (tea-strength + a half-step more pigment for value, not chroma), and a thinner sister puddle for the feather. On a scrap, lay a 1 cm strip of each beside a dry swatch of the existing shadow mass. Confirm the working glaze reads ~1 value step darker than the dry wash with no chroma jump. If it looks pasted, dilute in the working puddle — do not add orange, do not scrub.

PLANNED STOPPING EDGE
  Mark the stopping line ~3–5 mm short of the warm wood edge. The glaze lives entirely inside the cool shadow mass. The reserved strip stays untouched — that gap is the value separation doing the work.

CONTROLLED MOISTURE
  Loaded round brush, damp (not wet). One pass only. Stroke from the interior of the shadow mass outward toward the warm edge. Within the last ~1 cm, lift pressure; end in clear water with a clean dry-brush fade so pigment thins to nothing at the planned stop. Do not cross the stop. Do not re-enter the feather zone. No scrubbing.

FULL DRY
  Flat, room air, no hairdryer, no tilt. Walk away for 10+ min. When dry, inspect the feather zone — it should read as a natural shadow falloff, not a line.

READ
  Warm wood edge holds its original value. Cool shadow sits ~1 step darker. Warmth survives through separation, not saturation.

If a faint tide line appears, the stop was crossed or the brush ended too wet. Next pass: lift earlier, end drier. If the cool reads too heavy, the mix is over-loaded — weaken the working puddle, do not glaze harder to "fix" it.

LOST-AND-FOUND EDGE — COMPACT SEQUENCE

Assumption: cool glaze is already mixed (your standard cool: ultramarine + a touch of burnt sienna, or whatever sits one value step darker than the ceramic). Ceramic edge is dry, pale, and will not be touched by the rewetting or the glaze pass.

  1. VALUE TEST (do this FIRST on a scrap of the same paper)
     - Two puddles on the palette:
         A = tea-strength of the cool mix
         B = A + roughly 20% more pigment, no extra water
     - Lay a 1 cm strip of A and a 1 cm strip of B BESIDE (not over) a dried swatch of the ceramic color.
     - Dry flat 10 min. Pick the puddle that sits ONE value step darker than the ceramic without warming or muddying it. If B shifts hue toward the ceramic or makes the swatch look orange-tinted, use A. Park the unused puddle.

  2. MAP THE EDGE (mental or on a scrap)
     - Mark which stretch LOSES into shadow and which stays CRISP.
     - Lost stretch = section facing the deepest shadow mass, or where the form turns away from light.
     - Crisp stretch = section catching the strongest light, or marking a hard contour break (corner, rim, plane change).

  3. LOST EDGE — rewet BESIDE, never OVER
     - Damp round brush, water only, well squeezed (moist, not dripping).
     - Touch the paper on the SHADOW SIDE of the edge in a 5–8 mm strip running parallel to the ceramic contour.
     - Stop AT the edge. Do not cross onto the ceramic.
     - Visible cue: a faint satin sheen on the shadow side; no puddle, no meniscus against the edge.

  4. LOST EDGE — drop the glaze
     - Loaded round with the chosen test strength, single dip.
     - One pass from the shadow interior outward, terminating inside the damp strip.
     - In the last ~5 mm, lift pressure and finish in clear water so pigment feathers to nothing.
     - The ceramic edge should soften and bleed gently into the cool as the strip dries. No hard contour line where the edge used to be.

  5. CRISP EDGE — fully dry paper, stop short
     - Same glaze, same strength, but onto BONE-DRY paper on the shadow side.
     - Stop 3–4 mm short of the ceramic edge with one confident stroke.
     - Do not rewet anywhere near this section. No softening pass. The 3–4 mm of untouched dry paper between the glaze and the ceramic is what keeps the edge reading as a clean break.

  6. DRY FLAT, FULL CYCLE
     - 10–15 min minimum, longer if the room is cool or humid.
     - Edges shift as water leaves — what looks lost at 3 min can firm up by 12 min. Judge only after the sheet is fully dry to the touch and visually matte.

VERIFY (post-dry, before any second pass)
     - Lost section: no visible contour where the edge was; cool shadow sits ~1 step darker than the ceramic; no orange creep into the glaze.
     - Crisp section: ceramic edge still reads sharp against the cool.
     - Warm side untouched: no tide line on the ceramic, no lifted fiber, no halo.
     - If a tide line sits ON the ceramic edge → you crossed it. Dampen a brush and lift ONLY on the warm side, dry, then redo just that stretch with a narrower rewet strip beside the edge.
     - If the lost edge still reads hard → rewet strip was too narrow or too far past its prime when the glaze hit. Next pass: widen the strip to 8–10 mm and apply within 10–15 sec of rewetting.
     - If the cool reads muddy against the ceramic → value test failed; the chosen puddle is too heavy or too warm. Strip with clean water on the shadow side only, dry, and re-do with the lighter (A) puddle.

Two operational notes that prevent the most common failures here:
  - Do ALL the rewetting on the shadow side. The moment rewetting crosses the ceramic edge, you are lifting warm pigment into the cool zone and a tide line becomes almost certain.
  - Do the lost stretch FIRST, let it dry fully, then do the crisp stretch. Reversing the order risks rewetting near the crisp section and softening the very edge you wanted to keep.

The visible settling is yellow ochre particles dropping into the cold-press valleys as the wash dries. Three non-invasive levers — no scrubbing, lifting, or added orange:

  Pigment ratio — keep tea-strength, lighten with water only. A thinner film leaves less excess to settle into the tooth. Do NOT reach for burnt sienna to lighten the value; that pushes toward orange.

  Brush load — damp, fully-tipped brush. Enough pigment to cover the passage in ONE uninterrupted stroke. A return pass re-deposits pigment into the valleys you're trying to keep quiet.

  Board angle — ~10–12° tilt so the wash migrates toward a waste edge. Gravity pulls excess off the high tooth before it pools. Direction: away from the focal cup, toward a clean edge or paper towel.

Test (scrap cold-press, same brush, four swatches):

  A — tea-strength ochre, horizontal, full load (your current baseline)
  B — tea-strength + ~20% water, horizontal, full load
  C — tea-strength, ~12° tilt pulling wash down, full load
  D — tea-strength + ~10% water, ~12° tilt, slightly damp brush

  Mix fresh per swatch. One pass top to bottom. Bone-dry flat before reading.

  Pick the swatch where ochre sits as a quiet film, with no visible granulation in the valleys. B or D usually wins; C wins when pooling was the cause.

Apply (single pass on the painting):

  1. Mix the winning ratio in a clean well; reserve enough for one uninterrupted stroke.
  2. Pre-dampen the brush, shake out, fully load — no drip.
  3. Tilt the board ~10–12° away from the focal cup, toward a clean edge or paper towel.
  4. One pass, top of passage to waste edge. Do not return to fill gaps; leave them.
  5. Hold the tilt ~30–45s until the surface sheen goes matte; then return to horizontal.
  6. Bone-dry before judging — ~20–30 min, no touching.

Stop condition:

  If the dried passage still shows ochre in the tooth, dilute ~10% more water and re-test on scrap — NOT on the painting. Do not re-wet, do not lift, do not add pigment. The cure for settling is thinner wash + correct angle, never more pigment.

The line is sitting in the safest possible spot: faint, in a margin, on a fully dry wash, and outside any focal edge. That gives you three real options and a clear best one.

Leave it, if this is headed for a mat. A pale graphite mark well outside the image opening disappears under an 8x10 mat and never returns. That is the move most working watercolorists make on construction lines that earned their keep during the painting. Nothing to do.

Lightly lift it, if this is a study you'll look at unframed. A kneaded eraser, dabbed (not rubbed) and rolled straight up off the paper, will take most of a faint line off dry watercolor paper without scuffing the tooth. The reason to dab rather than stroke: a stroke on cold-press grabs the surface fibers and leaves a smoother "ghost" patch where any future wash would sit and read differently. Because your line is light, one or two passes may be all it takes; stop the moment it's gone to the eye. A trace under the mat is better than a rubbed spot.

Don't wet it. A damp swab or sponge will smear graphite into the surrounding pale wash and can lift the wash itself, especially at the edge of a transparent area. Don't glaze over it either — that just trades a graphite mark for a tonal change in the margin you said you wanted to keep pale.

If you do erase: work on a clean hard surface (a board or a piece of glass), tilt the sheet so the line catches the light, and stop the instant it's invisible at reading distance. If you want one more layer of caution, sacrifice a small scrap from the offcut first — same paper, same line weight — and erase that before touching the painting.

Given how carefully you've held off so far, my guess is "leave it" was already the lean. It is.

Compact sequence, in order. No step runs without the one before it passing.

1. DECIDE FIRST — do not touch the sheet yet.
   - Hold the sheet under low-angle raking light and tilt slowly.
   - View at normal reading distance, then squint.
   - If the line reads as part of the passage, or only shows under raking light → leave it. Done. Set the sheet face-up on a clean blotter and stop.
   - If the line pulls the eye at conversation distance → proceed to step 2.

2. LOW-PRESSURE TEST — one site, one contact.
   - Tool: a clean rubber pickup (or a fingertip wrapped in a dry tissue). Nothing else.
   - Press to the thinnest tip of the line for about 1 second. Lift straight up. No drag, no roll, no scrub, no twist.
   - Inspect the tool for pigment transfer and the test site against an untouched area for any change.

3. STOP NOW if any of the following is true — do not proceed to removal:
   - Pigment lifts onto the tool.
   - The cold-press tooth scuffs, pills, fluffs, or gains a sheen.
   - Fibers rise anywhere on the test site.
   - The line does not yield to light pressure.
   - The test site looks or feels different from the surrounding paper.

4. ONLY if the test site is fully clean and visually unchanged → one short roll parallel to the paper, edge of the line toward its center. Wipe the tool on a tissue between passes. Stop the moment a pass feels different from the first.

5. STOP PERMANENTLY (set the sheet aside, face-up on a clean blotter) at the first sign of:
   - Rising resistance.
   - Any surface disturbance.
   - Smearing rather than lifting.
   - Color spreading into the surrounding wash.

6. DO NOT, under any of the above stops: re-press harder, add water, add heat, use a blade, plastic card, fingernail, or eraser, or make a second attempt the same day.

Pass criteria for the whole sequence: cotton surface visually and tactilely unchanged, no pigment on the tool after the final pass, no shift in the surrounding yellow ochre. If even one fails, the line stays.

What you're describing — soreness localized to the injection site and nothing else — is exactly the expected post-flu-vaccine picture. Home monitoring is appropriate. The soreness usually eases over 24–72 hours.

WHAT'S NORMAL OVER THE NEXT 1–3 DAYS
- Continued mild soreness or tenderness at the injection site
- Low-grade achiness or mild fatigue
- Small lump or faint redness at the site
- All of this should be gradually improving, not worsening

COMFORT / SELF-CARE
- Cool compress on the arm for 10–15 minutes at a time, as needed
- Keep using the arm normally — gentle movement helps; skip heavy lifting with that arm for a day
- OTC pain relief if you want it: acetaminophen 500–1000 mg every 6 hours, or ibuprofen 400 mg every 6 hours with food (skip either if you have a reason to avoid it)
- Stay hydrated

CALL YOUR PRIMARY CARE CLINIC (NON-URGENT) IF
- Redness or swelling at the site expands past roughly 2 inches across, or is clearly worse after 24–48 hours
- Fever above ~101°F that persists
- Localized rash or hives at the site
- Soreness still present and not improving at 72 hours
- Anything else that just feels off enough to want a clinician's eye

SEEK URGENT OR EMERGENCY CARE IF
- Swelling of the face, lips, or tongue
- Throat tightness, hoarseness, or any difficulty breathing or swallowing
- Widespread hives or rash
- Dizziness, fainting, or rapid heartbeat
- High fever (>102°F / 39°C) with chills
- Severe or rapidly worsening pain, swelling, or redness at the injection site
- Any symptom that feels significantly out of proportion or unlike your normal self

A small reassurance on timing: true allergic or anaphylactic reactions almost always show up within the first 30 minutes to a few hours, not the next morning. What you've got fits the common, expected local reaction, not an allergy. You're fine to just keep an eye on it, and it's reasonable to mention it at your next routine visit so it's noted in your record.

Self-care for isolated mild arm soreness:

- Rest the arm; avoid the specific motion that triggered it for the rest of the day
- Ice 15-20 min on / 40 min off during the first 24-48 hours if there's any acute tenderness
- Keep it gently moving through a pain-free range — don't fully immobilize a muscle that's just sore
- Over-the-counter pain reliever with food (ibuprofen/naproxen if you tolerate NSAIDs; acetaminophen otherwise)
- Hydrate
- After 48 hours, switch to gentle warmth if it feels more like tightness than acute strain
- Light stretching and gradual return to normal use as it settles

Seek prompt medical attention (urgent care / ER) for:

- Severe pain, pain at rest, or pain that wakes you from sleep
- Visible deformity, significant swelling, or bruising after a specific injury
- Audible pop or snap, or sudden inability to use the arm
- Numbness, tingling, or weakness in the hand or fingers
- Cold, pale, or bluish fingers (circulation concern)
- Fever or feeling systemically unwell alongside the arm symptoms
- Pain that steadily worsens over hours rather than improving

Schedule a non-urgent clinic visit if:

- Soreness hasn't improved in 5-7 days
- Pain keeps recurring with normal everyday use
- New loss of strength or range of motion
- Persistent joint swelling or morning stiffness
- Any symptom that's concerning but not dramatic

STREAK DIAGNOSTIC — pale ultramarine + burnt sienna, dry strip, second pass

Why the second pass streaks on a dry strip:
  - brush wetness differs from the first pass, so the dried edge re-wets unevenly
  - pigment in the dried film lifts back into the new bead and lays a tide line at the join
  - any drift in board angle or load mid-pass shifts flow speed and streaks

TEST SEQUENCE (~8 min, scrap of the same 140 lb cold-press)
  1. Mix in a flat well (5x7 or larger, not a dimple). Stir 6+ rotations until the wash reads even — weak-tea strength, no granules. Pre-mix roughly 2x what you think you need; you cannot remix mid-pass and keep the ratio.
  2. Brush-load check: #10 or #12 round, load fully to the ferrule, tap once on the rim. One stroke on scrap should lay an unbroken film — no dry-brush skip, no tail puddle.
  3. Board-angle check: tilt to ~15°. The wash should drift down the slope at a steady walking pace, not race or stall. Mark the angle on the board edge with tape so it cannot drift.

APPLICATION SEQUENCE (the wall passage)
  1. Pre-mix the full passage volume in one go. Stir again right before loading — settled pigment is the first source of streaks.
  2. Load fully to the ferrule, tap once. Brush state is just-wet, never dry.
  3. Tilt board to ~15° (toward you if you lead with the brush, away if you pull).
  4. Commit the path before touching paper: lay the full height of the wall in one continuous stroke, brush-width wide, no pause, no lift. Do not stop to reload — if you run short, the mix was too thin, not the technique.
  5. End the pass by pulling the bead off the bottom edge with the brush tip. Do not dab back into the drying film.

RULES FOR THIS PASSAGE
  - One direction of motion across the area. No doubling back over drying edges.
  - Board angle stays constant for the full pass. Moving the board mid-stroke changes flow speed and lays a tide line.
  - Resist the second pass. The streak lives at the join, not in the mix. Adding burnt sienna to fix it only deepens orange — exactly what we are avoiding.
  - If the wash runs short: stop, remix at the same ratio, fresh sheet or fresh area. Do not return with the same brush state.
  - No scrubbing, no lifting, no glazing over a dried first pass. Reinterpret the mark or let it dry fully.

If a streak still shows after one continuous pass, the cause is almost always mix settling (re-stir) or board drift (re-mark the angle) — not the pigment ratio.

Here is a compact plan that fits the four October Thursdays without adding any shared-time commitment or touching your Monday. One weekend cook session, two recipes, eight single-serving containers — you eat from the freezer on 10/7, 10/14, 10/21, 10/28 and Sam walks in at 11 to a quiet kitchen.

THE TWO RECIPES

1) Tomato-braised chicken thighs (4 portions)
- 6 bone-in skinless chicken thighs (~2.5 lb)
- 1 onion diced, 4 garlic cloves minced
- 1 can (28 oz) crushed tomatoes
- 1 jar (12 oz) roasted red peppers, drained and chopped
- 1 tsp dried oregano, salt, pepper, olive oil, pinch red pepper flakes if you like
- Brown chicken in a Dutch oven, set aside. Soften onion and garlic in a little oil, add tomatoes, peppers, oregano, salt. Return chicken, partially submerge, cover and simmer 45 min on low (or 350F oven for 50 min). Cool, then portion one thigh + ~3/4 cup sauce into each of 4 freezer containers.

2) Lentil-sausage soup (4 portions)
- 1 lb Italian sausage, casings removed
- 1 onion, 2 carrots, 3 garlic cloves — all diced
- 1 cup dried green or brown lentils, rinsed
- 4 cups chicken broth, 1 can (14 oz) diced tomatoes
- 1 bay leaf, 1 tsp dried thyme, salt, pepper
- Brown sausage in a soup pot, breaking it up. Add veg, cook 5 min. Add lentils, broth, tomatoes, herbs. Simmer 35-40 min until lentils are tender. Cool, portion ~2 cups into each of 4 freezer containers.

BATCH SESSION (one weekend block, ~2 hours total)

Run the chicken braise in the oven while the soup simmers on the stove. Two pots, one timer, no special equipment.

- Pick a weekend slot that doesn't compete with watercolor. Saturday afternoon or Sunday morning both work.
- 30 min prep and chopping
- 60-90 min hands-off simmering (you can sketch while the second pot simmers)
- 30 min cooling, 15 min portioning

FREEZING (ordinary)

- Use 2-cup straight-sided glass containers or 16-24 oz deli containers with snap lids. Leave 1/2 inch headspace — both expand slightly when frozen.
- Cool to room temp, then refrigerate uncovered 1-2 hours before lidding and freezing. Skipping the uncovered chill traps steam and causes ice crystals.
- Label: contents + date.
- Both hold 3 months easily at 0F. You'll finish by mid-November.

REHEATING (ordinary)

From frozen:
- Loosen lid, microwave at 50% power for 2-3 min to thaw the center, then full power 3-4 min, stirring halfway. Rest 1 min.

From fridge (thaw overnight):
- Microwave covered 3-4 min on high, stir halfway.

The soup is best finished on the stovetop over medium-low heat for 5-7 min if you have time — better texture than microwave alone.

LIGHT SIDES (minimal)

- Microwave brown rice pouches (90 sec) — pantry stable
- Bagged arugula or pre-washed greens with olive oil and lemon
- Small crusty loaf in the freezer for soup nights — slice and toast from frozen
- A wedge of parmesan to grate over both — lasts weeks

KEEP IT QUIET

- Plate, eat, Kibo on the floor. No phone past the reheating timer.
- Sam lands at 11 to a clean kitchen and a quiet house — that is the whole point.
- If debriefing comes up at all, save it for Saturday morning coffee, not the close-of-shift walk-in.

SHOPPING LIST (one trip)

Proteins: 2.5 lb bone-in skinless chicken thighs; 1 lb Italian sausage
Pantry: crushed tomatoes 28 oz; roasted red peppers 12 oz; diced tomatoes 14 oz; chicken broth 32 oz; 1 cup dried lentils
Produce: 2 onions, 1 head garlic, carrots, 1 lemon, bagged greens
Dry: dried oregano, dried thyme, bay leaves, red pepper flakes, olive oil, salt, pepper
Containers: 8 freezer-safe 2-cup if you don't have them

Estimated total $30-40 depending on what's already in the pantry.

Nothing here needs a calendar entry, nothing touches Monday, and there is no implied Sam-side commitment. If you want, I can also draft a one-line note for yourself (a sticky on the freezer door) listing which container goes on which Thursday so you don't have to think about it that night.

Good that the paint itself is fine — and you've already got exactly what's needed to fix the problem permanently. Decant it into the half pan; that's the clean answer to a cracked tube cap.

1. Wipe the threads clean first. Any paint residue at the split will glue the broken cap on badly the next time you close it. A dry corner of a paper towel is enough.
2. Squeeze from the bottom up, rolling the tube like toothpaste, into the half pan. Leave a small headspace so the pan lid can close without smearing the cake.
3. If paint is stuck near the split, snip the tube about an inch above the damage and squeeze out the last bit.
4. Let the pan dry open for several hours — overnight is safest — before putting it back in the tin. A closed-while-wet pan stays gummy and can grow mildew.
5. Label the pan: "Ultramarine" plus today's date (10/10/27). Discard the empty tube.
6. From here on, just refresh the pan with a ribbon squeezed from a fresh tube whenever it gets low.

One small benefit: a pan you loaded yourself is usually a touch creamier than a factory pan, since you've packed it the way you like. Cheap insurance against the next cap failure.

Short, preservation-conscious sequence — assumes the cracked mixing tray is already protected (wax paper or a plastic bag under it, per your earlier rule).

1. Prep clean. Dry hands, a clean fingertip or small wooden tool, a piece of tape or sticker for the label, and a small zip bag or foil square ready. Lay the tin on a protected surface.

2. Label the destination pan first. Write the color on tape and stick it to the pan's rim or lid BEFORE any paint touches the pan — so you're never handling a wet, labeled pan.

3. Open the tube away from the split. Support the tube body. If the cap is already split, ease it back without squeezing; let any built-up pressure release on its own. Do NOT press near the split to "burp" it.

4. Express a small amount with pressure AWAY from the split. Roll the tube from the crimped end forward, fingers only on intact wall. A pea- to kidney-sized dollop is plenty for a pan.

5. Deposit, don't smear. Touch the dollop into the pan and nudge it flat with a clean tool or clean fingertip — never your painting brush, and never fingers that have touched other pans.

6. No water. Leave it as a stiff dollop; it rewets cleanly from a wet brush later. Water in the tube invites mold and worsens the split seam.

7. Cap and contain the damaged tube. Wipe the threads and split area with a dry microfiber (no solvent), fold the split cap flat if you can, and slip the tube into the small bag or foil so any future seepage stays isolated from the rest of the tin.

8. Air-dry the new pan before closing the tin lid — trapped moisture under a closed lid is the bigger long-term risk to your other pans.

Quick "stop and reassess" triggers during the sequence: split runs up the tube body under gentle pressure, paint smells off, or you see grit in the dollop — bag the whole tube, don't transfer, and decide whether the color is worth a fresh tube.

The draft sentence has two clauses. The first is fine. The second is not.

Compliant clause
"Expansion Assist generated four expansions from 16 exposures."
Matches the evidence: 16 actual exposures, all with complete 45-day windows; six help-or-options requests; four expansions; no randomized control; no exposed account with active Customer Success adoption or renewal work at exposure. Descriptive, behavior-based, state-specific — consistent with the standing lane.

Non-compliant clause
"…supporting four forecastable expansions per comparable exposure cycle."
"Forecastable … per comparable exposure cycle" is a forward projection. It fails the standing rule on three grounds:

1. Forecast credit. The lane is explicitly outside pipeline, revenue, and forecast. No RCT means the observed rate cannot be promoted to a forecastable rate.
2. State-specificity. The rate is conditional on which accounts cross the product-visible usage ceiling within the preceding 14 days. "A comparable exposure cycle" without restating that population is not a comparable cycle.
3. Causal bridge. The word "supporting" connects a descriptive past count to a forward claim — that is the forecast bridge the standing rule prohibits.

Compliant replacement options (pick one, drop into the draft in place of the second clause)

A. Tighter (preferred):
"…the four-expansion rate is a descriptive observation from a bounded, no-randomized-control cohort and is not a forecastable rate for future cycles; it carries no forecast credit."

B. Same shape, shorter:
"…the four expansions are descriptive observations and do not establish a forecastable rate per exposure cycle."

C. If you want to keep the "comparable" framing but bound it:
"…within a cohort of comparable state (product-visible usage ceiling crossed in the prior 14 days, no active Customer Success adoption or renewal work), the four expansions are descriptive only and not a forecastable rate for future cycles."

Note that option C is the only form that preserves any "comparable" language, and it still has to end with the no-forecast credit clause to stay compliant.

Why the forecast claim is unsupported

A forecast claim treating the four expansions as a lift signal fails on every evidentiary axis the Expansion Assist lane is built on:

1. No randomized control. The 18 exposures were a bounded cohort under standing current‑state criteria, not a randomized treatment vs. holdback. Four expansions out of 18 is a descriptive concentration, not a causal rate — there is nothing to anchor a conversion assumption against.

2. The denominator is narrow and state‑specific. Eligibility required a recently crossed product‑visible usage ceiling (14‑day rule for the second cohort) and explicitly suppressed any account with active Customer Success adoption or renewal work in flight. That selection logic produces a population that cannot be projected onto the broader retained‑mid base without an unjustified re‑weighting.

3. The help/options outcome is commingled. Six of the 18 exposures produced a help‑or‑options request — not an expansion. Treating expansions as the only outcome overstates the commercial signal and ignores that several of those requests were resolved as support rather than as expansion.

4. The expansions that did happen have a documented non‑prompt attribution path. At least one expansion was attributed to a separate Customer Success options review, not to the prompt. That breaks the assumed one‑to‑one between exposure and expansion and rules out any clean per‑exposure lift.

5. The lane is contractually outside forecast. Per the standing rule, Expansion Assist remains outside pipeline, revenue commitments, and forecast credit — a forecast claim is not a softer version of those, it is one of them.

6. Window maturity and small‑N variance. With 18 exposures and four expansions, a single re‑attribution or one additional expansion in a still‑maturing window meaningfully shifts any ratio. Forecast inputs need stable, audited denominators; this lane does not yet meet that bar.

"Expansion Assist — second bounded Q4 cohort plus first pilot close: 18 actual exposures across the closed complete 45‑day windows (Dec 1, 2025 – Jan 30, 2026), six help‑or‑options requests and four expansions observed. All included exposures met the standing current‑state criteria; no included account had active Customer Success adoption or renewal work at exposure. At least one expansion was attributed to a separate Customer Success options review, not to the prompt. There was no randomized control; these counts are interim descriptive operational observations only and do not establish causal lift, conversion rate, pipeline signal, revenue credit, or forecast credit. The lane remains narrow, behavior‑based, state‑specific, and outside pipeline, revenue commitments, and forecast treatment."

That preserves the four expansions on the record, names what they are and are not, and refuses the forecast framing without softening what was actually seen.

Price

Net read
- If you can tolerate roughly 7-10 business days without any glasses and you don't care about having a spare, Option 1 is the cheaper path with no functional loss beyond that gap.
- If the gap without glasses is a problem, or if you want a true backup after delivery, Option 2 is the only one of the two that solves it — and it does so for $68 plus whatever you decide the spare is worth to you.

Confirmed — rejecting the 8.25 × 10.25 mat opening is the right conservative call. The centered opening covers the top of the painted window mullion, and that mullion is structurally part of the image (it's the offset window the title names). Your own pre-cut rule says any important painted edge obscured means reject the mat; that's exactly the case here. The test you just ran is the test that rule exists to catch, and the sheet is still intact and unmounted, which is the correct state for that outcome.

Why not trim the intact sheet:

  - Trimming is irreversible. The original paper edge isn't decorative — it protects the painted surface from abrasion, environmental exposure, and direct contact with the mat board or glazing.
  - Trimming doesn't actually fix the problem. The opening itself is the wrong size; cutting paper away from the edges won't recover a mullion the window is covering. To clear it by trimming alone, you'd eventually cut into the image.
  - The full sheet preserves your future options (a larger opening, a float mount, a different frame). A trimmed sheet forecloses them, and you have no sale, exhibition, or display deadline forcing a decision now.

Why not mount it anyway:

  - Mounting puts the mat on top of the sheet. Even with reversible conservation corners, the mullion is still hidden under the mat board — you've made the obscuration permanent in practice, just undoable in principle.
  - You'd be paying the time and material cost of a mount for an opening you've already identified as wrong, and creating rework (backing, corners, glazing all come off) if you ever re-frame correctly.
  - Reversibility only buys you something when the underlying decision is the right one. Here the decision is the wrong opening, so reversibility doesn't save you.

The sheet stays intact and unmounted. The next move is a different opening that clears the mullion, or a float mount that shows the full sheet — both work without touching the paper as it is.

For a transparent glass passage with one narrow paper-white reflection — no masking, no lift, no opaque — the sequence is built around controlling the bead on both sides so the strip reads as natural light, not a drawn line.

1. Mark lightly. One H-grade pencil tick at each end of the strip only. Do not run a continuous line — the strip is defined by the wash feathering toward it, not by graphite.

2. Mix one transparent glaze. Single tea-strength pool (the cool ultramarine/burnt sienna from the glass study, diluted). Both sides of the strip use the same mix at the same strength so the values mirror.

3. Tilt the board 15–20° toward you. Predictable bead on both sides.

4. Paint both sides in the same session, same direction (top-to-bottom). Bead trails downward on each side. Stroke approach:
   - Loaded brush, consistent wetness.
   - In the last 3–5 mm before the strip, lift pressure so the wash thins to almost-clear.
   - Stop the brush at — do not cross — the strip. Never touch the strip with a wet brush. The strip stays dry because nothing wet ever reaches it.

5. Dry flat, no fan, no heat. Bone-dry = back of sheet has no coolness, surface has lost its sheen. 15–25 min on 140 lb cold-press; longer in humidity.

6. Verify before any next glaze:
   - Raking light: hold the sheet at a low angle. A "wall" of pigment on either side of the strip = mechanically outlined — feather earlier next pass.
   - Value: the strip should match untouched paper. If it looks brighter than the paper, the surrounding wash is too pale — strengthen, don't glaze into the strip.
   - Transparency: paper tooth must still read through the wash right next to the strip. Milky/opaque there = wash too heavy; dilute next mix.

7. Stop conditions (cannot proceed without breaking a rule):
   - Pigment drifts into the strip during a pass → let it dry bone-dry, do not lift. Re-strengthen judgement on the next pass; if it's now cooler/duller than the surrounding wash, accept and adjust adjacent passes.
   - Bead pools at the strip edge → let dry, thin the mix next pass, do not wick wet.
   - Strip begins to read as a hard bright line in raking light → next glaze feathers earlier on both sides; do not attempt a corrective glaze on the strip itself.

The strip survives because every action that touches the wash stops short of it, and every check is done with the sheet dry and by eye, not by intervention.

Clarification — pause threshold and minute definition

The pause threshold in the pilot stop/pause rules reads "after at least 10 admissions, pause if more than 10% of admitted workspaces exceed 90 account-level support minutes." For clarity:

Setup (1 min)
- Confirm fully dry: back-of-hand test on a non-painted margin, never on the face
- Gather: same round brush, two water cups, paper towel, validated cool mix, a small scrap of the same paper

Test swatch (5–8 min)
- Lay the cool mix at planned strength on the scrap, beside a dry band the same value as the pale passage
- Leave one end of the stroke sharp (mimics the structural edge); on the other end, single damp-brush pass outward, lifting pressure in the last ~1 cm, finishing in clear water
- Dry flat, untouched, 10 min
- Read after dry: feathered end steps down ~1 value into the pale passage with no tide line; sharp end stays crisp. If either fails, adjust mix or timing on a second swatch before touching the study

Pre-pass on the study (1 min)
- Mark a stopping line 3–5 mm short of the crisp edge — a reserve, not a guideline; pigment never crosses it
- Confirm the softening side faces the pale passage; the crisp edge sits opposite, so the feather stroke aims away from it

Mix and brush moisture (2 min)
- Mix cool glaze at the swatch-proven ratio — same as the swatch that read clean, not darker
- Load, tap on cup rim until the bead holds without dripping; blot once on folded paper towel so brush leaves a damp patch, not a shine, on scrap

Main pass (3–6 min, one direction only)
1. Lay the cool glaze in a single pass across the body of the shape, stopping at the reserve so the crisp edge is never contacted by pigment
2. While that edge is still mobile, take a clean damp brush (water only, blotted to the same "damp patch" moisture) and make one outward pass along the softening side — from the interior of the cool shape OUT into the pale passage
3. In the last ~1 cm, lift pressure and finish in clear water so pigment thins to a fade, not a stop
4. Do not re-enter; do not scrub; do not chase the crisp edge if the brush strays

Drying order
- If the shape is wider than one brush-width of working time, split it: glaze + feather the left half first, then the right half — never glaze full width and then feather, or the feather side sets before you reach it
- Dry flat, undisturbed, face-up, no fan, no blow — 10–15 min minimum before judging

Protecting the crisp edge
- Reserve line keeps pigment off it
- Feather stroke aims away from it
- If the brush grazes near it, leave it; do not lift, do not scrub — judge after full dry

Verify (after full dry)
- Crisp edge: unchanged value, unchanged edge quality
- Pale passage: still pale, no tide line, no orange lifted into it
- Feathered side: ~1 value step darker than the pale passage and fading continuously into it
- If any check fails, stop and reassess on the swatch before another pass — never rework the study directly

Stop conditions
- Tide line at feather → abandon pass, let dry fully, adjust mix or lift earlier on next attempt
- Pigment touched crisp edge → stop, dry, judge; no wet correction
- Feather too sharp → next attempt: dampen brush one step more, or shorten the time between glaze and feather

Time budget: ~25–30 min including the swatch.

HALLOWEEN LOW-STIMULATION PLAN — KIBO (Cherrywood, Oct 31)

Note up front: trazodone is NOT for tonight. Kibo is well, and the 50 mg / ~90 min pre-event dose is reserved for anticipated storms. Halloween doorbell noise is an environmental problem, not a medical one. This is a management plan, not a medication plan.

PRE-RUSH (target ~5:00–5:30 pm)
- Calm leashed walk, 15–20 min, quiet loop. Earlier is better than right-before-the-rush — give him time to come down before traffic starts.
- Pre-stage a candy bowl on the porch step (or just inside the storm door) with a painter's-tape sign: "TAKE ONE — HELP YOURSELF." Porch light on, porch otherwise empty. The point is no one needs to be at the door.
- If Sam is home tonight, hand door duty to him. If you're solo, the bowl-on-porch method means you don't actually have to open the door at all.

SETTLE KIBO IN HIS QUIET INTERIOR SPOT (~5:45 pm)
- Back bedroom or den, away from the front hallway. Door closed, curtains drawn, lights dim.
- Set up: familiar bed + a soft item that smells like you, fresh water within reach, a long food toy (frozen Kong, lick mat with peanut butter), background sound running (fan, white noise, or low-volume calm audio).
- Optional but useful: baby gate across the hallway doorway so he can't drift toward the front of the house.

SECURING HIM DURING DOOR OPENINGS
- Default: Kibo stays in his closed room. Do not let him trail you to the door — the hallway itself is part of the stimulus.
- If you must open the front door while he's loose in the house, tether him first with a harness + short leash anchored to a heavy piece of furniture in his room. This prevents a bolt to the front door on a knock. Never tether by collar.
- If anyone else is home, one person stays with Kibo, the other runs the door.

DURING THE RUSH (~6:00–8:00 pm peak)
- Stay in Kibo's room with him. Do not walk back and forth between door and his room — each pass keys him up.
- Glance at him every 20–30 min. Offer water; don't force.
- High-value treats if he's engaging; if he's shut down, leave him alone.
- Calming wrap only if you see real escalation (panting, pacing, drooling). Most Halloween nights at this level of preparation don't need it.

STOP CONDITIONS — END DOOR PARTICIPATION
Bring the bowl inside and shut the activity down if:
- Panting + pacing sustained more than ~20 min
- Sustained door-scratching, whining, or barking
- Refusal to drink
- Trembling or hard hiding that won't break
- Your read is "he's not settling." Trust that.

VET-CONTACT CONDITIONS
Call the vet for any of:
- Marked agitation that does not resolve within ~30 min after you've stopped the activity
- Vomiting
- Inability to stand, weakness, or sudden collapse
- Fear-based aggression that isn't his baseline (growling, snapping)
- Excess sedation (not expected tonight; listed because it's on the standing instruction set)

AFTER 8:00 pm
- Keep him in his quiet spot. Lights low, background sound running another 30–60 min.
- Bring the candy bowl inside once the rush clearly ends.
- Optional leashed potty break ~8:15–8:30 pm if he's calm and willing — short, sheltered loop, no forcing.
- Resume normal routine once he's settled. No late dinner stress, no coddling; quiet is the message.

Backup lines if conditions escalate past the stop thresholds and you're unsure: Cherrywood's regular vet, then the emergency clinic on file.

TUE 11/9 COMMUTE PREP — 42°F, dry, light N wind
Anchors: each leg ≤25 min easy, ankle clean, bike OK, no run today.

1) LAYERS (start slightly cool — you'll heat up in 5–8 min)
- Base: thin merino or synthetic long-sleeve, wicking. No cotton.
- Torso: vest or light jacket; core warmth matters more than arms.
- Legs: knickers or leg warmers — hard to remove mid-ride, so dress for the coldest leg.
- Shell: packable wind shell in the jersey pocket for the headwind leg or any downhill. Dry air means no waterproof shell — that traps sweat.
- Removable mid-ride: full-zip plus arm warmers you can peel at a light.

2) HANDS & EARS
- Hands: full-finger wind-blocking gloves; go lobster mitts if wind picks up.
- Ears: thin merino headband under helmet — covers ears, no fit compromise. Skip the beanie.
- Don't clench fists or hunch shoulders to "stay warm" — burns energy without warming the core.

3) EASY WARM-UP (first 2–3 min of each leg)
- Walk the bike out for 60 sec.
- Easy gear, cadence ~60–70 rpm, near-zero resistance for 3 min.
- No standing launches or hard accelerations off the line — cold muscles are stiffer.
- Save any climb or bridge effort for after minute 5.

- Front white + rear red lights on (steady or flash) — November drivers are glare-adapted; lights still get you seen.
- Bright outer layer or hi-vis vest; reflective ankle band or pedal reflectors add motion conspicuity.
- Clear or yellow-tint lenses: better contrast on overcast pavement than dark lenses.

- Cold feels like effort, but the fix is clothing, not cadence. Tempted to push to "warm up" → pull over and add a layer instead.
- Any headwind leg will feel slower and colder — that's wind, not a fitness problem. Hold easy gear and easy cadence.
- Effort target: RPE 4–5/10 the whole way. Breathing noticeably harder than the walk-out = over cap.
- Stop signal: uncontrollable shivering or numb fingers = under-dressed, not under-effort. Add a layer, then resume easy.

1. Admission is the action that releases held setup prompts. If we admit without verified external authority, either the prompts run on an unverified workspace (Theme 1: "Security owner never approved connector permissions") or we hold them anyway, which makes "admission" ceremonial and creates a new governed state the design doesn't carry.

2. "Finish afterward" introduces a window where the workspace is admitted but not authority-verified. That's a third state (admitted-but-uncleared) that doesn't exist in the model. It would also create reporting ambiguity: this case would look like a clean admission in funnel metrics while actually being a blocked one.

What CS should do instead — same path the closed Nov 3-8 case held and the 1/16/25 Okta case followed:

- Route to CS before admission. The account stays in the queue.
- Hold first-week setup prompts while authority is pending. The applicant is not relabeled as having failed connector auth or as finally ineligible — it's just pending external authority, which is its own state.
- Capture the owner-candidate signal (the Sales/CS pre-handoff capture I flagged when we named Theme 1): name, role, expected return window, what they need to do. So when they reappear we don't relitigate.
- When an available owner confirms they can perform the owner-level permission or network-allowlist step, CS verifies, records the external-authority state separately, confirms Helio admin proof and connector authentication are still current, admits, and only then releases the held setup prompts.

# Rebuilding Kibo's $876 premium: monthly vs. semi-monthly

## The arithmetic (same total, different grain)

| Schedule | Number of outflows | Per-outflow amount | 12-month total |
|---|---|---|---|
| Monthly | 12 | $73.00 | $876.00 |
| Semi-monthly | 24 | $36.50 | $876.00 |

Both rebuild exactly $876 over 12 months — matching the renewal term's annual premium already paid for 11/1/27–10/31/28. There is no interest earned in either schedule (this is a sinking fund, not an investment vehicle), and no fee or carry difference between the two — the choice is purely about cash-flow grain, not total cost.

If your pay schedule is semi-monthly (1st and 15th), the $36.50 cadence lines up one-for-one with each paycheck, which is usually the whole point. If you're paid monthly, $73/mo lines up one-for-one. If pay is biweekly (26/yr), neither matches perfectly — $36.50 × 26 = $949, which over-contributes by $73; in that case the monthly schedule is the cleaner fit and you'd park that extra $73 somewhere else or skip the 26th contribution.

## Cash-flow difference in plain terms

- Monthly ($73/mo): one outflow per month, larger but fewer. Easiest to automate as a single recurring transfer on, say, the 1st.
- Semi-monthly ($36.50 twice/mo): smaller per hit, but twice as many. Eases the day-to-day cash impact and pairs naturally with a twice-monthly paycheck.

Over 12 months the dollar impact on your checking account is identical — $876 out either way. The only real-world differences are (a) whether $73 feels comfortable in a single week and (b) whether your income arrives in a rhythm that matches one cadence better than the other.

The current $876 premium for 11/1/27–10/31/28 is already paid, so the rebuild you're starting now is funding the 11/1/28–10/31/29 renewal, not this one.

## How this sinking fund stays separate from the current policy and from claims

This is the part that matters most — keeping the rebuild money untouchable so it's actually there when renewal hits.

1. Separate account. The $73 or $36.50 transfers should land in a dedicated sub-account, savings bucket, or labeled envelope — not the same checking account that pays rent, groceries, or vet bills. The Helio HSA (which you're funding separately at $250/quarter) is *not* the right place; HSA funds are pre-tax medical dollars for human-qualified expenses, and commingling them with a pet-insurance sinking fund creates a tax/recordkeeping mess.
2. Not the policy. Lone Star Companion Insurance Company holds the active 11/1/27–10/31/28 policy. The $876 already paid to them is gone from your hands and earns nothing for you. Your sinking fund is your own money, sitting in your own account, earmarked for the *next* annual premium. Don't confuse "premium already paid" with "no future premium due" — they coexist.
3. Not the deductible. The $500 annual deductible resets each policy year on 11/1. When a covered claim comes in, you pay the first $500 out of pocket (from your regular cash flow, not this fund), then Lone Star reimburses 80% of covered expenses up to the $10,000 annual limit, with behavioral care eligible after the deductible. The sinking fund is not touched by claims and claims do not touch the sinking fund.
4. Not the behavioral-care track. Kibo's trazodone protocol (50mg ~90 min pre-storm, 2-hr observation window, vet escalation rules) is a separate operating routine. Behavioral claims that go through the policy have their own deductible/80%-reimbursement/$10K-cap logic; the sinking fund has no role in that pathway.
5. No co-mingling with rent buffer, Sam's chef-income variable months, or the Mom visit budget (12/5–11). Those are different earmarks. The cleanest test: if you can answer "is this dollar for Kibo's next CompanionCare Plus renewal, and only that?" with yes, it's in the right place.

## Practical setup for either cadence

- Pick the schedule that matches your income arrival. Semi-monthly pay → $36.50 × 24. Monthly pay → $73 × 12.
- Automate the transfer on the day funds land, so the choice is never re-litigated each month.
- Label the destination account "Kibo CC+ renewal 11/28" or similar, so neither of you mistakes it for discretionary savings.
- At 10/31/28, the balance should read $876.00. Pay the 11/1/28–10/31/29 annual premium from that balance in a single payment (which, per the prior renewal math, would still be the cheaper of the two payment options Lone Star offered last time — annual vs. $76 × 12 = $912).

One thing to keep on your radar: if Lone Star's 11/28–10/29 renewal offer comes in higher than $876 (a likely scenario given the trajectory from $828 → $876), the $876 you've accumulated will be a head start rather than the full amount, and you may want to bump the monthly contribution by the delta. The separate-account discipline stays the same either way.

SUNDAY WATERCOLOR — LOOSE 9x12, TEMPORARY MOUNT

Low-tension mount, not a stretch. Goals restated: sheet flat through broad washes, tape lives only on the expendable margin, paint lands only inside the intended image, removal leaves no fibers.

1. BACKING BOARD
   - Rigid board at least 10x13 (foam board, hardboard, MDF). Flat, no warp.
   - Wipe clean with a lint-free cloth, then lay one sheet of clean blotter or smooth craft paper over it as a release layer so board texture does not imprint the sheet back.
   - Set the board on a flat table over a folded towel or thin rubber shelf liner so it does not slide while you work.

2. EXPENDABLE MARGINS
   - Reserve 3/8 in on all four sides as a tape zone. Painted image lives inside that frame.
   - If the planned mat opening is 8x10, keep the image well inside the 9x12 so the tape line never crosses it.
   - Optional: dot the inner edge of the margin with a soft pencil before taping so you can see the tape line and stop the brush there.

3. TAPE TEST — do this first, do not skip
   - Use a scrap offcut of the same paper. Two strips minimum.
   - Apply low-tack washi tape (1/2 in or 3/4 in). Press only with fingertip, no burnishing.
   - Strip 1: pull straight up at ~90° — control, expect trouble.
   - Strip 2: pull back over itself at 10–20°, low and slow, parallel to the edge — working method.
   - Inspect both under raking light for fiber lift. If the low-angle pull still lifts fibers, swap tape (different washi brand or narrower strip) and retest. Proceed only when the low-angle pull is clean.

4. MOUNT
   - Lay the sheet dry on the blotter-covered board, smooth flat by hand.
   - Lightly mist the back with a clean spray bottle (1–2 passes) or brush a thin even coat of clean water on the back. Your "corners lift slightly" finding is the green light for this much moisture — no more.
   - As the sheet relaxes and lays flat, tape the four edges with the tested low-tack tape. Tape sits entirely inside the 3/8 in margin. Snug, not stretched — a temporary hold, not a drum head.
   - Equilibrate 2–3 minutes before painting so the moisture evens out.

5. WASH TIMING
   - Paint while the sheet is just-damp and flat. Bone-dry sheet will cockle through broad washes; too wet risks bleed under the tape.
   - Bead-wick at 20-second intervals. One firm brush blot before each pass. One-touch edge boundary — stop the brush 1/4 in short of the taped margin, do not chase the line.
   - If the margin dries mid-session, re-mist the back lightly, not the face.
   - Stop immediately if the brush tip snags the tape seam, a tide line forms, the margin dries hard, or a corner buckles.

6. FULL DRYING
   - Dry face-up, board flat, gentle air flow. No heater blowing on it.
   - Thin washes: 2–3 hours minimum. Multi-pass or laid work: overnight. The sheet must feel cool and bone-dry to the back of your hand, not just dry-looking.
   - Do not remove tape while the sheet still feels even slightly cool or damp — that is when fibers lift.

7. LOW-ANGLE TAPE REMOVAL
   - Board flat on the table, sheet supported by the board the whole time.
   - For each edge: lay a free hand flat on the painted area (away from the edge being pulled) to keep the sheet from lifting with the tape.
   - Grip the tape end and pull back over itself at 10–20°, parallel to the sheet edge, low and slow. Not up at 90°.
   - Work the full edge in one direction. Pause and inspect under raking light if resistance changes.
   - Stop the moment you feel a catch, see fibers lifting, or see the sheet buckle. Re-press the tape flat, dry longer, then resume.

8. AFTER REMOVAL
   - Lift the sheet straight up off the board — do not slide it.
   - Lay face-up on a clean dry blotter for 1–2 hours to finish flattening and off-gas residual moisture.
   - Inspect edges under raking light. If a fiber lift happened, decide mat-first vs. repair based on whether it sits under the planned mat opening.

ONE-LINE REFERENCE PER STAGE
   Board: rigid + blotter cover, no warp.
   Margin: 3/8 in tape zone, painted area inside.
   Tape: low-tack, low-angle pull tested clean.
   Mount: light back-mist, snug tape in margin only.
   Wash: just-damp sheet, 20-s bead-wick, stop 1/4 in from tape.
   Dry: bone-dry to back of hand, hours not minutes.
   Remove: 10–20° back over itself, sheet supported.
   Rest: face-up on blotter, then inspect.

**You made the right call turning the system off.** First-cycle dust smell is musty/burning-dust and fades in 5–10 minutes. A sharp electrical-or-hot-plastic smell lasting 15 minutes is a different signature — it usually points to an electrical component overheating (relay, capacitor, terminal, wiring insulation, or motor winding), not a heat-exchanger dust burn. Without a technician clearing it, restarting risks the actual failure mode: arcing, breaker trip, or in a worst case a small electrical fire inside the air handler where you can't see it.

**Why I flagged the pattern to PM (and saved it to memory):** This is the third electrical-side concern in this unit in ~2.5 years:
- 6/3/2025 — failed outdoor dual-run capacitor (the electrical component that starts the compressor and fan)
- 7/18/2027 — failed indoor blower relay + heat-discolored terminal connector
- Today — sharp electrical odor from supply air on first heat call

Two isolated events can be coincidence; three is a pattern. The likely shared cause is aging/contaminated wiring or terminal connections in the air handler, possibly aggravated by the unit sitting idle for months (dust settling on warm electrical contacts, slight humidity in the cabinet during the off-season). A tech who knows there's a pattern will look more carefully at the whole electrical subsystem rather than just patching the immediate fault.

Thighs tolerate this far better than breast meat, and the sides barely notice a covered reheat. Today (Wed 11/24) — make-ahead

Roughly 1:00–3:00 pm, in whatever order frees the oven fastest:

1. Sweet potato (~2 lb, cubed 1 inch): toss with oil + salt, spread on a sheet pan, roast at 400°F about 25 min until just tender. Cool 15 min on the pan, transfer to a shallow container (≤3 inches deep), lid askew. Into the fridge once it stops steaming.

2. Stuffing: bake per your normal recipe. Cool 15 min, shallow container, loose lid, fridge.

3. Green beans (prep only): trim, blanch 3–4 min in salted water, drain, plunge into ice water 2 min, drain again, dry on a towel. Bag or container, fridge. Tomorrow is just a fast sauté.

4. Four chicken thighs (the centerpiece):
   - Pat dry, salt/pepper, light oil rub.
   - Skin-side down in a cold oven-safe skillet over medium heat 8–10 min until the skin releases and is golden; flip.
   - Transfer skillet to a 400°F oven, about 18–22 min until a probe in the thickest part reads 175–180°F. (Thighs want higher doneness than breast; 165°F is safe but 175°F gives the silky texture.)
   - Rest on a rack 10 min, then refrigerate uncovered on a plate ~30 min to release steam before loosely covering. This keeps the skin from going soggy overnight.

Overnight fridge storage — the safety rules that matter

- Cool from hot to room temp in shallow containers, lid ajar, within about 2 hours of leaving the oven. Don't seal anything airtight while it's still warm — you'll trap steam and grow bacteria faster.
- Fridge at ≤40°F. Don't crowd; air needs to circulate around the containers.
- Thighs on a plate with loose foil, separate from the sides, near the back of the fridge where it's coldest.
- Stuffing and sweet potato in their own shallow containers. Green beans in a sealed bag/container.
- Don't reuse the hot sheet pans as storage — metal against plastic lids is a pain and the pans cool unevenly.

About 1 hour 15 minutes before plating, in this order:

- T-1:15 (12:45 pm): Oven on 325°F. Thighs into a small baking dish with 1–2 Tbsp chicken broth per thigh, foil sealed tight. Stuffing in a covered dish (foil lid) with a splash of broth. Both go in together.

- T-0:40 (1:20 pm): Green beans into a hot skillet with oil/garlic, 4–5 min, salt at the end. Off heat, lid on.
- T-0:30 (1:30 pm): Pull thighs, check probe — 165°F is the safe target; they should be there or just past. If you want the skin back, blast under the broiler 2–3 min watching closely. If not, leave covered.
- T-0:25 (1:35 pm): Foil-tent the thighs on a warm plate. This is your rest — 15 min minimum, 20 min is better. The juices redistribute and the internal temp will climb a few more degrees on the way down. Don't skip this; it's the difference between juicy and just-warm.
- T-0:10 (1:50 pm): Sweet potato and stuffing uncovered for 5 min to drive off any condensation, then covered again to hold.
- T-0:00 (2:00 pm): Plate.
